Quod cognovit venerabilis ille centurio qui dicebat: Domine, non sum dignus ut intres sub tectum meum, sed tantum dic verbo, et sanabitur puer meus, etc. Incipiebat enim mori. Hoc dicit Evangelista: primo, ad insinuandum cur regulus tantum festinavit ad Jesum, eumque tam obnixe deprecabatur; secundo, ad ostendendum miraculi magnitudinem, quia ejusdem potentiæ est mortuum suscitare, et lethali infirmitate laborantem seu agonizantem sanare.
paras.en: [[4:47|He having heard that Jesus was come from Judea into Galilee|Hic regulus quum audisset quod Jesus adveniret a Judæa, per Samariam, in Galilæam]], by way of Samaria. For Jesus had already become famous for His miracles, and for the Baptism with which He baptized by Himself and through His disciples, and also through the testimony of John the Baptist; and so His fame ran before Him. Hence we read in Matthew that [[Matt 4:24|his fame went throughout all Syria|abiit opinio ejus in totam Syriam]], which was certainly a great kingdom. He went to Him in Cana of Galilee, where he found Christ, [[4:47|and prayed him to come down|et rogabat eum ut descenderet]] to Capharnaum, which lay lower than Cana, [[4:47|and heal his son|et sanaret filium ejus]], who he thought could not be healed by Christ unless Christ were bodily present. For he did not yet know that Jesus is true God, present everywhere, and that the holy angels are His ministers[[Heb 1:7||]][[Ps 102:21||]], by whose ministry He could cure all the sick. This that venerable centurion knew, who said: [[Matt 8:8|Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed|Domine, non sum dignus ut intres sub tectum meum, sed tantum dic verbo, et sanabitur puer meus]], etc. [[4:47|For he was at the point of death|Incipiebat enim mori]] [*incipiebat mori*, literally “he was beginning to die”]. The Evangelist says this, first, to hint why the ruler made such haste to Jesus and besought Him so earnestly; secondly, to show the greatness of the miracle, since it belongs to the same power to raise the dead and to heal one labouring under a deadly sickness, or in his last agony.

paras.t: Dixit ergo Jesus ad eum: Nisi signa, id est miracula divinæ potentiæ ostensiva, et prodigia, hoc est miracula aliquid in longum et posterum indicantia, secundum Bedam; vel potius miracula virtutem divinam procul a sensu positam signantia; videritis, non creditis me esse omnipotentem Filium Dei, qui corporaliter absens, secundum divinitatem omnia impleo, et cuncta ubique facere queo. Occasione hujus verbi Augustinus dicit, quod regulus iste accessit ad Christum, non credens, sed tentans, volens experiri quis aut qualis esset, et quantum posset. Gregorius vero dicit oppositum, puta quod credidit, alias filio suo non peteret sospitatem. Cur ergo dicitur ei, Nisi signa videritis, non creditis? Respondit Gregorius, quod aliquid credidit, scilicet Jesum posse ægrum sanare; et aliquid non credidit, scilicet quod absens posset hoc facere.
paras.en: [[4:48|Jesus therefore said to him: Unless you see signs|Dixit ergo Jesus ad eum: Nisi signa]], that is, miracles that show forth the divine power, [[4:48|and wonders|et prodigia]], that is, miracles that point to something far off and to come, according to Bede; or rather, miracles that betoken the divine power, which lies far beyond the senses: unless you [[4:48|see|videritis]] these, [[4:48|you believe not|non creditis]] that I am the almighty Son of God, who, though bodily absent, fill all things by My Godhead[[Jer 23:24||]] and can do all things everywhere. On the occasion of this word Augustine says that this ruler came to Christ not believing but tempting, wishing to find out who and what He was, and how much He could do. Gregory, however, says the opposite, namely that he believed, for otherwise he would not have asked health for his son. Why then is it said to him, Unless you see signs, you believe not? Gregory answers that he believed something, namely that Jesus could heal the sick man, and did not believe something, namely that He could do it while absent.

paras.t: Porro, secundum Theophilum, regulus iste interfuit nuptiis in quibus aquam mutavit in vinum, ideo credidit Jesum posse agonizanti succurrere. Hoc tamen non apparet aliis probabile: quoniam nuptiæ illæ pauperum erant, nam et vinum defuit ibi, et secundum Hieronymum, Joannes evangelista exstitit sponsus; regulus autem iste potens valde præcipuus fuit in populo. Unde potius reor quod illud miraculum factum in nuptiis percepit auditu: propterea concepit fiduciam orandi pro salute filii sui. — Denique, quum dicat Apostolus, Judæi signa quærunt; et Jesus nunc ait, Nisi signa et prodigia videritis, non creditis: idcirco auctor Scholasticæ historiæ dicit, quod regulus iste creditur fuisse de plebe et semine Judæorum: quod alii non concedunt.
paras.en: Further, according to Theophilus, this ruler had been present at the marriage at which He changed water into wine, and so he believed that Jesus could help one in his last agony. But to others this does not seem probable, since that marriage was one of poor people, for the wine failed there[[John 2:3||]], and according to Jerome John the Evangelist was the bridegroom; whereas this ruler was very powerful and among the chief of the people. So I rather think that he had heard of the miracle done at the marriage, and for that reason took confidence to pray for his son's health. — Lastly, since the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 1:22|the Jews require signs|Judæi signa quærunt]], and Jesus now says, [[4:48|Unless you see signs and wonders, you believe not|Nisi signa et prodigia videritis, non creditis]], the author of the *Scholastic History* [Peter Comestor] says that this ruler is believed to have been of the common people and seed of the Jews; which others do not grant.

paras.t: Dicit ad eum regulus: Domine, descende priusquam moriatur filius meus. Imperfectio fidei reguli elucescit, non tantum in hoc quod corporalem Christi præsentiam credidit necessariam, sed etiam quia non cogitavit vel credidit quod posset suscitare defunctum. Nempe sic orat, Descende priusquam moriatur filius meus, quasi putet quod mortuum, etiam descendendo ad eum, suscitare non posset.
paras.en: [[4:49|The ruler saith to him: Lord, come down before that my son die|Dicit ad eum regulus: Domine, descende priusquam moriatur filius meus]]. The imperfection of the ruler's faith shines out, not only in that he believed Christ's bodily presence necessary, but also because he did not think or believe that He could raise the dead. For he prays thus, [[4:49|come down before that my son die|Descende priusquam moriatur filius meus]], as though he thought that, even by coming down to him, Christ could not raise him once dead.

paras.t: Dicit ei Jesus: Vade, filius tuus vivit vita naturali et convenienti, id est, in hoc momento, me operante atque secundum corpus absente, sanatus est. Credidit homo sermoni quem dixit ei Jesus, et ibat ad filium suum. Jam merito regulus appellatur homo, id est utens ratione ac rationabiliter agens, dum credit Christo, et voci ejus obedit, eundo non solum gressibus corporis, sed et mentis profectu proficiscens, videlicet ab imperfecta fide ad fidem perfectam.
paras.en: [[4:50|Jesus saith to him: Go thy way. Thy son liveth|Dicit ei Jesus: Vade, filius tuus vivit]] with a natural and fitting life; that is, at this moment, by My working, though I am bodily absent, he has been healed. [[4:50|The man believed the word which Jesus said to him and went his way|Credidit homo sermoni quem dixit ei Jesus, et ibat]] to his son. Now the ruler is rightly called a *man*, that is, one using reason and acting reasonably, when he believes Christ and obeys His voice, going not only with the steps of the body but advancing with the progress of the mind, namely from imperfect faith to perfect faith.

paras.t: Jam autem eo descendente, servi occurrerunt ei, et nuntiaverunt dicentes, quia filius ejus viveret, id est, incolumis esset. Tribus de causis obviaverunt servi hi regulo: Primo, ut bonum nuntium apportando, eum lætificarent quem tristissimum putaverunt. Servi quippe optantes amari a dominis suis, libenter annuntiant læta ac prospera, sicut patet de Chusi et Achimaas, qui exercitu David prævalente, et Absalone occiso, cupiebant regi David hoc nuntiare. Secundo, ut veritatem rei domino suo intimantes, eum ab itineris labore relevarent. Tertio, secundum Origenem, quoniam filio jam sanato, putabant præsentiam Christi superfluam, quem cum regulo putabant venturum.
paras.en: [[4:51|And as he was going down, his servants met him: and they brought word, saying, that his son lived|Jam autem eo descendente, servi occurrerunt ei, et nuntiaverunt dicentes, quia filius ejus viveret]], that is, was safe and sound. These servants went to meet the ruler for three reasons. First, to gladden with good news one whom they thought most sorrowful. For servants who wish to be loved by their masters gladly bring news of what is happy and prosperous, as is plain in Chusai and Achimaas, who, when David's army had prevailed and Absalom was slain, were eager to bring the news to king David[[2 Kings 18:21||]][[2 Kings 18:23||]] [2 Kings = 2 Samuel]. Secondly, that by making the truth of the matter known to their master they might spare him the toil of the journey. Thirdly, according to Origen, because, now that the son was healed, they thought the presence of Christ, whom they supposed to be coming with the ruler, unnecessary.

paras.t: Interrogabat ergo regulus horam ab eis, videlicet servis sibi occurrentibus, in qua melius habuerat filius ejus. Hoc quæsivit, ut certior fieret de veritate miraculi, ne forte filius suus a casu vel naturali causa esset sanatus. Tamen, si ante scivit quod filius suus lethaliter infirmabatur, scire potuit quod non valuit naturaliter reparari. Idcirco forte horam quæsivit, ut alios, præsertim domesticos suos, solidaret in fide. Et dixerunt ei: Quia heri hora septima reliquit eum subito et perfecte febris mortifera, in tantum quod postea nullum signum pristinæ infirmitatis in ipso apparuit: sicut socrus Petri febricitans, a Christo sanata mox surrexit atque ad mensam ministravit: quod in febricitantibus sanatis naturaliter non contingit.
paras.en: [[4:52|He asked therefore of them the hour wherein he grew better|Interrogabat ergo horam ab eis in qua melius]], namely of the servants who met him. He asked this to be more certain of the truth of the miracle, lest perhaps his son had been healed by chance or by a natural cause. Yet if he knew beforehand that his son was sick unto death, he could know that he could not be restored naturally. So perhaps he asked the hour in order to strengthen others, above all his household, in the faith. [[4:52|And they said to him: Yesterday at the seventh hour, the fever left him|Et dixerunt ei: Quia heri hora septima reliquit eum subito et perfecte febris]], suddenly and wholly, that deadly fever, so that afterwards no sign of the former sickness appeared in him: just as Peter's mother-in-law, sick of a fever, when healed by Christ rose at once and served at table[[Matt 8:14||]][[Matt 8:15||]], which does not happen naturally in those who are healed of a fever.

paras.t: Cognovit ergo pater filii jam sanati, videlicet regulus, cujus proprium nomen non explicatur: regulus nempe est nomen officii vel dignitatis, non personæ; quia illa hora, videlicet septima, erat in qua dixit ei Jesus: Filius tuus vivit. Et credidit ipse Jesum esse Christum filium Dei, et domus, id est familia, ejus tota, seu omnes sibi cohabitantes. Ex consideratione enim horæ, cognoverunt quod Jesus, etiam corporaliter absens, supernaturaliter operari curareque possit, et non qualitercumque, sed excellentissimo modo, utpote solo verbo, nutu atque imperio: quod non convenit puræ creaturæ. Verumtamen non videtur quibusdam quod explicite credidit Jesum esse Filium Dei naturalem, Deum verum, Deum et hominem: ad talem enim credulitatem homines tunc nondum tenebantur communiter. Sed sicut centurio qui stetit sub cruce, viso terræ motu et his quæ fiebant, et quia Jesus sic clamans exspirasset, credebat, Vere, inquiens, hic Filius Dei erat; sic credidit regulus iste. Credebant namque quod Jesus esset sanctus homo, magnus Propheta, Salvator mundi, Filius Dei: et hoc totum sic erat; sed ultra non determinabant an esset filius naturalis vel adoptivus.
paras.en: [[4:53|The father therefore knew|Cognovit ergo pater]] of the son now healed, namely the ruler, whose own name is not given: for *ruler* is the name of an office or dignity, not of a person; [[4:53|that it was at the same hour that Jesus said to him: Thy son liveth|quia illa hora, videlicet septima, erat in qua dixit ei Jesus: Filius tuus vivit]], namely the seventh. [[4:53|And himself believed|Et credidit ipse]] that Jesus was the Christ, the son of God, [[4:53|and his whole house|et domus ejus tota]], that is, his household, or all who lived with him. For from considering the hour they knew that Jesus, even when bodily absent, could work and heal supernaturally, and not in just any manner, but in the most excellent way, by a word, a nod and a command alone: which does not belong to a mere creature. Yet some think he did not believe explicitly that Jesus was the natural Son of God, true God, God and man: for men were not yet bound in common to such belief. But as the centurion who stood beneath the cross, seeing the earthquake and the things that were done[[Matt 27:54||]], and that Jesus, crying out in this manner, had given up the ghost, believed, saying, [[Mark 15:39|Indeed this man was the son of God|Vere, inquiens, hic Filius Dei erat]], so did this ruler believe. For they believed that Jesus was a holy man, a great Prophet, the Saviour of the world, the Son of God: and all this was so; but they went no further in determining whether He was a natural or an adopted son.

paras.t: Quidam præterea putaverunt quod regulus iste fuit ille centurio cujus puerum Christus in Capharnaum curasse describitur. Sed non est sic æstimandum. Primo, quoniam puer centurionis laborabat paralysi; iste filius febribus tabescebat. Secundo, quoniam ille fuit servus, secundum Lucam; iste filius fuit, secundum Joannem. Tertio, quoniam centurio rogavit Jesum in Capharnaum exsistentem, secundum Matthæum; regulus vero rogavit eum in Cana. Quarto, quia regulo tanquam defectuoso in fide, dicitur, Nisi signa videritis, non creditis; centurionis autem fides excellentissime commendatur, Christo dicente, Non inveni tantam fidem in Israel. Quinto, quia centurio Christi majestatem intelligens, dixit: Domine, non sum dignus ut intres sub tectum meum. Regulus econtrario ait: Domine, descende priusquam moriatur filius meus. Sexto, quia ad servum centurionis ire paratus fuit Salvator, dicendo, Ego veniam et curabo eum; ad filium vero reguli ire non acquievit.
paras.en: Some, moreover, have thought that this ruler was the centurion whose servant Christ is described as having healed in Capharnaum[[Matt 8:5||]]. But this is not to be thought. First, because the centurion's servant was suffering from palsy[[Matt 8:6||]], while this son was wasting with fever. Secondly, because that one was a servant, according to Luke[[Luke 7:2||]], while this one was a son, according to John. Thirdly, because the centurion besought Jesus when He was in Capharnaum, according to Matthew[[Matt 8:5||]]; but the ruler besought Him in Cana. Fourthly, because to the ruler, as one lacking in faith, it is said, [[4:48|Unless you see signs and wonders, you believe not|Nisi signa videritis, non creditis]]; but the centurion's faith is most highly commended, Christ saying, [[Matt 8:10|I have not found so great faith in Israel|Non inveni tantam fidem in Israel]]. Fifthly, because the centurion, understanding Christ's majesty, said: [[Matt 8:8|Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof|Domine, non sum dignus ut intres sub tectum meum]]. The ruler, on the contrary, says: [[4:49|Lord, come down before that my son die|Domine, descende priusquam moriatur filius meus]]. Sixthly, because the Saviour was ready to go to the centurion's servant, saying, [[Matt 8:7|I will come and heal him|Ego veniam et curabo eum]]; but He would not agree to go to the ruler's son.

paras.t: Quoniam ergo Filius Dei venit in mundum ostendere nobis viam ascendendi in cælum per veram humilitatem, idcirco obtulit se paratum proficisci ad famulum centurionis. Ad filium vero reguli ire non voluit, non utique ex contemptu personæ, sed ut doceat nos quod alia sunt judicia Dei, atque alia judicia hominum, et ut potius pensemus in hominibus naturam qua ad Dei imaginem facti sunt, quam accidentalia bona quibus in hoc mundo præfulgent, item ne dedignemur abjectas visitare personas, et ut agnoscamus quod tanto quis a Deo plus reputatur et sublimatur, quanto ab hominibus magis despicitur. Hinc scriptum est: Quod hominibus altum est, abominatio est ante Deum. De hoc multa conscripta sunt in Canonica Jacobi: quorum hoc unum est, Nonne Deus elegit pauperes in hoc mundo, divites in fide? Et illud: Si personas accipitis, peccatum operamini. Verumtamen sæcularis potestas aspernanda non est, sed honoranda, dicente Apostolo: Non est potestas nisi a Deo, et qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit. Unde, quantum ad exteriorem reverentiam, magis honorare oportet prælatos ac principes, rectores et officiales, quam personas privatas ac inopes; sed quantum ad reverentiam interiorem, ceteris paribus, possumus plus honorare, hoc est reputare ac beatificare, abjectos, egenos et simplices, quam sublimes, quia similiores sunt Christo, et eorum est regnum cælorum.
paras.en: Since, then, the Son of God came into the world to show us the way of going up to heaven through true humility, He offered Himself ready to go to the centurion's servant. But He would not go to the ruler's son: not, surely, out of contempt for his person, but to teach us that the judgments of God are one thing and the judgments of men another; that we should rather weigh in men the nature by which they are made to the image of God than the accidental goods with which they shine in this world; also that we should not disdain to visit lowly persons; and that we may know that the more a man is despised by men, the more he is esteemed and exalted by God. Hence it is written: [[Luke 16:15|that which is high to men is an abomination before God|Quod hominibus altum est, abominatio est ante Deum]]. Much is written of this in the Canonical Epistle of James, of which this is one saying: [[Jas 2:5|Hath not God chosen the poor in this world, rich in faith|Nonne Deus elegit pauperes in hoc mundo, divites in fide]]? And this: [[Jas 2:9|if you have respect to persons, you commit sin|Si personas accipitis, peccatum operamini]]. Yet the secular power is not to be despised but honoured, as the Apostle says: [[Rom 13:1|there is no power but from God|Non est potestas nisi a Deo]], and [[Rom 13:2|he that resisteth the power resisteth the ordinance of God|qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit]]. So as to outward reverence, prelates and princes, rulers and officers are to be honoured more than private persons and the needy; but as to inward reverence, other things being equal, we may honour more, that is, esteem more and count more blessed, the lowly, the needy and the simple than the exalted, because they are more like Christ, and [[Matt 5:3|theirs is the kingdom of heaven|eorum est regnum cælorum]].

paras.t: Quod autem in fine hujus capituli subditur, Hoc iterum secundum signum fecit Jesus, quum venisset a Judæa in Galilæam, non est intelligendum quod huc usque non fecit nisi duo miracula, quia ut dictum est, in Jerusalem multa fecit miracula, sed quod istud fuit secundum signum quantum ad miracula facta in Galilæa. Et secundum Bedam, ideo Evangelista hoc dicit, ut ostendat quod ea quæ supra descripsit, alii Evangelistæ omiserunt.
paras.en: As for what is added at the end of this chapter, [[4:54|This is again the second miracle that Jesus did, when he was come out of Judea. into Galilee|Hoc iterum secundum signum fecit Jesus, quum venisset a Judæa in Galilæam]], it is not to be understood that up to this time He had done only two miracles, since, as was said, He did many miracles in Jerusalem[[John 2:23||]]; but that this was the second sign as regards the miracles done in Galilee. And according to Bede the Evangelist says this to show that the other Evangelists left out what he has described above.

paras.t: Præterea, de moralitate hujus evangelicæ lectionis multa dici possent, et plurima dicta sunt; nec opus est ea quæ ab aliis plenissime dicta sunt, huic loco inserere atque repetere. Sed brevem tangam moralitatem quæ videtur congruenter posse aptari. Itaque, per regulum designatur spiritus rationalis seu intellectus, qui in regno animæ præsidet, omnesque potentias dirigit et gubernat: qui potius dicitur regulus quam rex, quia in ordine intellectualium essentiarum tenet infimum locum, in tantum ut naturaliter sit unibilis corpori. Unde secundum philosophos, sicut se habet materia prima in genere entium, sic anima rationalis in ordine intellectualium substantiarum. Filius hujus reguli est speculativus intuitus divinorum, qui est velut verbum prolesque mentis: qui infirmatur in Capharnaum, id est, in sensualitate et carne mortali multipliciter obfuscatur, impeditur, interrumpitur, deficit, languescit: quoniam deprimit terrena habitatio sensum multa cogitantem; et secundum Apostolum, invenitur alia lex in membris nostris, legi mentis repugnans, in tantum quod actus interioris hominis, propter ardorem sensualis concupiscentiæ ceterasque passiones, quasi febricitet.
paras.en: Further, many things could be said, and very many have been said, of the moral sense of this Gospel reading; nor is there need to put in and repeat here what others have said most fully. But I shall touch briefly on a moral sense that seems fittingly applicable. By the ruler, then, is signified the rational spirit, or intellect, which presides in the kingdom of the soul and directs and governs all its powers: and it is called a little king rather than a king because in the order of intellectual beings it holds the lowest place, so far that it is by nature able to be united to a body. Hence, according to the philosophers, as prime matter stands in the genus of beings, so does the rational soul in the order of intellectual substances. The son of this ruler is the speculative gazing upon divine things, which is as it were the word and offspring of the mind: and he is sick in Capharnaum, that is, in sensuality and mortal flesh he is in many ways darkened, hindered, interrupted, fails and languishes; for [[Wis 9:15|the earthly habitation presseth down the mind that museth upon many things|deprimit terrena habitatio sensum multa cogitantem]]; and, according to the Apostle, there is found [[Rom 7:23|another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind|alia lex in membris nostris, legi mentis repugnans]] [Denis: “in our members”], so much that the act of the inward man is, as it were, in a fever, through the heat of sensual concupiscence and the other passions.

paras.t: Accedat ergo regulus iste humili, affectuosa jugique prece ad Christum Dei sapientiam et virtutem, ut filium suum a prædictis incommodis curet, auferendo ab anima obstacula contemplationis cælestium, impedimenta amoris fervidi divinorum, omnemque instabilitatem, et passionum inordinationem ac impetum, quatenus revelata facie gloriam Domini speculetur. Et utique, quum intellectualitas nostra sit naturaliter tam imperfecta, obscura atque fallibilis, indigemus continuo clementissimoque divinæ bonitatis succursu, quatenus nec ad momentum derelinquamur a Deo et gratiæ ejus influxu, ab illustratione divinæ sapientiæ, ab inflammatione ignis Spiritus Sancti, a conservatione potestatis supremæ: alias intellectus noster errabit, voluntas frigescet, memoria quoque nutabit, et pleni erimus calamitate, passionibus, distractionibus et peccatis. Qui ista intelligit ac perpendit, nequaquam gloriatur in se ipso, non de se ipso præsumit, aliis se non præfert, pensans illud Apostoli: Qui se putat aliquid esse quum nihil sit, ipse se seducit; et quod apud Jeremiam legitur: Scio, Domine, quia non est hominis via ejus, nec viri est ut ambulet, et dirigat gressus suos.
paras.en: Let this ruler, then, come with humble, loving and unceasing prayer to Christ, the wisdom and power of God[[1 Cor 1:24||]], that He may cure his son of the ills just named, taking away from the soul the obstacles to the contemplation of heavenly things, the hindrances to a fervent love of divine things, and all unsteadiness, and the disorder and rush of the passions, so that with unveiled face it may behold the glory of the Lord. And indeed, since our intellectual nature is by nature so imperfect, so dark and so liable to error, we need the unceasing and most merciful help of the divine goodness, so that not for a moment may we be forsaken by God and by the inflowing of His grace, by the enlightening of the divine wisdom, by the kindling of the fire of the Holy Ghost, by the keeping of the supreme power: otherwise our intellect will go astray, our will grow cold, our memory waver, and we shall be full of calamity, passions, distractions and sins. He who understands and weighs this does not glory in himself at all, does not presume on himself, does not set himself above others, weighing that saying of the Apostle: [[Gal 6:3|if any man think himself to be some thing, whereas he is nothing, he deceiveth himself|Qui se putat aliquid esse quum nihil sit, ipse se seducit]]; and what we read in Jeremias: [[Jer 10:23|I know, O Lord, that the way of a man is not his: neither is it in a man to walk, and to direct his steps|Scio, Domine, quia non est hominis via ejus, nec viri est ut ambulet, et dirigat gressus suos]].

paras.t: Petat ergo regulus iste, seu intellectus noster, ut ipsemet Christus descendat ad sanandum filium suum, videlicet actum intellectualem, quoniam peccata auferre, gratiam dare, in voluntatem directe immediateque agere, solius est Dei. Nec curet si sibi dicatur a Christo, Nisi signa videritis, non creditis: quoniam fides quamvis sufficiens sit, tamen per experientiam divinæ miserationis et gratiæ, per evidentiam divinæ præsentiæ, roboratur atque perficitur. Non ergo sufficiat intellectui nostro præsentia angeli, imo nec sola divina præsentia Christi; sed corporalem ejus requirat præsentiam in Sacramento, quatenus corpus et sanguinem Dei propter se incarnati devotissime amplectatur, epuletur, contineat. Dicat igitur, non ex incredulitate, sed fervida dilectione, quæ inquieta est donec adsit dilectus: Domine, descende priusquam moriatur filius meus, hoc est, antequam actus intellectivus a sensualitate vincatur, a tentationibus superetur, et antequam amorosa contemplatio divinorum in interioribus exstinguatur. Oremus itaque Christum, ut per Sacramenti exhibitionem introeat spiritum nostrum, omnemque effectum superdignissimi Sacramenti illuc diffundat. Denique Moyses non contentus de ducatu angelico, ipsius Dei personalem requirebat præsentiam, dicens: Si non tu ipse præcedas nos, ne educas nos de loco isto: in quo enim scire poterimus invenisse nos gratiam in conspectu tuo, nisi ambulaveris nobiscum? Sic et Isaias clamavit: Utinam dirumperes cælos et descenderes.
paras.en: Let this ruler, then, that is, our intellect, ask that Christ Himself come down to heal his son, namely the act of the intellect; for to take away sins, to give grace, and to act directly and immediately upon the will belongs to God alone. Nor let him mind if Christ says to him, [[4:48|Unless you see signs and wonders, you believe not|Nisi signa videritis, non creditis]]: for faith, though it be sufficient, is yet strengthened and perfected by the experience of the divine mercy and grace and by the evidence of the divine presence. Let not the presence of an angel suffice our intellect, then, nor even the divine presence of Christ alone; but let it seek His bodily presence in the Sacrament, so that it may most devoutly embrace, feast upon and hold the body and blood of God, made flesh for its sake. Let it say, then, not from unbelief but from fervent love, which is restless until the beloved is present: [[4:49|Lord, come down before that my son die|Domine, descende priusquam moriatur filius meus]]; that is, before the act of the intellect is overcome by sensuality and overpowered by temptations, and before the loving contemplation of divine things is quenched within. Let us pray Christ, then, that through the giving of the Sacrament He may enter our spirit and pour out there the whole effect of that most worthy Sacrament. Moses, indeed, not content with the leading of an angel, sought the personal presence of God Himself, saying: [[Ex 33:15|If thou thyself dost not go before, bring us not out of this place|Si non tu ipse præcedas nos, ne educas nos de loco isto]]. [[Ex 33:16|For how shall we be able to know|in quo enim scire poterimus]] [[Ex 33:16|that we have found grace in thy sight, unless thou walk with us|invenisse nos gratiam in conspectu tuo, nisi ambulaveris nobiscum]]? So too Isaias cried out: [[Is 64:1|O that thou wouldst rend the heavens, and wouldst come down|Utinam dirumperes cælos et descenderes]].

paras.t: Porro, quum Christus viderit spiritum nostrum tam ferventer instanterque precantem, dicet per effectum: Vade, filius tuus vivit, hoc est, exaudita est deprecatio tua. Quo facto, tota domus spiritus nostri, videlicet omnia interiora animæ, cogitationes et affectiones, credent virtuose agendo, quoniam rationis imperio omnia subjicientur, et Deo obedient.
paras.en: Then, when Christ has seen our spirit praying so fervently and so instantly, He will say in effect: [[4:50|Go thy way. Thy son liveth|Vade, filius tuus vivit]], that is, thy prayer is heard. When this is done, [[4:53|his whole house|tota domus]] of our spirit, that is, all the inward parts of the soul, its thoughts and affections, will believe by acting virtuously, since all will be subject to the command of reason and will obey God.

paras.t: Et sicut regulus sollicitus fuit, Christumque accessit et instanter petiit pro sui carnalis filii corporali salute; sic omnis prælatus sollicitus esse, Christum accedere, eumque ferventer ac jugiter deprecari debet pro gregis sibi commissi spirituali sanitate. — Præterea multi usque in hodiernum diem sunt, qui licet habeant fidem informem et mortuam, non tamen credunt, loquendo de fide formata et viva seu operatoria, nisi signa et prodigia viderint, scilicet ultionem divinæ justitiæ, in aliquibus impiis, vel aliquid simile.
paras.en: And as the ruler was anxious, and came to Christ and besought Him instantly for the bodily health of his son according to the flesh, so every prelate ought to be anxious, to come to Christ, and to beseech Him fervently and unceasingly for the spiritual health of the flock entrusted to him. — Moreover, there are many even to this day who, though they have unformed and dead faith, yet do not believe (speaking of formed and living, or working, faith) [*fides informis*: faith without charity; *fides formata*: faith given life by charity] unless they see signs and wonders[[4:48||]], namely the vengeance of the divine justice upon some of the wicked, or something of the kind.

5.title: Expositio quinti capituli: Post hæc erat dies festus Judæorum, et ascendit Jesus Jerosolymam.
5.title_en: Exposition of the fifth chapter: “After these things was a festival day of the Jews: and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.”

paras.t: Hic rursum Evangelista commemorat signum magnificum a Christo peractum, ab aliis Evangelistis omissum, et de indiscreto zelo Judæorum, quomodo etiam Christus occasione hujus prodigii, magna et profunda ad Judæos locutus est.
paras.en: Here the Evangelist again records a magnificent sign done by Christ, which the other Evangelists left out; and he tells of the indiscreet zeal of the Jews, and also how Christ, on the occasion of this wonder, spoke great and deep things to the Jews.

paras.t: Post hæc quæ in præcedenti capitulo gesta narrantur, erat dies festus Judæorum. Non exprimitur quæ fuit ista festivitas; sed certum est quod fuit una de festivitatibus Judæorum præcipuis: et communiter dicitur quod erat solennitas Pentecostes, videlicet festum Novorum, quando Domino offerebantur primitiæ frugum. Et ascendit Jesus Jerosolymam, quæ erat altior situ Galilæa: ideo Christus eundo illuc a Galilæa ascendit. Ivit igitur, ut legem Mosaicam approbaret et impleret, humilitatisque et obedientiæ exemplum nobis relinqueret, salutaribus documentis atque miraculis populum Judæorum, ad quem fuerat specialiter missus, converteret. Dictum est enim, quod Judæi secundum præceptum legis, tenebantur in tribus præcipuis festis coram Domino apparere, hostiamque offerre in loco divini cultus divinitus prælecto, qui fuit Jerusalem a tempore David vel constructionis templi.
paras.en: [[5:1|After these things|Post hæc]] which are told as done in the preceding chapter, [[5:1|was a festival day of the Jews|erat dies festus Judæorum]]. Which feast this was is not stated; but it is certain that it was one of the chief feasts of the Jews, and it is commonly said that it was the solemnity of Pentecost, that is, the feast of the new fruits, when the firstfruits of the crops were offered to the Lord[[Num 28:26||]]. [[5:1|and Jesus went up to Jerusalem|Et ascendit Jesus Jerosolymam]], which lay higher than Galilee: so Christ, going there from Galilee, went up. He went, then, to approve and fulfil the law of Moses, to leave us an example of humility and obedience, and to convert by saving teachings and miracles the people of the Jews, to whom He had been specially sent[[Matt 15:24||]]. For it has been said that the Jews, by the precept of the law, were bound to appear before the Lord at the three chief feasts[[Deut 16:16||]], and to offer a victim in the place of divine worship chosen by God, which from the time of David, or of the building of the temple, was Jerusalem.

paras.t: Est autem Jerosolymis Probatica, id est ovinaria seu ovina, piscina, quæ cognominatur Hebraice Bethsaida, id est domus ovium vel pecorum. Hæc enim piscina prope templum fuit, in qua colligebantur aquæ pluviales, ut hostiæ templi, quæ communiter erant de ovibus, lavarentur in ea antequam immolarentur in templo coram Domino. Probatica autem dicitur a πρόβατον Græce, quod Latine dicitur ovis. Quinque porticus habens in gyro, videlicet quædam ædificia per quæ Nathinæi accedebant ad aquam causa lavandi hostias offerendas, quæ etiam jacebant in porticibus istis, quousque essent lotæ. Circumsepta itaque fuit piscina tam multis porticibus, ut ministri per plura loca haberent accessum ad aquam, et loca illa sufficerent ad continendum hostias Domino immolandas.
paras.en: [[5:2|Now there is at Jerusalem a pond, called Probatica|Est autem Jerosolymis probatica piscina]], that is, the sheep pool, [[5:2|which in Hebrew is named Bethsaida|quæ cognominatur Hebraice Bethsaida]], that is, house of sheep or of cattle. For this pool was near the temple, and the rain-water was gathered in it, so that the victims of the temple, which were commonly sheep, might be washed in it before they were sacrificed in the temple before the Lord. It is called *Probatica* from the Greek *probaton*, which in Latin is *ovis*, a sheep. [[5:2|having five porches|Quinque porticus habens]] round about, that is, certain buildings through which the Nathinites [the temple servants] came to the water to wash the victims to be offered; and the victims lay in these porches until they had been washed. So the pool was surrounded by so many porches that the ministers might have access to the water at several places, and that those places might be enough to hold the victims to be sacrificed to the Lord.

paras.t: In his porticibus jacebat multitudo magna languentium, diversis infirmitatibus tabescentium, utpote cæcorum, claudorum, aridorum, seu contractorum, exspectantium aquæ motum ab angelo fiendum, infirmitatis curativum. Angelus autem Domini descendebat secundum tempus, id est determinatis temporibus, tamen incertis et interruptis, in piscinam, et movebatur aqua ab angelo, motu forti ac turbulento, ita quod certum fuit motum illum ab angelo factum, non a vento, vel causa naturali. Et quoniam hora angelicæ descensionis fuit incerta, ideo languidi jacebant ibi continuo, quasi semper parati, et optantes se invicem prævenire in ingressu piscinæ. Cujus ratio subinfertur: Et qui prior descendebat in piscinam post motionem aquæ: piscina dici potest, vel ipsa aqua, vel receptaculum aquæ; sanus fiebat a quacumque detinebatur infirmitate, efficienter et principaliter a Deo, cui soli competit a qualibet invaletudine propria virtute liberare, instrumentaliter vero ab angelo, dispositive autem ab aqua, quæ ex descensu motioneque angeli quamdam sortiebatur efficaciam ad curandum.
paras.en: [[5:3|In these lay a great multitude of sick|In his porticibus jacebat multitudo magna languentium]], wasting with divers infirmities, [[5:3|of blind, of lame, of withered|cæcorum, claudorum, aridorum]], or crippled, [[5:3|waiting for the moving of the water|exspectantium aquæ motum]] that the angel would make, which healed their infirmity. [[5:4|And an angel of the Lord descended at certain times|Angelus autem Domini descendebat secundum tempus]], that is, at fixed times, yet uncertain and broken, [[5:4|into the pond|in piscinam]], [[5:4|and the water was moved|et movebatur aqua]] by the angel with a strong and turbulent motion, so that it was certain that motion was made by the angel, not by the wind or a natural cause. And since the hour of the angel's coming down was uncertain, the sick lay there continually, as though always ready, and each wishing to be before the others in getting into the pool. The reason for this is added: [[5:4|And he that went down first into the pond after the motion of the water|Et qui prior descendebat in piscinam post motionem aquæ]] (the pond may mean either the water itself or the basin that held it) [[5:4|was made whole of whatsoever infirmity he lay under|sanus fiebat a quacumque detinebatur infirmitate]]: effectively and principally by God, to whom alone it belongs to free from any sickness by His own power; instrumentally by the angel; and dispositively by the water, which, from the angel's coming down and moving it, gained a certain power to heal.

paras.t: Sed cur Dominus tantam reverentiam et virtutem contulit huic aquæ? Ad hoc aliqui dicunt, quod propter lignum dominicæ crucis, quod in ea natasse et circa passionem enatasse affirmant. Alii dicunt, quod ad præfigurandum virtutem Baptismatis Christi tunc propinquantis, in quo omnis qui descenderit, ab omni peccato purgatur. Quidam vero dicunt, quod propter dignitatem legalium hostiarum, quæ ibi lavabantur, et præsertim in quantum hostiæ illæ immolationem Christi in cruce præfigurabant, per quam totum genus humanum redemptum est. Mihi videtur convenienter dici, quod Deus ex sua misericordia, propter prædictos infirmos ac inopes fecit hanc gratiam.
paras.en: But why did the Lord give such reverence and power to this water? To this some say: because of the wood of the Lord's cross, which they affirm floated in it, and came up to the surface about the time of the Passion. Others say: to prefigure the power of Christ's Baptism, then drawing near, in which every one who goes down is cleansed of every sin. Some, again, say: because of the dignity of the victims of the law that were washed there, and above all inasmuch as those victims prefigured the sacrifice of Christ on the cross, by which the whole human race was redeemed. To me it seems fittingly said that God granted this grace in His mercy for the sake of those sick and needy people.

paras.t: Mystice, per piscinam intelligere possumus fontem Baptismatis, vel sacramentum Confessionis, in qua omnia lavantur, vel quotidianum baptismum lacrimarum sanctarum; per descensum vero angeli, operationem et influentiam Christi, qui est magni consilii angelus, et in quolibet trium prædictorum principaliter operatur, vimque curandi largitur. Sed figura non adæquatur figurato. Idcirco Christus agit in Baptismo et Confessione, non solum sæpe, sed indesinenter quotidie; nec solum curatur unus, videlicet primus, sed omnis quicumque sacramenta ista digne susceperit.
paras.en: Mystically, by the pool we can understand the font of Baptism, or the sacrament of Confession, in which all things are washed[[Ps 31:1||]], or the daily baptism of holy tears[[Prov 28:13||]]; and by the angel's coming down, the working and inflowing of Christ, who is the Angel of great counsel[[Is 9:6||]] [so the Septuagint of Isaias names Him], and who works principally in each of these three and bestows the power of healing. But the figure does not equal what it figures. Therefore Christ acts in Baptism and Confession not only often, but unceasingly, every day; and not one only is healed, namely the first, but every one who receives these sacraments worthily.

paras.t: Erat autem quidam homo ibi triginta et octo annos habens in infirmitate sua. Species hujus infirmitatis non explicatur, sed creditur fuisse paralysis, nam homo iste jacebat in lecto. Hunc quum vidisset Jesus oculo corporali, et compassionis affectu, et cognovisset quia jam multum tempus haberet, id est, diu infirmatus fuisset: hoc enim Jesus in se ipso a principio suæ incarnationis cognovit futurum, quod nunc vidit in præsenti; dicit ei: Vis sanus fieri? Certum est quod ista quæstio non processit ex ignorantia: imo quicumque alius scire potuit, quod omnes ibi jacentes et aquæ motum præstolantes, cupiebant sanari. Sed quærit, ut in ægro desiderium recipiendæ curationis provocet, sicque dignior sit ad beneficium sanitatis sumendum. Denique specialiter hunc unum affatur et curat, quia miserabilior fuit, et jam pro peccatis suis longissima molestia fuerat castigatus. Ideo Dominus qui vulneravit, medetur; et qui percussit, denuo sanat. Scriptum est enim in Tobia: Quum iratus fueris, misericordiam facies. Longanimiter ergo et patienter est sustinenda castigatio Dei, imo omnis molestia corporis atque adversitas, juxta quod scriptum est in Judith: Non ulciscamur nos pro his quæ patimur; sed reputantes peccatis nostris hæc ipsa supplicia minora esse, flagella Domini, quasi servi qui corripimur, ad emendationem et non ad perditionem nostram evenisse credamus.
paras.en: [[5:5|And there was a certain man there that had been eight and thirty years under his infirmity|Erat autem quidam homo ibi triginta et octo annos habens in infirmitate sua]]. The kind of infirmity is not stated, but it is believed to have been palsy, since this man lay in a bed. [[5:6|Him when Jesus had seen|Hunc quum vidisset Jesus]] with the eye of the body and with the affection of compassion, [[5:6|and knew that he had been now a long time|et cognovisset quia jam multum tempus haberet]], that is, had been long sick (for Jesus knew within Himself from the beginning of His incarnation, as something to come, what He now saw present), [[5:6|he saith to him: Wilt thou be made whole?|dicit ei: Vis sanus fieri?]] It is certain that this question did not come from ignorance: indeed anyone else could know that all who lay there awaiting the moving of the water wished to be healed. But He asks in order to stir up in the sick man the desire of receiving the cure, and so make him worthier to receive the benefit of health. Then He speaks to this one in particular and heals him, because he was the more pitiable, and had already been chastised for his sins by a very long affliction. So the Lord who wounded heals, and He who struck heals again[[Job 5:18||]][[Deut 32:39||]]. For it is written in Tobias: [[Tob 3:13|when thou hast been angry, wilt shew mercy|Quum iratus fueris, misericordiam facies]]. The chastisement of God, then, and indeed every bodily trouble and adversity, is to be borne with long-suffering and patience, according to what is written in Judith: [[Jdt 8:26|let us not revenge ourselves for these things which we suffer|Non ulciscamur nos pro his quæ patimur]]. [[Jdt 8:27|But esteeming these very punishments to be less than our sins deserve, let us believe that these scourges of the Lord, with which like servants we are chastised, have happened for our amendment, and not for our destruction|sed reputantes peccatis nostris hæc ipsa supplicia minora esse, flagella Domini, quasi servi qui corripimur, ad emendationem et non ad perditionem nostram evenisse credamus]].

paras.t: Respondit ei languidus: Domine. Vocat Jesum Dominum, quasi venerabilem virum; sed aliud nihil scivit de eo. Hominem servientem seu adjuvantem non habeo, ut quum turbata, id est ab angelo vehementer concussa et mota, fuerit aqua, mittat, id est, ante alios deferat, me in piscinam: dum venio enim ego, qui præ languore cito ire non valeo, alius languidus ante me descendit in aquam.
paras.en: [[5:7|The infirm man answered him: Sir|Respondit ei languidus: Domine]]. He calls Jesus *Domine* [Lord, or Sir], as a man worthy of respect; but he knew nothing else of Him. [[5:7|I have no man|hominem non habeo]] to serve or help me, [[5:7|when the water is troubled|ut, cum turbata fuerit aqua]], that is, violently shaken and moved by the angel, [[5:7|to put me into the pond|mittat me in piscinam]], that is, to carry me in before the others. [[5:7|For whilst I am coming|dum venio enim ego]], who for weakness cannot go quickly, [[5:7|another goeth down before me|alius languidus ante me descendit]], another sick man, into the water.

paras.t: Dicit ei Jesus, cujus dicere est facere: Surge, tolle grabatum tuum, et ambula. Et statim sanus factus est homo ille. In quo ostenditur omnipotentia Christi, tam inveteratum languorem, in instanti imperiose curantis. Virtus nempe divina quum sit infinita, operatur in instanti: quod naturæ non convenit, quia in transmutationibus rerum de contrario in contrarium, agit successive. Unde, secundum Dionysium, Natura non transit a distanti in distans, nisi per media. Et sustulit grabatum suum, et ambulavit.
paras.en: [[5:8|Jesus saith to him|Dicit ei Jesus]], for whom to say is to do: [[5:8|Arise, take up thy bed and walk|Surge, tolle grabatum tuum, et ambula]]. [[5:9|And immediately the man was made whole|Et statim sanus factus est homo]]. In this the omnipotence of Christ is shown, who with a command healed in an instant so long-standing a sickness. For since the divine power is infinite, it works in an instant: which does not belong to nature, since in the changes of things from contrary to contrary it acts successively. Hence, according to Dionysius, nature does not pass from one extreme to another except through what lies between. [[5:9|and he took up his bed and walked|Et sustulit grabatum suum, et ambulavit]].

paras.t: Per languidum istum ambulare non valentem, intelligitur piger et negligens mala consuetudine pressus, qui in delectatione vitiosa et usu peccati, quasi in grabato jacet. Huic, imo et omni peccatori, dicit Christus quotidie, per admonitionem sacræ Scripturæ: Vis sanus fieri? Quum enim Dominus ait per Ezechielem, Nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat; et per Zachariam, Convertimini ad me, et convertar ad vos; itemque per Joelem, Omnis quicumque invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit: quid aliud loquitur, nisi, Vis sanus fieri? tanquam dicat: Ego sum medicus animarum; fac quod in te est, acquiesce monitis meis, et sanabo te. Surge a ruina peccati, tolle grabatum tuum, id est, delectationem peccati in qua quiescis, aufer et porta super te per compunctionem et satisfactionem, quatenus quantum glorificasti te in deliciisque fuisti, tantum imponas tibi luctum et afflictionem, exemplo Prophetæ dicentis, Laboravi in gemitu meo, lavabo per singulas noctes lectum meum; et ambula regia via in divinis præceptis: de quibus in libro Proverbiorum legitur, Viæ ejus viæ pulchræ, et omnes semitæ ejus pacificæ. Imo viam mandatorum Dei percurre, implens illud Josue: Servite Domino corde perfecto atque verissimo. Quanto enim animo promptiori ac ferventiori fecerimus opera Dei, tanto amplius promeremur.
paras.en: By this sick man who cannot walk is understood the slothful and negligent man, weighed down by bad habit, who lies in sinful delight and the practice of sin as in a bed. To him, and indeed to every sinner, Christ says daily through the admonition of holy Scripture: [[5:6|Wilt thou be made whole?|Vis sanus fieri?]] For when the Lord says through Ezechiel, [[Ezech 33:11|I desire not the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way, and live|Nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat]][[Ezech 18:23||]][[Ezech 18:32||]] [Denis: “not the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live”]; and through Zacharias, [[Zach 1:3|Turn ye to me|Convertimini ad me]], [[Zach 1:3|and I will turn to you|et convertar ad vos]]; and again through Joel, [[Joel 2:32|every one that shall call upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved|Omnis quicumque invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit]]: what else does He say but, Wilt thou be made whole? As if He said: I am the physician of souls; do what is in you, consent to My warnings, and I will heal you. Rise from the ruin of sin, [[5:8|take up thy bed|tolle grabatum tuum]], that is, the delight of sin in which you rest; take it away and carry it on yourself by compunction and satisfaction, so that as much as you have glorified yourself and lived in delights, so much mourning and affliction you may lay upon yourself[[Apoc 18:7||]], after the example of the Prophet who says: [[Ps 6:7|I have laboured in my groanings, every night I will wash my bed|Laboravi in gemitu meo, lavabo per singulas noctes lectum meum]]; [[5:8|and walk|et ambula]] by the king's highway in the divine precepts, of which we read in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 3:17|Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceable|Viæ ejus viæ pulchræ, et omnes semitæ ejus pacificæ]]. Nay, run the way of God's commandments[[Ps 118:32||]], fulfilling that word of Josue: [[Jos 24:14|serve him with a perfect and most sincere heart|Servite Domino corde perfecto atque verissimo]]. For the readier and more fervent the mind with which we do the works of God, the more we merit.

paras.t: Erat autem sabbatum, id est quies et cessatio ab operibus servilibus, in die illo. Imo hæc dies fuit sabbatum, id est dies septima ac festiva. Dicebant ergo Judæi illi qui sanus fuerat factus: Sabbatum est, non licet tibi tollere grabatum tuum. Si Judæi putaverunt eum lectum suum portare sine speciali Dei commissione, et necessitate seu dispensatione, excusabiles erant. Tamen ad minus materialiter falsum locuti sunt. Labor enim exterior ad divinum honorem directe ordinatus seu pertinens, licebat in sabbato, quemadmodum sacerdotes sabbatis templum ornabant, hostias aptabant ac immolabant. Bajulatio autem lecti ab isto sanato, fuit ad ostensionem divinæ potentiæ et gloriam Christi: velut si quis die dominica miraculose liberatus a carcere, deferat ad ecclesiam vincula sua ad glorificandum Deum. Fuit quoque ex dispensatione summi dispensatoris, qui legem dedit, et ad spiritualem legis intelligentiam introduxit. Unde subjungitur: Respondit eis iste sanatus: Qui me sanum fecit a paralysi, imo a labe peccati: quoniam Christus, cujus perfecta sunt opera, sanavit in anima quos curavit in corpore; ille mihi dixit: Tolle grabatum tuum, et ambula, id est, ea potestate qua me miraculose curavit, eadem auctoritate mihi præcepit quod facio.
paras.en: [[5:9|And it was the sabbath that day|Erat autem sabbatum in die illo]]: *sabbath*, that is, rest and ceasing from servile works. Nay, this day was the sabbath, that is, the seventh day and a feast day. [[5:10|The Jews therefore said to him that was healed: It is the sabbath. It is not lawful for thee to take up thy bed|Dicebant ergo Judæi illi qui sanus fuerat factus: Sabbatum est, non licet tibi tollere grabatum tuum]]. If the Jews thought he was carrying his bed without a special commission from God, and without necessity or dispensation, they were excusable. Yet at least materially they spoke falsely. For outward labour directly ordered to, or belonging to, the honour of God was lawful on the sabbath, just as the priests on the sabbath adorned the temple and prepared and sacrificed the victims[[Num 28:9||]]. And the carrying of the bed by this man who had been healed was for the showing of the divine power and the glory of Christ: as if someone, miraculously freed from prison on a Sunday, should carry his chains to the church to glorify God. It was also by the dispensation of the supreme Dispenser, who gave the law and led men into its spiritual understanding. Hence it is added: [[5:11|He answered them: He that made me whole|Respondit eis iste sanatus: Qui me sanum fecit]] of the palsy, nay of the stain of sin (for Christ, whose works are perfect[[Deut 32:4||]], healed in soul those whom He cured in body), [[5:11|he said to me: Take up thy bed and walk|ille mihi dixit: Tolle grabatum tuum, et ambula]]; that is, with the same authority, the power by which He cured me miraculously, He commanded me what I am doing.

paras.t: Interrogaverunt ergo eum: Quis est ille homo qui dixit tibi, Tolle grabatum tuum, et ambula? tanquam dicant: Ostende nobis talem tam malum et legis contemptorem, ut culpam tuam puniamus in eo. Isti qui curatorem hujus paralytici purum hominem æstimabant, homines erant, eo modo quo dicit Apostolus: Quum sit inter vos zelus et contentio, nonne carnales estis, et secundum hominem ambulatis?
paras.en: [[5:12|They asked him therefore: Who is that man who said to thee: Take up thy bed and walk?|Interrogaverunt ergo eum: Quis est ille homo qui dixit tibi, Tolle grabatum tuum, et ambula?]] As if they said: Show us this man, so wicked and so contemptuous of the law, that we may punish your fault in him. These men, who thought the healer of this paralytic a mere man, were *men* in the way the Apostle means when he says: [[1 Cor 3:3|whereas there is among you envying and contention, are you not carnal and walk you not according to man?|Quum sit inter vos zelus et contentio, nonne carnales estis, et secundum hominem ambulatis?]]

paras.t: Is autem qui sanus fuerat effectus, nesciebat quis esset, id est, nomen et famam Christi ignoravit, nec quidquam audivit de eo: et forte oblitus fuit dispositionis Christi in vultu ac habitu, ita quod neque per circumlocutionem et signa indicare potuit quisnam esset: quo modo Ochozias rex Israel cognovit Eliam, audito quod homo pilosus et zonam pelliceam circa renes habens, famulis suis obviasset, ut legitur in libris Regum. Jesus enim statim recessit ab homine isto, sicut subjungitur: Jesus autem declinavit a turba constituta in loco ubi paralyticum istum sanavit, vel ubi turba eum de grabati bajulatione redarguit. Declinavit autem a turba, erudiens nos ut post perpetrationem excellentium operum, fugiamus humanum honorem hominumque applausum, amantes nesciri; secundo, quia interdum ad tempus divertendum est a calumniatoribus, et ingratis cedendum; item, ut quietum locum quæramus ad vacandum Deo: in turba enim plurima occurrunt devotionis ac puritatis obstacula. Et forte ad litteram Christus recessit a turba, habens aliud salutare opus alibi expedire.
paras.en: [[5:13|But he who was healed knew not who it was|Is autem qui sanus fuerat effectus, nesciebat quis esset]], that is, he did not know Christ's name or fame, nor had he heard anything of Him; and perhaps he had forgotten Christ's look and bearing, so that he could not point out who He was even by describing Him and by signs, in the way that Ochozias king of Israel knew Elias on hearing that a hairy man with a girdle of leather about his loins had met his servants, as we read in the books of Kings[[4 Kings 1:8||]]. For Jesus at once withdrew from this man, as is added: [[5:13|for Jesus went aside from the multitude standing in the place|Jesus autem declinavit a turba constituta in loco]] where He had healed this paralytic, or where the crowd had rebuked him for carrying his bed. He went aside from the crowd, teaching us, after doing excellent works, to flee human honour and the applause of men, loving to be unknown; secondly, because at times one must turn aside for a while from slanderers and give way to the ungrateful; also, that we may seek a quiet place to be free for God, since in a crowd there are very many hindrances to devotion and purity. And perhaps, in the letter, Christ withdrew from the crowd because He had some other saving work to do elsewhere.

paras.t: Postea invenit eum Jesus in templo, ad quod sanatus iste convenit ut Deo ageret gratias. Sic et nos, si Jesum invenire et ab eo inveniri optamus, intremus templum ejus materiale ac spirituale, visitando ecclesiam, et redeundo ad propriam mentem per contemplationem et vitæ nostræ discussionem, atque internam in omni virtute exercitationem. Dominus enim in templo sancto suo. Et dixit illi: Ecce sanus factus es mente et corpore; jam noli peccare, id est, propositum habe cavendi omne peccatum pro posse, ne deterius tibi aliquid contingat, id est, ne major pœna tibi in præsenti, vel æterna damnatio infligatur: quoniam recidivantes atque ingrati graviorem pœnam merentur. Ex quibus elicitur, quod æger iste propter peccata sua incidit languorem præfatum. Quomodo autem Deus diversis de causis homines nunc flagellat, infra, Deo præstante, dicetur, ubi de cæco nato agetur.
paras.en: [[5:14|Afterwards, Jesus findeth him in the temple|Postea invenit eum Jesus in templo]], to which this man who had been healed had come to give thanks to God. So we too, if we long to find Jesus and to be found by Him, should enter His temple, both the material and the spiritual: by visiting the church, and by going back into our own mind through contemplation, through searching out our life, and through inward exercise in every virtue. For [[Ps 10:5|The Lord is in his holy temple|Dominus enim in templo sancto suo]]. [[5:14|and saith to him: Behold thou art made whole|Et dixit illi: Ecce sanus factus es]] in mind and body: [[5:14|sin no more|jam noli peccare]], that is, have the purpose of avoiding every sin as far as you can, [[5:14|lest some worse thing happen to thee|ne deterius tibi aliquid contingat]], that is, lest a greater punishment be laid on you in this life, or eternal damnation; for those who fall back and are ungrateful deserve a heavier punishment. From this it is drawn that this sick man fell into the sickness spoken of because of his sins. How God scourges men now for various reasons will be told below, God granting, where the man born blind is treated[[John 9:3||]].

paras.t: Abiit ille homo, et nuntiavit Judæis quia Jesus esset qui fecit eum sanum. Dicunt aliqui, quod malitiose hoc fecit, tanquam ingratus. Et hoc videtur ex eo quod Judæi eum increpabant de lecti sui portatione, et quum se excusasset per commissionem sui sanatoris, Judæi dixerunt: Ubi est ille? Ex quibus conjicere potuit quod Judæi volebant culpam retorquere in illum. Propter quod publicando Jesum, exposuit eum calumniatorum persecutioni. Alii dicunt oppositum, scilicet, quod simplici animo hoc egit, ne esset ingratus, et ut Christum glorificaret. Et probant per hoc quod Jesus sanavit istum in mente sicut in corpore: ideo non fuit tam improbus. Sed quidquid sit de veritate rei, istud argumentum facile solveretur per evangelicam veritatem: quia ut legitur in Luca, quum Jesus decem leprosos curasset, unus dumtaxat reversus est gratias agens, et alii facti fuerunt ingrati. Propter quod Christus dicebat: Nonne decem mundati sunt? Et novem ubi sunt? Non est inventus qui rediret et daret gloriam Deo, nisi hic alienigena. Nihilo minus omnes illi etiam mente sanati fuerunt; sed rursus in culpam prolapsi sunt, et forte a sacerdotibus subversi. Sic dici posset de isto. Potius tamen arbitror, quod non malitiose, sed bona intentione fecit quod dictum est, putans Judæos agnito actore miraculi meliorandos.
paras.en: [[5:15|The man went his way and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him whole|Abiit ille homo, et nuntiavit Judæis quia Jesus esset qui fecit eum sanum]]. Some say that he did this maliciously, as an ungrateful man. And this seems so from the fact that the Jews were rebuking him for carrying his bed, and when he excused himself by the command of his healer, the Jews said, Where is he? From which he could gather that the Jews meant to turn the blame upon Him. So, by making Jesus known, he exposed Him to the persecution of slanderers. Others say the opposite, namely that he did it with a simple mind, so as not to be ungrateful, and to glorify Christ. And they prove it by this, that Jesus healed this man in mind as in body; so he was not so wicked. But whatever the truth of the matter, this argument would easily be answered from the truth of the Gospel. For, as we read in Luke, when Jesus had cured ten lepers, only one came back giving thanks[[Luke 17:12||]][[Luke 17:15||]], and the others became ungrateful. For which reason Christ said: [[Luke 17:17|Were not ten made clean? And where are the nine?|Nonne decem mundati sunt? Et novem ubi sunt?]] [[Luke 17:18|There is no one found to return and give glory to God, but this stranger|Non est inventus qui rediret et daret gloriam Deo, nisi hic alienigena]]. Nevertheless all of them were healed in mind too; but they fell back into sin, perhaps led astray by the priests. The same could be said of this man. Yet I rather think that he did what was said not maliciously but with a good intention, thinking that the Jews, once they knew who had done the miracle, would be made better.

paras.t: Propterea persequebantur Judæi Jesum, detrahendo et comminando, quia hæc faciebat in sabbato, scilicet, quod hominem curavit, et ei lectum ferre præcepit. Jesus autem respondit eis, ostendens se non esse legis vel sabbati transgressorem, sed Patri æterno conformem in operando. Quemadmodum enim apud Matthæum excusat discipulos sabbato spicas evellentes et confricantes, a transgressione sabbati, per hoc quod David simile fecit; sic nunc excusat se a transgressione sabbati, per hoc quod Pater eodem modo operatur ut ipse. Pater meus cælestis et naturalis, usque modo operatur: id est, a principio mundi usque in præsens, imo et usque in sempiternum, indesinenter agit in rebus, totum universum in esse conservando, gubernando, corrupta restaurando; agit quoque animas rationales quotidie creando, impios justificando, purgatos ab omni reatu in cælis beatificando, panem et vinum in corpus et sanguinem Christi transsubstantiando; et alia ineffabilia jugiter operatur, præsertim in Ecclesia triumphanti, quæ ignoramus. Pauca quippe videmus operum ejus, ut dicitur in Ecclesiastico, ubi et scribitur: Multa sunt abscondita majora his. Quod vero in Genesi legitur, Requievit Deus ab omni opere quod patrarat, intelligendum est quantum ad productionem novarum specierum entis. Et ego operor, sicut et Pater, imo eadem quæ Pater, quia indivisus ab illo in natura et opere. Quemadmodum ergo Deus Pater prædicta omnia operans etiam sabbato, non arguitur quasi sabbati violator; ita nec ego argui debeo, qui confractum restauravi, et ad demonstrationem divinæ virtutis, eidem præcepi grabatum bajulare.
paras.en: [[5:16|Therefore did the Jews persecute Jesus|Propterea persequebantur Judæi Jesum]], by disparaging and threatening Him, [[5:16|because he did these things on the sabbath|quia hæc faciebat in sabbato]], namely, that He cured the man and bade him carry his bed. [[5:17|But Jesus answered them|Jesus autem respondit eis]], showing that He was no transgressor of the law or of the sabbath, but conformed to the eternal Father in working. For as in Matthew He excuses His disciples, who plucked and rubbed ears of corn on the sabbath, from breaking the sabbath, because David did the like[[Matt 12:1||]][[Matt 12:3||]], so now He excuses Himself from breaking the sabbath because the Father works in the same way as He. [[5:17|My Father|Pater meus]], heavenly and by nature, [[5:17|worketh until now|usque modo operatur]]: that is, from the beginning of the world until now, nay for ever, He acts unceasingly in things, keeping the whole universe in being, governing it and restoring what has decayed; He works also by creating rational souls every day, justifying the wicked, making blessed in heaven those cleansed of all guilt, changing the bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ; and He works continually other unspeakable things, above all in the Church triumphant, which we do not know. For [[Ecclus 43:36|we have seen but a few of his works|Pauca quippe videmus operum ejus]], as is said in Ecclesiasticus, where it is also written: [[Ecclus 43:36|There are many things hidden from us that are greater than these|Multa sunt abscondita majora his]]. And what we read in Genesis, [[Gen 2:2|he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done|Requievit Deus ab omni opere quod patrarat]], is to be understood of the bringing forth of new species of being. [[5:17|and I work|Et ego operor]], as does the Father, nay the same things as the Father, because I am undivided from Him in nature and in working. As, then, God the Father, who works all these things on the sabbath too, is not accused of violating the sabbath, so neither ought I to be accused, who have restored a broken man and, to show the divine power, bade him carry his bed.

paras.t: Ad intelligendum hæc verba sublimia, oportet advertere quod aliquid est causa alterius dupliciter: Primo, quantum ad illius inceptionem, et quoad esse ipsius, sed non quoad permanentiam ejus: quemadmodum homo generans est causa filii sui, et artifex causa ædificii. Unde, si pater vel artifex moriatur, nihilo minus filius et ædificium permanent atque subsistunt. In talibus ergo causatum non dependet a sua causa, quantum ad permanentiam. — Secundo, unum est causa alterius, quantum ad inceptionem et permanentiam ejus: quemadmodum sol est causa luminis et diei. Unde, si ad momentum sol deesset, dies deficeret. Et hoc modo est Deus causa rerum: creaturæ enim plus dependent a Creatore, quam aliquid creatum a causa creata. Propterea, si Deus relinqueret ens creatum sibi ipsi, suæ omnipotentiæ manutenentiam in ictu oculi subtrahendo seu suspendendo, mox universa mundanæ machinæ fabrica in nihil decideret, atque in se ipsa annihilata deficeret, sicut ex nihilo in esse surrexit. Et hoc ipsum, si non fallitur Albertus, scripsit et docuit Aristoteles in epistola de Principio universi. Hinc quoque, non solum secundum Platonem et Proclum, sed etiam teste principe theologorum sacratissimo Dionysio, Deus est causa rerum, non solum quasi nunc causans, sed quasi incessabiliter eas producens, propter incessantem suæ conservationis influentiam indesinentemque illarum dependentiam.
paras.en: To understand these lofty words, we must note that one thing is the cause of another in two ways. First, as to its beginning and as to its being, but not as to its lasting: as a man who begets is the cause of his son, and a builder the cause of a building. So if the father or the builder dies, the son and the building none the less last and subsist. In such things, then, what is caused does not depend on its cause as to its lasting. — Secondly, one thing is the cause of another both as to its beginning and as to its lasting: as the sun is the cause of light and of the day. So if the sun were missing for a moment, the day would fail. And in this way God is the cause of things: for creatures depend more on the Creator than anything made depends on a created cause. Therefore, if God left created being to itself, withdrawing or suspending for the twinkling of an eye the upholding of His omnipotence, the whole fabric of the world's frame would at once fall into nothing and, annihilated, fail in itself, just as it rose from nothing into being. And this very thing, if Albert is not mistaken, Aristotle wrote and taught in his letter *On the Principle of the Universe*. Hence too, not only according to Plato and Proclus, but also on the witness of the most holy Dionysius, prince of theologians, God is the cause of things not as causing them only once, but as producing them unceasingly, because of the unceasing inflowing of His conservation and their unceasing dependence.

paras.t: Hinc igitur asserit Filius Dei: Pater meus usque modo operatur. Non enim minoris potentiæ est creata manutenere in esse, et totum universum conservare in nihilo (quia nihil est extra universum fulciens ipsum, nisi Deus), quam eadem produxisse atque in nihilo collocasse. Hinc Proclus subtilissimus Platonicus scripsit in Elementatione sua theologica: Totus mundus ab intellectu substantiam habet; etsi perpetuus sit, non propter hoc non procedit ab intellectu, sed et procedit semper, et conversus est semper, et perpetuus secundum essentiam, et insolubilis secundum ordinem.
paras.en: Hence, then, the Son of God asserts: [[5:17|My Father worketh until now|Pater meus usque modo operatur]]. For it takes no less power to keep created things in being, and to hold up the whole universe in nothing (since there is nothing outside the universe that props it up, except God), than to have brought them forth and set them in nothing. Hence Proclus, a most subtle Platonist, wrote in his *Elements of Theology*: “The whole world has its substance from intellect; and though it be everlasting, it does not on that account fail to proceed from intellect: it both proceeds always and has always turned back, and is everlasting in its essence and indissoluble in its order.”

paras.t: Judæi ergo ex verbis Christi jam præinductis intelligentes quod Jesus comparasset se Deo in virtute et operatione, dixissetque se esse naturalem Filium Dei, Patri æqualem, putaverunt eum blasphemum, et fecerunt quod subditur. Propterea ergo, videlicet, quia æquavit se Patri, magis quærebant eum Judæi interficere, quia non solum solvebat sabbatum, secundum eorum falsam opinionem, sed et Patrem suum dicebat Deum, æqualem se faciens, id est esse dicens, Deo Patri. Sæpe in Scripturis, et etiam in communi modo loquendi, sumitur Facere pro Dicere vel Cogitare. Quoniam ergo secundum legem, gravior graviusque punienda fuit blasphemia, quam transgressio sabbati, ideo Judæi quærebant Jesum quasi blasphemum occidere.
paras.en: The Jews, then, understanding from the words of Christ just given that Jesus had made Himself like God in power and in working, and had said that He was the natural Son of God, equal to the Father, thought Him a blasphemer, and did what follows. [[5:18|Hereupon therefore|Propterea ergo]], namely because He made Himself equal to the Father, [[5:18|the Jews sought the more to kill him, because he did not only break the sabbath|magis quærebant eum Judæi interficere, quia non solum solvebat sabbatum]], according to their false opinion, [[5:18|but also said God was his Father, making himself equal to God|sed et Patrem suum dicebat Deum, æqualem se faciens, id est esse dicens, Deo]], that is, saying that He was equal to God the Father. Often in the Scriptures, and in the common way of speaking too, *to make* is taken for *to say* or *to think*. Since, then, by the law blasphemy was graver and more gravely to be punished than breaking the sabbath, the Jews sought to kill Jesus as a blasphemer.

paras.t: Sed quia Judæis visum fuit quod Jesus derogavit honori divino æquando se Patri æterno, idcirco Christus ostendit quod per hoc non derogavit Patri. Respondit itaque Jesus, et dixit eis: Amen, amen dico vobis, non potest Filius a se facere quidquam, nisi quod viderit Patrem facientem. Sed ex hoc Arius et Eunomius arguerunt quod Filius esset ex se infirmus, et per consequens minor Patre, et pura creatura: et satis difficile apparet quomodo sit verus Deus atque omnipotens, quia a se non potest quidquam. Sed non est impossibile ista dissolvere. Ut enim ostenderet Christus se a Patre recepisse, et habere quidquid est et habet, ita dicit, Non potest Filius a se facere quidquam: tanquam dicat, A me ipso non sum, sed esse et potestatem accepi a Patre. Itaque, Non potest a se, id est virtute non accepta, ut in eo est, facere quidquam, quia Filius non habet nisi virtutem acceptam, hoc est a Patre sibi communicatam. Denique, secundum Hilarium et Thomam in Summa contra gentiles, quamvis Filius non potest a se quidquam facere, potest tamen per se omnia facere, utpote propria virtute, quæ quum sit una numero in Patre et Filio ac Spiritu Sancto, est causa quod quælibet divina Persona est causa omnium rerum principalis atque omnipotens, et nulla est instrumentalis respectu alterius. — Quod vero adjecit, Nisi quod viderit Patrem facientem, non est sic intelligendum quasi alia sit visio seu intellectualis cognitio Filii, et alia Patris: imo sicut in Patre et Filio est unus numero intellectus, ita et visio una. Nihilo minus Pater videt Filium ejusque opera, et econtra: quoniam in utroque est plenitudo Divinitatis, quæ omnem perfectionem et actualitatem supersimplicissime prorsusque incomprehensibiliter comprehendit. Neque enim sic Filius videt Patrem et opera ejus, quasi aliquid aliud sit visio illa quam Filii deitas atque essentia. Quemadmodum ergo per eamdem essentiam Pater Filiusque subsistunt et Deus sunt, sic eadem visione Filius videt Patrem et opera ejus, Pater quoque Filium et opera ejus. Hæc est una interpretatio hujus loci.
paras.en: But since it seemed to the Jews that Jesus took away from the divine honour by making Himself equal to the eternal Father, Christ therefore shows that by this He took nothing away from the Father. [[5:19|Then Jesus answered and said to them: Amen, amen, I say unto you, the Son cannot do any thing of himself, but what he seeth the Father doing|Respondit itaque Jesus, et dixit eis: Amen, amen dico vobis, non potest Filius a se facere quidquam, nisi quod viderit Patrem facientem]]. From this Arius and Eunomius argued that the Son was weak of Himself, and so less than the Father, and a mere creature; and it seems hard enough to see how He is true God and almighty, since of Himself He can do nothing. But it is not impossible to solve this. For to show that He received from the Father, and has from Him, whatever He is and has, Christ says, [[5:19|the Son cannot do any thing of himself|Non potest Filius a se facere quidquam]]; as though He said, I am not from Myself, but I have received being and power from the Father. So *He cannot of Himself*, that is, by a power not received, as far as lies in Him, *do anything*, since the Son has only a power received, that is, communicated to Him by the Father. Further, according to Hilary, and Thomas in the *Summa contra Gentiles*, though the Son can do nothing *of* Himself, He can do all things *by* Himself, namely by His own power; and since this power is one in number in the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost, it is the reason why each divine Person is the principal and almighty cause of all things, and none is an instrument with respect to another. — As for what He added, [[5:19|but what he seeth the Father doing|nisi quod viderit Patrem facientem]], it is not to be understood as though the seeing, or intellectual knowing, of the Son were one and that of the Father another: rather, as there is one intellect in number in the Father and the Son, so there is one seeing. None the less the Father sees the Son and His works, and the other way about, since in each is the fulness of the Godhead, which contains all perfection and actuality in a most utterly simple and wholly incomprehensible way. For the Son does not see the Father and His works as though that seeing were something other than the Son's Godhead and essence. As, then, by the same essence the Father and the Son subsist and are God, so by the same seeing the Son sees the Father and His works, and the Father the Son and His works. This is one interpretation of this place.

paras.t: Potest autem et ita exponi: Non potest Filius a se facere quidquam, nisi quod viderit Patrem facientem. Tanquam diceret: Hoc quod Filius videt facere Patrem, hoc etiam potest ipse Filius facere a se, id est per se propriaque quamvis collata virtute; alia vero non potest facere Filius. Et sic Christus per verba hæc probat se non posse peccare: quod ei imposuerunt Judæi. Si enim Filius nihil potest facere nisi quod viderit Patrem facientem, tunc procul dubio, sicut Pater non potest peccare, ita nec Filius. — Postremo, verba ista intelligi possent de Christo secundum assumptam naturam, secundum quam certum est quod non potest facere quidquam a se.
paras.en: It can also be expounded thus: [[5:19|the Son cannot do any thing of himself, but what he seeth the Father doing|Non potest Filius a se facere quidquam, nisi quod viderit Patrem facientem]]. As though He said: What the Son sees the Father doing, that the Son Himself can also do of Himself, that is, by Himself and by His own power, though a power given; but other things the Son cannot do. And so by these words Christ proves that He cannot sin, which the Jews laid to His charge. For if the Son can do nothing but what He sees the Father doing, then beyond doubt, as the Father cannot sin, neither can the Son. — Lastly, these words could be understood of Christ according to the nature He assumed, according to which it is certain that He can do nothing of Himself.

paras.t: Insuper Christus testatur, quod Pater non est factor principalior nec universalior Filio, et quod opera amborum sunt indivisa, ita quod Pater et Filius sunt unus factor, Creator et gubernator, non duo factores: per quod hæresim Arianorum confundit. Quæcumque enim ille, videlicet Pater, fecerit, hæc eadem opera et Filius secundum naturam divinam similiter facit, id est æque principaliter et auctoritative, non instrumentaliter et ministrative. Per hoc ergo quod ait, Quæcumque, ostenditur quod operatio Patris non extenditur ultra operationem Filii. Propterea Filius est prima et universalis causa, prout in Apocalypsi loquitur: Ego sum Alpha et Omega, primus et novissimus, principium et finis. Unde in Michæa habetur: Et tu, turris Gregis nebulosa, ad te veniet potestas prima, regnum filiæ Jerusalem. Ubi per potestatem primam, ad litteram intelligitur Christus, qui teste Apostolo, est virtus et sapientia Patris, portans omnia verbo virtutis suæ. Hoc quoque in Proverbiis manifeste ostenditur, ubi Sapientia de Deo effatur: Quando præparabat cælos aderam; quando appendebat fundamenta terræ, cum eo eram cuncta componens. Per hoc autem quod ait, Hæc, docet quod eadem numero sunt opera Patris et Filii. Quumque natura sit operationis principium, sequitur quod Patris et Filii sit una natura: una utique numero, non genere vel specie, quia divina natura multiplicari non potest. Per hoc vero quod subditur, Similiter facit, patet quod Pater operatur per Verbum seu Filium, non sicut artifex per ministrum vel instrumentum, sed sicut amicus per amicum, rex per regem, judex per judicem, non subalternatum, sed comparem.
paras.en: Moreover, Christ testifies that the Father is not a more principal or more universal maker than the Son, and that the works of both are undivided, so that the Father and the Son are one maker, Creator and ruler, not two makers: and by this He confounds the heresy of the Arians. [[5:19|for what things soever he doth|Quæcumque enim ille, videlicet Pater, fecerit]], namely the Father, [[5:19|these the Son also doth in like manner|hæc … et Filius … similiter facit]], the same works, according to the divine nature: that is, equally as principal and with authority, not as an instrument or a minister. By saying *what things soever*, then, He shows that the working of the Father does not reach beyond the working of the Son.
