Therefore the Son is the first and universal cause, as He says in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 22:13|I am Alpha and Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End|Ego sum Alpha et Omega, primus et novissimus, principium et finis]][[Apoc 1:8||]][[Apoc 21:6||]]. Hence we have in Micheas: [[Mich 4:8|And thou, O cloudy tower of the flock|Et tu, turris Gregis nebulosa]], [[Mich 4:8|unto thee shall it come: yea the first power shall come, the kingdom to the daughter of Jerusalem|ad te veniet potestas prima, regnum filiæ Jerusalem]]: where by *the first power* is understood, in the letter, Christ, who, on the witness of the Apostle, is the power and wisdom of the Father[[1 Cor 1:24||]], [[Heb 1:3|upholding all things by the word of his power|portans omnia verbo virtutis suæ]]. This too is plainly shown in Proverbs, where Wisdom says of God: [[Prov 8:27|When he prepared the heavens, I was present|Quando præparabat cælos aderam]]; when He poised the foundations of the earth[[Prov 8:29||]], [[Prov 8:30|I was with him forming all things|cum eo eram cuncta componens]]. By saying *these*, He teaches that the works of the Father and of the Son are the same in number. And since nature is the principle of working, it follows that the Father and the Son have one nature: one in number, surely, not in genus or species, since the divine nature cannot be multiplied. And by what is added, *in like manner*, it is plain that the Father works through the Word, or Son, not as a craftsman through a servant or a tool, but as a friend through a friend, a king through a king, a judge through a judge: not one placed beneath Him, but His equal.

paras.t: Pater enim diligit Filium, hoc supra scriptum atque expositum est. Et nunc addi potest, quod dilectio non est principium emanationis Filii a Patre, quia non procedit a Patre per voluntatem, aut libere libertate contingentiæ vel ad utrumlibet, sed naturali emanatione. Nihilo minus Pater diligit Filium vere et intensive, infinite, sumendo dilectionem absolute, ita quod habet se quasi concomitanter ad emanationem.
paras.en: [[5:20|For the Father loveth the Son|Pater enim diligit Filium]]: this was written and explained above[[John 3:35||]]. And now it can be added that love is not the principle of the Son's coming forth from the Father, since He does not proceed from the Father by will, nor freely with the freedom of contingency, that is, of being able to go either way, but by natural emanation. None the less the Father loves the Son truly, intensely and infinitely, taking love absolutely, so that love goes along, as it were, with the emanation.

paras.t: Denique multæ sunt rationes dilectionis, quæ maxime et superexcellenter inveniuntur inter Patrem et Filium, imo inter tres supersublimes, æternas, increatas Personas, hoc est in ipsa Trinitate, una, superessentiali, simplicissima Deitate. Interdum enim dicimus, quod agnitio est causa dilectionis, videlicet ut via ad dilectionem; interdum, quod bonum est causa dilectionis tanquam objectum; interdum vero similitudo appellatur causa amoris; sed et communicatio est causa amoris; sæpeque dicimus, quod nihil sic accendat amorem, quomodo si quis sciat se amari ab alio. Quum ergo Pater et Filius se invicem perfectissime comprehendant, et Filius Patri omnino simillimus sit, uterque quoque infinitæ bonitatis et sanctitatis exsistat, Paterque dederit Filio totum quod suum est, puta divinam essentiam, quam transfundit in eum, et Filius tantum bonum a Patre susceperit, Pater etiam sciat se amari a Filio immenso amore, et econtra; hinc constat, quod in divinis Personis sit quomodolibet omniformiterque plenissima ratio mutuæ dilectionis. Quæ quum sit infiniti ardoris, et rei summæ, præsentis, perfectissime quoque conjunctæ, liquet quod dilectio trium Personarum ad invicem sit vere immensæ dulcedinis infinitæque pacis. Et dulce, sanctum ac deiforme est, hoc nunc fideliter contemplari, sincere adspicere, atque in contemplatione tam alta cordialiter affici, divinæ beatitudini congratulari, a sensibus rapi, in divitias gloriæ absorberi. Beatus qui sic gustat quam dulcis et felix est Deus; beati mundi corde, studiosi et affectuosi in obsequio Dei, ferventes atque solliciti quomodo Creatorem suum honorent, eumque ab aliis honorari conspiciant. Maledictus vero qui facit opus Dei negligenter, qui intimorate ambulat coram Altissimo.
paras.en: Further, there are many reasons for love, and they are found most fully and supremely between the Father and the Son, nay among the three most exalted, eternal and uncreated Persons, that is, in the Trinity itself, the one, superessential and most simple Godhead. For sometimes we say that knowledge is the cause of love, as the way to love; sometimes that the good is the cause of love, as its object; sometimes likeness is called the cause of love; communication too is a cause of love; and we often say that nothing so kindles love as knowing oneself loved by another. Since, then, the Father and the Son comprehend each other most perfectly, and the Son is altogether most like the Father, and each is of infinite goodness and holiness, and the Father has given the Son all that is His, namely the divine essence, which He pours into Him, and the Son has received so great a good from the Father, and the Father knows Himself loved by the Son with an immense love, and the other way about: it is plain from this that in the divine Persons there is, in every way and every form, the fullest ground of mutual love. And since this love is of infinite ardour, and of a thing supreme, present and most perfectly united, it is clear that the love of the three Persons for one another is truly of immense sweetness and infinite peace. And it is sweet, holy and godlike now to contemplate this faithfully, to gaze on it sincerely, to be moved in heart in so high a contemplation, to rejoice with the divine beatitude, to be rapt from the senses and swallowed up in the riches of glory. Blessed is he who thus tastes how sweet and happy God is[[Ps 33:9||]]; [[Matt 5:8|Blessed are the clean of heart|beati mundi corde]], zealous and loving in the service of God, fervent and anxious how they may honour their Creator and see Him honoured by others. But cursed is he who does the work of God negligently[[Jer 48:10||]], who walks before the Most High without fear[[Mich 6:8||]].

paras.t: Et omnia demonstrat ei quæ ipse facit, id est, Deus Pater dat Filio notitiam omnium operum suorum: generando enim Filium, dat ei divinam essentiam, et per consequens æternam et infinitam sapientiam omnium intuitivam. Sic ergo Pater demonstrat Filio, non quasi ignoranti, aut præexsistenti et demum instructo, sed quasi totum suum esse, posse ac nosse a Patre suscipienti. Quidquid enim Patris est, communicatum est Filio, et resplendet in eo sicut in naturali et plena imagine Patris. Et quoniam Filius propter nos instruendos ac redimendos homo factus fuit, et inter homines socialiter vixit, idcirco altitudinem sapientiæ suæ aptavit et proportionavit capacitati intelligentiæ nostræ, loquendo nobis de rebus incomprehensibilibus ac divinis humano modo, quatenus sic ea aliqualiter caperemus. Unde de æternis loquitur nobis per verba temporalia secundum omnes differentias temporis, quia et ipsa æternitas comprehendit ac continet omne tempus. Sicque loquendo nunc subditur:
paras.en: [[5:20|and sheweth him all things which himself doth|Et omnia demonstrat ei quæ ipse facit]]; that is, God the Father gives the Son the knowledge of all His works: for in begetting the Son He gives Him the divine essence, and consequently the eternal and infinite wisdom that sees all things. So the Father shows them to the Son, not as to one ignorant, or as to one already existing and then taught, but as to one who receives all His being, power and knowledge from the Father. For whatever is the Father's is communicated to the Son, and shines in Him as in the natural and full image of the Father. And since the Son was made man to teach and redeem us, and lived among men as one of them[[John 1:14||]][[Bar 3:38||]], He fitted and proportioned the height of His wisdom to the capacity of our understanding, speaking to us of incomprehensible and divine things in a human way, so that we might in some measure grasp them. Hence He speaks to us of eternal things in words of time, according to all the differences of time, since eternity itself comprehends and contains all time. And speaking in this way He now adds:

paras.t: Et majora his demonstrabit ei opera, id est mirabilia excellentiora signis quæ hucusque in Jerusalem feci: nam illuminatio cæci nati et suscitatio Lazari, major fuit quam curatio paralytici. Convenientius tamen opera ista majora intelliguntur spiritualia miracula Christi in conversione hominum facta, secundum quod majus dicitur impium justificare, quam mundum creare. Christus enim quosdam omnino mirabiliter convertit et sibi attraxit. Sed et miracula facta in passione, in resurrectione, ascensione, et Spiritus Sancti missione, magna nimis fuerunt. Itaque, per hoc quod ait, Demonstrabit, non datur intelligi quod Filius secundum divinam naturam aliquid accipiat in futuro: imo nec secundum humanam naturam hoc ei proprie competebat, præsertim quum anima Christi, a suæ conditionis exordio, plena fuerit sapientia, virtute et gratia. Sed loquitur sic propter duo: Primo, quia ut dictum est, æterna emanatio Verbi seu receptio Filii a Patre, omne tempus includit. Secundo, quoniam in Scripturis dicitur aliquid fieri, quum aliis innotescit. Quoniam ergo postea innotuerunt Judæis majora opera Christi, quam hucusque, propterea dixit Filius, quod Pater demonstraturus esset sibi opera præclariora. Ut sit sensus: Majora his demonstrabit, id est, se ei demonstrasse ostendet, opera, quando videlicet talia fient.
paras.en: [[5:20|and greater works than these will he shew him|Et majora his demonstrabit ei opera]]; that is, wonders more excellent than the signs I have done until now in Jerusalem: for the enlightening of the man born blind and the raising of Lazarus were greater than the curing of the paralytic. More fittingly, however, these greater works are understood as Christ's spiritual miracles done in the conversion of men, in the sense in which it is said to be a greater thing to justify the wicked than to create the world. For Christ converted some and drew them to Himself in a wholly wonderful way. And the miracles done in the Passion, the Resurrection, the Ascension and the sending of the Holy Ghost were exceedingly great too. So by saying *will shew* it is not given to be understood that the Son, according to the divine nature, receives anything in the future; nor did this properly belong to Him according to His human nature either, above all since the soul of Christ from the first beginning of its making was full of wisdom, power and grace. But He speaks so for two reasons. First because, as was said, the eternal emanation of the Word, or the Son's receiving from the Father, includes all time. Secondly, because in the Scriptures a thing is said to be done when it becomes known to others. Since, then, greater works of Christ than those done until then afterwards became known to the Jews, the Son said that the Father would show Him more glorious works. So the sense is: *Greater than these will He shew Him*, that is, He will make it plain that He has shown Him, *works*, namely when such things come to pass.

paras.t: Ut vos miremini. Si admiratio accipiatur secundum se, sistendo in ea, tunc non fuit finis hujuscemodi demonstrationis miraculorumque Christi, sed consecuta est ad opera Christi: sicque, Ut, ponitur concomitanter, non causaliter. Juxta quem sensum dicit Apostolus: Mittet illis Deus spiritum erroris, ut credant mendacio; et Psalmista, Tibi soli peccavi, et malum coram te feci, ut justificeris in sermonibus tuis. Si autem sumatur miratio prout inducit ad fidem, videlicet, ut est via ad conversionem, sic potest dici finis mirabilium operum Christi: sic tamen, ut ista miratio conversionem mirantis includat. Ad hoc quippe fecit Christus miracula, ut Judæi videndo admirandoque crederent.
paras.en: [[5:20|that you may wonder|Ut vos miremini]]. If wonder is taken in itself, stopping at it, then it was not the end of this showing and of Christ's miracles, but followed upon Christ's works; and so *that* is put to mean what goes along with it, not its cause. In this sense the Apostle says: God [[2 Thess 2:10|shall send them the operation of error, to believe lying|Mittet illis Deus spiritum erroris, ut credant mendacio]] [Denis: “the spirit of error”]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 50:6|To thee only have I sinned, and have done evil before thee: that thou mayst be justified in thy words|Tibi soli peccavi, et malum coram te feci, ut justificeris in sermonibus tuis]]. But if wondering is taken as it leads to faith, that is, as the way to conversion, then it can be called the end of Christ's wonderful works: yet in such a way that this wonder includes the conversion of the one who wonders. For Christ did miracles to this end, that the Jews, seeing and wondering, might believe.

paras.t: Advertendum quoque, quod licet ea quæ dicta sunt ab illo loco, Pater diligit Filium, accipi possint de Filio etiam secundum humanitatem assumptam, secundum quam Pater notificavit seu demonstravit Filio omnia opera sua, quoniam quidquid Deus cognoscit scientia visionis, videlicet omnia quæ unquam fuerunt, sunt, vel erunt, cognoscit et anima Christi; illud tamen, Quæcumque ille fecerit, scilicet Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit, non convenit Christo, nisi ut vero Deo. Imo per illud verbum aperte confunditur hæresis Arii dicentis, quod Filius sit pura creatura. Sic enim Pater fecisset Filium. Si ergo quæcumque facit Pater, facit et Filius, sequitur quod Filius fecisset se ipsum, loquendo semper de Filio secundum naturam suam superiorem.
paras.en: It is to be noted also that, although what is said from the words [[5:20|For the Father loveth the Son|Pater diligit Filium]] onward can be taken of the Son according to the humanity He assumed too (according to which the Father made known, or showed, all His works to the Son, since whatever God knows by the knowledge of vision, namely all things that ever were, are or will be, the soul of Christ knows also), yet the words [[5:19|for what things soever he doth, these the Son also doth in like manner|Quæcumque ille fecerit, scilicet Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit]], namely the Father, do not belong to Christ except as true God. Indeed by that word the heresy of Arius, who said that the Son is a mere creature, is openly confounded. For on that view the Father would have made the Son. If, then, whatever the Father does the Son also does, it follows that the Son would have made Himself: speaking always of the Son according to His higher nature.

5.title: Prosecutio elucidationis hujus capituli quinti, ab eo loco quo dicitur: Sicut enim Pater suscitat mortuos et vivificat.
5.title_en: Continuation of the explanation of this fifth chapter, from the place where it is said: “For as the Father raiseth up the dead and giveth life.”

paras.t: Dixit jam Christus paulo ante, quia quæcumque facit Pater, facit similiter Filius, et quod majora Pater opera demonstraret Filio, quam hucusque fecit Filius coram Judæis. Nunc Christus declarat hoc quasi exemplificando. Sicut enim Pater suscitat mortuos morte naturæ, et morte culpæ, hoc est mortuos corporaliter per discessum animæ, et mortuos spiritualiter per amissionem caritatis et gratiæ, et vivificat eos. Mortuos namque corporaliter, suscitat atque vivificat Pater, animam corpori reuniendo, ut totum compositum habeat vitam naturæ sicut et ante mortem habebat. Unde in libris Regum inducitur: Dominus mortificat et vivificat, deducit ad inferos et reducit. Deus enim habet imperium vitæ et mortis. Mortuos vero spiritualiter (de quibus ait Salvator apud Matthæum, Dimitte mortuos sepelire mortuos suos), suscitat, itemque vivificat Pater, culpam delendo et gratiam restituendo, prout ad Ephesios Apostolus dicit: Quum essemus mortui peccatis, convivificavit nos Christo. Sic et Filius, quos vult vivificat: non utique alios aut pauciores quam Pater, sed eosdem et æque multos, quoniam operatio Patris et Filii ad extra, est penitus indivisa. Et idem dicendum est de Spiritu Sancto, de quo fatur Apostolus: Hæc omnia operatur unus atque idem Spiritus, dividens singulis prout vult. Unde de Filio nunc dicitur, Quos vult vivificat, ad insinuandum quod Filius agit sponte, imperialiter et propria auctoritate, tanquam verus Deus, secundum quod dicit Apostolus: Omnia operatur secundum propositum voluntatis suæ. Quod autem Filius spiritualiter suscitet, claret ex verbo Apostoli: Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis, et illuminabit te Christus. Sed quum de Patre dictum est, Sicut Pater suscitat mortuos et vivificat: quare de Filio non subditur, Sic et Filius, quos vult suscitat et vivificat, nisi quia suscitatio in vivificatione includitur?
paras.en: Christ said a little before that whatever the Father does the Son does in like manner, and that the Father would show the Son greater works than the Son had done until then before the Jews. Now Christ makes this plain, as it were by an example. [[5:21|For as the Father raiseth up the dead|Sicut enim Pater suscitat mortuos]], dead by the death of nature and by the death of guilt, that is, dead bodily through the departure of the soul, and dead spiritually through the loss of charity and grace, [[5:21|and giveth life|et vivificat]] to them. For the Father raises up and gives life to those who are bodily dead by joining the soul again to the body, so that the whole composite has the life of nature as it had before death. Hence it is brought in in the books of Kings: [[1 Kings 2:6|The Lord killeth and maketh alive, he bringeth down to hell, and bringeth back again|Dominus mortificat et vivificat, deducit ad inferos et reducit]]. For God has the power of life and death[[Wis 16:13||]]. And those who are spiritually dead (of whom the Saviour says in Matthew, [[Matt 8:22|let the dead bury their dead|Dimitte mortuos sepelire mortuos suos]]) the Father raises up and likewise gives life to, by blotting out guilt and restoring grace; as the Apostle says to the Ephesians: [[Eph 2:5|Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together in Christ|Quum essemus mortui peccatis, convivificavit nos Christo]]. [[5:21|so the Son also giveth life to whom he will|Sic et Filius, quos vult vivificat]]: not, surely, to others or to fewer than the Father, but to the same and to just as many, since the working of the Father and the Son outside themselves is wholly undivided. And the same must be said of the Holy Ghost, of whom the Apostle speaks: [[1 Cor 12:11|But all these things, one and the same Spirit worketh, dividing to every one according as he will|Hæc omnia operatur unus atque idem Spiritus, dividens singulis prout vult]]. So it is now said of the Son, *to whom he will*, to hint that the Son acts of His own accord, with sovereign power and by His own authority, as true God, according to what the Apostle says: [[Eph 1:11|who worketh all things according to the counsel of his will|Omnia operatur secundum propositum voluntatis suæ]]. And that the Son raises up spiritually is clear from the Apostle's word: [[Eph 5:14|Rise, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead: and Christ shall enlighten thee|Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis, et illuminabit te Christus]]. But since it was said of the Father, *as the Father raiseth up the dead and giveth life*, why is it not added of the Son, *so the Son also raiseth up and giveth life to whom he will*, unless because raising up is included in giving life?

paras.t: Neque enim Pater judicat quemquam, sed omne judicium dedit Filio. Quomodo verum est hoc? Si enim indivisa sunt opera Patris ac Filii, quemcumque judicat Filius, judicat Pater. Iterum, quomodo Pater non judicat, sed Filius, quum infra Filius dicat, Ego non judico quemquam, est qui quærat et judicet, scilicet Pater? Et si Pater non judicat quemquam, quomodo verum est illud in Job, Absit a Deo impietas et ab Omnipotente iniquitas, opus enim hominis reddet ei, et juxta vias singulorum restituet? Denique, quod convenit Deo absolute, secundum naturam Divinitatis, convenit cuilibet divinæ Personæ. Judicare autem homines universos convenit Deo, secundum quod Deus, videlicet secundum propriam naturam. Aliter vane constituisset filios hominum: quod pro inconvenienti habet Psalmista; et contrariatur his quæ in libro Job continentur, videlicet: Universorum finem ipse considerat; rursusque, Omnipotens causas singulorum intuebitur. Hinc quoque per Jeremiam asseritur: Domine Deus, fortissime, magnus consilio et incomprehensibilis cogitatu, cujus oculi aperti sunt super omnes filios Adam, ut reddas unicuique secundum vias suas et secundum fructum adinventionum suarum.
paras.en: [[5:22|For neither does the Father judge any man: but hath given all judgment to the Son|Neque enim Pater judicat quemquam, sed omne judicium dedit Filio]]. How is this true? For if the works of the Father and the Son are undivided, whomever the Son judges, the Father judges. Again, how does the Father not judge, but the Son, when further on the Son says, *I judge not any man; there is one that seeketh and judgeth*[[John 8:15||]][[John 8:50||]], namely the Father? And if the Father judges no man, how is that true which is in Job: [[Job 34:10|far from God be wickedness, and iniquity from the Almighty|Absit a Deo impietas et ab Omnipotente iniquitas]]. [[Job 34:11|For he will render to a man his work, and according to the ways of every one he will reward them|opus enim hominis reddet ei, et juxta vias singulorum restituet]]? Further, what belongs to God absolutely, according to the nature of the Godhead, belongs to each divine Person. And to judge all men belongs to God as God, that is, according to His own nature. Otherwise He would have made the sons of men in vain[[Ps 88:48||]], which the Psalmist holds unfitting; and it would go against what is contained in the book of Job, namely: [[Job 28:3|the end of all things he considereth|Universorum finem ipse considerat]]; and again, [[Job 35:13|the Almighty will look into the causes of every one|Omnipotens causas singulorum intuebitur]]. Hence it is also asserted through Jeremias: O Lord God, [[Jer 32:18|most mighty|fortissime]], [[Jer 32:19|Great in counsel, and incomprehensible in thought: whose eyes are open upon all the ways of the children of Adam, to render unto every one according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his devices|magnus consilio et incomprehensibilis cogitatu, cujus oculi aperti sunt super omnes filios Adam, ut reddas unicuique secundum vias suas et secundum fructum adinventionum suarum]] [Denis: “upon all the children of Adam”].

paras.t: Verum omnia ista atque similia, una solutione solvuntur et concordantur. Oportet ergo advertere, quod in judicio quatuor considerantur: primo, auctoritas judicandi seu judiciaria potestas; secundo, ipsa discretio boni a malo, videlicet interior approbatio boni, atque interior detestatio mali. Quantum ad hæc duo, judicium convenit toti Trinitati singulisque Personis. Tertio, ipsa prolatio sententiæ sensibilis atque exterior: et quoad hoc, Pater non judicat quemquam, sed solus Filius secundum naturam assumptam. Imo hoc modo Deus Trinitas judicabit auctoritative, per Christum hominem exsecutive, juxta illud Actuum: Deus statuit diem in quo judicaturus est orbem terræ in æquitate, in viro quem statuit. Tunc enim manifeste veniet Deus noster, et non silebit, quando in die judicii videbunt in quem transfixerunt. Quarto, consideratur in judicio ipsa retributio pœnæ vel gloriæ: et sic quoque soli Deo principaliter secundum divinam naturam judicium convenit, præsertim quantum ad gloriæ collationem. Porro, quod Filius ait, Ego non judico quemquam, intelligendum est de judicio retributionis, quantum ad primum Christi adventum, in quo non venit judicare, sed judicari. Sic ergo, Pater non judicat quemquam, id est, non profert judicialem sententiam, modo prætacto, sed omne judicium, id est universalem exsecutionem judicii, dedit Filio secundum naturam quam induit, sicut infra plenius ostendetur. Unde habetur in Psalmo: Deus, judicium tuum regi da. Et juxta Apostolum, Omnes nos stare oportet ante tribunal Christi.
paras.en: But all these and the like are solved and brought into agreement by one solution. We must note, then, that four things are considered in judgment. First, the authority of judging, or judicial power; secondly, the discerning itself of good from evil, that is, the inward approval of good and the inward detesting of evil. As to these two, judgment belongs to the whole Trinity and to each Person. Thirdly, the pronouncing itself of the sentence, outwardly and to the senses; and as to this, the Father judges no man, but the Son alone, according to the nature He assumed. Indeed in this way God the Trinity will judge with authority, and through Christ the man as the one who carries it out, according to that word of the Acts: [[Acts 17:31|he hath appointed a day wherein he will judge the world in equity, by the man whom he hath appointed|Deus statuit diem in quo judicaturus est orbem terræ in æquitate, in viro quem statuit]]. For then [[Ps 49:3|God shall come manifestly: our God shall come, and shall not keep silence|manifeste veniet Deus noster, et non silebit]], when on the day of judgment [[John 19:37|They shall look on him whom they pierced|videbunt in quem transfixerunt]]. Fourthly, there is considered in judgment the repaying itself of punishment or glory; and in this way too judgment belongs principally to God alone, according to the divine nature, above all as to the bestowing of glory. Further, what the Son says, *I judge not any man*, is to be understood of the judgment of retribution as regards Christ's first coming, in which He came not to judge but to be judged. So, then, *the Father judgeth not any man*, that is, He does not pronounce the judicial sentence in the way just touched on, *but hath given all judgment*, that is, the universal carrying out of judgment, *to the Son*, according to the nature He put on, as will be shown more fully below. Hence we have in the Psalm: [[Ps 71:2|Give to the king thy judgment, O God|Deus, judicium tuum regi da]]. And according to the Apostle, [[2 Cor 5:10|we must all be manifested before the judgment seat of Christ|Omnes nos stare oportet ante tribunal Christi]] [Denis: “we must all stand before the judgment seat of Christ”, as in Rom 14:10].

paras.t: Hunc autem honorem Pater impendit Filio incarnato, ut omnes intellectuales creaturæ honorificent Filium, exhibendo ei cultum et adorationem latriæ soli Deo debitam, sicut honorificant Patrem, impendendo ei latriæ cultum. Sed honoratio ista non convenit Filio secundum illam naturam qua convenit ei prædicta exsecutio judicii, sed secundum naturam qua consubstantialis et coæqualis est Patri. Nihilo minus Pater dedit Filio secundum naturam assumptam hoc judicium, ut per hoc innotescat omnibus quod homo ille est verus Deus, sicque honorificetur sicut et Pater. Unde verbum istud consonat dicto Apostoli ad Philippenses, loquentis de Filio secundum naturam humanam: Humiliavit semetipsum factus obediens usque ad mortem: propter quod et Deus exaltavit illum, ut in nomine Jesu omne genu flectatur, cælestium, terrestrium et infernorum.
paras.en: This honour the Father bestows on the incarnate Son, [[5:23|That all men may honour the Son|ut omnes intellectuales creaturæ honorificent Filium]], all intellectual creatures, showing Him the worship and adoration of *latria* due to God alone [*latria*: the worship given to God only], [[5:23|as they honour the Father|sicut honorificant Patrem]], paying Him the worship of *latria*. But this honouring does not belong to the Son according to that nature by which the carrying out of judgment just spoken of belongs to Him, but according to the nature by which He is consubstantial and co-equal with the Father. None the less the Father has given this judgment to the Son according to the nature He assumed, so that by this it may become known to all that that man is true God, and so He may be honoured as the Father is. So this word agrees with the saying of the Apostle to the Philippians, speaking of the Son according to His human nature: [[Phil 2:8|He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death|Humiliavit semetipsum factus obediens usque ad mortem]]: [[Phil 2:9|For which cause, God also hath exalted him|propter quod et Deus exaltavit illum]], [[Phil 2:10|That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth|ut in nomine Jesu omne genu flectatur, cælestium, terrestrium et infernorum]].

paras.t: Quæritur, si Pater non judicat quemquam, sed omne judicium dedit Filio, quomodo verum est illud in Job: Quem constituit alium super terram? aut quem posuit super orbem quem fabricatus est? Et respondendum, quod Pater non sic constituit Christum judicem ac principem mundi, quasi ipse desierit habere providentiam rerum: sed Pater seu Deus Trinitas, est principalis provisor, judex et rex universi; Christus vero secundum quod homo, prælatus est omni creaturæ quasi minister Dei et exsecutor.
paras.en: It is asked: if the Father judges no man, but has given all judgment to the Son, how is that true which is in Job: [[Job 34:13|What other hath he appointed over the earth? or whom hath he set over the world which he made?|Quem constituit alium super terram? aut quem posuit super orbem quem fabricatus est?]] The answer is that the Father did not so appoint Christ judge and prince of the world as though He Himself had ceased to have providence over things; but the Father, or God the Trinity, is the principal provider, judge and king of the universe, while Christ, as man, is set over every creature as God's minister and the one who carries out His will.

paras.t: Qui non honorificat Filium per latriæ cultum: est autem latria, virtus quæ Deo cultum et cerimoniam affert; non honorificat Patrem qui misit illum, quum utriusque sit una majestas, et tanta dilectio, concordia, atque justitiæ ac sanctitatis conformitas, vel potius unitas et identitas, quod qui unum offendit, offendit et alium, præsertim quum sit amborum una voluntas. Præterea, qui non credit in Filium, mendacem facit Patrem, et Spiritui gratiæ ingerit contumeliam, quia non credit in testimonium quod testificati sunt Pater et Spiritus Sanctus de Christo in baptismo et transfiguratione, in diversis miraculis et distributionibus gratiarum, in Scripturis utriusque Testamenti, et in omni sanctitate et excellentia Christi.
paras.en: [[5:23|He who honoureth not the Son|Qui non honorificat Filium]] with the worship of *latria* (and *latria* is the virtue that brings worship and ceremony to God) [[5:23|honoureth not the Father who hath sent him|non honorificat Patrem qui misit illum]], since the majesty of both is one, and so great is their love, concord and likeness in justice and holiness, or rather their unity and sameness, that whoever offends the one offends the other also, above all since the will of both is one. Moreover, he who does not believe in the Son [[1 John 5:10|maketh him a liar|mendacem facit]], the Father, and does insult to the Spirit of grace, because [[1 John 5:10|he believeth not in the testimony|non credit in testimonium]] that the Father and the Holy Ghost have borne to Christ at His baptism[[Matt 3:16||]][[Matt 3:17||]] and transfiguration[[Matt 17:5||]], in divers miracles and distributions of graces, in the Scriptures of both Testaments, and in all the holiness and excellence of Christ.

paras.t: Honorificandus est ergo Filius interiori exteriorique latriæ cultu, videlicet reverentia cordiali, oratione et laude, præceptorumque observatione. Omnes itaque qui Patrem Filio asseruerunt majorem, non honorificaverunt Patrem, cujus Filio dilecto ac unico derogaverunt: cujus contumelia redundat in Patrem, præsertim quum hoc maxime ad commendationem bonitatis, potestatis et sapientiæ Dei pertineat, quod Filium sibi prorsus æqualem producere et voluit, et novit, et potuit, quamvis (ut dixi) voluntas non præcessit generationem Verbi quasi origo ipsius, sed potius concomitanter se habet ad eam. Imo Spiritus Sanctus, qui est amor et emanatio voluntatis, non sic procedit a voluntate, quasi libere ad utrumlibet effluat atque spiretur: sic enim posset non procedere, haberetque esse contingens. Sed procedit per modum naturalis emanationis, secundum quod voluntas Patris ac Filii est quædam natura.
paras.en: The Son, then, is to be honoured with the inward and outward worship of *latria*, that is, with heartfelt reverence, with prayer and praise, and with keeping His commandments. So all who asserted that the Father is greater than the Son did not honour the Father, for they took away from His beloved and only Son; and the insult to the Son redounds upon the Father, above all since it belongs most of all to the praise of God's goodness, power and wisdom that He willed, knew how, and was able to bring forth a Son wholly equal to Himself: although (as I said) His will did not go before the generation of the Word as its origin, but rather goes along with it. Indeed the Holy Ghost, who is love and the emanation of the will, does not so proceed from the will as though He flowed forth and were breathed forth freely, as able to go either way: for so He might not proceed, and would have contingent being. But He proceeds by way of natural emanation, inasmuch as the will of the Father and the Son is a kind of nature.

paras.t: Deinde Filius Dei ostendit quomodo spiritualis vivificatio fiat. Amen, amen dico vobis, quia qui verbum meum audit, non auribus corporis tantum, sed etiam cordis, de quibus dicitur alibi: Qui habet aures audiendi, audiat. Itaque, Qui verbum meum audit, id est, sermonibus meis consentit, et credit ei qui misit me, id est Patri cælesti, recipiendo testimonium quod ipse perhibet mihi, vel credendo ei fide formata, hoc est credendo in ipsum, habet vitam æternam jam in spe et in merito, atque in dispositione propinqua, et cito sortiturus ac possessurus est eam in re, in mercede, in actu. Hoc enim modo viatores dicuntur beati, quamvis variis persecutionibus concutiantur, prout scriptum est in Matthæo: Beati pauperes spiritu, beati qui lugent, beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam. Et in judicium non venit, id est, judicium damnationis non incurret, de quo fatetur Apostolus ad Corinthios: Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur. Omnes tamen judicabimur judicio retributionis. Sed transiet a morte corporali, quam omnes quasi debitum solvunt propter originale peccatum, in vitam gloriæ sempiternæ, quum fuerit liber ab omni reatu, de qua dicit Apostolus: Vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo. Talis etiam in præsenti transit per cordis salutarem immutationem, a morte culpæ ad vitam virtutis et gratiæ. Nam et prudentia carnis, mors est, et si secundum carnem vixerimus, moriemur. Qui ergo carnalem prudentiam deserit, et veram sapientiam recipit, transit a morte in vitam.
paras.en: Next the Son of God shows how spiritual quickening comes about. [[5:24|Amen, amen, I say unto you that he who heareth my word|Amen, amen dico vobis, quia qui verbum meum audit]], not with the ears of the body only, but also with those of the heart, of which it is said elsewhere: [[Matt 13:9|He that hath ears to hear, let him hear|Qui habet aures audiendi, audiat]]. So *he who heareth my word*, that is, consents to My words, [[5:24|and believeth him that sent me|et credit ei qui misit me]], that is, the heavenly Father, receiving the testimony He bears to Me, or believing Him with formed faith, that is, believing in Him, [[5:24|hath life everlasting|habet vitam æternam]] already in hope and in merit and in near disposition, and will soon obtain and possess it in reality, in reward, in act. For in this way wayfarers are called blessed, though shaken by divers persecutions, as is written in Matthew: [[Matt 5:3|Blessed are the poor in spirit|Beati pauperes spiritu]], [[Matt 5:5|Blessed are they that mourn|beati qui lugent]], [[Matt 5:10|Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake|beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam]]. [[5:24|and cometh not into judgment|Et in judicium non venit]], that is, will not incur the judgment of damnation, of which the Apostle says to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 11:31|But if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged|Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur]]. Yet we shall all be judged with the judgment of retribution. [[5:24|but is passed from death|Sed transiet a morte]], bodily death, which all pay as a debt because of original sin, [[5:24|to life|in vitam]] of everlasting glory, when he is free of all guilt; of which the Apostle says: [[Col 3:3|your life is hid with Christ in God|Vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo]]. Such a man passes in this present life too, through a saving change of heart, from the death of guilt to the life of virtue and grace. For [[Rom 8:6|the wisdom of the flesh is death|prudentia carnis, mors est]], and [[Rom 8:13|if you live according to the flesh, you shall die|si secundum carnem vixerimus, moriemur]] [Denis: “if we live”]. So he who forsakes the wisdom of the flesh and receives true wisdom passes from death to life.

paras.t: Amen, amen dico vobis, quia venit hora, et nunc est, utpote tempus gratiæ, de quo dicit Apostolus: Quum venit plenitudo temporis; et Petrus in Actibus, Omnes (inquit) Prophetæ annuntiaverunt dies istos. Quando mortui, id est peccatores vita gratiæ destituti: de qua morte Paulus testatur, Vidua quæ in deliciis vivit, vivens mortua est; audient exteriori et interiori auditu, vocem, id est prædicationem, Filii Dei. Multi enim Judæorum per verba Christi correcti atque conversi fuerunt, præsertim post ejus passionem et ascensionem. Quotidie quoque mortui seu injusti, audiendo verbum Christi ab ejus vicariis ac ministris, spiritualiter reviviscunt, sicut subjungitur: et qui audierint verbum Christi modo jam dicto, vivent vita gratiæ in via, et vita gloriæ in patria, dummodo perseverent usque in finem, quoniam sola perseverantia coronatur. Et hoc sciendum, quod nemo audit salubriter verbum Dei, nisi Christus per inspirationem Spiritus Sancti cor ejus tetigerit, et erudierit mentem ejus, fundendo radium sapientiæ in intellectum ipsius. Propter quod in Isaia scribitur: Erigit mane, mane erigit mihi aurem, ut audiam quasi magistrum; Dominus Deus aperuit mihi aurem, ego autem non contradico.
paras.en: [[5:25|Amen, amen, I say unto you, that the hour cometh, and now is|Amen, amen dico vobis, quia venit hora, et nunc est]], namely the time of grace, of which the Apostle says: [[Gal 4:4|when the fulness of the time was come|Quum venit plenitudo temporis]]; and Peter in the Acts: [[Acts 3:24|all the prophets|Omnes (inquit) Prophetæ]] (he says) [[Acts 3:24|have told of these days|annuntiaverunt dies istos]]. [[5:25|when the dead|Quando mortui]], that is, sinners bereft of the life of grace, of which death Paul testifies: [[1 Tim 5:6|she that liveth in pleasures is dead while she is living|Vidua quæ in deliciis vivit, vivens mortua est]] [Denis: “the widow that liveth in pleasures”]; [[5:25|shall hear|audient]], with outward and inward hearing, [[5:25|the voice of the Son of God|vocem Filii Dei]], that is, His preaching. For many of the Jews were corrected and converted by Christ's words, above all after His Passion and Ascension. And every day the dead, or unjust, hearing the word of Christ from His vicars and ministers, come to life again spiritually, as is added: [[5:25|and they that hear shall live|et qui audierint, vivent]]: they who hear the word of Christ in the way just said shall live with the life of grace on the way and the life of glory in the fatherland, provided they persevere to the end[[Matt 10:22||]][[Matt 24:13||]], since perseverance alone is crowned. And this is to be known: that no one hears the word of God to his salvation unless Christ, by the inspiration of the Holy Ghost, has touched his heart and taught his mind, pouring a ray of wisdom into his understanding. For which reason it is written in Isaias: [[Is 50:4|he wakeneth in the morning, in the morning he wakeneth my ear, that I may hear him as a master|Erigit mane, mane erigit mihi aurem, ut audiam quasi magistrum]]; [[Is 50:5|The Lord God hath opened my ear, and I do not resist|Dominus Deus aperuit mihi aurem, ego autem non contradico]].

paras.t: Secundo exponi potest hic locus de particulari corporum resurrectione, secundum quam Christus suscitavit filium viduæ, filiam archisynagogi, et Lazarum. Sed tunc quæstio est, quomodo corporaliter mortui dicantur audire vocem Filii Dei. Quod enim non vivit, non utique audit. Et respondendum, quod dicuntur audire vocem Christi metaphorice, quoniam ad imperium Christi sic corpus exstinctum et anima separata quasi obediendo reassociantur et componuntur, sicut obediunt qui realiter imperantis eloquium audiunt, et tanquam jussionem Christi vere audissent. Sic quippe dicimus quod mare cognovit Christum, quando sub pedibus ejus mansit indivisum. Sic quoque ait Psalmista: Mare vidit, et fugit; et, Sol cognovit occasum suum.
paras.en: Secondly, this place can be expounded of the particular resurrection of bodies, by which Christ raised the widow's son[[Luke 7:14||]], the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue[[Matt 9:25||]], and Lazarus[[John 11:43||]]. But then the question is how those bodily dead are said to hear the voice of the Son of God. For what does not live surely does not hear. And the answer is that they are said to hear the voice of Christ by a figure of speech, since at Christ's command the lifeless body and the separated soul are joined again and put together as though obeying, just as those obey who really hear the words of one who commands, and as though they had truly heard Christ's bidding. So we say that the sea knew Christ when it stayed undivided beneath His feet[[Matt 14:25||]]. So too the Psalmist says: [[Ps 113:3|The sea saw and fled|Mare vidit, et fugit]]; and, [[Ps 103:19|the sun knoweth his going down|Sol cognovit occasum suum]].

paras.t: Insuper declaratur, quod Christus ad utramque hanc vivificationem idoneus sit tanquam fons vitæ. Sicut enim Pater habet vitam intellectualem, non vegetativam, sensitivam, vel secundum locum motivam, in semetipso; sic dedit, id est, generando communicavit naturali diffusione seu originatione, non libera ad utrumlibet, et Filio vitam, non solum similem, sed numero eamdem, habere in semetipso. Pater nempe sic habet vitam in se, quod ipse est hæc vita. Quæ etiam vita est in se ipsa omnino perfecta, omnem nobilitatem beatitudinemque vivendi cum incomprehensibili simplicitate complectens: ita quod est vita superessentialis, fontana, superjucunda et superbeatissima; vita vere purissima, vivacissima, prorsusque superplenissima, omnis vitæ fontale principium, in quo est omnium bonorum atque pulchrorum ac desiderabilium superdives possessio. Simili modo habet Filius secundum divinam naturam, vitam in semetipso, quoniam ipse est vita hæc. Suntque Pater et Filius una vita, quæ divina est essentia prout est actus purus: Pater ergo generando communicans Filio divinam essentiam, communicavit et dedit ei vitam et sapientiam. Quum ergo sit Filius tam superexuberans fons vitæ, palam quod possit vivificare quoscumque voluerit. Et potestatem dedit ei, et judicium facere. Quum Filius a Patre habeat quidquid habet, constat quod Filius, etiam ut Deus, habet a Patre judiciariam potestatem. Sed de hujus potestatis datione non est nunc sermo. Subditur enim: quia Filius hominis est. Ergo intelligendum de potestate subauctoritatis in judicando, videlicet de potestate exsequendi judicium pro prolatione sententiæ: quæ potestas data est a tota Trinitate Christo homini, quia Filius hominis est. Quod dupliciter intelligi potest. Primo sic: Quia Filius hominis est, id est merito suæ humiliationis, incarnationis, humanæ conversationis, ac passionis. Christus enim per ista meruit sibi ipsi judiciariam potestatem in exsequendo. Nec obstat quod habuit eam ab instanti suæ incarnationis propter hypostaticam unionem cum Verbo. Non enim est inconveniens aliquid alicui deberi et convenire ob causas diversas: quemadmodum etiam corpori Christi debebatur vel competebat glorificatio, ratione beatitudinis animæ suæ; nihilo minus per suam passionem promeruit eam, et sæpe oravit pro ea.
paras.en: Moreover, it is made plain that Christ is fit for both these quickenings, as the fountain of life. [[5:26|For as the Father hath life|Sicut enim Pater habet vitam]], intellectual life, not vegetative or sensitive or the life that moves from place to place, [[5:26|in himself|in semetipso]], [[5:26|so he hath given|sic dedit]], that is, by begetting He has communicated by natural outpouring, or origin, not free to go either way, [[5:26|to the Son also to have life in himself|et Filio habere vitam in semetipso]]: a life not only like His own but the same in number. For the Father so has life in Himself that He Himself is this life. And this life is in itself wholly perfect, embracing all the nobility and beatitude of living with incomprehensible simplicity: so that it is a superessential life, a fountain-life, surpassingly delightful and surpassingly blessed; a life truly most pure, most living and altogether over-full, the fountainhead of all life, in which is the more than rich possession of all good, beautiful and desirable things. In like manner the Son, according to the divine nature, has life in Himself, since He is this life. And the Father and the Son are one life, which is the divine essence as pure act: so the Father, by begetting and communicating the divine essence to the Son, communicated and gave Him life and wisdom. Since, then, the Son is so overflowing a fountain of life, it is plain that He can give life to whomever He will. [[5:27|And he hath given him power to do judgment|Et potestatem dedit ei, et judicium facere]]. Since the Son has from the Father whatever He has, it is clear that the Son, even as God, has the power of judging from the Father. But it is not of the giving of this power that He now speaks. For it is added: [[5:27|because he is the Son of man|quia Filius hominis est]]. It is to be understood, then, of the power of judging under authority, that is, of the power of carrying out judgment by pronouncing sentence: a power given by the whole Trinity to Christ the man, *because he is the Son of man*. This can be understood in two ways. First thus: *because he is the Son of man*, that is, by the merit of His humbling, incarnation, life among men and passion. For by these Christ merited for Himself the judicial power of carrying out judgment. Nor does it stand in the way that He had it from the instant of His incarnation because of the hypostatic union with the Word. For it is not unfitting that something should be owed to someone and belong to him for different reasons: as glorification was owed to, or belonged to, the body of Christ by reason of the beatitude of His soul, and yet He merited it by His passion and often prayed for it.

paras.t: Secundo sic: Quia Filius hominis est, id est propter convenientiam quam habet ad exercendum judicium ex parte humanitatis assumptæ. Decet enim judicem ab omnibus judicandis manifeste videri, ut stent coram eo, et loquantur pro se, si potuerint. Nulla autem divina Persona secundum propriam naturam apta est judicare hoc modo. Non enim videri potest manifeste nisi a Beatis. Imo a quocumque manifeste videtur, beatus est. Quum ergo persona Filii sit secundum humanam naturam a bonis malisque visibilis, ideo datum est ei judicium facere, quia Filius hominis est. Ideo Petrus loquitur in Actibus Apostolorum: Ipse est qui constitutus est a Deo judex vivorum et mortuorum. Et David ait de Christo: Judicabit in nationibus, implebit ruinas. Hoc sanctus Job cognovit adfuturum, quum dixit: Credo quod Redemptor meus vivit, et in novissimo die de terra surrecturus sum, et in carne mea videbo Deum salvatorem meum. Videre enim in carne propria ipsum Deum, non videtur proprie posse intelligi nisi de Deo incarnato atque visibili: præsertim quum sanctus Job subjecerit, Quem visurus sum ego ipse, et oculi mei conspecturi sunt: quod de corporalibus oculis dictum videtur, quoniam Job loquitur de vera corporum resuscitatione atque perfecta membrorum reparatione.
paras.en: Secondly thus: [[5:27|because he is the Son of man|Quia Filius hominis est]], that is, because of the fitness He has for exercising judgment on the side of the humanity He assumed. For it befits a judge to be seen plainly by all who are to be judged, so that they may stand before him and speak for themselves if they can. But no divine Person, according to His own nature, is fit to judge in this way. For He cannot be seen plainly except by the Blessed[[Ex 33:20||]][[1 John 4:12||]]; indeed, whoever sees Him plainly is blessed. Since, then, the Person of the Son, according to His human nature, is visible to good and wicked alike, it is therefore given Him to do judgment, *because he is the Son of man*. That is why Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: [[Acts 10:42|it is he who was appointed by God to be judge of the living and of the dead|Ipse est qui constitutus est a Deo judex vivorum et mortuorum]]. And David says of Christ: [[Ps 109:6|He shall judge among nations, he shall fill ruins|Judicabit in nationibus, implebit ruinas]]. Holy Job knew this would come to pass when he said: [[Job 19:25|For I know that my Redeemer liveth, and in the last day I shall rise out of the earth|Credo quod Redemptor meus vivit, et in novissimo die de terra surrecturus sum]]. [[Job 19:26|and in my flesh I shall see my God|et in carne mea videbo Deum]] [Denis: “God my Saviour”]. For to see God Himself in one's own flesh does not seem properly understandable except of God incarnate and visible; above all since holy Job added: [[Job 19:27|Whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold|Quem visurus sum ego ipse, et oculi mei conspecturi sunt]]; which seems said of the bodily eyes, since Job is speaking of the true raising of bodies and the perfect restoring of their members.

paras.t: Et ne Judæi verbis istis præ admiratione discrederent, addit Filius Dei aliud mirabilius, quatenus mirabilia reddantur credibilia per facta mirabiliora. Nolite mirari admiratione inordinata, dejectiva, incredula, hoc quod dixi, mihi datam potestatem judicandi, quum majora acturus sim; quia veniet hora, videlicet dies judicii: de qua alibi legitur, De die illa et hora nemo scit; in qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt, id est omnes defuncti quantum ad corpus in sepulcris locati, quantum vero ad animam in inferno, in limbo, purgatorio, vel in cælo exsistentes (unde dicuntur esse in monumentis ratione partis, per synecdochen: quemadmodum Abraham dicitur sepultus in spelunca duplici; et Maria Magdalene, Tulerunt, inquit, Dominum, id est corpus Domini de monumento), audient vocem Filii Dei, id est, ad imperium Christi resurgent, quemadmodum per Danielem prænuntiatum est: Qui dormiunt in pulvere terræ, evigilabunt. Isaias quoque prædixit: Vivent mortui tui, interfectique mei resurgent. Ista est vox Christi de qua dicit Apostolus: Quoniam ipse Dominus in jussu et in voce Archangeli et in tuba Dei, descendet de cælo. De qua apud Matthæum prædixit Salvator: Media nocte clamor factus est: Ecce sponsus venit, exite obviam ei. Qualiter vero quamque celeriter fiet resuscitatio corporum, pandit Apostolus: In momento, in ictu oculi, in novissima tuba: canet enim tuba, et mortui resurgent incorrupti. Quomodo autem mortui dicantur audire, jam patuit.
paras.en: And lest the Jews, for wonder at these words, should disbelieve them, the Son of God adds something more wonderful still, so that wonderful things may be made believable by things more wonderful. [[5:28|Wonder not at this|Nolite mirari hoc]], with a disordered, downcast and unbelieving wonder, namely what I have said, that the power of judging is given to Me, since I shall do greater things: [[5:28|for the hour cometh|quia veniet hora]], namely the day of judgment, of which we read elsewhere: [[Matt 24:36|of that day and hour no one knoweth|De die illa et hora nemo scit]]; [[5:28|wherein all that are in the graves|in qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt]], that is, all the dead, laid in tombs as to the body, but as to the soul being in hell, in limbo, in purgatory or in heaven (and so they are said to be *in the graves* by reason of a part, by synecdoche, as Abraham is said to be buried in the double cave[[Gen 25:9||]], and Mary Magdalen says, [[John 20:13|they have taken away my Lord|Tulerunt, inquit, Dominum]], that is, the Lord's body, from the tomb), [[5:28|shall hear the voice of the Son of God|audient vocem Filii Dei]], that is, shall rise again at Christ's command, as was foretold through Daniel: [[Dan 12:2|those that sleep in the dust of the earth, shall awake|Qui dormiunt in pulvere terræ, evigilabunt]]. Isaias too foretold: [[Is 26:19|Thy dead men shall live, my slain shall rise again|Vivent mortui tui, interfectique mei resurgent]]. This is the voice of Christ of which the Apostle says: [[1 Thess 4:15|For the Lord himself shall come down from heaven with commandment and with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God|Quoniam ipse Dominus in jussu et in voce Archangeli et in tuba Dei, descendet de cælo]]. Of it the Saviour foretold in Matthew: [[Matt 25:6|And at midnight there was a cry made: Behold the bridegroom cometh. Go ye forth to meet him|Media nocte clamor factus est: Ecce sponsus venit, exite obviam ei]]. And how and how swiftly the raising of bodies will come about, the Apostle makes known: [[1 Cor 15:52|In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet: for the trumpet shall sound and the dead shall rise again incorruptible|In momento, in ictu oculi, in novissima tuba: canet enim tuba, et mortui resurgent incorrupti]]. How the dead are said to hear has already been made plain.

paras.t: Et procedent qui bona fecerunt, id est finaliter consummati atque inventi in operibus meritoriis, in resurrectionem vitæ, id est, felicem immutationem consequentur. Omnes enim resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur. Nam immutabuntur qui mutabuntur in melius, adipiscentes resurrectionem pertingentem in vitam gloriosam atque cælestem. Qui vero mala egerunt, id est in iniquitatibus deprehensi, et in vitiis mortalibus hinc sublati, qui sibi finem ultimum constituerunt in rebus caducis, adhærentes creaturæ potius quam Creatori, procedent in resurrectionem judicii, id est, resurrectionem habebunt damnosam ac miseram, pertingentem ad reprobationis judicium de quo dixit Apostolus: Eos qui foris sunt Deus judicabit. In quali enim dispositione seu affectione anima recedit a corpore, in tali æternaliter permanet, et secundum eam judicatur præmiumque æternum sortitur a Deo: sicut angeli apostatantes inconvertibiliter manent in dispositione illa mentali ac vitiosa in qua erant quum dejicerentur a cælo. Propter quod asserit Damascenus: Quod in angelis est casus, hoc in hominibus est mors; et Salomon in Ecclesiaste, Si ceciderit lignum ad austrum aut ad aquilonem, in quocumque loco ceciderit, ibi erit.
paras.en: [[5:29|And they that have done good things shall come forth|Et procedent qui bona fecerunt]], that is, those found at the end perfected in meritorious works, [[5:29|unto the resurrection of life|in resurrectionem vitæ]], that is, they will obtain a happy change. For [[1 Cor 15:51|We shall all indeed rise again: but we shall not all be changed|Omnes enim resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur]]. For they will be changed who are changed for the better, gaining a resurrection that reaches to a glorious and heavenly life. [[5:29|but they that have done evil|Qui vero mala egerunt]], that is, those caught in their iniquities and taken hence in mortal vices, who set their last end in perishable things, cleaving to the creature rather than the Creator[[Rom 1:25||]], [[5:29|unto the resurrection of judgment|procedent in resurrectionem judicii]], that is, they will have a ruinous and wretched resurrection, reaching to the judgment of reprobation, of which the Apostle said: [[1 Cor 5:13|them that are without, God will judge|Eos qui foris sunt Deus judicabit]]. For in whatever disposition or affection the soul leaves the body, in that it remains for ever, and according to it it is judged and receives its eternal reward from God: as the apostate angels remain unchangeably in that disposition of mind, and that vicious one, in which they were when they were cast down from heaven. For which reason Damascene asserts: “What a fall is for the angels, death is for men”; and Solomon in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 11:3|If the tree fall to the south, or to the north, in what place soever it shall fall, there shall it be|Si ceciderit lignum ad austrum aut ad aquilonem, in quocumque loco ceciderit, ibi erit]].

paras.t: Postremo, per hoc quod ait Evangelista, vel potius Christus per eum, Qui bona fecerunt, et qui mala egerunt, etc.; patet insania æstimantium fidem sine operibus posse salvare. Nec tamen putandum, quod illi dumtaxat salvabuntur qui opera caritatis vel saltem interiorem ejus actum habuerunt: salvabuntur enim infantes baptizati, et naturaliter stolidi Baptismatis fonte renati. His vero quæ de distinctione resurgentium dicta sunt, consonat illud Danielis: Evigilabunt, alii in vitam æternam, alii in opprobrium, ut videant semper.
paras.en: Lastly, by what the Evangelist says, or rather Christ through him, [[5:29|they that have done good things|Qui bona fecerunt]], and [[5:29|they that have done evil|qui mala egerunt]], etc., the madness of those who think that faith without works can save is made plain. Yet it is not to be thought that only those will be saved who have had the works of charity, or at least its inward act: for baptized infants will be saved, and those simple by nature who have been born again in the font of Baptism. And with what has been said of the distinction among those who rise again agrees that word of Daniel: [[Dan 12:2|shall awake: some unto life everlasting, and others unto reproach, to see it always|Evigilabunt, alii in vitam æternam, alii in opprobrium, ut videant semper]].

paras.t: Quoniam ergo Filius Dei qui factus est caro et frater noster, advocatus, propitiator et proximus noster, habet vitam fontalem, supereffluentem et indefectibilem in semetipso, accedamus semper ad eum cum plena fiducia, ut gloriose vivificet nos, et de plenitudine torrentis suæ dulcissimæ vitæ corda nostra saltem perfundat, etsi nondum inebriet. Denique vox ejus terribilis, quam omnes mortui audient, qua totus tinniet mundus, et tartarea claustra patebunt, jugiter insonet auribus nostræ mentis; et cogitemus quam horrendum sit incidere in manus Dei viventis, quam metuendum erit illud judicium, quam inæstimabilis angustia impiorum.
paras.en: Since, then, the Son of God, who was made flesh[[John 1:14||]] and is our brother[[Matt 28:10||]][[Heb 2:11||]], our advocate and propitiation[[1 John 2:1||]][[1 John 2:2||]] and our neighbour, has in Himself a fountain-life, overflowing and unfailing, let us always draw near to Him with full confidence, that He may give us glorious life, and from the fulness of the torrent of His most sweet life may at least steep our hearts, even if He does not yet make them drunk. Lastly, let His terrible voice, which all the dead shall hear, at which the whole world shall ring and the gates of hell shall open, sound unceasingly in the ears of our mind; and let us think [[Heb 10:31|It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God|quam horrendum sit incidere in manus Dei viventis]], how dreadful that judgment will be, how beyond reckoning the anguish of the wicked.

5.title: Explanatio residuæ partis hujus capituli quinti: Non possum ego a me ipso facere quidquam.
5.title_en: Explanation of the remaining part of this fifth chapter: “I cannot of myself do any thing.”

paras.t: Quoniam multa magnifica perhibuit Christus de semetipso, videlicet, quod Pater non judicat quemquam, sed Filius omnes, et quod quos vult, vivificat, omnesque in sepulcris repositos suscitabit. Ne ergo videatur inaniter loqui, vel Patri derogare, vel secundum personarum acceptionem et inordinatam aliquam affectionem judicare, refert omne bonum suum ad Deum Patrem, quasi ad fontem derivantem, non derivatum, et dicit se omnia agere prout a Patre accepit, cujus in omnibus quærit gloriam, promovetque honorem.
paras.en: Christ has borne witness to many great things about Himself: namely, that the Father judges no man, but the Son judges all; that He gives life to whom He will; and that He will raise up all who are laid in the tombs. So that He may not seem to speak idly, or to take away from the Father, or to judge with respect of persons and some disordered affection, He refers all His good to God the Father, as to the fountain from which it flows and which does not flow from another, and says that He does all things as He has received from the Father, whose glory He seeks in all things and whose honour He furthers.

paras.t: Itaque ait: Non possum ego a me ipso facere quidquam. Hoc est quod jam in isto capitulo paulo ante locutus est: Non potest Filius a se facere quidquam. Et quod nunc adjicit, Sed sicut audio, judico, aliud nihil est quam quod ibi subjecit, Nisi quod viderit Patrem facientem. Quæ verba jam ante satis prolixe tractata sunt, et nunc breviter perstringam. Non possum a me ipso facere quidquam, id est, nil valeo virtute non accepta, secundum quod est in me: quia quum sim a Patre, non habeo potestatem nisi ab eo, ideo nihil possum nisi virtute communicata a Patre. Sed sicut audio, judico, id est, secundum sapientiam infallibilem mihi a Patre per generationem æternam collatam, in judicando procedo, idcirco errare non valeo. Unde subjungitur: et judicium meum justum est. Justus enim Dominus, et justitias dilexit; æquitatem vidit vultus ejus. Itaque Filio Dei, secundum naturam divinam, idem est videre opera Patris, et audire a Patre. Per hoc enim quod Pater generando transfundit in Filium totam sapientiam suam, Filius videt Patrem et opera ejus; audireque dicitur a Deo Patre, quum tamen totum sit ibi supersimplicissimo et superineffabili modo.
paras.en: So He says: [[5:30|I cannot of myself do any thing|Non possum ego a me ipso facere quidquam]]. This is what He said a little before in this chapter: [[5:19|the Son cannot do any thing of himself|Non potest Filius a se facere quidquam]]. And what He now adds, [[5:30|As I hear, so I judge|Sed sicut audio, judico]], is nothing else than what He added there, [[5:19|but what he seeth the Father doing|Nisi quod viderit Patrem facientem]]. These words have been treated at some length already, and I shall now touch on them briefly. *I cannot of myself do any thing*, that is, I can do nothing by a power not received, as far as lies in Me: since I am from the Father, I have no power except from Him, and so I can do nothing except by power communicated by the Father. *As I hear, so I judge*: that is, I proceed in judging according to the unerring wisdom given Me by the Father through eternal generation, and so I cannot go astray. Hence it is added: [[5:30|And my judgment is just|et judicium meum justum est]]. [[Ps 10:8|For the Lord is just, and hath loved justice: his countenance hath beheld righteousness|Justus enim Dominus, et justitias dilexit; æquitatem vidit vultus ejus]]. So for the Son of God, according to the divine nature, to see the works of the Father and to hear from the Father are the same. For because the Father, by begetting, pours His whole wisdom into the Son, the Son sees the Father and His works; and He is said to hear from God the Father, though all is there in a most utterly simple and more than unspeakable way.

paras.t: Possunt quoque ista magis proprie, quamvis non magis litteraliter, exponi de Filio secundum naturam assumptam. Sic enim palam est, quod non potest facere quidquam a se ipso, sicut nec ceteri homines. Sola equidem gratia differt humanitas Christi ab aliis, secundum quod dicit Augustinus: Tolle gratiam, quid est ille homo, nisi quod tu? Sicque judicat per exsecutionem, sicut audivit, id est, sicut per scientiam infusam interiori auditu divinitus didicit.
paras.en: These words can also be expounded more properly, though not more literally, of the Son according to the nature He assumed. For so it is plain that He can do nothing of Himself, any more than other men. For the humanity of Christ differs from others by grace alone, as Augustine says: “Take away grace, and what is that man but what you are?” And so He judges, as the one who carries out judgment, *as He has heard*, that is, as He has learned from God by inward hearing through infused knowledge.

paras.t: Ait ergo: Judicium meum justum est, quoniam do unicuique sicut meretur, quia non quæro voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem ejus qui misit me. Nonne juxta præinducta, Patris et Filii est una voluntas? Quomodo ergo Filius quærit voluntatem Patris, non suam? Et respondendum, quod sicut in Christo est duplex natura, puta divina et humana, sic voluntas duplex in eo consistit. Quod ergo nunc asserit de voluntate sua, intelligendum est de voluntate sua humana. Et quia humana natura constat ex intellectivo ac sensitivo, seu anima rationali et parte sensitiva, propterea ponitur duplex voluntas hominis: Una superior, utpote appetitus intellectivus, qui proprie appellatur voluntas: et de hac intelligi potest, quod Filius non quærit voluntatem suam, quoniam istam voluntatem immobiliter a principio suæ creationis subjecit voluntati divinæ, et quoniam ordinavit eam omnemque actum ejus, ad voluntatem divinam et ejus honorem sicut ad ultimum finem. Alia est voluntas hominis inferior, quæ dicitur appetitus naturalis et sensitivus, quo Christus abhorruit mortem: de qua voluntate accipi solet quod ait in passione, Non mea voluntas fiat, sed tua. Et de ista magis proprie accipi potest quod dictum est: Non quæro voluntatem meam, id est aliquid privati amoris et ad se reflexæ affectionis, sed voluntatem Patris, id est ea quæ placita ei sunt. Unde Apostolus dicit, quod Christus non placuit sibi, id est, in sui ipsius complacentia non quievit, secundum quod homo, nec quæsivit beneplacitum suæ voluntatis humanæ, in quantum humanæ, sed ut Deo subjectæ et in omnibus ei conformatæ: quod non est aliud nisi quærere voluntatem Dei. Imo, sic et nos quærere et implere possumus propriam voluntatem, non in quantum est nostra, et ad se conversa, sed ut est divina caritate et lege evangelica informata. Neque enim opus est meritorium nisi fuerit voluntarium, et quanto opus bonum fit promptiori voluntate, tanto est Deo acceptius et præmii amplioris, eo quod Deus respiciat affectum potius quam effectum.
paras.en: He says, then: [[5:30|my judgment is just|Judicium meum justum est]], since I give to every one as he deserves[[Jer 17:10||]], [[5:30|because I seek not my own will. but the will of him that sent me|quia non quæro voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem ejus qui misit me]]. But, by what was said before, are not the Father and the Son one will? How then does the Son seek the Father's will and not His own? The answer is that as there is a twofold nature in Christ, namely divine and human, so there is a twofold will in Him. What He now says of His will, then, is to be understood of His human will. And since human nature is made up of the intellective and the sensitive, or of the rational soul and the sensitive part, a twofold will is placed in man. One is the higher, namely the intellective appetite, which is properly called the will; and of this it can be understood that the Son does not seek His own will, since from the beginning of its creation He subjected this will unchangeably to the divine will, and ordered it and its every act to the divine will and honour as to its last end. The other is man's lower will, called the natural and sensitive appetite, by which Christ shrank from death[[Matt 26:39||]]: and of this will is usually taken what He said in the Passion, [[Luke 22:42|not my will, but thine be done|Non mea voluntas fiat, sed tua]]. And of this can more properly be taken what is said here, *I seek not my own will*, that is, anything of private love and of affection turned back upon itself, *but the will of the Father*, that is, the things that please Him. Hence the Apostle says that [[Rom 15:3|Christ did not please himself|Christus non placuit sibi]]: that is, as man He did not rest in pleasing Himself, nor seek the good pleasure of His human will as human, but as subject to God and conformed to Him in all things; which is nothing else than to seek the will of God. Indeed, in this way we too can seek and fulfil our own will: not as it is ours and turned back on itself, but as it is formed by divine charity and the Gospel law. For no work is meritorious unless it is willing; and the readier the will with which a good work is done, the more acceptable it is to God and the greater its reward, since God looks at the affection rather than the effect.

paras.t: Si ego testimonium perhibeo de me ipso, testimonium meum non est verum. Infra ait Salvator, quum sibi dixissent Judæi, Tu de te ipso testimonium perhibes, testimonium tuum non est verum: Et si ego testimonium perhibeo de me ipso, testimonium meum verum est. Quomodo ergo nunc ait, Si ego testimonium perhibeo de me ipso, testimonium meum non est verum? Et nonne ipse est veritas, quæ nec fallit nec fallitur? Secundum assumptam quoque humanitatem confirmatus fuit in bono, ita quod mentiri non potuit, nec peccare. Denique tempore passionis perhibuit de se ipso testimonium coram Caipha et Pilato, quum dixit: Amodo videbitis Filium hominis venientem in nubibus cæli; itemque, Ego in hoc natus sum, et ad hoc veni in mundum, ut testimonium perhibeam veritati.
paras.en: [[5:31|If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true|Si ego testimonium perhibeo de me ipso, testimonium meum non est verum]]. Further on, when the Jews had said to Him, [[John 8:13|Thou givest testimony of thyself. Thy testimony is not true|Tu de te ipso testimonium perhibes, testimonium tuum non est verum]], the Saviour says: [[John 8:14|Although I give testimony of myself, my testimony is true|Et si ego testimonium perhibeo de me ipso, testimonium meum verum est]]. How then does He now say, *If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true*? And is He not the Truth[[John 14:6||]], which neither deceives nor is deceived? According to the humanity He assumed, too, He was confirmed in good, so that He could neither lie nor sin. And in the time of the Passion He bore witness to Himself before Caiphas and Pilate, when He said: [[Matt 26:64|hereafter you shall see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of the power of God and coming in the clouds of heaven|Amodo videbitis Filium hominis venientem in nubibus cæli]]; and again, [[John 18:37|For this was I born, and for this came I into the world; that I should give testimony to the truth|Ego in hoc natus sum, et ad hoc veni in mundum, ut testimonium perhibeam veritati]].

paras.t: Ad hoc quidam respondent, quod Christus dixit interdum testimonium suum de se ipso non esse verum, ad ostendendum assumptæ carnis humanitatem; interdum vero dixit illud esse verum, ad insinuandum sui cum Patre æqualitatem: ita quod testimonium Christi de se ipso fuit verum, et non verum, verum quidem secundum divinitatem, sed nondum verum secundum humanitatem. Quomodo autem hoc stare possit, non video, nisi intelligatur quod testimonium Christi de se ipso secundum humanitatem prolatum non est verum, loquendo de humanitate ejus seorsum, seclusa de divinitate et gratia. Sic enim fortasse, potuisset esse erroneum atque inefficax. Facilior ergo et aptior videtur esse expositio Chrysostomi sic exponentis: Si ego testimonium perhibeo de me ipso, testimonium meum non est verum, secundum vestram æstimationem, quamvis secundum exsistentiam sit verissimum ac sufficientissimum.
paras.en: To this some answer that Christ sometimes said that His testimony of Himself was not true, to show the humanity of the flesh He had taken, and sometimes said it was true, to hint at His equality with the Father: so that Christ's testimony of Himself was true and not true, true according to the Godhead, but not yet true according to the humanity. But how this can stand I do not see, unless it is understood that Christ's testimony of Himself given according to the humanity is not true when we speak of His humanity apart, with the Godhead and grace set aside; for so perhaps it could have been mistaken and without force. Easier and more fitting, then, seems the exposition of Chrysostom, who expounds thus: *If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true*, in your estimation, though in reality it is most true and most sufficient.

paras.t: Alius est qui testimonium perhibet de me, et scio quia verum est testimonium quod perhibet de me. Per hunc alium, intelligi potest Pater, qui in baptismo testatus est, Hic est Filius meus dilectus; qui etiam per miracula Christi in nomine Patris facta, testimonium præstitit Filio. De testimonio etenim Patris scriptum est in epistola Petri: Accepit a Deo Patre honorem et gloriam, voce ad eum delapsa a magnifica gloria: Hic est Filius meus dilectus in quo mihi complacui; ipsum audite. Sed et Spiritus Sanctus testimonium Christo perhibuit, juxta illud Joannis: Spiritus est qui testificatur quoniam Christus est veritas. Potest quoque per hunc alium intelligi Joannes Baptista, qui fuit verus testis Christi, secundum quod pater ejus Zacharias plenus Spiritu Sancto prædixit: Tu, puer, Propheta Altissimi vocaberis, etc. De cujus testimoniis Christo exhibitis, jam multa præclara, pulcherrima atque sublimia dicta sunt primo tertioque capitulis.
paras.en: [[5:32|There is another that beareth witness of me: and I know that the witness which he witnesseth of me is true|Alius est qui testimonium perhibet de me, et scio quia verum est testimonium quod perhibet de me]]. By this other can be understood the Father, who at the baptism testified, [[Matt 3:17|This is my beloved Son|Hic est Filius meus dilectus]], and who also gave testimony to the Son through the miracles of Christ done in the Father's name. For of the Father's testimony it is written in the epistle of Peter: [[2 Pet 1:17|he received from God the Father honour and glory, this voice coming down to him from the excellent glory: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Hear ye him|Accepit a Deo Patre honorem et gloriam, voce ad eum delapsa a magnifica gloria: Hic est Filius meus dilectus in quo mihi complacui; ipsum audite]]. The Holy Ghost too bore witness to Christ, according to that word of John: [[1 John 5:6|it is the Spirit which testifieth that Christ is the truth|Spiritus est qui testificatur quoniam Christus est veritas]]. By this other can also be understood John the Baptist, who was a true witness of Christ, as his father Zachary, filled with the Holy Ghost, foretold: [[Luke 1:76|And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest|Tu, puer, Propheta Altissimi vocaberis]], etc. Of the testimonies he gave to Christ many excellent, most beautiful and lofty things have already been said in the first and third chapters[[John 1:26||]][[John 3:27||]].

paras.t: Vos misistis ad Joannem Baptistam sacerdotes et Levitas, ut interrogarent an esset Christus; et testimonium perhibuit veritati, videlicet mihi, qui sum via, veritas et vita, dicens: Non sum ego Christus; et, Medius vestrum stetit, cujus ego non sum dignus ut solvam corrigiam calceamenti ejus: ut dictum est. Vel, Testimonium perhibuit veritati, id est ei quod verum fuit; vel veritati proportionali, videlicet, se esse vocem clamantis in deserto, et Christi præconem, me vero esse Christum, in Spiritu Sancto baptizantem. Ego autem ab homine testimonium non accipio, id est, testimonium humanum non requiro, quasi indigens illo, vel ut ex hoc mihi aliquid accrescat, majorisque auctoritatis exsistam quantum ad me, sicut homo indiget testimonio Dei. Sed hæc dico, videlicet, quod Deus Pater et Joannes mihi testimonium præbuerunt, ut vos salvi sitis, credendo in me per testificationem illorum. Non enim ob suam indigentiam vel profectum, sed propter nostram salutem, voluit Christus testes habere, ut sic crederemus in eum.
paras.en: [[5:33|You sent to John|Vos misistis ad Joannem]] the Baptist priests and Levites, to ask whether he was the Christ; [[5:33|and he gave testimony to the truth|et testimonium perhibuit veritati]], that is, to Me, who am [[John 14:6|the way, and the truth, and the life|via, veritas et vita]], saying: [[John 1:20|I am not the Christ|Non sum ego Christus]]; and, [[John 1:26|there hath stood one in the midst of you|Medius vestrum stetit]], [[John 1:27|the latchet of whose shoe I am not worthy to loose|cujus ego non sum dignus ut solvam corrigiam calceamenti ejus]], as has been said. Or, *he gave testimony to the truth*, that is, to what was true; or to the truth in proportion, namely that he was [[John 1:23|the voice of one crying in the wilderness|vocem clamantis in deserto]] and Christ's herald, and that I am the Christ, baptizing in the Holy Ghost[[John 1:33||]]. [[5:34|But I receive not testimony from man|Ego autem ab homine testimonium non accipio]], that is, I do not require human testimony as though I needed it, or so that something might be added to Me by it and I might be of greater authority in Myself, as man needs the testimony of God. [[5:34|but I say these things|Sed hæc dico]], namely that God the Father and John have given testimony to Me, [[5:34|that you may be saved|ut vos salvi sitis]], by believing in Me through their witness. For Christ willed to have witnesses not for His own need or profit, but for our salvation, that so we might believe in Him.

paras.t: Insuper Christus ostendit quod testimonium Joannis fuit idoneum, propter ipsius magnam perfectionem. Ille erat, per similitudinem quamdam, lucerna ardens et lucens. Primo enim fuit similis lucernæ, quoniam sicut lucerna non est essentialiter lux, nec lucet per se, sed per lumen constitutum in ea, sic Joannes non erat lux per essentiam, nec splendebat ex se, sed ex participatione lucis divinæ, videlicet per gratiam Christi sibi infusam, quæ fulsit per corpus Joannis in verbo et opere, sicut lumen lucernæ fulget per cornua ejus. Et sicut lucerna cum lumine suo obfuscatur superveniente luce diei, sic Christo verbis atque miraculis radiante, cœpit obfuscari Joannes, secundum quod ipse prædixit: Illum oportet crescere, me autem minui. Fuit quoque Joannes lucerna ardens igne divini amoris, ex quo congratulatus est excellentiæ Christi, sicut ait: Amicus sponsi qui stat et audit eum, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi. Arsit etiam Joannes zelo justitiæ, quo increpavit Herodem, et flamma dilectionis proximorum. Habuitque verba vehementer ignita, dicendo: Genimina viperarum, quis ostendit vobis fugere a ventura ira? facite ergo dignos fructus pœnitentiæ. Fuit insuper lucens radiis sapientiæ, exemplari et optima conversatione prædicationeque splendida.
paras.en: Moreover, Christ shows that John's testimony was fitting because of his great perfection. [[5:35|He was a burning and a shining light|Ille erat lucerna ardens et lucens]] [*lucerna*, a lamp], by a certain likeness.
