paras.en: [[6:13|They gathered up therefore|Collegerunt ergo]], the Apostles chiefly, [[6:13|and filled twelve baskets with the fragments|et impleverunt duodecim cophinos fragmentorum]], namely each Apostle his own basket, if indeed the Apostles alone gathered: which does not appear, since because of the multitude of those eating they would have been long busied in going round and gathering. But did not Christ, the uncreated Wisdom of God, [[Wis 8:1|She reacheth, therefore, from end to end|attingens a fine usque ad finem]], and appointing all things [[Wis 11:21|in measure, and number, and weight|in numero, mensura ac pondere]], ordain not without a deep mystery that twelve baskets of fragments should remain, according to the twelvefold number of the Apostles? Why then did it so happen? Certainly not by chance, but by his governing, by whose working the multiplication just recalled was done. For it is plain that by bread is signified saving doctrine, to the taste of which Wisdom invites, saying: [[Prov 9:5|Come, eat my bread|Venite, comedite panem meum]]. By the fragments are signified imperfect sharings of that perfect doctrine. And perfect doctrine belongs to Christ. The Apostles, by sharing in Christ's doctrine, gathered as it were fragments and parts of the perfect doctrine from the fountain of wisdom. The vessels or baskets of these fragments were the hearts of the Apostles, in which they carried the fragments of Christ's wisdom through the whole world, scattered them and shared them. Hence, to prefigure so great a mystery, twelve baskets of fragments were filled, according to the number of the most blessed Apostles.

paras.t: Collegerunt ergo tantas reliquias, ex quinque panibus hordeaceis, id est ex panibus in quos multiplicati fuerunt quinque panes prædicti, qui erant quasi semina omnium panum antepositorum edentibus. Quinque etenim panes non habuerunt immediate tanta fragmenta. Apud Marcum adjungitur: Et de piscibus. Ex quo perpenditur quod etiam ex duobus piscibus tanti cibi piscium processerunt, quod discipuli Christi congregaverunt reliquias inde, quamvis non fiat plena narratio de hoc.
paras.en: They gathered so great remains, then, [[6:13|of the five barley loaves|ex quinque panibus hordeaceis]], that is, from the loaves into which the five loaves aforesaid were multiplied, which were as it were the seeds of all the loaves set before those eating. For five loaves would not of themselves have held so many fragments. In Mark there is added: [[Mark 6:43|and of the fishes|Et de piscibus]]. From which it is gathered that from the two fishes too there came so great a quantity of fish that Christ's disciples gathered the remains of it, though no full account is given of this.

paras.t: Sed quid biberunt hæ turbæ? Certum videtur quod si non habuerunt aliunde potum, Christus dedit cibariis istis virtutem agendi quod efficit potus, ita quod sitim perpessi non sunt. Opera nempe Christi summi opificis, perfecta fuerunt: quos ergo refecit, perfecte refecit.
paras.en: But what did these crowds drink? It seems certain that, if they had no drink from elsewhere, Christ gave these foods the power of doing what drink does, so that they did not suffer thirst. For the works of Christ, the supreme craftsman, [[Deut 32:4|The works of God are perfect|Opera nempe Christi summi opificis, perfecta]] [Denis: “the works of Christ … were perfect”]: those, then, whom he refreshed, he refreshed perfectly.

paras.t: Illi ergo homines, quum vidissent, imo et manducando experti fuissent, quod Jesus fecerat signum, dicebant: Quia hic tanti miraculi factor, est vere Propheta, non qualiseumque, sed qui venturus est, id est, venturus esse prænuntiatus est per alios Prophetas, in mundum hunc inferiorem, ad salvandum eum, id est ad homines redimendos. Non ergo solum confessi sunt Jesum esse prophetam, sed veraciter esse summum illum Prophetam de cujus adventu alii cecinerunt: de quo et Moyses dixit, Prophetam suscitabit vobis Dominus.
paras.en: [[6:14|Now those men, when they had seen|Illi ergo homines, quum vidissent]], nay, had experienced by eating, [[6:14|what a miracle Jesus had done, said|quod Jesus fecerat signum, dicebant]]: [[6:14|This is of a truth the prophet|Quia hic est vere propheta]], the doer of so great a miracle, not any prophet whatever, but [[6:14|that is to come|qui venturus est]], that is, who was foretold by the other Prophets as to come, [[6:14|into the world|in mundum]], this lower world, to save it, that is, to redeem men. So they confessed not only that Jesus was a prophet, but that he was truly that supreme Prophet of whose coming the others sang: of whom Moses too said, [[Acts 3:22|A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you|Prophetam suscitabit vobis Dominus]][[Deut 18:15||]].

paras.t: Quæritur, an Christus fuit propheta. Videtur quod non, quia ut homo, erat præ universis electis excellentissimus comprehensor: comprehensoribus autem seu Beatis in patria, non convenit ratio prophetiæ, propter perfectionem eorum. Prophetia enim, ut Thomas et multi secum testantur, imperfectionem notitiæ comprehendit. Et respondendum, quod Christus fuit vere et verus propheta, quia secundum aliquid fuit viator et hominum conversator, prædicens eis cum quibus conversabatur, futura contingentia atque præsentia eis ignota. Propheta enim dicitur quasi procul videns, id est, ea agnoscens atque annuntians his inter quos habet vitam communem, quæ procul sunt ab aliorum notitia, puta futura, vel præsentia qua in absentia horum quibus loquitur fiunt: ut si quis in episcopatu Leodiensi consistens, dicat illic præsentibus quæ fiunt in Asia, Domino revelante. Quamvis autem Deus et Beati talia sciant atque denuntient, non tamen prophete dicendi sunt, quoniam eum hominibus communem non habent conversationem. Quamvis vero intellectualis cognitio Christi fuit perfecta, non proprie prophetalis, tamen secundum notitiam imaginativæ potentia, habuit convenientiam cum Prophetis, quia in imaginatione animæ Christi formari poterant formæ sensibiles, per quas occulta atque futura representabantur animæ suæ, ut viatriei, secundum partem suam inferiorem.
paras.en: It is asked whether Christ was a prophet. It seems not: since as man he was, beyond all the elect, the most excellent of those who have attained [*comprehensor*, one who enjoys the vision of God]; and the nature of prophecy does not belong to those who have attained, or the Blessed in the fatherland, because of their perfection. For prophecy, as Thomas and many with him testify, includes imperfection of knowledge. The answer is that Christ was truly and a true prophet, since in a certain respect he was a wayfarer [*viator*, one still on the way to the fatherland] and dwelt among men, foretelling to those with whom he lived future contingent things, and present things unknown to them. For a prophet is so called as one seeing far off, that is, knowing and announcing to those among whom he has his common life things that are far from the knowledge of others, namely things future, or things present that happen in the absence of those to whom he speaks: as if someone living in the diocese of Liège should tell those present there what is happening in Asia, by the Lord's revealing. And though God and the Blessed know and announce such things, yet they are not to be called prophets, since they have no common life with men. And though Christ's intellectual knowledge was perfect, not properly prophetic, yet as to the knowledge of the imaginative power he had something in common with the Prophets, since in the imagination of Christ's soul sensible forms could be formed by which hidden and future things were represented to his soul, as a wayfarer's, according to its lower part.

paras.t: Postremo, de moralitate hujus evangelicæ lectionis tanta ab expositoribus dicta sunt, ut non videatur opus aliquid addere, nec illa repetere. Sed quoniam Scriptura est velut infinita abyssus atque inexhaustibile pelagus, ita quod de ejus expositione, præsertim morali, tanta dici non possint quin in infinitum plura dici prævaleant, nunc aliquid moralitatis tangendum est.
paras.en: Lastly, so much has been said by the expositors on the moral sense of this gospel reading that there seems no need to add anything, nor to repeat it. But since Scripture is like a boundless abyss and an inexhaustible sea, so that so much cannot be said of its exposition, above all the moral one, that more cannot be said without end, something of the moral sense is now to be touched on.

paras.t: In primis ergo, quod Jesus facto ac […] abiit trans mare Galilææ, hoc figuraliter signat, quod Judæis in sua pravitate atque perfidia obstinatis, transiit Jesus ad gentes, illas per Apostolorum prædicationem vocando ad fidem. Per locum enim […] desertum quem Jesus ingressus est per mare, significatur gentilitas, olim a Deo relicta, sterilis et vitiosa. De qua Isaias prædixit: Lætabitur deserta et invia; et rursus, Multi filii desertæ magis quam ejus quæ habet virum. Porro, per mare figuratur abundantia persecutionum atque amaritudo passionis Christi. Unde ait in Psalmo: Omnes fluctus tuos induxisti super me; itemque, Salvum me fac, Deus, quoniam intraverunt aquæ usque ad animam meam. Per mare ergo, hoc est per passionem, Christus transivit ad gentes: et convenienter per mare Galilææ, quæ interpretatur transmigratio, quia per passionem migravit a Synagoga, desponsando sibi Ecclesiam ex gentilitate conversam. Nam ante passionem jussit Christus Apostolis: In viam gentium ne abieritis; sed ite ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel. Ad has quippe et ipse primo ac specialiter missus fuit, secundum quod profitetur: Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel. Post passionem autem mandavit discipulis: Euntes in mundum universum, prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ; et, Docete omnes gentes.
paras.en: First, then, that Jesus in deed and […] [a line of the scan is unreadable here] [[6:1|went over the sea of Galilee|abiit trans mare Galilææ]] signifies figuratively that, the Jews being obstinate in their wickedness and unbelief, Jesus passed over to the Gentiles, calling them to the faith by the preaching of the Apostles. For by the place […] desert, which Jesus entered by way of the sea[[Mark 6:32||]], is signified the Gentile world, once forsaken by God, barren and full of vice. Of which Isaias foretold: [[Is 35:1|The land that was desolate and impassable shall be glad|Lætabitur deserta et invia]]; and again, [[Is 54:1|many are the children of the desolate, more than of her that hath a husband|Multi filii desertæ magis quam ejus quæ habet virum]]. Further, by the sea is figured the abundance of persecutions and the bitterness of Christ's passion. Hence he says in the Psalm: [[Ps 87:8|all thy waves thou hast brought in upon me|Omnes fluctus tuos induxisti super me]]; and again, [[Ps 68:2|Save me, O God: for the waters are come in even unto my soul|Salvum me fac, Deus, quoniam intraverunt aquæ usque ad animam meam]]. By the sea, then, that is, by the passion, Christ passed over to the Gentiles: and fittingly by the sea of Galilee, which is interpreted *transmigration*, since by the passion he migrated from the Synagogue, espousing to himself the Church converted from among the Gentiles. For before the passion Christ commanded the Apostles: [[Matt 10:5|Go ye not into the way of the Gentiles|In viam gentium ne abieritis]]; [[Matt 10:6|But go ye rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel|sed ite ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel]]. For to these he himself was first and specially sent, according to what he professes: [[Matt 15:24|I was not sent but to the sheep, that are lost of the house of Israel|Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel]]. But after the passion he commanded the disciples: [[Mark 16:15|Go ye into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature|Euntes in mundum universum, prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ]]; and, [[Matt 28:19|teach ye all nations|Docete omnes gentes]].

paras.t: Quum itaque Jesus hoc modo ad gentes processisset, secuta est eum maxima multitudo, quia innumerabiles gentes ad fidem conversæ sunt, Christi vestigia imitantes, atque per fidem, dilectionem et opera bona, post ipsum euntes, tendendo de via ad patriam, de exsilio ad paradisum, de terra ad cœlum: et hoc, quia viderunt signa quæ fecit Dominus Jesus per suos Apostolos ceterosque discipulos, in his qui infirmabantur, quos spiritualiter corporaliterque curavit. Innumerabilia namque miracula fecerunt prædicatores Christi inter gentes. Nam et per […] contactum sudariorum Pauli, sanabantur […] per superpositionem baculi Petri ac vestium evangelistæ Joannis, suscitabantur defuncti. Propter quod dicitur in Marco: Illi profecti prædicaverunt ubique, Domino cooperante, et sermonem confirmante sequentibus signis.
paras.en: When Jesus had thus gone forth to the Gentiles, [[6:2|a great multitude followed him|secuta est eum maxima multitudo]], since countless nations were converted to the faith, imitating Christ's footsteps, and going after him by faith, love and good works, making their way from the road to the fatherland, from exile to paradise, from earth to heaven: and this [[6:2|because they saw the miracles which he did on them that were diseased|quia videbant signa quæ faciebat super his qui infirmabantur]], the Lord Jesus, through his Apostles and his other disciples, whom he cured spiritually and bodily. For the preachers of Christ worked countless miracles among the Gentiles. For by […] the touch of Paul's handkerchiefs the sick were healed[[Acts 19:12||]] […] by the laying on of Peter's staff and of the garments of John the Evangelist the dead were raised. For this reason it is said in Mark: [[Mark 16:20|But they going forth preached every where: the Lord working withal, and confirming the word with signs that followed|Illi profecti prædicaverunt ubique, Domino cooperante, et sermonem confirmante sequentibus signis]] [the lower part of the page (PDF 396) is badly damaged in the scan's text; “[…]” marks lines that could not be read].

paras.t: Subiit ergo in montem Jesus: hoc est, in die ascensionis, dato Apostolis præcepto prædicandi gentibus, Eritis (inquiens) mihi testes usque ad ultimum terræ, tunc ascendit super omnes cælos, quemadmodum in Actibus plenius edocetur. Et Psalmista predixit: Ascendisti in altum, cepisti captivitatem; et, Psallite Domino qui ascendit super eclum coli ad orientem. summo etenim cœlo egressio ejus, et occursus ejus usque ad summum ejus. Et ibi sedebat ad dexteram Patris, cum discipulis suis, id est universis beatis angelis animabusque glorificatis. Omnes namque cives regni cœlestis, tam angeli quam anima gloriose, purgantur, illuminantur, et perficiuntur a Christo, etiam secundum naturam assumptam, secundum divinum Dionysium: merito ergo nuncupantur discipuli ejus.
paras.en: [[6:3|Jesus therefore went up into a mountain|Subiit ergo in montem Jesus]]: that is, on the day of the ascension, having given the Apostles the command to preach to the Gentiles, saying [[Acts 1:8|you shall be witnesses unto me in Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and Samaria, and even to the uttermost part of the earth|Eritis … mihi testes … usque ad ultimum terræ]], he then went up above all the heavens, as is taught more fully in the Acts[[Acts 1:9||]]. And the Psalmist foretold: [[Ps 67:19|Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive|Ascendisti in altum, cepisti captivitatem]]; and, [[Ps 67:34|Who mounteth above the heaven of heavens, to the east|qui ascendit super cœlum cœli ad orientem]] [Denis: “Sing ye to the Lord, who mounteth …”]. [[Ps 18:7|His going out is from the end of heaven, And his circuit even to the end thereof|a summo cælo egressio ejus. Et occursus ejus usque ad summum ejus]]. [[6:3|And there he sat with his disciples|et ibi sedebat cum discipulis suis]], at the right hand of the Father, that is, with all the blessed angels and glorified souls. For all the citizens of the heavenly kingdom, angels as well as glorious souls, are purged, enlightened and perfected by Christ, even according to the nature he assumed, according to the divine Dionysius: rightly, then, are they called his disciples.

paras.t: Tunc denique sublevavit Jesus oculos suæ inexcogitabilis pietatis, et vidit quia multitudo maxima venit ad eum: quia in omnibus finibus terræ, innumerabiles gentes convertebantur ad ipsum. Unde et Paulus in epistola ad Colossenses, testatur Evangelium suo tempore esse prædicatum in omni creatura quæ sub cœlo est.
paras.en: Then at last [[6:5|Jesus therefore had lifted up his eyes|sublevavit Jesus oculos]], the eyes of his unthinkable kindness, [[6:5|and seen that a very great multitude cometh to him|et vidit quia multitudo maxima venit ad eum]]: since in all the ends of the earth countless nations were being converted to him. Hence Paul too, in the epistle to the Colossians, testifies that in his time the Gospel [[Col 1:23|is preached in all the creation that is under heaven|prædicatum in omni creatura quæ sub cœlo est]].

paras.t: Quumque vidisset eos spirituali alimonia indigentes, et justitiam esurientes, dedit atque proposuit eis quinque panes, animam viatricem dulciter atque fortissime reficientes. — Primus panis, est ipsa superbenedicta Divinitas, qua sicut comprehensores alit per speciem, reficitque indesinenter per sui ipsius suavissimam fruitionem, sic alit viatores per fidem, et roborat per contemplationem ac futurorum gaudiorum piissimam prælibationem. — Secundus panis, est corpus Salvatoris sub speciebus sacramentalibus tectum, panis vivus, verusque cibus, de quo infra plenissimus erit sermo: de quo ait Apostolus, Panis quem sumimus, nonne communicatio corporis Domini est? Hunc itaque panem, qui est viaticum nostrum, Christiani tanto ardentius cupsunt, quanto devotiores ac sanctiores exstiterunt. — Tertius panis, est divina Scriptura canonica utriusque Testamenti. De quo in Ecclesiastico legitur: Cibabit illum pane vitæ et intellectus; et alio loco, Sapientiam omnium antiquorum exquiret sapiens, et in Prophetis vacabit. Hic panis adeo dulcis est, ut hominem studiosum faciat omnem corporalem cibum atque carnales delicias fastidire ac aspernari. Quamobrem dicit Hieronymus: Ama studia Scripturarum, et ventris delicias non amabis. Et Apostolus: Quæcumque (inquit) scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, ut per patientiam et consolationem Scripturarum, spem habeamus. Hine nempe in libris Machabæorum Jonathas fassus est: Nos nullo horum indigemus, habentes solatio sanctos libros qui in manibus nostris sunt.
paras.en: And when he had seen them in need of spiritual nourishment and hungering after justice, he gave and set before them five loaves, sweetly and most strongly refreshing the wayfaring soul. The first loaf is the superblessed Godhead itself, which, as it feeds those who have attained by sight and refreshes them unceasingly by the most sweet enjoyment of itself, so feeds wayfarers by faith, and strengthens them by contemplation and the most loving foretaste of the joys to come. The second loaf is the body of the Saviour hidden under the sacramental species, the living bread and true food, of which there will be the fullest discussion below[[6:32||]]: of which the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 10:16|And the bread which we break, is it not the partaking of the body of the Lord?|Panis quem sumimus, nonne communicatio corporis Domini est?]] [Denis: “The bread which we take, is it not the communion of the body of the Lord?”]. This bread, then, which is our viaticum, Christians desire the more ardently the more devout and holy they are. The third loaf is the divine canonical Scripture of both Testaments. Of which we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 15:3|With the bread of life and understanding, she shall feed him|Cibabit illum pane vitæ et intellectus]]; and in another place, [[Ecclus 39:1|The wise man will seek out the wisdom of all the ancients, and will be occupied in the prophets|Sapientiam omnium antiquorum exquiret sapiens, et in Prophetis vacabit]]. This bread is so sweet that it makes a studious man loathe and spurn all bodily food and carnal delights. Wherefore Jerome says: Love the study of the Scriptures, and you will not love the delights of the belly. And the Apostle: [[Rom 15:4|For what things soever were written were written for our learning: that, through patience and the comfort of the scriptures, we might have hope|Quæcumque … scripta sunt … spem habeamus]]. Hence in the books of the Machabees Jonathas confessed: [[1 Mach 12:9|We, though we needed none of these things having for our comfort the holy books that are in our hands|Nos nullo horum indigemus, habentes solatio sanctos libros qui in manibus nostris sunt]].

paras.t: Quartus panis, est gratia gratum faciens, cum spiritualibus bonis sibi inseparabiliter annexis, quæ sunt tres virtutes theologicæ, septem dona Spiritus Sancti, ceteræque virtutes infusæ, et fructus Spiritus: quibus anima spiritualiter impinguatur, armatur, fecundatur, invincibilisque efficitur. Unde, secundum Apostolum: Optimum est gratia stabiliri cor. Et pœnitens ait: Percussus sum ut fœnum, et aruit cor meum, quia oblitus sum comedere panem meum. Hic panis gratie in anima nostra spiritualem vitam initiat, deiformem similitudinem præstat, atque ad omne bonum facit idoneum. Ideo incessanter orare debemus Dominum pro gratiæ incremento, quia quo illa magis in mente perficitur, tanto ad omnes operationes meritorias reddimur fortiores atque proniores, ita ut laborem vix sentiamus.
paras.en: The fourth loaf is sanctifying grace, with the spiritual goods inseparably joined to it, which are the three theological virtues, the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, the other infused virtues, and the fruits of the Spirit: by which the soul is spiritually fattened, armed, made fruitful and made invincible. Hence, according to the Apostle: [[Heb 13:9|it is best that the heart be established with grace|Optimum est gratia stabiliri cor]]. And the penitent says: [[Ps 101:5|I am smitten as grass, and my heart is withered: because I forgot to eat my bread|Percussus sum ut fœnum, et aruit cor meum, quia oblitus sum comedere panem meum]]. This bread of grace begins the spiritual life in our soul, bestows a godlike likeness, and makes it fit for every good. So we ought to pray to the Lord unceasingly for the increase of grace, since the more it is perfected in the mind, the stronger and readier we are made for all meritorious works, so that we scarcely feel the labour.

paras.t: Quintus panis, est promissio futurorum bonorum, qui facit nos agiles et animo infatigabiles in cultu divino, scientes quod non sunt condignæ passiones ad mercedem nobis promissam, paratam, mox dandam. De hoc pane dicit Archiapostolus in sua Canonica: Videntes Jesum exsultabitis lætitia inenarrabili et glorificata, reportantes fructum fidei vestræ, salutem animarum vestrarum; et ipse Salvator, Fulgebunt justi sicut sol in regno Patris eorum. Joannes quoque in sua epistola: Carissimi, nunc filii Dei sumus, et nondum apparuit quid erimus; scimus quia quum apparuerit, similes ei erimus, quia videbimus eum sicuti est. Quicumque manducat hunc panem, considerando futura atque cœlestia præmia mente pervigili ac profunda, non suecumbit laboribus; non deficit in adversis, non frangitur prosperis, nec quærit laudes humanas; non pigrescit, sed viam mandatorum, non solum ambulat, sed percurrit.
paras.en: The fifth loaf is the promise of the good things to come, which makes us nimble and unwearied in mind in the worship of God, knowing that [[Rom 8:18|the sufferings of this time are not worthy|non sunt condignæ passiones]] to be compared with the reward promised us, prepared, and soon to be given. Of this bread the chief Apostle says in his Canonical Epistle: [[1 Pet 1:8|shall rejoice with joy unspeakable and glorified|exsultabitis lætitia inenarrabili et glorificata]], [[1 Pet 1:9|Receiving the end of your faith, even the salvation of your souls|reportantes fructum fidei vestræ, salutem animarum vestrarum]] [Denis: “Seeing Jesus, you shall rejoice … bearing away the fruit of your faith”]; and the Saviour himself: [[Matt 13:43|Then shall the just shine as the sun, in the kingdom of their Father|Fulgebunt justi sicut sol in regno Patris eorum]]. John too in his epistle: [[1 John 3:2|Dearly beloved, we are now the sons of God: and it hath not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he shall appear we shall be like to him: because we shall see him as he is|Carissimi, nunc filii Dei sumus, et nondum apparuit quid erimus ; scimus quia quum apparuerit, similes ei erimus, quia videbimus eum sicuti est]]. Whoever eats this bread, by considering the things to come and the heavenly rewards with a watchful and deep mind, does not sink under labours; does not fail in adversity, is not broken by prosperity, nor seeks human praise; does not grow sluggish, but not only walks in the way of the commandments, but runs it[[Ps 118:32||]].

paras.t: Preterea, predietis quinque panibus adduntur duo pisces, suavem gustum præstantes. Primus piscis, est actualis experientia divine dulcedinis, qua gustata desipit omnis caro. Ad quam hortatur Propheta: Gustate, et videte quoniam suavis est Dominus. Unde et Paulus testatur ad Corinthios: Sicut abundant passiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abundat consolatio nostra; et Psalmista, Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam. Secundus piscis, est absorptio, resolutio seu salutaris illa defectio mentis in Deo, de qua loquitur Jeremias: Factus est sermo Domini in corde meo quasi ignis exæstuans, et defeci, ferre non sustinens; itemque Psalmographus, Defecit caro mea et cor meum, Deus cordis mei et pars mea Deus in æternum; Sponsa quoque in Canticis, Anima mea liquefacta est ut dilectus locutus est. Hunc piscem gustamus, dum anima nostra supra se rapta, atque in divitias Creatoris expansæ ac dilatata, reverberatur, pre affectu dissolvitur, a se ipsa omnibusque creatis alienatur, et in solo Deo sensificatur.
paras.en: Besides, to these five loaves are added two fishes, giving a sweet taste. The first fish is the actual experience of the divine sweetness, which once tasted, all flesh grows insipid. To which the Prophet exhorts: [[Ps 33:9|O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet|Gustate, et videte quoniam suavis est Dominus]]. Hence Paul too testifies to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 1:5|For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us: so also by Christ doth our comfort abound|Sicut abundant passiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abundat consolatio nostra]]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 93:19|According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, thy comforts have given joy to my soul|Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam]]. The second fish is the absorption, the melting, or that saving fainting of the mind in God, of which Jeremias speaks: [[Jer 20:9|and there came in my heart as a burning fire, shut up in my bones, and I was wearied, not being able to bear it|Factus est … in corde meo quasi ignis exæstuans … ferre non sustinens]] [Denis: “The word of the Lord became in my heart as a burning fire, and I fainted, not being able to bear it”]; and again the Psalmist, [[Ps 72:26|For thee my flesh and my heart hath fainted away: thou art the God of my heart, and the God that is my portion for ever|Defecit caro mea et cor meum, Deus cordis mei et pars mea Deus in æternum]] [the margin prints Ps. lxxii, 26]; the Bride too in the Canticle, [[Cant 5:6|My soul melted when he spoke|Anima mea liquefacta est ut dilectus locutus est]]. We taste this fish when our soul, rapt above itself, and spread out and enlarged in the riches of the Creator, is beaten back, melts away for love, is estranged from itself and all created things, and has its taste in God alone.

paras.t: Dum ergo fideles his panibus ac piscibus fuerint satiati a Christo supra fœnum, hoc est in carne ista mortali, de qua Isaias effatur, Omnis caro fœnum; dicunt: Quia hic est vere Propheta, impletor et finis ac Dominus Prophetarum, qui venturus est in mundum, Ecclesiam suam usque ad finem seculin spiritualiter visitando, et in fine sæculorum visibiliter descendendo et vivos ac mortuos judicando. Ex hujuscemodi enim refectione interna, certissime noscunt, laudant, ac diligunt clementiam atque potentiam Salvatoris, quemadmodum dicit Propheta: Duo hæc audivi: quia potestas Dei est, et tibi, Domine, misericordia.
paras.en: When, then, the faithful have been filled by Christ with these loaves and fishes upon the grass, that is, in this mortal flesh, of which Isaias declares, [[Is 40:6|All flesh is grass|Omnis caro fœnum]] [the margin is read as Is. ix; the words are Is 40:6], they say: [[6:14|This is of a truth the prophet|Quia hic est vere Propheta]], the fulfiller and end and Lord of the Prophets, [[6:14|that is to come into the world|qui venturus est in mundum]], visiting his Church spiritually until the end of the world, and at the end of the ages coming down visibly and judging the living and the dead. For from this inward refreshment they know most certainly, praise and love the mercy and power of the Saviour, as the Prophet says: [[Ps 61:12|these two things have I heard, that power belongeth to God|Duo hæc audivi: quia potestas Dei est]], [[Ps 61:13|And mercy to thee, O Lord|et tibi, Domine, misericordia]].

6.title: Prosecutio explanationis hujus capituli sexti, ab eo loco quo dicitur: Jesus ergo quum cognovisset quia venturi essent ut raperent et facerent eum regem.
6.title_en: Continuation of the explanation of this sixth chapter, from the place where it is said: “Jesus therefore, when he knew that they would come to take him by force and make him king.”

paras.t: Pandit deinceps gloriosissimus Evangelista effectum præinducti miraculi quinque panum duorumque piscium, et cetera signa ac documenta Christi describit.
paras.en: The most glorious Evangelist next sets out the effect of the miracle of the five loaves and two fishes related above, and describes the other signs and teachings of Christ.

paras.t: Jesus ergo quum cognovisset, id est, se cognoscere demonstrasset. Omnia quippe ut Deus cognovit a principio æternitatis. Omnia quoque ut homo cognovit ab exordio incarnationis. Sed dicitur aliquid quasi de novo cognovisse, quando per effectum aliquem demonstravit se hoc ipsum agnoscere. Quia venturi essent illi quos tam miraculose pavit de quinque panibus piscibusque duobus, ut raperent et facerent eum regem. Cur ait, Ut raperent, quasi violentiam illaturi? Puto quod ideo, quoniam Jesum præsumebant, quem noverant humilitatem ac paupertatem docere, non debere acquiescere eis in accipiendo dominium. Propterea decreverunt eum, quamvis nolentem ac renitentem, facere regem. Vel ideo dicit, Ut raperent, quoniam cum ingenti tumultu, affectu et gaudio, voluerunt eum sibi in regem præficere. Sed quomodo hoc audebant? quum Romani, quibus erant subjecti, jam sub periculo mortis prohibuissent ne aliqua plebs assumeret sibi regem præter imperatorem, vel sine Romanorum consensu; et etiam quia Judæi isti Jesum regem facere volentes, sciebant quod principes sacerdotum, Scribæ ac Pharisæi, oderint jam Christum, et ægre acciperent quod aliqua pars Judæorum præficeret eum sibi in principem. Dicendum, quod isti viso præscripto miraculo multiplicationis panum ac piscium, confessi fuerunt Jesum esse præcipuum illum Prophetam ab aliis prænuntiatum quod esset Salvator mundi. Sicque considerabant quod esset Christus in lege promissus, et per consequens regnaturus, atque hæreditarius rex Israel: quemadmodum per Jeremiam fuit prædictum, Ecce dies veniunt, dicit Dominus, et suscitabo David germen justum, et regnabit Rex, et sapiens erit; et per Isaiam, Super solium David et super regnum ejus sedebit. Voluerunt ergo scripturas illas implere, et Jesum super se temporaliter corporaliterque regnare: errantes in hoc, quod putabant scripturas illas de temporali carnalique regno intelligendas, quasi primus adventus Messiæ promissus esset in majestate et gloria, ut dominaretur, et non potius in omnimoda abjectione, paupertate et humilitate, ut occideretur.
paras.en: [[6:15|Jesus therefore, when he knew|Jesus ergo quum cognovisset]], that is, when He had shown that He knew. For as God He knew all things from the beginning of eternity; and as man too He knew all things from the first moment of the Incarnation. But He is said to have come to know something as if anew when by some effect He showed that He knew that very thing. [[6:15|that they would come|Quia venturi essent]], those whom He had fed so miraculously with five loaves and two fishes, [[6:15|to take him by force and make him king|ut raperent et facerent eum regem]]. Why does he say *to take him by force*, as though they meant to do Him violence? I think it is because they took it for granted that Jesus, whom they knew to teach humility and poverty, would not consent to them in accepting dominion; therefore they resolved to make Him king, however unwilling and resisting He might be. Or else he says *to take him by force* because they wanted to set Him over themselves as king with a great tumult, eagerness and joy. But how did they dare this, when the Romans, to whom they were subject, had already forbidden on pain of death that any people should take to itself a king other than the emperor, or without the consent of the Romans[[John 19:12||]]; and also since these Jews who wanted to make Jesus king knew that the chief priests, the Scribes and the Pharisees already hated Christ, and would take it ill that any part of the Jews should set Him over themselves as prince? The answer is that these men, having seen the miracle described above, the multiplying of the loaves and fishes, confessed that Jesus was that chief Prophet foretold by the others, who was to be the Saviour of the world. And so they reckoned that He was the Christ promised in the law, and consequently that He would reign, and was the hereditary king of Israel, as was foretold by Jeremias: [[Jer 23:5|Behold the days come, saith the Lord, and I will raise up to David a just branch: and a king shall reign, and shall be wise|Ecce dies veniunt, dicit Dominus, et suscitabo David germen justum, et regnabit Rex, et sapiens erit]]; and by Isaias: [[Is 9:7|he shall sit upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom|Super solium David et super regnum ejus sedebit]]. They wanted, then, to fulfil those scriptures, and to have Jesus reign over them in a temporal and bodily way; erring in this, that they thought those scriptures were to be understood of a temporal and carnal kingdom, as if the first coming of the Messias had been promised in majesty and glory, that He might rule, and not rather in utter abjection, poverty and humility, that He might be slain.

paras.t: Quæritur, quum Christus etiam secundum naturam assumptam fuerit rex et sacerdos a principio incarnationis, tanquam omni creaturæ prælatus atque inter Deum et homines mediator constitutus, incipiens ex utero virgineæ Genitricis se ipsum offerre pro nobis, quomodo voluerunt eum facere regem. Dicendum, quod a principio fuit rex auctoritate ac potestate; sed voluerunt eum facere regem, quantum ad usum seu exsecutionem potestatis. Denique voluerunt eum facere regem, specialiter propter tria quæ consideraverunt in ipso, et specialiter spectant ac requiruntur ad regem: primo quia viderunt eum pium, compassivum ac liberalem, sicut in satiatione sua fuerunt experti; secundo, quia viderunt eum valde sapientem in omnibus; tertio, quia viderunt eum potentem supra naturam, sicque credebant se defendendos ab ipso. Idcirco nec Romanos, nec pontifices proprios attenderunt.
paras.en: It is asked: since Christ, even according to the nature He assumed, was king and priest from the beginning of the Incarnation, as set over every creature and appointed mediator between God and men, beginning from the womb of His virgin Mother to offer Himself for us, how was it that they wanted to make Him king? The answer is that from the beginning He was king in authority and power; but they wanted to make Him king as to the use or exercise of the power. Further, they wanted to make Him king chiefly on account of three things which they saw in Him, and which belong especially to a king and are required in one: first, because they saw that He was kind, compassionate and generous, as they had found by experience when they were filled; secondly, because they saw that He was very wise in all things; thirdly, because they saw that He was powerful above nature, and so they believed they would be defended by Him. That is why they paid no heed either to the Romans or to their own high priests.

paras.t: Fugit, id est festinanter ascendit, iterum in montem, in quem primo ascendit, ut dictum est, et a quo descendit, occurrendo turbæ quam pavit; ipse solus, ut nemo sciret ubi esset, et ut quietius oraret: non quod multitudo potuit ejus contemplationem impedire, vel solitudo juvare, sed ut nos suo informaret exemplo, videlicet, ut post occupationem, quamvis divinam, cum aliis habitam, festinemus solitarium locum expetere, illicque nos ipsos recolligere, venialia commissa abstergere, contemplationi et orationi vacare. Ascendit etenim Christus in montem orare, secundum Matthæum et Marcum.
paras.en: [[6:15|fled|Fugit]], that is, He went up in haste, [[6:15|again into the mountains|iterum in montem]], into which He had first gone up, as was said, and from which He had come down to meet the crowd which He fed; [[6:15|himself alone|ipse solus]], so that no one should know where He was, and that He might pray more quietly: not that the multitude could hinder His contemplation, or solitude help it, but to instruct us by His example: namely, that after business had with others, even though it be divine, we should make haste to seek a solitary place, and there gather ourselves together again, wipe away the venial sins we have committed, and give ourselves to contemplation and prayer. For Christ went up into the mountain to pray, according to Matthew[[Matt 14:23||]] and Mark[[Mark 6:46||]].

paras.t: Præterea, quod Christus promovendus in regem, fugit, quæsitus vero ad crucifigendum, paratum se obtulit, confundit superbiam, ambitionem, mollitiem nostram. Ipse enim idcirco hæc fecit, ut doceat nos honores prælationesque fugere, adversa autem æquanimiter sustinere. Sed, heu! pauci videntur qui non mallent præesse quam subesse, jubere quam obedire, honorari quam sperni; qui ingerunt semetipsos, non vocati a Deo tanquam Aaron. Pauci adversitatibus gaudent magis quam prosperis. In istis nondum exstinctus est amor privatus, nondum veraciter et perfecte se diligunt, nondum utuntur hoc mundo velut exsilio, hac vita ut via, præsentibus in ordine ad futura. Verumtamen scimus, teste Apostolo, quia qui sunt Christi, carnem suam crucifixerunt cum vitiis et concupiscentiis.
paras.en: Moreover, in that Christ, when He was to be raised to kingship, fled, but when He was sought to be crucified, offered Himself ready, He puts to shame our pride, our ambition, our softness. For He did these things to teach us to flee honours and prelacies, and to bear adversities with an even mind. But alas! few are seen who would not rather be over others than under them, command than obey, be honoured than despised; who thrust themselves forward, not [[Heb 5:4|called by God, as Aaron was|vocati a Deo tanquam Aaron]]. Few rejoice in adversities more than in prosperity. In these men private love [*amor privatus*: love of one's own good for oneself, apart from God and neighbour] is not yet extinguished; they do not yet love themselves truly and perfectly, do not yet use this world as an exile, this life as a road, and present things as ordered to those to come. Yet we know, on the Apostle's witness, that [[Gal 5:24|they that are Christ's have crucified their flesh, with the vices and concupiscences|qui sunt Christi, carnem suam crucifixerunt cum vitiis et concupiscentiis]].

paras.t: Ut autem sero factum est, descenderunt discipuli ejus ad mare. Hoc quod jam hic recitatur de navigatione discipulorum, in aliquibus differre videtur a navigatione quam alii Evangelistæ describunt post miraculum panum. Hic enim habetur, quod discipuli ejus descenderunt ad mare, quasi proprio motu hoc facientes. Sed apud Matthæum legitur, quod Christus jussit eos ingredi navim; et apud Marcum, quod coegit eos ad hoc. Itemque hic dicitur, quod Jesus et discipuli venerunt Capharnaum; ibi vero habetur, quod venerunt in terram Genesar, sive Genesareth. Rursusque hic dicitur, quod quum discipuli voluissent Jesum in navim accipere, statim fuit navis ad terram; ibi autem, quod introiit navim. Ob hæc dicit Chrysostomus, quod non sit eadem res gesta de qua loquuntur Matthæus et Joannes, quamvis in multis conveniat.
paras.en: [[6:16|And when evening was come, his disciples went down to the sea|Ut autem sero factum est, descenderunt discipuli ejus ad mare]]. What is told here of the disciples' voyage seems in some points to differ from the voyage which the other Evangelists describe after the miracle of the loaves. For here we have that His disciples went down to the sea as if doing so of their own accord; but in Matthew we read that Christ bade them go into the boat[[Matt 14:22||]], and in Mark that He compelled them to it[[Mark 6:45||]]. Again, here it is said that Jesus and the disciples came to Capharnaum; but there we have that they came into the land of Genesar[[Matt 14:34||]], or Genesareth[[Mark 6:53||]]. And again, here it is said that when the disciples wished to take Jesus into the ship, [[6:21|presently the ship was at the land|statim fuit navis ad terram]]; but there, that He went into the ship[[Matt 14:32||]][[Mark 6:51||]]. For these reasons Chrysostom says that the event Matthew and John speak of is not the same, though it agrees in many things.

paras.t: Augustinus vero dicit oppositum: et hoc verius puto, ut patet ex circumstantia evangelicæ narrationis. Rationes vero Chrysostomi solverentur, dicendo ad primam, quod quamvis discipuli inviti separabantur a Christo, libenter tamen secundum rationem obediebant: et ergo descenderunt ad navim secundum imperium Christi. Ad secundam dicendum, quod Genesar quandoque est nomen civitatis, et quandoque regionis in qua, vel juxta quam, est civitas Capharnaum sita: sicque veniendo Capharnaum, venerunt et Genesar, id est in illam provinciam. Vel dicendum, quod primo applicuerunt Capharnaum, postea Genesar. Ad tertiam dicendum, quod quamvis Joannes dicat navim statim fuisse ad terram, non tamen negat Jesum navim intrasse. — Secundum hanc ergo positionem exponenda est littera hæc, ut dictis Matthæi ac Marci concordet.
paras.en: Augustine, however, says the opposite, and this I think the truer, as is clear from the circumstances of the Gospel narrative. Chrysostom's reasons would be answered thus. To the first: although the disciples were parted from Christ unwillingly, yet they obeyed willingly, according to reason; and so they went down to the ship at Christ's command. To the second it must be said that Genesar is sometimes the name of a city, and sometimes of the region in which, or near which, the city of Capharnaum lies; and so in coming to Capharnaum they came also to Genesar, that is, into that province. Or it may be said that they put in first at Capharnaum, and afterwards at Genesar. To the third it must be said that although John says the ship was presently at the land, he does not deny that Jesus went into the ship. — According to this position, then, the letter here is to be expounded so as to agree with what Matthew and Mark say.

paras.t: Et quum ascendissent discipuli navim, juxta præceptum Christi, venerunt trans mare Tiberiadis præmemoratum, in Capharnaum. Hoc, secundum Bedam, dicitur per anticipationem. Unde infra recitat Evangelista ordinem facti, quomodo illuc venerunt. Et tenebræ jam factæ erant, id est principium noctis, et non venerat ad eos Jesus, videlicet ad discipulos suos in navim. Unde secundum Matthæum, vespere facto, fuit adhuc Jesus solus in monte. Et secundum Marcum, quum sero factum esset, fuit navicula in medio mari. Sic spiritualiter, dum Christus qui est lux vera non adest, tenebræ adsunt, caligo ignorantiæ et peccati, tribulatio atque tentatio.
paras.en: [[6:17|And when they had gone up into a ship|Et quum ascendissent discipuli navim]], according to Christ's command, [[6:17|they went over the sea|venerunt trans mare]] of Tiberias mentioned before, [[6:17|to Capharnaum|in Capharnaum]]. This, according to Bede, is said by anticipation; hence the Evangelist tells further on the order of events, how they came there. [[6:17|And it was now dark|Et tenebræ jam factæ erant]], that is, the beginning of the night, [[6:17|and Jesus was not come unto them|et non venerat ad eos Jesus]], that is, to His disciples in the ship. Hence according to Matthew, when evening was come, Jesus was still alone on the mountain[[Matt 14:23||]]; and according to Mark, when it was late, the boat was in the midst of the sea[[Mark 6:47||]]. So, spiritually, while Christ, who is [[John 1:9|the true light|lux vera]], is not present, darkness is present: the darkness of ignorance and of sin, tribulation and temptation.

paras.t: Mare autem, vento magno flante, et aquas agitante seu commovente, exsurgebat, intumescentibus fluctibus ejus in tantum, quod navis jactabatur in fluctibus. Pariformiter, absente auxilio atque præsentia Christi, motus vitiosi insurgunt in nobis.
paras.en: [[6:18|And the sea|Mare autem]], [[6:18|by reason of a great wind that blew|vento magno flante]] and stirring or troubling the waters, [[6:18|arose|exsurgebat]], its waves swelling so high that the ship was tossed on the waves. In like manner, when the help and presence of Christ are absent, vicious motions rise up in us.

paras.t: Quum remigassent ergo discipuli quasi stadia viginti quinque aut triginta. Causa remigationis, secundum alios Evangelistas, fuit quoniam ventus fuit eis contrarius: propterea non poterant procedere, sed nitebantur ad Christum redire. Sic viri devoti, dum tempestatibus persecutionum variisque tribulationibus agitantur, convertuntur et revertuntur ad Christum, ut ejus gratiosa præsentia consolentur, dicentes cum Psalmista: Usquequo, Domine, oblivisceris me in finem? Usquequo avertis faciem tuam a me? Unde et in Jona habetur: Quum angustiaretur in me spiritus meus, Domini recordatus sum. Stadium dicitur octava pars milliaris.
paras.en: [[6:19|When they had rowed therefore|Quum remigassent ergo]] (the disciples) [[6:19|about five and twenty or thirty furlongs|quasi stadia viginti quinque aut triginta]]. The cause of the rowing, according to the other Evangelists, was that the wind was against them[[Matt 14:24||]][[Mark 6:48||]]: so they could not go forward, but strove to get back to Christ. So devout men, when they are tossed by the storms of persecutions and by various tribulations, turn and return to Christ, that they may be comforted by His gracious presence, saying with the Psalmist: [[Ps 12:1|How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me unto the end? how long dost thou turn away thy face from me?|Usquequo, Domine, oblivisceris me in finem? Usquequo avertis faciem tuam a me?]] Hence also in Jonas we read: [[Jon 2:8|When my soul was in distress within me, I remembered the Lord|Quum angustiaretur in me spiritus meus, Domini recordatus sum]]. A furlong [*stadium*] is said to be the eighth part of a mile.

paras.t: Vident Jesum ambulantem super mare circa quartam vigiliam noctis, videlicet in ultima noctis parte, propinquante aurora. Ex quo patet quod discipuli tota pene nocte in labore et periculo erant. Ambulavit autem Jesus super mare per dotem agilitatis, secundum Hugonem. Quod communiter non tenetur; sed quod divina virtute sic incessit, gravitate sui corporis non agente in aquam eam dividendo, sicut divina virtute ignis interdum non agit suo calore in corpus humanum, ut patet in Daniele de tribus pueris, et aliis multis in novo Testamento.
paras.en: [[6:19|they see Jesus walking upon the sea|Vident Jesum ambulantem super mare]] [[Mark 6:48|about the fourth watch of the night|circa quartam vigiliam noctis]][[Matt 14:25||]], that is, in the last part of the night, as dawn drew near. From this it is plain that the disciples were in toil and danger almost the whole night. Now Jesus walked upon the sea by the dowry of agility [*dos agilitatis*: one of the gifts of the glorified body, by which it moves at once wherever the soul wills, without hindrance], according to Hugh. This is not commonly held; rather it is held that He went thus by divine power, the weight of His body not acting on the water so as to part it, just as by divine power fire sometimes does not act with its heat on a human body, as is plain in Daniel in the case of the three children[[Dan 3:50||]], and in many others in the New Testament.

paras.t: Et proximum navi fieri, id est appropinquare naviculæ. Sic utique quando in maximis tribulationibus sumus, ita ut vix de evasione speremus, si suspiramus ad Jesum, mox experimur piissimum ejus occursum, fitque proximus navi, id est Ecclesiæ adversitatibus laboranti. Propter quod dicit Apostolus: Fidelis Deus, qui non patietur vos tentari ultra id quod potestis. Unde orat Propheta: Quum deficiet virtus mea, ne derelinquas me. Inconcussibiliter ergo speremus in eo, dicentes cum sancto Job: Etiamsi occiderit me, in ipso sperabo. Imo in tribulatione Deus præcipue adest, quamvis non sentiatur, sed quasi abscondat se, adspiciens nostrum certamen. Dum ergo affligimur, impugnamur, tentamur, pensemus Deum præsentem et nostrum conflictum considerantem, sicque animemur, viriliter militantes et de subsidio Dei certissime confidentes, scientes verum esse quod ait: Cum ipso sum in tribulatione, eripiam eum, et glorificabo eum.
paras.en: [[6:19|and drawing nigh to the ship|Et proximum navi fieri]], that is, coming near the boat. So indeed, when we are in the greatest tribulations, so that we scarcely hope to escape, if we sigh to Jesus we soon experience His most loving coming to meet us, and He draws nigh to the ship, that is, to the Church labouring in adversities. Therefore the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 10:13|God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that which you are able|Fidelis Deus, qui non patietur vos tentari ultra id quod potestis]]. Hence the Prophet prays: [[Ps 70:9|when my strength shall fail, do not thou forsake me|Quum deficiet virtus mea, ne derelinquas me]]. Let us then hope in Him unshakeably, saying with holy Job: [[Job 13:15|Although he should kill me, I will trust in him|Etiamsi occiderit me, in ipso sperabo]]. Nay, in tribulation God is especially present, though He is not felt, but as it were hides Himself, watching our combat. While, then, we are afflicted, assailed, tempted, let us think of God as present and looking upon our conflict, and so take heart, fighting manfully and trusting most surely in God's help, knowing that what He says is true: [[Ps 90:15|I am with him in tribulation, I will deliver him, and I will glorify him|Cum ipso sum in tribulatione, eripiam eum, et glorificabo eum]].

paras.t: Et timuerunt, propter novitatem rei, et quia putabant esse phantasma, secundum alios Evangelistas. Timebant enim ne forte esset spiritus malignus in specie Christi, et ne læderentur aut mergerentur ab eo. Unde et præ timore exclamaverunt, Deum invocando. Ille autem dicit eis: Ego sum qui videor esse, videlicet magister quem quæritis, quem amatis, qui possum succurrere; nolite timere inordinato timore, nimis timendo propriæ pelli, et de illusione phantastica. Sed est timor divinus ac salutaris, quo timemus culpam incidere, Deum offendere, gloria spoliari. De quo ait Scriptura: Qui sine timore est, non potest justificari; et, Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus.
paras.en: [[6:19|And they were afraid|Et timuerunt]], because of the strangeness of the thing, and because they thought it was an apparition, according to the other Evangelists[[Matt 14:26||]][[Mark 6:49||]]. For they feared that it might perhaps be an evil spirit in the likeness of Christ, and that they might be harmed or sunk by it. Hence also they cried out for fear, calling upon God. [[6:20|But he saith to them|Ille autem dicit eis]]: [[6:20|It is I|Ego sum]], He who I seem to be, namely the master whom you seek, whom you love, who am able to help you; [[6:20|Be not afraid|nolite timere]] with an inordinate fear, fearing too much for your own skin, and fearing a phantom illusion. But there is a divine and wholesome fear, by which we fear to fall into sin, to offend God, to be robbed of glory. Of this the Scripture says: [[Ecclus 1:28|he that is without fear, cannot be justified|Qui sine timore est, non potest justificari]]; and: [[Prov 28:14|Blessed is the man that is always fearful|Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus]].

paras.t: Voluerunt ergo eum discipuli accipere in navim. Amor est enim virtus unitiva: ideo magistro suo carissimo cupiebant corporaliter quoque adesse.
paras.en: [[6:21|They were willing therefore to take him into the ship|Voluerunt ergo eum discipuli accipere in navim]], that is, the disciples were. For love is a unitive virtue: therefore they longed to be with their dearest master in body also.

paras.t: Quum autem dixerat Christus, Ego sum, statim post hoc, non tamen immediate, jussit tempestatem cessare. Omittit hoc loco Joannes quod alii Evangelistæ scripserunt, videlicet, quod quum Jesus dixisset, Ego sum, Petrus dixit: Domine, si tu es, jube me venire ad te super aquas. Cui respondit, Veni. Quum vero Petrus tenderet super aquas, videns ventum validum timuit; et quum mergi cœpisset, clamavit: Domine, salva me. Dixitque Jesus: Modicæ fidei, quare dubitasti? Et apprehendens manum Petri, intravit cum eo naviculam, et protinus ventus cessavit. Et statim fuit navis ad terram, id est juxta Capharnaum, ad quam ibant navigio, non pedestres. Christo enim navim ingresso, navis divina virtute, ductu forte angelico, in brevissimo et quasi imperceptibili temporis spatio, pervenit ad littus.
paras.en: Now when Christ had said, [[6:20|It is I|Ego sum]], straight after this, though not immediately, He commanded the storm to cease. John here leaves out what the other Evangelists wrote, namely that when Jesus had said, It is I, Peter said: [[Matt 14:28|Lord, if it be thou, bid me come to thee upon the waters|Domine, si tu es, jube me venire ad te super aquas]]. And He answered him: [[Matt 14:29|Come|Veni]]. But as Peter made his way over the waters, [[Matt 14:30|seeing the wind strong, he was afraid: and when he began to sink, he cried out, saying: Lord, save me|videns ventum validum timuit; et quum mergi cœpisset, clamavit: Domine, salva me]]. And Jesus said: [[Matt 14:31|O thou of little faith, why didst thou doubt?|Modicæ fidei, quare dubitasti]] And taking Peter by the hand, He went into the boat with him, and at once the wind ceased[[Matt 14:32||]]. [[6:21|And presently the ship was at the land|Et statim fuit navis ad terram]], that is, near Capharnaum, [[6:21|to which they were going|ad quam ibant]] by boat, not on foot. For when Christ had entered the boat, the boat, by divine power, perhaps under the guidance of an angel, reached the shore in a very short and as it were imperceptible space of time.

paras.t: Sic itaque fecit Christus quatuor magna miracula uno tempore: primum, quod ipse super undas incessit; secundum, quod ejus virtute Petrus similiter fecit; tertium, quod tempestatem tam subito fecit quiescere; quartum, quod navim tam repente fecit ad littus pertingere. — Sic spiritualiter dat Christus famulis suis electis virtutem ambulandi atque calcandi super aquas tribulationum præsentium, et vincendi cuncta adversa, ita ut omne gaudium existiment, quum in diversas tentationes inciderint. Quum vero Jesus ingreditur navim, hoc est Ecclesiam, seu corda fidelium, statim cum insperata celeritate, est navis ad terram optatam; quia tunc subito consolantur, et patriam contemplantur, eamque desiderio sancto introeunt, habentes conversationem in cœlis, qui paulo ante fluctuabant in imis. Estque hæc mutatio dexteræ Excelsi, qui vulnerat et medetur, et tunc, et quomodo placuerit.
paras.en: So Christ worked four great miracles at one time: first, that He Himself walked upon the waves; second, that by His power Peter did the same; third, that He made the storm grow calm so suddenly; fourth, that He made the boat reach the shore so quickly. — So, spiritually, Christ gives His chosen servants the power to walk and tread upon the waters of present tribulations, and to overcome all adversities, so that they count it all joy when they fall into divers temptations[[Jas 1:2||]]. And when Jesus enters the boat, that is, the Church, or the hearts of the faithful, at once, with unhoped-for speed, the boat is at the land they long for; for then of a sudden they are comforted, and contemplate their heavenly fatherland, and enter it by holy desire, having their conversation in heaven[[Phil 3:20||]], who a little before were tossed about in the depths. And [[Ps 76:11|this is the change of the right hand of the most High|hæc mutatio dexteræ Excelsi]], who [[Job 5:18|woundeth, and cureth|vulnerat et medetur]], both when and as it shall please Him.

paras.t: Altera die post miraculum panum, turba quæ stabat trans mare Tiberiadis, hoc est ex opposito urbis Capharnaum, circa locum quo die præcedenti a Christo pasta fuit: rediit enim ad illum locum, ut quæreret et regem faceret Jesum; vidit quia navicula alia non erat ibi nisi una, id est, die præcedenti non fuit ibi nisi una navis, in qua navigaverunt discipuli; et quia non introisset cum discipulis suis Jesus in navim præfatam, quæ sola exstitit ibi, sed soli discipuli ejus abiissent in illa navi. Aliæ vero supervenerunt naves a Tiberiade urbe prædicta, juxta locum, id est usque ad locum, ubi manducaverant panem turba quinque millium virorum, gratias agentes Domino, qui eos tam mirabiliter pavit. Istæ naves venerunt postea, scilicet post recessum discipulorum.
paras.en: [[6:22|The next day|Altera die]] after the miracle of the loaves, [[6:22|the multitude that stood on the other side of the sea|turba quæ stabat trans mare]] of Tiberias, that is, opposite the city of Capharnaum, about the place where it had been fed by Christ the day before (for it had gone back to that place, to seek Jesus and make Him king), [[6:22|saw that there was no other ship there but one|vidit quia navicula alia non erat ibi nisi una]]: that is, on the day before there had been only one boat there, in which the disciples sailed; [[6:22|and that Jesus had not entered into the ship with his disciples|et quia non introisset cum discipulis suis Jesus in navim]], the boat just mentioned, which alone was there, [[6:22|but that his disciples were gone away alone|sed soli discipuli ejus abiissent]] in that boat. [[6:23|But other ships came in from Tiberias|Aliæ vero supervenerunt naves a Tiberiade]], the city already named, [[6:23|nigh unto the place|juxta locum]], that is, as far as the place, [[6:23|where they had eaten the bread|ubi manducaverant panem]], the multitude of five thousand men, giving thanks to the Lord who had fed them so wonderfully [Denis reads *gratias agentes Domino*, the people “giving thanks to the Lord”; the Vulgate has *gratias agente Domino*, “the Lord giving thanks”]. These boats came afterwards, that is, after the disciples had gone.

paras.t: Quum ergo vidisset turba quia Jesus non esset ibi, hoc est in loco manducationis jam dictæ, neque discipuli ejus, ascenderunt in naviculas illas quæ supervenerunt, et venerunt Capharnaum, quærentes Jesum. Et quum invenissent eum trans mare, in Capharnaum vel prope, dixerunt ei cum admiratione: Rabbi, quando huc venisti? id est, quando et quomodo transvadasti hoc mare sine navigio? vel, per quem modum venisti ad locum hunc, quum sciamus te non intrasse cum discipulis tuis unicam illam naviculam?
paras.en: [[6:24|When therefore the multitude saw that Jesus was not there|Quum ergo vidisset turba quia Jesus non esset ibi]], that is, in the place of the eating just spoken of, [[6:24|nor his disciples|neque discipuli ejus]], they went up into the boats that had come in, [[6:24|and came to Capharnaum, seeking for Jesus|et venerunt Capharnaum, quærentes Jesum]]. [[6:25|And when they had found him on that other side of the sea|Et quum invenissent eum trans mare]], in Capharnaum or near it, [[6:25|they said to him|dixerunt ei]] in wonder: [[6:25|Rabbi, when camest thou hither?|Rabbi, quando huc venisti]] That is, when and how didst thou cross this sea without a boat? Or, in what way didst thou come to this place, since we know that thou didst not go into that one boat with thy disciples?

paras.t: Respondit eis Jesus, non ad interrogationem eorum, vel quia indigni erant audire tantum mysterium, vel quia non credidissent, vel quia non fuit eis necesse hoc scire. Idcirco primo redarguit carnalitatem eorum, et deinceps moralem doctrinam proposuit. Et dixit: Amen, amen dico vobis, quæritis me, non quia vidistis signa, id est non propter spiritualem rationem, non ex admiratione sincera ac vera dilectione mirabilium operum Dei, sed quia manducastis ex panibus, et saturati estis, hoc est ex affectu carnali et aviditate alimoniæ corporalis, cupientes frequentius satiari a me sine vestro labore. Dominus Jesus scrutans corda et renes, discretor intentionum, vidit interiorem imperfectionem istorum, qui voluerunt eum regem facere propter corporalia commoda, ut otiosam deliciosamque sub ejus dominio agerent vitam, putantes quod semper posset eos usque ad satietatem nutrire, sine ipsorum sollicitudine ac labore, qui semel tam mirabiliter paverat ipsos: ideo eum quærebant, atque redargui meruerunt. Non est tamen putandum quod omnes fuerint tales, quia nonnulli ex devotione piisque causis eum comitabantur.
paras.en: [[6:26|Jesus answered them|Respondit eis Jesus]], not to their question: either because they were unworthy to hear so great a mystery, or because they would not have believed, or because it was not necessary for them to know this. And so He first rebuked their carnal-mindedness, and then set forth moral teaching. [[6:26|and said: Amen, amen, I say to you, you seek me|Et dixit: Amen, amen dico vobis, quæritis me]], [[6:26|not because you have seen miracles|non quia vidistis signa]], that is, not for a spiritual reason, not out of a sincere wonder at God’s marvellous works and a true love of them, [[6:26|but because you did eat of the loaves and were filled|sed quia manducastis ex panibus, et saturati estis]]: that is, out of carnal affection and greed for bodily nourishment, wishing to be filled by me again and again without labour of your own. The Lord Jesus, [[Ps 7:10|the searcher of hearts and reins|scrutans corda et renes]], the discerner of intentions[[Heb 4:12||]], saw the inward imperfection of these men, who wanted to make Him king for bodily advantages, so as to lead an idle and pleasant life under His rule, thinking that He who had once fed them so wonderfully could always feed them to the full without care or labour of their own. That is why they sought Him, and they deserved to be rebuked. Yet it is not to be thought that all were such, for some followed Him out of devotion and for holy reasons.

paras.t: Operamini, hoc est, operando acquirite et adipisci studete, non solum vel principaliter cibum qui perit, hoc est escam corpoream, quæ in substantiam aliti transmutatur amittendo propriam formam, sicque corrumpitur, sed qui permanet in vitam æternam, id est, manducantem confortat, in ipsoque permanet quousque perducatur ad patriam; quem cibum spiritualem animas vitaliter reficientem, Filius hominis dabit vobis. Cibus iste intelligi potest ipsum Verbum incarnatum, vel corpus dominicum, vel actio virtuosa, et quidquid spiritualiter alit mentem, perducens eam ad vitam beatam. Primo enim quærendum est regnum Dei et justitia ejus; et deinde licitum est, cum moderata sollicitudine ac labore honesto quærere sustentaculum vitæ, escam, potum, vestitum et domum: præsertim quum dicat Apostolus, Qui non laborat, nec manducet; et Psalmista, Labores manuum tuarum quia manducabis, beatus es, et bene tibi erit.
paras.en: [[6:27|Labour|Operamini]], that is, by working acquire, and strive to obtain, not only or chiefly [[6:27|the meat which perisheth|cibum qui perit]], that is, bodily food, which is changed into the substance of the one it nourishes, losing its own form, and so is corrupted, [[6:27|but for that which endureth unto life everlasting|sed qui permanet in vitam æternam]]: that is, which strengthens the one who eats it, and remains in him until he is brought to the heavenly fatherland; which spiritual food, giving life and refreshment to souls, [[6:27|the Son of man will give you|Filius hominis dabit vobis]]. This food may be understood as the incarnate Word Himself, or the Lord’s body, or virtuous action, and whatever feeds the mind spiritually, leading it to the life of bliss. For first we must seek [[Matt 6:33|the kingdom of God, and his justice|regnum Dei et justitia ejus]]; and after that it is lawful, with moderate care and honest labour, to seek the support of life, food, drink, clothing and a house: especially since the Apostle says, [[2 Thess 3:10|if any man will not work, neither let him eat|Qui non laborat, nec manducet]]; and the Psalmist, [[Ps 127:2|For thou shalt eat the labours of thy hands: blessed art thou, and it shall be well with thee.|Labores manuum tuarum quia manducabis, beatus es, et bene tibi erit]].

paras.t: Huic vero quod nunc loquitur Christus, Operamini non cibum qui perit, concordat quod ait apud Matthæum: Ne solliciti sitis animæ vestræ quid manducetis, neque corpori vestro quid induamini. Et aliud nihil intendit per hæc, nisi ut tanto sollicitiores simus pro interna refectione, spirituali confortatione, gratiosa pinguedine animæ, quam corporis, quanto præstantior est immortalis anima summæ Trinitatis imagine decorata, vili isto ac corruptibili corpore, et quanto majus damnum imminet si anima negligatur, quam si corpus maceretur. Denique, sicut lecatores non contentantur qualicumque alimento, sed delicatissima fercula quærunt; sic nos, si veri religiosi sumus, non debemus inferiorum virtutum actionibus animas nostras tantum vel præsertim reficere, sed nobilissimarum virtutum epulas degustare, insistendo præcipue actibus fidei, spei et caritatis, deinde actibus latriæ aliarumque virtutum cardinalium. Sed ad talia nemo idoneus est, nisi per virtutes morales fuerint in eo passiones reformatæ vitiaque exstincta.
paras.en: With what Christ says here, [[6:27|Labour not for the meat which perisheth|Operamini non cibum qui perit]], agrees what He says in Matthew: [[Matt 6:25|be not solicitous for your life, what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall put on|Ne solliciti sitis animæ vestræ quid manducetis, neque corpori vestro quid induamini]]. And by these words He means nothing else than that we should be as much more careful for the inward refreshment, the spiritual strengthening and the gracious fatness of the soul than of the body, as the immortal soul, adorned with the image of the most high Trinity, is more excellent than this vile and corruptible body, and as the loss threatening is greater if the soul is neglected than if the body is wasted. Lastly, as gluttons are not content with any food whatever, but seek the most delicate dishes, so we, if we are true religious, ought not to refresh our souls only or chiefly with the acts of the lower virtues, but to taste the banquet of the noblest virtues, applying ourselves above all to acts of faith, hope and charity, and then to acts of *latria* [the worship due to God alone, an act of the virtue of religion] and of the other cardinal virtues. But no one is fit for such things unless through the moral virtues his passions have been set in order and his vices put out.

paras.t: Hunc enim cibum spiritualem, Pater signavit Deus, hoc est, Deus Pater præcipue requirendum ostendit. Vel: Hunc Filium hominis, Pater signavit Deus, id est, hominibus per incarnationis mysterium demonstravit, quatenus cibum spiritualem nobis conferret. Signavit quoque Pater Filium suum in baptismo, Hic est, inquiens, Filius meus dilectus; et per columbam, atque per alia testimonia quibus probatur Jesus esse Christus Filius Dei.
paras.en: [[6:27|For him|Hunc enim]], this spiritual food, [[6:27|hath God, the Father, sealed|Pater signavit Deus]] [*signavit*: “sealed”, that is, marked out or pointed out]: that is, God the Father has shown that it is above all to be sought. Or: Him, the Son of man, hath God the Father sealed, that is, He has shown Him to men through the mystery of the Incarnation, that He might bestow spiritual food on us. The Father also sealed His Son in His baptism, saying: [[Matt 3:17|This is my beloved Son|Hic est, inquiens, Filius meus dilectus]]; and by the dove[[Matt 3:16||]], and by the other testimonies by which Jesus is proved to be the Christ, the Son of God.

paras.t: Dixerunt ergo ad eum Judæi: Quid faciemus ut operemur opera Dei? id est, quid agendo erimus Deo obedientes, seu opera ei placentia exsequentes, ut prædictum panem spiritualem consequi mereamur? Respondit Jesus, et dixit eis: Hoc est opus Dei, id est actio placita Deo, et donum ipsius quo panis iste acquiritur, ut credatis in eum quem misit ille, id est credere in me Jesum Christum, missum a Deo Patre seu Trinitate. Sumuntur itaque hoc loco Facere et Operari, multum late atque communiter, prout omnem actum interiorem et exteriorem includunt, ita quod interior fidei actus vocetur opus et factio Dei, quoniam donum ipsius est, qui fidem ipsam infundit, et omnia opera nostra operatur in nobis.
paras.en: [[6:28|They said therefore unto him|Dixerunt ergo ad eum]], the Jews: [[6:28|What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?|Quid faciemus ut operemur opera Dei?]] That is, by doing what shall we be obedient to God, or carry out works pleasing to Him, so that we may deserve to obtain the spiritual bread spoken of? [[6:29|Jesus answered and said to them: This is the work of God|Respondit Jesus, et dixit eis: Hoc est opus Dei]], that is, the action pleasing to God, and His gift by which this bread is gained, [[6:29|that you believe in him whom he hath sent|ut credatis in eum quem misit ille]]: that is, to believe in me, Jesus Christ, sent by God the Father, or by the Trinity. So *to do* and *to work* are taken here very broadly and generally, as including every act, inward and outward, so that the inward act of faith is called a work and a doing of God, since it is His gift who infuses faith itself, and works all our works in us[[Is 26:12||]].

paras.t: Dixerunt ergo ei: Quod ergo tu facis signum, ut videamus, et credamus tibi? Hoc est, quod miraculum tam præclarum ac singulare operaris, ut illo conspecto, credamus tibi tanquam regi Messiæ et Christo Filio Dei? Quid operaris? id est, nil tale facis, propter quod dignum sit tibi sic credere. Superius dictum est, quod crediderunt in Jesum, viso miraculo quinque panum. Quomodo ergo nunc reprehenduntur de incredulitate? Est respondendum, quod loquuntur sicut homines passionati, qui secundum omnem ventum mutantur. Unde satiati, quasi blandiendo dixerunt, Hic est vere Propheta qui venturus est in mundum; nunc vero increpati, dicunt, Quid operaris? Imperfecta ergo atque instabilis fuit fides eorum de Christo. Et forte, quæ dicta sunt de credentibus, et istis, non sunt referenda ad eosdem. In tanta enim turba erant diversi diversimode sentientes.
paras.en: [[6:30|They said therefore to him: What sign therefore dost thou shew that we may see and may believe thee?|Dixerunt ergo ei: Quod ergo tu facis signum, ut videamus, et credamus tibi?]] That is, what miracle so glorious and singular dost thou work, that when we have seen it we may believe thee as the king Messias and the Christ, the Son of God? [[6:30|What dost thou work?|Quid operaris]] That is, thou doest nothing of the kind, for which it would be right to believe thee so. It was said above that they believed in Jesus when they had seen the miracle of the five loaves. How then are they now reproached with unbelief? The answer is that they speak like men swayed by their passions, who change with every wind. So when they had been filled they said, as if to flatter Him, [[6:14|This is of a truth the prophet that is to come into the world|Hic est vere Propheta qui venturus est in mundum]]; but now that they have been rebuked, they say, What dost thou work? Their faith in Christ, then, was imperfect and unstable. And perhaps what was said of those who believed, and of these, is not to be referred to the same people; for in so great a crowd there were different men thinking in different ways.

paras.t: Quod autem Christus nil operetur, comparatione Moysis probant. Patres nostri manducaverunt manna in deserto, sicut scriptum est in Psalmo, quantum ad sensum: Panem de cælo dedit eis manducare. Tanquam dicerent: Tu nos semel satiasti, multiplicando panes hordeaceos: sed quid est hoc, respectu cibationis patrum nostrorum egredientium de Ægypto, qui quadraginta annis refecti sunt pane cœlesti sub Moysis principatu? secundum quod Exodi sextodecimo Dominus dixit: Ecce ego pluam vobis panes de cœlo.
paras.en: That Christ works nothing, they prove by comparison with Moses: [[6:31|Our fathers did eat manna in the desert|Patres nostri manducaverunt manna in deserto]], [[6:31|as it is written|sicut scriptum est]] in the Psalm (as to the sense): [[6:31|He gave them bread from heaven to eat|Panem de cælo dedit eis manducare]][[Ps 77:24||]][[Ps 77:25||]][[Ps 104:40||]]. As if they said: Thou hast filled us once, by multiplying the barley loaves; but what is this, compared with the feeding of our fathers when they went out of Egypt, who for forty years were fed with bread from heaven under the rule of Moses? According to what the Lord said in the sixteenth chapter of Exodus: [[Ex 16:4|Behold I will rain bread from heaven for you|Ecce ego pluam vobis panes de cœlo]].

paras.t: Dixit ergo eis Jesus: Amen, amen dico vobis, non Moyses dedit vobis, hoc est patribus vestris, panem de cælo. Hoc tripliciter verum est: primo, quoniam Moyses non dedit eis hunc panem, sed Deus omnipotens ministerio angelorum formavit, dedit ac pluit manna; secundo, quoniam panis ille non descendit de cœlo proprie dicto, videlicet de cœlo empyreo, sidereo, seu aliquo orbe cœlesti altioris naturæ præ elementis, sed de cœlo aerio; tertio, quoniam manna non fuit panis verus, sed figuralis ac typicus. Sed sciendum, quod verum quandoque distinguitur contra fictum seu falsum, et sic fuit verus panis; quandoque autem contra figurativum, et sic non erat verus panis, sed typicus, præfigurans panem cœlestem ac spiritualem, qui datur nobis in Sacramento. De quo subditur: sed Pater meus dat vobis, quantum in se est, hoc est, paratum ad dandum se exhibet, panem de cælo verum, non figuralem tantum. Et quis sit panis ille subjungitur.
paras.en: [[6:32|Then Jesus said to them: Amen, amen, I say to you|Dixit ergo eis Jesus: Amen, amen dico vobis]]; [[6:32|Moses gave you not|non Moyses dedit vobis]], that is, your fathers, [[6:32|bread from heaven|panem de cælo]]. This is true in three ways. First, because Moses did not give them this bread, but almighty God, by the ministry of angels, formed, gave and rained down the manna. Secondly, because that bread did not come down from heaven properly so called, that is, from the empyrean heaven [the highest heaven, the dwelling of God and the blessed], from the starry heaven, or from any heavenly sphere of a higher nature than the elements, but from the heaven of the air. Thirdly, because the manna was not true bread, but figurative and typical. But it is to be known that the true is sometimes set against the feigned or false, and in this sense it was true bread; and sometimes against the figurative, and in this sense it was not true bread, but typical, prefiguring the heavenly and spiritual bread which is given to us in the Sacrament. Of which it is added: [[6:32|but my Father giveth you|sed Pater meus dat vobis]], as far as lies in Him, that is, He shows Himself ready to give, [[6:32|the true bread from heaven|panem de cælo verum]], not a figurative one only. And what that bread is, is added next.

paras.t: Panis enim Dei, hoc est a Deo Patre datus, est ille qui descendit de cœlo, id est unigenitus Filius Dei, seu Verbum incarnatum, et dat vitam gratiæ mundo, hoc est hominibus in ipsum credentibus. Ipse igitur Christus est verus panis mentem reficiens, tam ratione suæ divinitatis, per quam reficit angelos, et gratiam causat in nobis, quam ratione suæ humanitatis, cujus virtute et merito omne spirituale bonum consequimur, quasi per causam mediatam ac instrumentalem, quia de plenitudine ejus omnes accipimus, gratiam pro gratia, ut dictum est primo capitulo. Denique panis iste descendit de cœlo empyreo, in quo Deus specialiter habitare censetur, non locum mutando, sed nostram naturam induendo, seque hominibus visibiliter ostendendo. Et quoniam anima Christi fuit creata a Deo, et corpus ejus immediate formatum a Spiritu Sancto, potest dici quod etiam secundum assumptam humanitatem descendit de cœlo, secundum sensum expositum.
paras.en: [[6:33|For the bread of God|Panis enim Dei]], that is, given by God the Father, [[6:33|is that which cometh down from heaven|est ille qui descendit de cœlo]], that is, the only-begotten Son of God, or the Word incarnate, [[6:33|and giveth life|et dat vitam]] of grace [[6:33|to the world|mundo]], that is, to men who believe in Him. Christ Himself, then, is the true bread that refreshes the mind, both by reason of His divinity, by which He refreshes the angels and causes grace in us, and by reason of His humanity, by whose power and merit we obtain every spiritual good, as through a mediate and instrumental cause; for [[John 1:16|of his fulness we all have received: and grace for grace|de plenitudine ejus omnes accipimus, gratiam pro gratia]], as was said in the first chapter. Lastly, this bread came down from the empyrean heaven, in which God is held to dwell in a special way: not by changing place, but by putting on our nature and showing Himself visibly to men. And since the soul of Christ was created by God, and His body formed immediately by the Holy Ghost, it can be said that even according to the humanity He assumed He came down from heaven, in the sense explained.

paras.t: Dixerunt ergo ad eum carnales Judæi: Domine, semper da nobis panem hunc. Non petierunt panem cœlestem, de quo Christus loquebatur, sed corporalem, de quo eum loqui putabant. Optabant enim corporaliter refici pane meliori quam fuerat manna. Et sicut mulier Samaritana non intellexit Christum loquentem de aqua spirituali, sed dixit, Domine, da mihi hanc aquam, ut non veniam huc haurire, nec sitiam; sic isti non intellexerunt Christum loquentem de pane spirituali, sed dixerunt, Semper da nobis panem hunc, videlicet, ut sine labore et cura tam optimo pane vescerentur.
paras.en: [[6:34|They said therefore unto him|Dixerunt ergo ad eum]], the carnal Jews: [[6:34|Lord, give us always this bread|Domine, semper da nobis panem hunc]]. They did not ask for the heavenly bread of which Christ was speaking, but for bodily bread, of which they thought He spoke; for they longed to be fed in the body with a better bread than the manna had been.
