And as the Samaritan woman did not understand Christ when He spoke of spiritual water, but said, [[John 4:15|Sir, give me this water, that I may not thirst, nor come hither to draw|Domine, da mihi hanc aquam, ut non veniam huc haurire, nec sitiam]], so these did not understand Christ speaking of spiritual bread, but said, [[6:34|give us always this bread|Semper da nobis panem hunc]]: that is, so that they might feed on such excellent bread without labour or care.

paras.t: Dixit autem eis Jesus: Ego sum panis vitæ, hoc est conferens vitam gratiæ in via, et vitam gloriæ in patria. Nec solum conservo ac roboro vitam istam, sicut cibus corporeus conservat atque fortificat vitam naturæ præsentem; sed etiam causo vitam hanc spiritualem, quum deest: quod cibus corporalis non valet efficere quantum ad vitam naturæ.
paras.en: [[6:35|And Jesus said to them: I am the bread of life|Dixit autem eis Jesus: Ego sum panis vitæ]], that is, conferring the life of grace on the way, and the life of glory in the fatherland [that is, in this life, where we are wayfarers, and in heaven]. Nor do I only preserve and strengthen this life, as bodily food preserves and fortifies the present life of nature; but I also cause this spiritual life when it is lacking, which bodily food cannot do with regard to the life of nature.

paras.t: Qui venit ad me, non esuriet; et qui credit in me, non sitiet in æternum. Huic simile est quod supra dixit Salvator, Qui biberit ex aqua quam ego dabo ei, non sitiet in æternum; quod illic prolixe diversisque modis expositum est, quibus perlectis, patet intellectus loci præsentis. Qui enim venit ad Christum per caritatem et gratiam, non esuriet post hanc vitam, quoniam satiabitur satietate æterna, quum viderit Deum per speciem. Nec sitiet in æternum, quamvis ad tempus sitiat durante vita præsenti, in qua beati sunt qui esuriunt et sitiunt justitiam. In futuro etenim sæculo incessanter potabitur torrente voluptatis Dei, ubi fluminis impetus lætificat civitatem Dei. Quomodo autem intelligi possit quantum ad vitam præsentem, quod scilicet veniens ad Christum et credens in ipsum, non sitiat neque esuriat in præsenti, et quomodo hoc non discordet ab eo quod in Ecclesiastico inducitur, Qui edunt me, adhuc esurient, et qui bibunt me, adhuc sitient, elucescit ex dictis in expositione quarti capituli.
paras.en: [[6:35|He that cometh to me shall not hunger: and he that believeth in me shall never thirst|Qui venit ad me, non esuriet; et qui credit in me, non sitiet in æternum]]. Like this is what the Saviour said above: [[John 4:13|he that shall drink of the water that I will give him shall not thirst for ever|Qui biberit ex aqua quam ego dabo ei, non sitiet in æternum]]; which was there explained at length and in various ways, and when these are read through, the meaning of the present passage is plain. For he who comes to Christ by charity and grace shall not hunger after this life, since he will be filled with an everlasting fulness when he sees God face to face [*per speciem*: by sight of His very form, as opposed to by faith][[Ps 16:15||]]. Nor shall he thirst for ever, though for a time he thirsts while the present life lasts, in which [[Matt 5:6|Blessed are they that hunger and thirst after justice|beati sunt qui esuriunt et sitiunt justitiam]]. For in the world to come he will be given to drink without ceasing [[Ps 35:9|of the torrent of thy pleasure|torrente voluptatis]] (the pleasure of God), where [[Ps 45:5|The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful|fluminis impetus lætificat civitatem Dei]]. But how it can be understood of the present life, namely that he who comes to Christ and believes in Him does not thirst or hunger in this present time, and how this does not conflict with what is said in Ecclesiasticus, [[Ecclus 24:29|They that eat me, shall yet hunger: and they that drink me, shall yet thirst|Qui edunt me, adhuc esurient, et qui bibunt me, adhuc sitient]], is made clear by what was said in the exposition of the fourth chapter[[John 4:13||]].

paras.t: Deinde Christus ostendit, quod quantum in se fuit, ipse obtulit panem vitæ Judæis, sed ipsi propter suam incredulitatem, eum non gustaverunt. Sed dixi vobis, quia, id est quod, et vidistis me oculo corporali, secundum quod homo sum, et non credidistis verbis meis, nec in me, quod sim unigenitus Filius Dei et Christus vobis promissus. Obtuli ergo vobis hunc panem, ostendendo vobis me ipsum; sed non manducastis, quia non credidistis: qui enim credit, manducat.
paras.en: Then Christ shows that, as far as lay in Him, He offered the bread of life to the Jews, but they, because of their unbelief, did not taste it. [[6:36|But I said unto you|Sed dixi vobis]] [[6:36|that|quia]] [*quia*, which can also mean “because”, here stands for *quod*, “that”], [[6:36|you also have seen me|et vidistis me]] with the bodily eye, according as I am man, [[6:36|and you believe not|et non credidistis]] my words, nor in me, that I am the only-begotten Son of God and the Christ promised to you. I offered you, then, this bread, by showing you Myself; but you did not eat, because you did not believe: for he who believes, eats.

paras.t: Sed ne putaremus omnes Judæos deserendos, vel propter illorum incredulitatem misericordiam Dei evacuandam, declarat quibus dandus sit panis iste vitalis atque vivificus. Omne genus hominum quod dat mihi Pater, id est, quos Pater per inspirationem internam inclinat ad me, vel quos ab æterno elegit ac prædestinavit in me, utpote quos decrevit per meam incarnationem ac passionem salvare, ad me veniet, nunc per fidem et gratiam, in futuro autem per beatificam visionem, imo et per localem sui exaltationem usque ad cœlum empyreum. De his nempe dicit Apostolus ad Ephesios: Deus elegit nos in Christo ante mundi constitutionem, ut essemus sancti et immaculati in conspectu ejus; et in Psalmo ait Pater ad Filium, Postula a me, et dabo tibi gentes hæreditatem tuam, etc.
paras.en: But lest we should think that all the Jews were to be forsaken, or that the mercy of God was to be made void because of their unbelief, He declares to whom this living and life-giving bread is to be given. [[6:37|All|Omne]] the race of men [[6:37|that the Father giveth to me|quod dat mihi Pater]], that is, those whom the Father inclines to Me by inward inspiration, or whom He has chosen and predestined in Me from eternity[[Rom 8:29||]], as those whom He has decreed to save through My incarnation and passion, [[6:37|shall come to me|ad me veniet]]: now by faith and grace, but in the world to come by the beatific vision, and indeed also by being raised bodily, in place, up to the empyrean heaven. Of these indeed the Apostle says to the Ephesians: God [[Eph 1:4|chose us|elegit nos]] in Christ [[Eph 1:4|before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and unspotted in his sight|ante mundi constitutionem, ut essemus sancti et immaculati in conspectu ejus]]; and in the Psalm the Father says to the Son: [[Ps 2:8|Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance|Postula a me, et dabo tibi gentes hæreditatem tuam]], etc.

paras.t: Et eum qui venit ad me, per mentis suæ conversionem, fidem et caritatem, vel qui facit quod in se est, quamvis nondum gratiam habeat, non ejiciam foras, id est, non separabo eum a grege electorum meorum, nec a pietate mea eum excludam, sed incorporabitur mihi, et si Pater meus dederit eum mihi (modo prætacto), finaliter salvus erit. Non enim est Christus personarum acceptor, sed in omni gente, qui timet eum et operatur justitiam, acceptus est illi. Ecce quanta est misericordia Salvatoris. Nullum quantumcumque abjectum vel impium, despicit aut relinquet, si convertatur ad ipsum, faciendo quod in se est. Cujus ratio subditur:
paras.en: [[6:37|and him that cometh to me|Et eum qui venit ad me]] by the conversion of his mind, by faith and charity, or who does what is in him [*facit quod in se est*: does all that lies in his power], though he has not yet grace, [[6:37|I will not cast out|non ejiciam foras]]: that is, I will not separate him from the flock of My elect, nor shut him out from My loving-kindness, but he shall be made one body with Me; and if My Father has given him to Me (in the way just mentioned), he will be saved in the end. For Christ is not [[Acts 10:34|a respecter of persons|personarum acceptor]], [[Acts 10:35|But in every nation, he that feareth him and worketh justice is acceptable to him|sed in omni gente, qui timet eum et operatur justitiam, acceptus est illi]]. Behold how great is the mercy of the Saviour! No one, however abject or wicked, does He despise or forsake, if he turns to Him, doing what is in him. The reason of which is added:

paras.t: Quia descendi de cœlo, humanam naturam assumendo (ut dictum est plenius), non ut faciam voluntatem meam, id est proprium beneplacitum, sed voluntatem ejus qui misit me, puta Patris cœlestis. Quomodo intelligendum est hoc? Nonne Patris et Filii, secundum naturam divinam, est una numero voluntas, sicut et una essentia? Quod enim dicitur absolute in tribus Personis, non numeratur. Sed voluntas Christi humana, fuit divinæ voluntati inflexibiliter subjecta, unita et conformata, non solum propter beatificam fruitionem animæ Christi, sed insuper propter hypostaticam humanæ naturæ unionem cum Verbo. Et respondendum, quod Christus loquitur de voluntate humana, quæ licet fuerit Deo semper conformis, non tamen Christus fecit eam in quantum fuit sua, sed in quantum erat voluntati paternæ subjecta. Idcirco formaliter dicitur voluntatem Patris fecisse, quoniam illa fuit ratio ob quam fecit quod suæ voluntati humanæ complacuit. Unde Christus loqui videtur secundum generalem modum loquendi, secundum quem aliquis subditus vel amicus dicit de suo prælato vel dilecto, Non facio quod mihi placet, sed quod illi; quamvis quidquid placuerit illi, sibi quoque summe complaceat.
paras.en: [[6:38|Because I came down from heaven|Quia descendi de cœlo]] by taking human nature (as has been said more fully), [[6:38|not to do my own will|non ut faciam voluntatem meam]], that is, My own good pleasure, [[6:38|but the will of him that sent me|sed voluntatem ejus qui misit me]], namely of the heavenly Father. How is this to be understood? Is there not, according to the divine nature, one will of the Father and the Son, one in number, as there is also one essence? For what is said absolutely of the three Persons is not multiplied [that is, what belongs to the divine nature itself, not to one Person as distinct from another, is one and not three]. And the human will of Christ was inflexibly subject, united and conformed to the divine will, not only because of the beatific fruition of Christ's soul, but moreover because of the hypostatic union of the human nature with the Word. And the answer is that Christ is speaking of His human will, which, though it was always conformed to God, Christ nevertheless did not do in so far as it was His own, but in so far as it was subject to the Father's will. Therefore He is said, formally [that is, as to the reason for which He acted], to have done the will of the Father, since that was the reason why He did what pleased His human will. Hence Christ seems to speak according to the common way of speaking, in which a subject or a friend says of his superior or of the one he loves: I do not do what pleases me, but what pleases him; although whatever pleases the other also pleases himself in the highest degree.

paras.t: Quæritur, quum Deus sit sua voluntas, quomodo potest quis facere voluntatem Dei, quum nullus possit facere Deum. Et respondendum, quod voluntatem Dei dicimur facere, dum ejus præceptis paremus, vel consiliis acquiescimus. Frequenter enim sumitur voluntas pro signo voluntatis, videlicet pro præcepto vel consilio, vel pro re volita.
paras.en: It is asked: since God is His own will, how can anyone do the will of God, when no one can make God? [*facere* means both to do and to make.] And the answer is that we are said to do the will of God when we obey His precepts or comply with His counsels. For *will* is often taken for the sign of the will [the *voluntas signi*, as distinguished from the will of God's good pleasure], namely for a precept or a counsel, or for the thing willed.

paras.t: Denique verbis istis incomparabilis nobis commendatur humilitas Christi, qui quum sit verus Deus, Patri æqualis, tam humiliter asserit se venisse, non ut propriam impleat voluntatem, sed Patris. Confunditur ergo et condemnatur superbia nostra, rebellio nostra, duritia nostra, qui ad murmurandum, repugnandum et intumescendum, tam proni consistimus. Contemplemur igitur efficaciterque sectemur Caput nostrum, propriam voluntatem penitus abnegantes, secundum quod ipse alibi docet: Qui vult venire post me, abneget semetipsum, et tollat crucem suam quotidie, et sequatur me. Quo enim sincere propter Deum propriam voluntatem magis relinquimus, frangimus, abnegamus, eo amplius Deus se ipsum ingerit nobis, ita quod eum possidere incipimus, et nostris desideriis acquiescit, offerens se copiosissime mentibus nostris. Unde Isaias inducit: Si glorificaveris Dominum dum non invenitur voluntas tua, tunc delectaberis super Domino, et sustollam te super altitudinem terræ, ait Dominus. Hanc abnegationem efficit vera caritas Dei, quoniam amor, secundum Dionysium, non sinit amantem esse sui ipsius, sed amati.
paras.en: Lastly, in these words the incomparable humility of Christ is commended to us, who, though He is true God, equal to the Father, so humbly declares that He came not to fulfil His own will, but the Father's. Confounded, then, and condemned is our pride, our rebellion, our hardness, who are so prone to murmuring, resisting and swelling up. Let us therefore contemplate and follow in deed our Head, wholly denying our own will, as He Himself teaches elsewhere: [[Luke 9:23|If any man will come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me|Qui vult venire post me, abneget semetipsum, et tollat crucem suam quotidie, et sequatur me]]. For the more sincerely we leave, break and deny our own will for God's sake, the more fully God pours Himself into us, so that we begin to possess Him; and He yields to our desires, offering Himself most abundantly to our minds. Hence Isaias brings in: If thou [[Is 58:13|glorify him|glorificaveris Dominum]] while [[Is 58:13|thy own will is not found|non invenitur voluntas tua]], [[Is 58:14|Then shalt thou be delighted in the Lord, and I will lift thee up above the high places of the earth|tunc delectaberis super Domino, et sustollam te super altitudinem terræ]], saith the Lord. This self-denial is brought about by true charity towards God, since love, according to Dionysius, does not suffer the lover to be his own, but the beloved's [Dionysius the Areopagite, On the Divine Names, ch. 4].

paras.t: Hæc est autem voluntas, hoc est res placens ac volita, ejus qui misit me Patris, ut omne quod dedit mihi (modo jam explanato) non perdam ex eo, hoc est, nullum electorum perire permittam, quia etsi ad tempus erraverit, finaliter perire non valet. Propter quod fertur in Psalmo: Quum ceciderit non collidetur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam; rursusque, Impulsus eversus sum ut caderem, et Dominus suscepit me. Sed resuscitem illud in novissimo die, hoc est in die judicii universalis: de quo sanctus Job ait, In novissimo die de terra surrecturus sum. Omnes quippe resurgemus (nec dubium quin per omnipotentiam Christi) in momento, in ictu oculi, in novissima tuba, secundum Apostolum. Dies autem judicii appellatur novissimus, quia ex tunc motus cœli cessabit, et per consequens tempus, quod est mensura motus cœlestis. Tempore autem cessante, cessabunt dies et nox proprie sumpti.
paras.en: [[6:39|Now this is the will|Hæc est autem voluntas]], that is, the thing pleasing and willed, [[6:39|of the Father who sent me|ejus qui misit me Patris]], [[6:39|that of all that he hath given me|ut omne quod dedit mihi]] (in the way already explained) [[6:39|I should lose nothing|non perdam ex eo]], that is, I will let none of the elect perish; for even if one should go astray for a time, he cannot perish in the end. For which reason it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 36:24|When he shall fall he shall not be bruised, for the Lord putteth his hand under him|Quum ceciderit non collidetur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam]]; and again: [[Ps 117:13|Being pushed I was overturned that I might fall: but the Lord supported me|Impulsus eversus sum ut caderem, et Dominus suscepit me]]. [[6:39|but should raise it up again in the last day|Sed resuscitem illud in novissimo die]], that is, on the day of the general judgment, of which holy Job says: [[Job 19:25|in the last day I shall rise out of the earth|In novissimo die de terra surrecturus sum]]. For, according to the Apostle, [[1 Cor 15:51|We shall all indeed rise again|Omnes quippe resurgemus]] (and doubtless by the almighty power of Christ) [[1 Cor 15:52|In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet|in momento, in ictu oculi, in novissima tuba]]. Now the day of judgment is called the last, because from then on the motion of the heavens will cease, and in consequence time, which is the measure of the heavenly motion. And when time ceases, day and night, properly so called, will cease.

paras.t: Hæc est enim voluntas Patris mei qui misit me, ut omnis qui videt Filium per contemplationem fidelem, et credit in eum per fidem formatam. Loquitur autem de visione ænigmatica, non de visione clara per speciem. Visio enim Dei per speciem, fidem excludit. De visione vero ista obscura dicit Apostolus: Videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate; et, Nunc cognosco ex parte. Habeat vitam æternam pro mercede in patria, id est claram notitiam Dei. Visio enim per speciem, est tota merces. Patet ergo quod voluntas Patris est salus, conservatio atque redemptio nostra. Unde etiam protestatur Apostolus: Hæc est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra. Sed quia vita ista æterna, est subjective in anima, idcirco de corporis glorificatione adjecit: et ego resuscitabo eum in novissimo die, hoc est, de morte naturæ seu somno mortis ipsum excitabo, corpus resolutum in cineresque redactum redintegrando, eique animam copulando, ut beatitudo animæ mox redundet in corpus, et utrumque pariter glorificetur.
paras.en: [[6:40|And this is the will of my Father that sent me|Hæc est enim voluntas Patris mei qui misit me]], [[6:40|that every one who seeth the Son|ut omnis qui videt Filium]] by faithful contemplation, [[6:40|and believeth in him|et credit in eum]] by formed faith [*fides formata*: faith quickened by charity]. He speaks of the dim vision [*visio ænigmatica*: seeing as in a riddle], not of the clear vision face to face; for the vision of God face to face excludes faith. Of this dark vision the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 13:12|We see now through a glass in a dark manner|Videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate]]; and: [[1 Cor 13:12|Now I know in part|Nunc cognosco ex parte]]. [[6:40|may have life everlasting|Habeat vitam æternam]] as a reward in the fatherland, that is, the clear knowledge of God; for the vision face to face is the whole reward. It is plain, then, that the will of the Father is our salvation, preservation and redemption. Hence also the Apostle declares: [[1 Thess 4:3|this is the will of God, your sanctification|Hæc est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra]]. But since this eternal life is in the soul as in its subject, He therefore added, concerning the glorifying of the body: [[6:40|And I will raise him up in the last day|et ego resuscitabo eum in novissimo die]], that is, I will rouse him from the death of nature, or the sleep of death, restoring the body that has been dissolved and brought to ashes, and joining the soul to it again, so that the blessedness of the soul may at once overflow into the body, and both may be glorified together.

paras.t: Murmurabant ergo Judæi de illo, quia dixisset: Ego sum panis vivus, qui de cœlo descendi. Et dicebant: Nonne hic est Jesus filius Joseph, cujus nos novimus patrem, et matrem? Quomodo ergo dicit hic, Quia de cœlo descendi? Isti Judæi increduli multipliciter erraverunt. Primo, quia murmurabant. In quo imitati sunt patres suos, qui Deum gravissime offendisse leguntur, murmurando contra eum in solitudine. Verba enim quæ isti intelligere propria subtilitate non poterant, debebant humiliter investigasse ac didicisse, nec debuerunt ambigere de veritate loquentis, cujus in tantis miraculis experti erant sanctitatem atque potentiam, assistentiamque divinam. Secundo, quia putabant Jesum naturali ordine ex commixtione viri ac feminæ natum. Et ergo putabant quod Joseph esset pater ejus carnalis; Mariam quoque a viro cognitam reputabant. Tertio, quoniam æstimabant Jesum esse purum hominem, idcirco non descendisse de cœlo, quia natus in terra ex homine.
paras.en: [[6:41|The Jews therefore murmured at him|Murmurabant ergo Judæi de illo]], [[6:41|because he had said: I am the living bread which came down from heaven|quia dixisset: Ego sum panis vivus, qui de cœlo descendi]]. [[6:42|And they said: Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then saith he: I came down from heaven?|Et dicebant: Nonne hic est Jesus filius Joseph, cujus nos novimus patrem, et matrem? Quomodo ergo dicit hic, Quia de cœlo descendi?]] These unbelieving Jews went wrong in many ways. First, in that they murmured. In this they imitated their fathers, who are read to have offended God most grievously by murmuring against Him in the wilderness[[Ex 16:2||]][[Ex 16:7||]][[Ex 16:8||]][[Num 11:1||]][[Num 14:2||]][[Num 14:11||]][[Num 14:27||]][[Num 14:29||]][[Num 14:35||]][[Num 20:13||]]. For the words which these men could not understand by their own subtlety they ought humbly to have searched into and learned; nor should they have doubted the truthfulness of the speaker, whose holiness and power, and the divine assistance with Him, they had experienced in so many miracles. Second, in that they thought that Jesus was born in the natural order, of the union of man and woman. And so they thought that Joseph was His father according to the flesh; and they supposed that Mary too had known man. Third, since they reckoned Jesus to be a mere man, they therefore thought He had not come down from heaven, since He was born on earth of a human being.

paras.t: Respondit ergo Jesus, et dixit eis: Nolite murmurare in invicem, quoniam grande peccatum est. Itaque, nolite murmurare, quasi aliquid falsi dixerim. Nec tamen mirum si murmuratis. Et utriusque ratio subditur, scilicet, quod verba Christi nullam falsitatem continebant, et quod mirum non fuit murmurare Judæos.
paras.en: [[6:43|Jesus therefore answered and said to them: Murmur not among yourselves|Respondit ergo Jesus, et dixit eis: Nolite murmurare in invicem]], for it is a great sin. Murmur not, then, as though I had said something false. And yet it is no wonder if you murmur. And the reason for both is given next: namely, that the words of Christ contained no falsehood, and that it was no wonder that the Jews murmured.

paras.t: Nemo potest venire ad me, id est, non solum non venit, sed nec potest venire ad me interiori accessu per fidem et caritatem, nisi Pater qui misit me, traxerit eum, hoc est, per suam caritatem et pietatem inclinaverit atque perduxerit mentem ejus ad me, infundendo ei fidem et gratiam, quibus mihi spiritualiter uniatur et incorporetur. Non est enim volentis neque currentis, sed Dei miserentis, cujus donum est omne bonum quod inest nobis.
paras.en: [[6:44|No man can come to me|Nemo potest venire ad me]], that is, not only does no man come, but no man can come to me by inward approach through faith and charity, [[6:44|except the Father, who hath sent me, draw him|nisi Pater qui misit me, traxerit eum]], that is, by His charity and loving-kindness incline and lead his mind to me, pouring into him faith and grace, by which he may be spiritually united to me and made one body with me. For [[Rom 9:16|it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy|Non est enim volentis neque currentis, sed Dei miserentis]], whose gift is every good that is in us[[Jas 1:17||]].

paras.t: Tractus iste interior est, non violentus neque coactus, sed amorosus atque spontaneus, ex divina caritate procedens. Deus namque movet unumquodque secundum propriam suam naturam. Rationalem ergo creaturam convertit et movet ad Christum intellectualiter, sponte ac libere. Denique tractus iste, inter caritatem trahentis et unionem tracti cum ipso, est medius. Sine quo tractu nihil possumus: quia quum Christus sit finis noster, seu terminus supernaturalis, non possumus ad ipsum moveri sive pertingere, nisi aliunde trahamur, puta a Patre cœlesti, imo a tota Trinitate, cujus indivisa sunt opera: sicut nec terra potest ascendere, nisi ab alia elevetur. Et quum homo sit gravis, quia corpus quod corrumpitur aggravat animam; et potestas ejus infirma, quia non sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid a nobis quasi ex nobis; via quoque longa, periculosa atque difficilis, nam et arcta est via angustaque porta quæ ducit ad vitam: patet quod maxime indigemus hoc tractu. Ideo semper dicamus cum Sponsa: Trahe me post te.
paras.en: This drawing is inward, not violent or forced, but loving and spontaneous, proceeding from the divine charity. For God moves each thing according to its own nature. So He turns and moves the rational creature to Christ in a manner fitting an intellect, of its own accord and freely. Further, this drawing stands midway between the charity of Him who draws and the union of the one drawn with Him. Without this drawing we can do nothing: for since Christ is our end, or supernatural goal, we cannot be moved towards Him or reach Him unless we are drawn from elsewhere, namely by the heavenly Father, nay, by the whole Trinity, whose works are undivided [that is, whatever God works outside Himself is the work of all three Persons together]: just as earth cannot rise unless it is lifted by something else. And since man is heavy, for [[Wis 9:15|the corruptible body is a load upon the soul|corpus quod corrumpitur aggravat animam]]; and his power is weak, for, [[2 Cor 3:5|Not that we are sufficient to think any thing of ourselves, as of ourselves|non sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid a nobis quasi ex nobis]]; and the way too is long, dangerous and hard, for [[Matt 7:14|narrow is the gate, and strait is the way that leadeth to life|arcta est via angustaque porta quæ ducit ad vitam]]: it is plain that we have the greatest need of this drawing. Therefore let us always say with the Bride: [[Cant 1:3|Draw me|Trahe me]] after thee.

paras.t: Præterea tractus iste ex divina (ut dictum est) caritate procedit, juxta illud Jeremiæ: In caritate perpetua dilexi te; ideo attraxi te miserans. Quod tripliciter fit. Quosdam etenim trahit Deus flagellis: quæ tamen ex dilectione infliguntur, Domino contestante, Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo. Propter quod ait Osee: In funiculis Adam traham eos, in vinculis caritatis. Isti funiculi, sunt pœnalitates originale peccatum sequentes, quibus affligimur, et ad Deum converti monemur. Quosdam vero trahit Deus beneficiis, ut eum qui dixit: Cantabo Domino qui tribuit mihi bona; et, Quid retribuam Domino pro omnibus quæ retribuit mihi? Isaiam quoque audi dicentem: Miserationum Domini recordabor; laudem Domini super omnibus quæ reddidit nobis Dominus, et quæ largitus est nobis secundum indulgentiam suam. Quosdam vero trahit promissis, ut qui contemplatione præmiorum cœlestium convertuntur: quemadmodum de Moyse dicit Apostolus ad Hebræos, quod adspexit in remunerationem; et Psalmista, Inclinavi (inquit) cor meum ad faciendas justificationes tuas in æternum, propter retributionem. — Aliqui insuper trahuntur solo amore dilecti.
paras.en: Moreover this drawing proceeds (as was said) from the divine charity, according to that of Jeremias: [[Jer 31:3|I have loved thee with an everlasting love, therefore have I drawn thee, taking pity on thee|In caritate perpetua dilexi te; ideo attraxi te miserans]]. And this is done in three ways. For some God draws by scourges, which are nevertheless inflicted out of love, as the Lord witnesses: [[Apoc 3:19|Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise|Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo]]. Wherefore Osee says: [[Osee 11:4|I will draw them with the cords of Adam, with the bands of love|In funiculis Adam traham eos, in vinculis caritatis]]. These cords are the penalties that follow upon original sin, by which we are afflicted and admonished to turn to God. Others God draws by benefits, like him who said: [[Ps 12:6|I will sing to the Lord, who giveth me good things|Cantabo Domino qui tribuit mihi bona]]; and, [[Ps 115:3|What shall I render to the Lord, for all the things that he hath rendered to me?|Quid retribuam Domino pro omnibus quæ retribuit mihi?]] Hear Isaias too, saying: [[Is 63:7|I will remember the tender mercies of the Lord, the praise of the Lord for all the things that the Lord hath bestowed upon us|Miserationum Domini recordabor; laudem Domini super omnibus quæ reddidit nobis Dominus]], and [[Is 63:7|which he hath given them according to his kindness|quæ largitus est nobis secundum indulgentiam suam]]. Others again He draws by promises, as those who are converted by the contemplation of the heavenly rewards: as the Apostle says of Moses, writing to the Hebrews, that [[Heb 11:26|he looked unto the reward|adspexit in remunerationem]]; and the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:112|I have inclined my heart to do thy justifications for ever, for the reward.|Inclinavi (inquit) cor meum ad faciendas justificationes tuas in æternum, propter retributionem]] And some, besides, are drawn by the love of the Beloved alone.

paras.t: A quibusdam additur quintus modus trahendi, qui est per occultam virtutem Spiritus Sancti et inspirationem internam. Sed iste modus generalis est omnibus præinductis, quoniam sine occulto influxu sive instinctu Spiritus Sancti, nec flagellis, nec donis, neque promissis, nec aliquo alio modo traheremur ad Christum. Illa autem tractio qua trahimur ad Deum solo ejus amore, præstantior est atque divinior, imo omnino deifica est: quia per eam ad Deum convertimur, eumque diligimus, honoramus, exquirimus, quoniam est in se ipso naturaliter atque totaliter bonus, sanctus, summus, perfectus. Unde hoc ipsum ad filios spectat carissimos.
paras.en: Some add a fifth way of drawing, which is by the hidden power of the Holy Ghost and inward inspiration. But this way is common to all those set out before, since without the hidden inflowing or prompting of the Holy Ghost we should be drawn to Christ neither by scourges, nor by gifts, nor by promises, nor in any other way. But that drawing by which we are drawn to God by His love alone is more excellent and more divine, nay, wholly deifying: for by it we are turned to God, and love, honour and seek Him, because He is in Himself, by nature and wholly, good, holy, supreme and perfect. Hence this belongs to the dearest sons.

paras.t: Et ego resuscitabo eum in novissimo die. Quid est hoc? Nonne et eos quos Pater non trahit, suscitaturus est Filius? Cur ergo quasi pro præmio spondet tracto, quod suscitabit eum in die novissimo? Et respondendum, juxta Apostolum, quod omnes utique resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur. Nunc ergo loquitur Christus de suscitatione beatæ immutationis, hoc est glorificationis in carne, quoniam anima propter naturalem inclinationem ad corpus, non est perfecte beata donec corpori glorificando reuniatur, vel potius glorificato fuerit copulata.
paras.en: [[6:44|And I will raise him up in the last day|Et ego resuscitabo eum in novissimo die]]. What does this mean? Will not the Son raise up also those whom the Father does not draw? Why then does He promise the one who is drawn, as if for a reward, that He will raise him up at the last day? The answer, according to the Apostle, is that [[1 Cor 15:51|We shall all indeed rise again: but we shall not all be changed|omnes utique resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur]]. So Christ is speaking here of the raising up of blessed change, that is, of glorification in the flesh; for the soul, because of its natural inclination to the body, is not perfectly blessed until it is reunited to the body that is to be glorified, or rather until it is joined to it glorified.

paras.t: Insuper probat Christus testimonio Prophetarum, quod multi sint, Patre trahente, convertendi ad ipsum. Est scriptum in Prophetis, id est in libris eorum: Et erunt tempore gratiæ omnes homines docibiles Dei, id est apti doceri vel docti a Deo. Sic tamen ut sit distributio pro generibus singulorum, non pro singulis generum: quomodo alibi dicitur, Et benedicentur in ipso omnes tribus terræ; et item in Daniele, Omnes gentes, tribus et linguæ servient ei: quum tamen comparatione aliorum, pauci sint qui Christo veraciter serviunt, sicut sunt pauci electi. Unde ad insinuandum quod post incarnationem Filii Dei, per prædicationem Evangelii essent incomparabiliter plures divinitus illustrandi atque ad Christum convertendi, quam ante, dicta sunt verba præallegata, et quod nunc Christus allegat: Erunt omnes docibiles Dei. Quocirca sciendum quod Christus, Apostoli et Evangelistæ frequenter allegant Scripturas veteris Testamenti potius quantum ad sensum, quam quoad formam verborum. Unde quod dicitur nunc, Erunt omnes docibiles Dei, invenitur non solum in uno Propheta, sed in multis, quantum ad sensum, quamvis in nullo inveniatur quoad formam sermonis. Scriptum est enim in Isaia: Repleta est terra scientia Domini, quasi aquæ maris operientes; et rursus, Ponam omnes filios tuos doctos a Domino. Jeremias quoque: Omnes a majore eorum usque ad minorem, cognoscent me.
paras.en: Further, Christ proves by the testimony of the Prophets that many are to be converted to Him, the Father drawing them. [[6:45|It is written in the prophets|Est scriptum in Prophetis]], that is, in their books: [[6:45|And they shall all be taught of God|Et erunt tempore gratiæ omnes homines docibiles Dei]]: that is, in the time of grace all men shall be apt to be taught, or taught, by God. Yet so that the distribution is over the kinds of individuals, not over the individuals of each kind [that is, “all” means men of every kind, not every single man]: as it is said elsewhere, [[Ps 71:17|And in him shall all the tribes of the earth be blessed|Et benedicentur in ipso omnes tribus terræ]]; and again in Daniel, [[Dan 7:14|all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him|Omnes gentes, tribus et linguæ servient ei]]: though in comparison with the rest, few are they who truly serve Christ, just as the chosen are few[[Matt 20:16||]][[Matt 22:14||]]. So, to intimate that after the Incarnation of the Son of God, through the preaching of the Gospel, incomparably more would be divinely enlightened and converted to Christ than before, the words alleged above were spoken, and those which Christ now alleges: [[6:45|they shall all be taught of God|Erunt omnes docibiles Dei]]. Wherefore it should be known that Christ, the Apostles and the Evangelists often allege the Scriptures of the Old Testament as to their sense rather than as to the form of the words. Hence what is said now, [[6:45|they shall all be taught of God|Erunt omnes docibiles Dei]], is found not in one Prophet only but in many, as to the sense, though in none is it found in the form of the words. For it is written in Isaias: [[Is 11:9|the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the covering waters of the sea|Repleta est terra scientia Domini, quasi aquæ maris operientes]]; and again, [[Is 54:13|All thy children shall be taught of the Lord|Ponam omnes filios tuos doctos a Domino]]. Jeremias too: [[Jer 31:34|all shall know me from the least of them even to the greatest|Omnes a majore eorum usque ad minorem, cognoscent me]].

paras.t: Omnis homo viator qui audivit auribus cordis a Patre intus loquente, id est, divinum instinctum advertit, et didicit per inspirationem internam, id est, quem Pater docuit de his quæ spectant ad fidem: qualis fuit qui ait, Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus; venit ad me per fidem et operationem, per caritatem et obedientiam. Ideo dicit Propheta: Beatus homo quem tu erudieris, Domine, et de lege tua docueris eum. Non ergo ad conversionem hominis sufficit vox prædicatoris, nisi fuerit Deus interius instruens.
paras.en: [[6:45|Every one|Omnis]] still in this life [*homo viator*, a wayfarer, one still on the way to the heavenly homeland] [[6:45|that hath heard|qui audivit]] with the ears of the heart [[6:45|of the Father|a Patre]] speaking within, that is, who has heeded the divine prompting, [[6:45|and hath learned|et didicit]] by inward inspiration, that is, whom the Father has taught about the things that belong to faith (such was he who said: [[Ps 84:9|I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me|Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus]]), [[6:45|cometh|venit]] to me by faith and working, by charity and obedience. Therefore the Prophet says: [[Ps 93:12|Blessed is the man whom thou shalt instruct, O Lord: and shalt teach him out of thy law.|Beatus homo quem tu erudieris, Domine, et de lege tua docueris eum]] So the voice of the preacher is not enough for a man's conversion, unless God is instructing him within.

paras.t: Denique Thomas in Summa contra gentiles redarguit Origenem dicentem, quod Deus dicitur causa bonorum nostrorum, solum quia est causa habituum infusorum per quos meritorie operamur, videlicet gratiæ habitualis, fidei, spei et caritatis. Dicit itaque Thomas, quod etiam quandoque Deus est proxima causa actionum nostrarum interiorum, Isaia testante, qui ait: Domine, dabis pacem nobis, omnia enim opera nostra operatus es in nobis; et item Apostolus: Deus est qui operatur in vobis et velle et perficere, pro bona voluntate, hoc est ex sua pietate voluntaria voluntateque pia, non meritis vestris. Dicit insuper Thomas, quod semper acquiescimus actuali inspirationi quæ nobis a Deo infunditur. Et fundatur hoc verbum Thomæ in auctoritate Augustini, dicentis: Gratia quæ occulte humanis cordibus divina largitate tribuitur, a nullo corde duro respuitur, quoniam ideo datur ut duritia cordis penitus auferatur.
paras.en: Further, Thomas, in the Summa contra gentiles, refutes Origen, who says that God is called the cause of our good things only because He is the cause of the infused habits by which we act meritoriously, namely of habitual grace, faith, hope and charity. So Thomas says that God is also at times the proximate cause of our inward acts, as Isaias witnesses, who says: [[Is 26:12|Lord, thou wilt give us peace: for thou hast wrought all our works for us|Domine, dabis pacem nobis, omnia enim opera nostra operatus es in nobis]]; and likewise the Apostle: [[Phil 2:13|it is God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will|Deus est qui operatur in vobis et velle et perficere, pro bona voluntate]], that is, out of His own willing loving-kindness and loving will, not by your merits. Thomas says besides that we always consent to the actual inspiration that is poured into us by God [*actual* grace: a passing movement of God in the soul, as distinct from *habitual* grace, which abides]. And this saying of Thomas is founded on the authority of Augustine, who says: The grace which is secretly bestowed on human hearts by the divine bounty is rejected by no hard heart, since it is given for this very purpose, that the hardness of the heart may be wholly taken away [Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, ch. 8].

paras.t: Ad propositum igitur: Omnis qui audivit didicitque a Patre, hoc est, actualem illustrationem immediate a Deo percepit, venit per consensum ad Christum, quoniam omnis talis veraciter acquiescit. Non tamen omnis talis salvatur, sed qui prædestinatus est, finaliter perseverans.
paras.en: To the point, then: [[6:45|Every one that hath heard of the Father and hath learned|Omnis qui audivit didicitque a Patre]], that is, who has received an actual enlightenment immediately from God, [[6:45|cometh|venit]] by consent to Christ, since every such man truly consents. Yet not every such man is saved, but he who is predestined, persevering to the end.

paras.t: Sed ne ex verbis inductis aliquis æstimaret Deum Patrem esse oculo carnis visibilem, vel intellectu comprehensibilem, addidit Christus: Non quia Patrem æternum vidit quisquam hominum oculo corporali, vel etiam intellectuali, loquendo de visione comprehensionis perfectæ: quia sic solus Deus comprehendit se ipsum, immensus immensum. Loquendo autem de visione Dei per speciem quam habent Sancti in patria, sic nullus purus viator vidit Deum visione fixa ac cœliformi, quamvis Moyses et Paulus credantur Deum in hac vita vidisse per speciem, in raptu quodam non diu durante. De hoc dictum est plenius primo capitulo, super illud: Deum nemo vidit unquam. Sed quoniam Christus hæc proferens homo fuit, ne Judæi putarent eum non vidisse Patrem, subjecit: nisi is qui est a Deo, hoc est Filius natus a Patre, vel missus a Deo Trinitate. Filius enim in quantum homo, missus ac originatus est a se ipso secundum quod Deus. Ac vidit Patrem visione perfectæ comprehensionis, in quantum est Deus, et item visione beatificæ fruitionis, secundum quod homo, ab incarnationis exordio. Ex hoc sequi videtur, quod Christus non loquitur de visione corporali, quia sic nec ipse videt Patrem. Porro, per hoc quod ait, Nisi is qui est a Patre, non excluditur Spiritus Sanctus quin et ipse comprehendat Patrem, quum dicat Apostolus, quod Spiritus scrutatur profunda Dei, et quæ Dei sunt nemo novit, nisi Spiritus ejus.
paras.en: But lest anyone should think from the words brought forward that God the Father is visible to the eye of flesh, or comprehensible by the intellect, Christ added: [[6:46|Not that any man hath seen the Father|Non quia Patrem æternum vidit quisquam]], the eternal Father, with the bodily eye, or even with the eye of the intellect, speaking of the vision of perfect comprehension: for in that way God alone comprehends Himself, the infinite the infinite. But speaking of the vision of God by sight [*per speciem*: seeing God as He is, as opposed to knowing Him by faith] which the Saints have in the homeland, in that way no mere wayfarer has seen God with a fixed and heavenly vision, though Moses and Paul are believed to have seen God by sight in this life, in a certain rapture that did not last long. Of this more was said in the first chapter, on the words: [[John 1:18|No man hath seen God at any time|Deum nemo vidit unquam]]. But since Christ, in saying these things, was a man, lest the Jews should think that He had not seen the Father, He added: [[6:46|but he who is of God|nisi is qui est a Deo]], that is, the Son born of the Father, or sent by God the Trinity. For the Son, inasmuch as He is man, is sent by and has His origin from Himself according as He is God. And He saw the Father with the vision of perfect comprehension inasmuch as He is God, and likewise with the vision of beatific enjoyment according as He is man, from the first moment of the Incarnation. From this it seems to follow that Christ is not speaking of bodily vision, since in that way not even He sees the Father. Further, by His saying, [[6:46|but he who is of God|Nisi is qui est a Patre]], the Holy Ghost is not excluded from Himself comprehending the Father, since the Apostle says that [[1 Cor 2:10|the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God|Spiritus scrutatur profunda Dei]], and [[1 Cor 2:11|the things also that are of God, no man knoweth, but the Spirit of God|quæ Dei sunt nemo novit, nisi Spiritus ejus]].

paras.t: Amen, amen dico vobis, qui credit in me fide caritate ornata, habet nunc vitam æternam in spe, in merito, in radice, in dispositione propinqua. Habet enim causam meritoriam spemque idoneam ingrediendi vitam æternam, seu obtinendi beatificam divinæ essentiæ visionem. Vel, habet vitam gratiæ realiter in præsenti. Qui enim credit in Christum, habet Christum. Et utique Christus est vita æterna, quemadmodum contestatur: Ego sum via, veritas et vita. Joannes quoque in prima sua ait Canonica: Hic est verus Deus et vita æterna.
paras.en: [[6:47|Amen, amen, I say unto you: He that believeth in me|Amen, amen dico vobis, qui credit in me]] with a faith adorned by charity, [[6:47|hath everlasting life|habet nunc vitam æternam]] now, in hope, in merit, in its root, in near disposition. For he has the meritorious cause, and a well-founded hope, of entering eternal life, or of obtaining the beatific vision of the divine essence. Or, he has the life of grace really in the present. For he who believes in Christ has Christ. And Christ is indeed eternal life, as He testifies: [[John 14:6|I am the way, and the truth, and the life|Ego sum via, veritas et vita]]. John too says in his first canonical Epistle: [[1 John 5:20|This is the true God and life eternal|Hic est verus Deus et vita æterna]].

paras.t: Ego sum panis vitæ substantialiter atque causaliter. Panis sum omnia pascens: non tamen in quemquam convertor, aut mutor, sed fideliter manducantem converto in me. Sum etiam panis vitæ, quia sumentibus digne do vitam gratiæ in præsenti, et vitam gloriæ in futuro. De hoc verbo superius dicta sunt plura.
paras.en: [[6:48|I am the bread of life|Ego sum panis vitæ]], in My substance and as its cause. I am the bread that feeds all things: yet I am not turned into anyone, or changed, but him who eats faithfully I turn into Myself. I am also the bread of life because to those who receive Me worthily I give the life of grace in the present, and the life of glory in the future. Much was said about this saying above[[6:35||]].

paras.t: Deinde inanem gloriationem Judæorum de manna præsumentium, Christus evacuat. Patres vestri manducaverunt manna in deserto, et mortui sunt. Palam est quod mortui sunt morte naturæ. Sed quia mox subditur, Hic est panis de cœlo descendens, ut si quis manducaverit ex ipso non moriatur, certum est quod loquitur de morte culpæ. Hoc enim Christus adjecit, distinguendo inter panem vitæ quem ipse dat, et manna. Sed numquid omnes patres Judæorum qui manna edebant, mortui sunt morte culpæ? Non utique, quia nec Moyses, nec Aaron, nec Josue, nec ceteri justi illius exercitus. Loquitur ergo Salvator de patribus Judæorum quorum vestigia isti sectabantur, puta incredulis seu perversis, qui dixerunt: Anima nostra nauseat super cibo isto levissimo. Illis quippe fuit panis ille insipidus. Justis vero optime sapiebat, quemadmodum in libro Sapientiæ scribitur: Panem de cœlo præstitisti eis, omne delectamentum in se habentem et omnis saporis suavitatem: ad quod enim quisque volebat, convertebatur. De illis vero carnalibus tantum, non carnalibus simul et spiritualibus patribus, loquitur Christus Judæis alio loco: Murmuratores, filii murmuratorum, implete mensuram patrum vestrorum.
paras.en: Next Christ empties the vain boasting of the Jews, who presumed upon the manna. [[6:49|Your fathers did eat manna in the desert: and are dead.|Patres vestri manducaverunt manna in deserto, et mortui sunt]] It is plain that they died the death of nature. But since there follows at once, [[6:50|This is the bread which cometh down from heaven: that if any man eat of it, he may not die|Hic est panis de cœlo descendens, ut si quis manducaverit ex ipso non moriatur]], it is certain that He speaks of the death of guilt. For Christ added this to distinguish between the bread of life which He Himself gives, and the manna. But did all the fathers of the Jews who ate the manna die the death of guilt? By no means: neither Moses, nor Aaron, nor Josue, nor the other just men of that host. So the Saviour is speaking of those fathers of the Jews whose footsteps these men were following, namely the unbelieving or perverse, who said: [[Num 21:5|our soul now loatheth this very light food|Anima nostra nauseat super cibo isto levissimo]]. For to them that bread was tasteless. But to the just it tasted most sweet, as is written in the book of Wisdom: Thou [[Wis 16:20|gavest them bread from heaven|Panem de cœlo præstitisti eis]], [[Wis 16:20|having in it all that is delicious, and the sweetness of every taste|omne delectamentum in se habentem et omnis saporis suavitatem]]: for [[Wis 16:21|it was turned to what every man liked|ad quod enim quisque volebat, convertebatur]]. Of those fathers who were carnal only, and not of those who were both carnal and spiritual, Christ speaks to the Jews in another place: Murmurers, sons of murmurers, [[Matt 23:32|Fill ye up then the measure of your fathers|implete mensuram patrum vestrorum]] [the words “murmurers, sons of murmurers” are not in the Gospel; Denis seems to have added them, perhaps thinking of Matt 23:31, “you are the sons of them that killed the prophets”].

paras.t: Subditur ergo de pane vero vitali, non figurali dumtaxat, quamvis et panis vitæ quem dat Christus, sit aliquo modo figurativus illius panis cœlestis in patria de quo in Luca habetur: Beatus qui manducabit panem in regno Dei. Hic panis vitæ de quo dictum est, utpote Verbum incarnatum, vel corpus dominicum, est panis de cœlo descendens. Verbum enim descendit per incarnationem, et novi effectus productionem. Corpus autem descendit, quia virtute Spiritus Sancti formatum, non quia de cœlo allatum. Descendens, inquam, ad hoc, ut si quis ex ipso manducaverit, manducatione sacramentali et spirituali simul, vel spiritualiter dumtaxat (de quibus in sequenti articulo plenius dicam, Deo præstante), non moriatur morte culpæ in præsenti, vel morte damnationis æternæ in futuro, quæ est mors secunda.
paras.en: So there follows, about the true life-giving bread, not merely a figure (though the bread of life which Christ gives is also in some way a figure of that heavenly bread in the homeland, of which we have in Luke: [[Luke 14:15|Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God|Beatus qui manducabit panem in regno Dei]]): [[6:50|This|Hic]] bread of life of which we have spoken, namely the Word incarnate, or the Lord's body, [[6:50|is the bread which cometh down from heaven|est panis de cœlo descendens]]. For the Word came down by the Incarnation, and by bringing about a new effect. And the body came down because it was formed by the power of the Holy Ghost, not because it was brought from heaven. It cometh down, I say, to this end, [[6:50|that if any man eat of it|ut si quis ex ipso manducaverit]], by sacramental and spiritual eating together, or by spiritual eating only (of which I shall speak more fully in the following article, God granting), [[6:50|he may not die|non moriatur]] the death of guilt in the present, or the death of eternal damnation in the future, which is the second death[[Apoc 2:11||]][[Apoc 20:6||]][[Apoc 20:14||]][[Apoc 21:8||]].

6.title: Elucidatio residuæ partis hujus capituli sexti, ab eo loco quo dicitur: Ego sum panis vivus, qui de cœlo descendi.
6.title_en: Explanation of the remaining part of this sixth chapter, from the place where it is said: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven.”

paras.t: Sacramentum Eucharistiæ instituit Christus dupliciter: primo, verbo seu assertione; secundo, facto seu consecratione. De prima autem institutione nunc agitur. Et quoniam sacramentum istud incomprehensibilissimum utilissimumque consistit, ideireo ad excludendum omnem errorem ac dubitationem, Christus apertissime tractat de sacramento hoc ipso.
paras.en: Christ instituted the sacrament of the Eucharist in two ways: first, by word or assertion; second, by deed or consecration. It is of the first institution that he now treats. And since this sacrament is most incomprehensible and most profitable, therefore, to shut out all error and doubt, Christ treats of this very sacrament most openly.

paras.t: Ego sum panis vivus: quia secundum naturam divinam essentialiter vita sum vivens in me ipso, et vitam gratiæ vitamque gloriæ causo in aliis, omnes electos reficiens et confortans. Porro, secundum naturam assumptam sum panis vivus, quoniam propter unionem cum Verbo, habeo plenitudinem omnium gratiarum et gloriam perfectissimæ fruitionis in Deo, atque per corpus et sanguinem meum, fidelium animas alo ac poto, gratiam illis præstando per modum causæ instrumentalis ac meritoriæ. Humanitas etenim Christi est instrumentum animatum, conjunctum ac proprium Verbi, per quod et cujus virtute ac merito, omnia divina nobis præstantur gratiarum charismata: sicut et corpus nostrum est instrumentum animatum, unitum et proprium animæ rationalis, per quod anima agit et effluit. Qui de cœlo descendi per incarnationis mysterium et novi effectus productionem, non per localem descensum, ut dictum est sæpius.
paras.en: [[6:51|I am the living bread|Ego sum panis vivus]]: since according to the divine nature I am essentially life, living in myself, and I cause the life of grace and the life of glory in others, refreshing and strengthening all the elect. Further, according to the nature assumed I am the living bread, since, because of the union with the Word, I have the fullness of all graces and the glory of most perfect enjoyment in God, and by my body and blood I feed and give drink to the souls of the faithful, bestowing grace on them by way of an instrumental and meritorious cause. For Christ's humanity is the living, conjoined and proper instrument of the Word, through which and by whose power and merit all the divine gifts of grace are bestowed on us: just as our body too is the living, united and proper instrument of the rational soul, through which the soul acts and flows out. [[6:51|which came down from heaven|Qui de cœlo descendi]], by the mystery of the incarnation and the producing of a new effect, not by a descent from place to place, as has been said often.

paras.t: Si quis manducaverit, non sacramentaliter tantum, sed sacramentaliter et spiritualiter, vel ad minus spiritualiter cum proposito manducandi sacramentaliter quum fuerit opportunum, ex hoc pane, vivet in æternum vita spirituali, quæ nunc in ipso inchoatur, et virtute sacramenti perficitur, atque in patria consummatur. Nunc enim vivit, bene agendo per gratiam; et in futuro vivet, Deum videndo per glorias lumen, dummodo finaliter perseveret in hujus manducationis effectu. Vivet itaque in æternum, quantum est ex parte sacramenti, quod tantæ efficaciæ est, ut possit vitam æternam influere. — Quum quilibet communicans recipiat panem istum totum ac integrum, non partem dumtaxat, cur ait, Si quis manducaverit ex hoc pane, et non potius, Si quis manducaverit hunc panem? Dicendum, quod ad insinuandum quod panis iste inconsumptibilis est, nunquam deficiens.
paras.en: [[6:52|If any man eat|Si quis manducaverit]], not sacramentally only, but sacramentally and spiritually, or at least spiritually with the purpose of eating sacramentally when it shall be opportune, [[6:52|of this bread, he shall live for ever|ex hoc pane, vivet in æternum]], with the spiritual life, which is now begun in him, and is perfected by the power of the sacrament, and consummated in the fatherland. For now he lives by doing well through grace; and in the future he will live by seeing God through the light of glory, provided that he perseveres to the end in the effect of this eating. *He shall live for ever*, then, so far as lies with the sacrament, which is of such efficacy that it can pour in eternal life. But since every communicant receives this bread whole and entire, not a part only, why does he say *If any man eat of this bread*, and not rather *If any man eat this bread*? It must be said that it is to suggest that this bread cannot be used up, and never fails.

paras.t: Preterea, ad intelligendum omnia quæ de isto sacramento jam asseruntur, oportet scire quod in Sacramento altaris sunt tria: Primum est sacramentum tantum, videlicet species panis et vini post consecrationem. Secundum est res et sacramentum, videlicet corpus et sanguis Christi. Tertium est res tantum, utpote gratia sacramentalis, vel unitas corporis mystici. Species itaque panis et vini dicuntur sacramentum, quoniam rei sacræ sunt signum, videlicet corporis et sanguinis Christi. Corpus vero est sacramentum respectu sui effectus, qui est gratia, vel respectu sui signati, quod est corpus mysticum, puta Ecclesia. Quum igitur aliquis accipit corpus et sanguinem sub speciebus sacramentalibus, et non participat sacramenti hujus effectum, scilicet gratiam atque Ecclesiæ incorporationem, propter suam incapacitatem, indignitatem et pravitatem, qua ponit obicem gratis, dicitur manducare sacramentaliter tantum. Quum vero sumendo sacramentum, recipit ejus salutarem effectum, manducat sacramenlaliter et spiritualiter. Dum autem sortitur effectum præfatum, nec tamen suscipit sacramentum, manducat spiritualiter solum.
paras.en: Further, to understand all that is now said of this sacrament, we must know that in the Sacrament of the altar there are three things. The first is the sacrament only [*sacramentum tantum*], namely the species of bread and wine after the consecration. The second is the reality and sacrament [*res et sacramentum*], namely the body and blood of Christ. The third is the reality only [*res tantum*], namely sacramental grace, or the unity of the mystical body. The species of bread and wine, then, are called the sacrament, since they are the sign of a sacred thing, namely of the body and blood of Christ. The body is a sacrament in respect of its effect, which is grace, or in respect of what it signifies, which is the mystical body, namely the Church. When, then, someone receives the body and blood under the sacramental species and does not share in the effect of this sacrament, namely grace and incorporation into the Church, because of his incapacity, unworthiness and wickedness, by which he puts an obstacle to grace, he is said to eat sacramentally only. But when in taking the sacrament he receives its saving effect, he eats sacramentally and spiritually. And when he obtains the said effect and yet does not receive the sacrament, he eats spiritually only.

paras.t: Et panis quem ego dabo, per me ipsum in Cœna, hoc sacramentum instituendo discipulisque tradendo, et in ara crucis panem hunc Patri offerendo, et. deinceps per meos ministros, videlicet sacerdotes, quibus convenit sacramentum istud consecrare atque porrigere aliis; caro ea est, quæ alit mentem fidelium: tum quia Verbo unita, tum quoniam gratiis plena per redundantiam, et quia Divinitatis gratiam creantis est instrumentum, itemque merito suæ actionis ac passionis; pro mundi vita, id est pro spirituali vivificatione hominum viatorum in mundo degentium. Ad hunc enim finem, ut a morte culpæ ac miseriæ eriperemur, vitamque gratie et gloriæ consequeremur, dedit Christus corpus suum in cruce in pretium, et in sacramento in edulium atque remedium. Quotidie quoque dat panem istum pro vita nostra, hoc est, ad hoc ut in vita gratie roboremur ac perficiamur.
paras.en: [[6:52|and the bread that I will give|Et panis quem ego dabo]], by myself at the Supper, by instituting this sacrament and handing it to the disciples, and by offering this bread to the Father on the altar of the cross, and afterwards through my ministers, namely the priests, to whom it belongs to consecrate this sacrament and hand it to others, [[6:52|is my flesh|caro mea est]], which feeds the mind of the faithful: both because it is united to the Word, and because it is full of graces by overflow, and because it is the instrument of the Godhead creating grace, and also by the merit of its action and passion; [[6:52|for the life of the world|pro mundi vita]], that is, for the spiritual quickening of wayfaring men living in the world. For to this end, that we might be snatched from the death of guilt and misery and obtain the life of grace and glory, Christ gave his body on the cross as a price, and in the sacrament as food and remedy. Daily too he gives this bread for our life, that is, so that we may be strengthened and perfected in the life of grace.

paras.t: Verumtamen non est sic intelligendum quod ait, Pro mundi vita, quod per receptionem hujus sacramenti, vita gratia in homine inchoetur: imo, qui sine vita gratiæ ad hoc sacramentum accederet, amplius moreretur in anima, reusque fieret corporis Domini. Quum enim sacramentum istud sit cibus spiritualis, ideo, sicut cibus corporalis non datur nec prodest nisi viventi vita natura, sic cibus hic spiritualis non convenit nec proficit nisi viventi vita gratia.
paras.en: Yet what he says, *for the life of the world*, is not to be understood as if by the receiving of this sacrament the life of grace were begun in a man: on the contrary, he who came to this sacrament without the life of grace would die the more in his soul, and become guilty of the body of the Lord[[1 Cor 11:27||]]. For since this sacrament is spiritual food, therefore, as bodily food is not given to, nor profits, any but one living with the life of nature, so this spiritual food does not befit nor profit any but one living with the life of grace.

paras.t: Litigabant ergo, id est, verbis contendebant, Judæi, hæc ab ore Christi audientes, et carnaliter ac ruditer capientes, ad invicem dicentes ex infidelitate et inordinata admiratione: Quomodo potest hic, quem tenemus pro puro homine et filio Joseph, nobis carnem suam dare ad manducandum ? quasi dicant: Hoc impossibile est atque inutile. Christus vero testatur hoc esse, non solum non inutile, sed insuper necessarium ad salutem ipsorum.
paras.en: [[6:53|The Jews therefore strove|Litigabant ergo Judæi]], that is, contended in words, hearing these things from Christ's mouth and taking them carnally and crudely, [[6:53|among themselves, saying|ad invicem dicentes]], out of unbelief and disordered wonder: [[6:53|How can this man give us his flesh to eat|Quomodo potest hic nobis carnem suam dare ad manducandum?]], this man whom we hold to be a mere man and the son of Joseph? as though they said: This is impossible and useless. But Christ testifies that it is not only not useless, but moreover necessary for their salvation.

paras.t: Dicit ergo eis Jesus: Amen, amen dico vobis, nisi manducaveritis carnem Filii hominis, in Sacramento, sacramentaliter et spiritualiter, vel spiritualiter ad minus, per fidem et votum accedendo gratiamque Christi participando, et biberitis ejus sanguinem modo prædicto, non habebitis vitam spiritualem in vobis, sed carebitis gratia in præsenti et gloria in futuro. Quemadmodum enim membra corporis naturalis moriuntur ac pereunt, nisi capiti connectantur, et ab eo motum sensumque participent; sic homines, ex quibus quasi ex membris constituitur mysticum corpus Christi, vita gratie destituuntur, nisi capiti, quod est Christus, per sacram communionem nectantur, recipiendo ab illo vitam spiritualem et motum meritorium. Preterea, sicut corpus sine corporeo cibo non sustentatur, nec permanet in vita naturali, sic anima sine hoc cibo vivifico non persistit in vita gratiæ spirituali.
paras.en: [[6:54|Then Jesus said to them: Amen, amen, I say unto you: except you eat the flesh of the Son of man|Dicit ergo eis Jesus: Amen, amen dico vobis, nisi manducaveritis carnem Filii hominis]], in the Sacrament, sacramentally and spiritually, or at least spiritually, by approaching by faith and desire and sharing in the grace of Christ, [[6:54|and drink his blood|et biberitis ejus sanguinem]] in the way just said, [[6:54|you shall not have life in you|non habebitis vitam spiritualem in vobis]], the spiritual life, but you will be without grace in the present and glory in the future. For as the members of a natural body die and perish unless they are joined to the head and receive movement and sense from it, so men, of whom as of members the mystical body of Christ is made up, are bereft of the life of grace unless they are joined by holy communion to the head, which is Christ[[Col 1:18||]], receiving from him spiritual life and meritorious movement. Further, as the body without bodily food is not sustained nor remains in natural life, so the soul without this life-giving food does not persist in the spiritual life of grace.

paras.t: Sed verba inducta intelligenda non sunt quasi sanguis Christi seorsum sumendus sit a vulgo communicante. In primitiva tamen Ecclesia hoc fiebat; sed nunc ordinatum est aliter, propter effusionis perieulum. Sanguinem ergo Christi accipit populus spiritualiter, et etiam aliquo modo realiter, quia in Sacramento corporis continetur et sanguis, sicut econtra. Licet enim transsubstantiatio panis directe terminetur ad carnem Salvatoris, et conversio vini ad sanguinem ejus, ex naturali tamen concomitantia, sub utraque specie sunt quatuor: quia sub specie panis est corpus Christi, vi conversionis; anima vero, sanguis et Verbum, sunt ibi ex naturali sequela, quum non sint separata ab invicem. Pariformiter sub specie vini, est sanguis directe, puta ex vi conversionis; earo autem, anima et Verbum concomitantur.
paras.en: But the words cited are not to be understood as if the blood of Christ were to be taken separately by the common people at communion. In the early Church, indeed, this was done; but now it is ordered otherwise, because of the danger of spilling. The people, then, receive the blood of Christ spiritually, and also in some way really, since in the Sacrament of the body the blood too is contained, and conversely. For although the transubstantiation of the bread ends directly in the flesh of the Saviour, and the conversion of the wine in his blood, yet by natural concomitance [that is, because what is really united cannot be apart] four things are under each species: since under the species of bread is the body of Christ, by the force of the conversion; but the soul, the blood and the Word are there by natural consequence, since they are not separated from one another. In like manner under the species of wine is the blood directly, namely by the force of the conversion; but the flesh, the soul and the Word accompany it.

paras.t: Qui manducat meam carnem et bibit meum sanguinem, non sacramentaliter tantum, sicut jam dictum est, habet vitam æternam, quoniam habet me ipsum, et habet vitam gratie, qua virtute hujus sacramenti continuatur, donec ad vitam gloriæ sempiterna pertingat. Futuram quoque beatitudinem jam habet in spe, virtute et gratia hujus sacramenti. Et ego resuscitabo eum in novissimo die, ut me Deum et hominem videat oculis carnis et cordis per propriam speciem, quem nunc cernit per fidem. Carnalibus enim oculis videbimus Christum in humanitate, mentalibus vero in divinitate.
paras.en: [[6:55|He that eateth my flesh and drinketh my blood|Qui manducat meam carnem et bibit meum sanguinem]], not sacramentally only, as has just been said, [[6:55|hath everlasting life|habet vitam æternam]], since he has me myself, and has the life of grace, which by the power of this sacrament is continued until it reaches the everlasting life of glory. He has future beatitude too already in hope, by the power and grace of this sacrament. [[6:55|and I will raise him up in the last day|Et ego resuscitabo eum in novissimo die]], so that he may see me, God and man, with the eyes of the flesh and of the heart, in my own form, whom he now sees by faith. For with the eyes of the flesh we shall see Christ in his humanity, but with the eyes of the mind in his divinity.

paras.t: Caro enim mea vere est cibus, et sanguis meus vere est potus. Hoc ait Salvator, ne putaretur parabolice loqui more consueto, ita quod carnem suam diceret panem, quia signaretur per panem, et esset sub forma panis solum sicut in signo, vel propter aliquam proprietatem cum pane cibus diceretur: quomodo dicit Apostolus, Petra erat Christus, quoniam figuravit Christum; et Isaias, Vere fœnum est populus, propter convenientiam quamdam; et infra ait de se ipso Salvator, Ego sum vitis vera. Ad insinuandum ergo quod caro sua sit vere et substantialiter sub specie panis, veraciterque sumatur a communicante, sanguis quoque ipsius vere sub specie vini contineatur et recipiatur. adjecit: Caro mea, id est corpus: sumitur enim nunc caro, non prout ossa excludit, sed pro toto corpore nervos, venas ac ossa habente; vere est cibus animæ, non corporis, quia non visibiliter nee corporaliter sumitur, quamvis verum corpus sumatur. Et potius dicit, Caro, quam Corpus, quia nunc loquitur de corpore suo in quantum est alimonia spiritus: caro autem magis dicit quid comestibile, quam corpus. Et sanguis meus vere est potus refrigerans, rigans, inebrians mentem, non ventrem. Omnia quippe sacramenta novæ legis ordinantur ad spiritualem vitam. Spiritualis autem vita per Baptismum acquiritur, quia Baptismus est regeneratio spiritualis; et per Confirmationem augetur. Oportet ergo ut per aliquod sacramentum nutriatur: et hoc est Eucharistiæ, quæ est spirituale alimentum hujusmodi vite. Cibum autem oportet realiter addi atque uniri eibato: idcirco in sacramento hoc Christus realiter continetur. substantialiterque communicanti unitur. Et simile est de sanguine, qui est potus. Præterea, quoniam sacramentum istud est cibus, ideo quidquid operatur cibus materialis in corpore manducantis, hoc agit hic cibus spiritualis in anima digne recipientis. Quemadmodum ergo cibus corporeus naturalem vitam sustentat, confortat, ad perfectionem deducit, deperditum reparat, delectat, impinguat; sic cibus iste vivifieus vitam spiritualem ac deiformem in anima fulcit, roborat, perficit, amissa bona restaurat, exhilarat et impinguat, divitias gratiæ accumulando in anima. Unde effectus sacramenti istius, sunt collatio gratiæ, adeptio gloriæ, remissio peccati mortalis obliti ac venialium, diminutio pœnæ, mitigatio fomitis, preservatio a malis futuris, secundum quod dicit Chrysostomus: Sicut leones flammam spirantes, sic ab illa mensa discedimus terribiles facti diabolo.
paras.en: [[6:56|For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed|Caro enim mea vere est cibus, et sanguis meus vere est potus]]. The Saviour says this lest he be thought to speak in a parable after his usual manner, so that he called his flesh bread because it was signified by bread and was under the form of bread only as in a sign, or was called food because of some property in common with bread: as the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 10:4|and the rock was Christ|Petra erat Christus]], since it figured Christ; and Isaias, [[Is 40:7|Indeed the people is grass|Vere fœnum est populus]], because of a certain likeness [the margin is read as Is. xi, 7; the words are Is 40:7]; and below the Saviour says of himself, [[John 15:1|I am the true vine|Ego sum vitis vera]]. To suggest, then, that his flesh is truly and substantially under the species of bread and is truly taken by the communicant, and his blood also truly contained and received under the species of wine, he added: *my flesh*, that is, body: for flesh is taken here not as it excludes bone, but for the whole body having sinews, veins and bones; *is meat indeed* of the soul, not of the body, since it is not taken visibly or bodily, though the true body is taken. And he says *flesh* rather than *body*, since he is now speaking of his body in so far as it is nourishment of the spirit: and *flesh* means something eatable more than *body* does. *And my blood is drink indeed*, cooling, watering, inebriating the mind, not the belly. For all the sacraments of the new law are ordered to the spiritual life. Spiritual life is acquired by Baptism, since Baptism is spiritual regeneration; and it is increased by Confirmation. So it must be nourished by some sacrament: and this is the Eucharist, which is the spiritual food of this life. And food must be really added to and united with the one fed: therefore in this sacrament Christ is really contained, and substantially united to the communicant. And it is the same with the blood, which is drink. Further, since this sacrament is food, whatever material food works in the body of the one eating, this spiritual food does in the soul of the one who receives it worthily. As, then, bodily food sustains, strengthens, brings to perfection the natural life, repairs what was lost, delights and fattens, so this life-giving food props up, strengthens and perfects the spiritual and godlike life in the soul, restores lost goods, gladdens and fattens, heaping up the riches of grace in the soul. Hence the effects of this sacrament are the bestowing of grace, the gaining of glory, the remission of mortal sin forgotten and of venial sins, the lessening of punishment, the easing of the *fomes* [the tinder of sin, the inclination to evil left by original sin], and preservation from evils to come, according to what Chrysostom says: Like lions breathing flame, so we go away from that table made terrible to the devil.

paras.t: Voluit quoque Christus in hoc sacramento veraciter contineri ac suscipi, ad ostendendum perfectum fervorem suæ incomprehensibilis caritatis ad nos, et propter nostram utilitatem, quia ex reali præsentia atque immediata unione Christi nobiscum, consequimur maxima bona, sicut subjungitur.
paras.en: Christ willed, too, to be truly contained and received in this sacrament, to show the perfect fervour of his incomprehensible charity towards us, and for our benefit, since from the real presence and immediate union of Christ with us we obtain the greatest goods, as is added next.

paras.t: Qui manducat meam carnem sacramentaliter et spiritualiter, et bibit meum sanguinem eodem modo, in me manet per caritatem et gratiam, et mihi incorporatur. Talis utique habitat in adjutorio Altissimi, et in protectione Dei cœli commoratur. Et ego in illo permaneo, per salutares hujus sacramenti effectus, per gratiosam custodiam, per inhabitationem benignam. Nam et per eadem dona quibus Deus ad nos converti et in nobis esse ac habitare quasi in templo asseritur, in quantum ea infundit atque conservat, nos quoque ad eum redimus, et in ipso subsistimus ac manemus. Palam est quod speciebus sacramentalibus jam consumptis, desinat Christus esse in communicante per præsentiam carnis et sanguinis; permanet tamen in eo per præsentiam suæ divinitatis, et per effectus sacramenti prætactos. Communicans ergo manet in Christo, sicut membrum in capite, recipiendo influentiam ejus; et Christus manet in illo, sicut caput in membro, influendo in illud.
paras.en: [[6:57|He that eateth my flesh|Qui manducat meam carnem]] sacramentally and spiritually, [[6:57|and drinketh my blood|et bibit meum sanguinem]] in the same way, [[6:57|abideth in me|in me manet]] by charity and grace, and is incorporated into me. Such a one indeed [[Ps 90:1|dwelleth in the aid of the most High, shall abide under the protection|habitat in adjutorio Altissimi, et in protectione Dei]] [Denis: “… abideth under the protection of the God of heaven”]. [[6:57|and I in him|Et ego in illo]] abide, by the saving effects of this sacrament, by gracious guarding, by kindly indwelling. For by the same gifts by which God is said to turn to us and to be and dwell in us as in a temple, in so far as he pours them in and keeps them, we too return to him, and subsist and abide in him. It is plain that once the sacramental species are consumed, Christ ceases to be in the communicant by the presence of his flesh and blood; yet he abides in him by the presence of his divinity, and by the effects of the sacrament spoken of. The communicant, then, abides in Christ as a member in the head, by receiving his influence; and Christ abides in him as the head in a member, by flowing into it.

paras.t: Ecce quanta beatitudo, dignitas et gloria devotorum, qui tam prestantissimo alimento vescuntur, et Christo tam intime copulantur, tantisque gratie donis deificis adimplentur; quanta denique est dilectio, dignatio, liberalitas et misericordia Christi veri Dei, qui nobis pauperculis et indignis sic præstat, sic unit, sic ingerit semetipsum. Nonne veraciter monstrat quod deliciæ ejus sunt esse cum filiis hominum, et quam paratus est dare nobis omnem gratiam suam, quibus tam ineffabiliter præstat se ipsum ?
paras.en: Behold how great is the beatitude, dignity and glory of the devout, who feed on so surpassing a food, are so intimately joined to Christ, and are filled with such godlike gifts of grace; how great, lastly, is the love, condescension, liberality and mercy of Christ the true God, who so gives, so unites, so bestows himself on us poor and unworthy creatures. Does he not truly show that [[Prov 8:31|my delights were to be with the children of men|deliciæ ejus sunt esse cum filiis hominum]] [Denis: “his delights are to be with the children of men”], and how ready he is to give us all his grace, to whom he gives himself so ineffably?

paras.t: Non ergo simus ingrati tanto benefactori et tam incomprehensibilibus beneficiis ejus; sed fervido animo, sollicita mente reverentique corde ei ministremus, ad ejus mensam nos præparemus, ad ejus mansionem in nobis nos dignificemus, venialia cuncta pro posse vitando, mentem ad Christum frequenter erigendo, cordis custodiæ jugiter insistendo. Tune enim poterimus fructum multiplicem hujus sacramenti percipere, ejusque dulcedinem mirabiliter degustare: quod aliter non contingit. Quamvis enim venialia et distrætio improvisa, sacramenti hujus principales effectus non impediant, impediunt tamen experimentalem gustum suavitatis ipsius. Dicamus ergo mente intenta ac grata cum Propheta, Benedic, anima mea, Domino, et noli oblivisci omnes retributiones ejus: imo, totum psalmum in quo continetur iste versicutus, quia præcipue applieabilis est ad regratiandum Christo pro beneficiis istis.
paras.en: Let us not, then, be ungrateful to so great a benefactor and for his so incomprehensible benefits; but with fervent spirit, careful mind and reverent heart let us serve him, prepare ourselves for his table, make ourselves worthy of his dwelling in us, avoiding all venial sins as far as we can, often lifting up the mind to Christ, and keeping constantly to the guard of the heart. For then we shall be able to receive the manifold fruit of this sacrament, and taste its sweetness wonderfully: which does not happen otherwise. For although venial sins and unforeseen distraction do not hinder the chief effects of this sacrament, they do hinder the tasting by experience of its sweetness. Let us say, then, with attentive and grateful mind, with the Prophet: [[Ps 102:2|Bless the Lord, O my soul, and never forget all he hath done for thee|Benedic, anima mea, Domino, et noli oblivisci omnes retributiones ejus]]; nay, the whole psalm in which this verse is contained, since it is especially fitting for giving thanks to Christ for these benefits.

paras.t: Sicut misit me vivens Pater, id est Pater eternus omnis vite fontale principium, qui est substantialiter sua vita, et ego vivo propter Patrem. Hoc præcipue intelligendum est de Christo secundum naturam assumptam, ut sit sensus: Et ego vivo propter Patrem, id est, vitam meam refero ad Patrem, videlicet ad honorem et gloriam ejus, sicut ad superiorem et ultimum finem. Imo, sic Christus retulit vitam suam ad totam Trinitatem, quæ est omnis creatæ naturæ ultimus finis. Potest quoque exponi de Christo secundum naturam divinam, hoc modo: Vivo propter Patrem, id est, a Patre vitam accepi, non aliam, sed eamdem quam possidet ipse. Et qui manducat me sacramentaliter ac spiritualiter, et ipse vivet per caritatem et gratiam, propter me, id est, ad honorem et gloriam meam ordinabit vitam suam: quemadmodum ait Apostolus, Omne quodcumque facitis in verbo vel opere, in gloriam Dei facite. Vel, Vivet propter me, id est, a me spiritualis vitæ augmentum recipiet, et vivifieabitur quotidie magis perfecte. In hoc enim sacramento continetur fons gratie, qui communicanem perfundit atque vivificat, nisi obicem ponat.
