paras.en: [[6:58|As the living Father hath sent me|Sicut misit me vivens Pater]], that is, the eternal Father, the fountain-principle of all life, who is substantially his own life, [[6:58|and I live by the Father|et ego vivo propter Patrem]]. This is to be understood chiefly of Christ according to the nature assumed, the sense being: *and I live by the Father*, that is, I refer my life to the Father, namely to his honour and glory, as to the higher and last end. Nay, Christ so referred his life to the whole Trinity, which is the last end of all created nature. It can also be explained of Christ according to the divine nature, in this way: *I live by the Father*, that is, I have received life from the Father, not another, but the same that he himself possesses. [[6:58|so he that eateth me|Et qui manducat me]], sacramentally and spiritually, [[6:58|the same also shall live|et ipse vivet]] by charity and grace, [[6:58|by me|propter me]], that is, will order his life to my honour and glory: as the Apostle says, [[Col 3:17|All whatsoever you do in word or in work|Omne quodcumque facitis in verbo vel opere]], [[1 Cor 10:31|do all to the glory of God|in gloriam Dei facite]]. Or, *shall live by me*, that is, shall receive from me the increase of spiritual life, and be quickened daily more perfectly. For in this sacrament is contained the fountain of grace, which floods and quickens the communicant, unless he puts an obstacle.

paras.t: Hic est panis supersubstantialis, qui de cœlo summo descendit: in quo patet nobilitas ac desiderabilitas ejus. Quomodo autem Christo secundum utramque naturam conveniat esse panem, et descendisse de cœlo, jam dictum est sæpius. Non sicut manducaverunt patres vestri manna: id est, panis iste præstantior et efficacior est quam manna, quum sit verus cibus, non figurativus, gratiam conferens, non promittens. Manna autem fuit figura hujus panis; nec contulit gratiam, sed præsignavit. Per hoc enim quod omne delectamentum continebat, figuravit quod sacramentum Eucharistiæ omnem spiritualem dulcedinem, virtutem et gratiam contineret. Et mortui sunt. Omnes enim illi qui manna comederunt, mortui sunt morte naturali ac corporali; sed quidam eorum, quibus isti increduli Juda similes erant, mortui sunt morte culpa.
paras.en: [[6:59|This is the bread that came down from heaven|Hic est panis … quæ de cœlo … descendit]] [Denis: “This is the supersubstantial bread, which came down from the highest heaven”]: in which its nobility and desirability are plain. How it belongs to Christ according to both natures to be bread, and to have come down from heaven, has been said often already. [[6:59|Not as your fathers did eat manna|Non sicut manducaverunt patres vestri manna]]: that is, this bread is more excellent and more effective than manna, since it is true food, not figurative, conferring grace, not promising it. Manna was a figure of this bread; and it did not confer grace, but signified it. For by containing every delight[[Wis 16:20||]], it figured that the sacrament of the Eucharist would contain all spiritual sweetness, power and grace. [[6:59|and are dead|Et mortui sunt]]. For all those who ate the manna died a natural and bodily death; but some of them, whom these unbelieving Jews were like, died the death of guilt.

paras.t: Qui manducat hunc panem digne, cum debita reverentia et devotione, in memoriam dominicæ passionis atque eximiæ caritatis Christi, dijudicans corpus Domini. Instituit enim Christus hoc sacramentum in memoriam suæ amarissimæ passionis et ardentissime dilectionis, quatenus toties suæ dilectionis nos flamma æcenderet, et ad ejus sectanda vestigia pronos efficeret, quoties sacramentum istud superdignissimum, angelis adorandum, susciperemus. Vivet in æternum, in anima per spiritualem virtutem et gratiam hujus panis, imo et tandem vivet vita beata ac immortali in corpore et anima, suscitatus atque feliciter immutatus a Christo.
paras.en: [[6:59|He that eateth this bread|Qui manducat hunc panem]] worthily, with due reverence and devotion, in memory of the Lord's passion and of the surpassing charity of Christ, [[1 Cor 11:29|discerning the body of the Lord|dijudicans corpus Domini]]. For Christ instituted this sacrament in memory of his most bitter passion and most ardent love, so that as often as we received this most worthy sacrament, to be adored by angels, he might kindle us with the flame of his love and make us ready to follow his footsteps. [[6:59|shall live for ever|Vivet in æternum]], in the soul by spiritual power and grace; nay, and at last he shall live a blessed and immortal life in body and soul, raised up and happily changed by Christ.

paras.t: Hæc verba præinducta dixit Jesus in synagoga docens, in Capharnaum metropoli Galilææ. Potest autem per synagogam intelligi vel congregatio Judæorum, vel domus in qua ad audiendum atque orandum confluxerant. Quamvis enim Judæi non poterant immolare nisi in templo Jerusalem, in singulis tamen urbibus habebant domum vel synagogam, in qua convenerunt ad audiendum verbum Dei et lectionem legis ac Prophetarum, et ad deprecandum Dominum. Docuit ergo Christus in civitate præcipua, in loco patenti in populo magno, quasi non timens reprehendi, nec falsa annuntians. Unde in passione respondit: Ego palam locutus sum mundo, ego semper docui in synagogis, etc. Omnis enim qui facit veritatem, venit ad lucem.
paras.en: [[6:60|These things he said, teaching in the synagogue, in Capharnaum|Hæc dixit in synagoga docens, in Capharnaum]], the chief city of Galilee. By the synagogue may be understood either the congregation of the Jews, or the house in which they had flocked together to hear and to pray. For although the Jews could not offer sacrifice except in the temple at Jerusalem, yet in each city they had a house or synagogue in which they came together to hear the word of God and the reading of the law and the Prophets, and to pray to the Lord. Christ, then, taught in the chief city, in an open place, among a great people, as one not afraid of being reproved nor announcing false things. Hence in his passion he answered: [[John 18:20|I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in the synagogue|Ego palam locutus sum mundo, ego semper docui in synagogis]], etc. For [[John 3:21|But he that doth truth cometh to the light|Omnis enim qui facit veritatem, venit ad lucem]] [Denis: “every one that doth truth …”].

paras.t: Multi ergo audientes ex discipulis ejus, id est, multi discipulorum Christi audientes Christum tam alta et incomprehensibilia de se ipso, et corporis sui edulio ac sanguinis poculo pradieantem, dixerunt: Durus, id est ad intelligendum difficilis, et rationi vel veritati contrarius, est hic sermo, ille præcipuus quo dixit: Panis quem ego dabo, earo mea est, etc. Quis potest eum audire, quum sonet tam male? quasi dicant: Blasphemare videtur, et obturanda sunt aures. Verba siquidem Christi de comestione suæ carnis potuque sanguinis, carnaliter intelligebant, putantes quod sic promitteret se daturum suum corpus ad manducandum sanguinemque ad potandum, quomodo alii cibi ac potus apponuntur.
paras.en: [[6:61|Many therefore of his disciples, hearing it, said|Multi ergo audientes ex discipulis ejus, dixerunt]], that is, many of Christ's disciples, hearing Christ preach such high and incomprehensible things of himself, and of the food of his body and the cup of his blood, said: [[6:61|This saying is hard|Durus est hic sermo]], that is, hard to understand, and contrary to reason or truth, this chief saying in which he said, *The bread that I will give is my flesh*, etc. [[6:61|and who can hear it|Quis potest eum audire]], since it sounds so ill? as though they said: He seems to blaspheme, and our ears must be stopped. For they understood Christ's words on the eating of his flesh and the drinking of his blood carnally, thinking that he was promising to give his body to be eaten and his blood to be drunk in the way other foods and drinks are set before men.

paras.t: Sciens autem Jesus apud semetipsum, id est in luce propria notitiæ, absque exteriori perceptione, quia murmurarent de hoc quod dixit se panem vivum descendentem de eclo, vel de hoc quod dixit se præstiturum carnem suam ad manducandum, discipuli ejus, non veri ac humiles, sed superbi, dixit eis: Hoc vos scandalizat, hoc est, ad ruinam peccati, ad murmurationem perfidiamque inducit, non ex parte mei, sed ex vestra imperfectione ? Fuit ergo ibi scandalum passivum, non activum. Si ergo videritis Filium hominis ascendentem in corpore glorificato ubi erat prius, id est ad cœlum, in quo fuit ante incarnationem, non secundum naturam humanam, sed divinam ? Unde ad insinuandum unitatem persona utriusque naturæ in Christo, dicitur Filius hominis fuisse in eclo, antequam descendit in Virginem.
paras.en: [[6:62|But Jesus, knowing in himself|Sciens autem Jesus apud semetipsum]], that is, in the proper light of his knowledge, without outward perception, [[6:62|that his disciples murmured at this|quia murmurarent de hoc discipuli ejus]], namely that he had said he was the living bread come down from heaven, or that he had said he would give his flesh to be eaten (his disciples, not true and humble ones, but proud), [[6:62|said to them: Doth this scandalize you|dixit eis: Hoc vos scandalizat]], that is, lead you to the downfall of sin, to murmuring and unbelief, not on my part but from your imperfection? There was, then, passive scandal there, not active [that is, they took offence where none was given]. [[6:63|If then you shall see the Son of man ascend up where he was before|Si ergo videritis Filium hominis ascendentem in corpore glorificato ubi erat prius]], ascending in his glorified body, that is, to heaven, in which he was before the incarnation, not according to the human nature but according to the divine? Hence, to suggest the unity of person of both natures in Christ, the Son of man is said to have been in heaven before he came down into the Virgin.

paras.t: His verbis Christus evacuavit atque dissolvit scandalum discipulorum. Per hoc enim quod prædixit se in conspectu ipsorum, si secum manerent, ascensurum in eclum, patere potuit quod descendit de cœlo, et quod non daret corpus suum ad manducandum carnaliter, eo modo quo aliæ carnes eduntur, non sine earum divisione, laceratione et consumptione: quoniam naturale est unumquodque redire ad locum suæ originis; imo, secundum philosophos, unumquodque convertitur ad id a quo processit. Caro quoque sic comesta, non potuisset ascendere.
paras.en: By these words Christ took away and dissolved the scandal of the disciples. For by foretelling that he would ascend into heaven in their sight, if they stayed with him, it could become plain that he had come down from heaven, and that he would not give his body to be eaten carnally, in the way other flesh is eaten, not without being divided, torn and consumed: since it is natural for each thing to return to the place of its origin; nay, according to the philosophers, each thing turns back to that from which it proceeded. And flesh eaten in that way could not have ascended.

paras.t: Spiritus, id est spiritualis intellectus verborum quæ dixi de manducatione eorporis mei, est qui vivificat animam vita gratiæ; caro autem carnaliter intellecta, et per se, non prodest quidquam communicanti. Imo, qui verba inducta carnaliter accipit, et carnem non nisi sacramentaliter edit, non solum non vivificatur, sed animæ mortem illabitur. Verumtamen verba prætacta, ad litteram, non mystice, intelligenda sunt de vero corpore Christi; sed ipsum verum corpus spiritualiter contemplandum est atque sumendum, quoniam modus quo est in sacramento, est supernaturalis et incorporalis. Hine quoque dicit Apostolus: Littera occidit, spiritus autem vivificat. Quemadmodum ergo scientia sine caritate non prodest, sed obest, quum inflet, non quia in se mala, sed propter abusum habentis, et sicut corpus naturale sine anima mortuum est; sic caro sine spiritu non prodest quidquam, etiam nee caro Christi, quia sine gratia Spiritus Sancti et spirituali intellectu, non confert quidquam, sed communieantem damnationi facit obnoxium, eo quod carnem tam sanctam sumat indigne, non spiritualiter ac discrete. Verum, sicut scientia maxime prodest, si adsit dilectio, sic caro Christi, adjuncto spiritu. Sic etiam caro Apostolorum prædicando et discurrendo profuit nobis, operante Spiritu Sancto. Unde quod ait, Spiritus est qui vivificat, accipi potest de Spiritu Sancto seu gratia ejus.
paras.en: [[6:64|It is the spirit that quickeneth|Spiritus est qui vivificat]], that is, the spiritual understanding of the words I have spoken of the eating of my body quickens the soul with the life of grace; [[6:64|the flesh profiteth nothing|caro autem carnaliter intellecta, et per se, non prodest quidquam]], flesh understood carnally, and by itself, profits nothing to the communicant. Nay, he who takes the words cited carnally, and eats the flesh only sacramentally, is not only not quickened, but falls into the death of the soul. Yet the words just mentioned are to be understood literally, not mystically, of the true body of Christ; but that true body is to be contemplated and taken spiritually, since the mode in which it is in the sacrament is supernatural and incorporeal. Hence too the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 3:6|For the letter killeth: but the spirit quickeneth|Littera occidit, spiritus autem vivificat]]. As, then, knowledge without charity does not profit but harms, since it puffs up[[1 Cor 8:1||]], not because it is evil in itself, but because of the abuse of him who has it, and as a natural body without a soul is dead; so the flesh without the spirit profits nothing, not even the flesh of Christ, since without the grace of the Holy Ghost and spiritual understanding it confers nothing, but makes the communicant liable to damnation, because he takes flesh so holy unworthily, not spiritually and with discernment. But as knowledge profits most if love is present, so does the flesh of Christ when the spirit is joined to it. So too the flesh of the Apostles profited us by their preaching and going about, the Holy Ghost working. Hence what he says, *It is the spirit that quickeneth*, can be taken of the Holy Ghost or his grace.

paras.t: Verba quæ ego locutus sum vobis, de corpore et sanguine meo, spiritus et vita sunt, id est, spiritualem intellectum requirunt, quantum ad modum intelligendi, sicque vivificant mentem per gratiam et sapientiæ lucem. Corpus quippe Christi est in sacramento per modum incorporalem ac indivisibilem: quoniam, non est ibi sieut in loco, vel per propriam dimensionem, sed per dimensionem panis, quamvis proprie dimensiones ejus sint ibi concomitanter, sicut et cetera quædam accidentia Christi, quia non minus splendet in manibus sacerdotis, quam in throno majestatis. Sed sunt quidam ex vobis discipulis meis, qui non credunt verbis qua dixi, quum tamen tot tantisque testimoniis scire possint me esse Christum, et per consequens falsa docere non posse. Et quia non credunt, non sunt veri discipuli: addiscentem enim oportet credere. Nec valent verba predicta spiritualiter intelligere, quum Isaias testetur: Nisi credideritis, non intelligetis.
paras.en: [[6:64|The words that I have spoken to you|Verba quæ ego locutus sum vobis]], of my body and blood, [[6:64|are spirit and life|spiritus et vita sunt]], that is, require a spiritual understanding as to the manner of understanding, and so quicken the mind by grace and the light of wisdom. For the body of Christ is in the sacrament in an incorporeal and indivisible manner: since it is not there as in a place, or by its own dimension, but by the dimension of the bread, though its own dimensions are there by concomitance, as also certain other accidents of Christ, since he shines no less in the priest's hands than on the throne of majesty. [[6:65|But there are some of you that believe not|Sed sunt quidam ex vobis discipulis meis, qui non credunt]], my disciples, the words I have spoken, though by so many and so great testimonies they could know that I am the Christ, and in consequence cannot teach what is false. And because they do not believe, they are not true disciples: for a learner must believe. Nor can they understand the words spoken spiritually, since Isaias testifies: *Unless you believe, you shall not understand*[[Is 7:9||]] [the margin gives Is. vii, 9, according to the Septuagint; the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have “If you will not believe, you shall not continue”].

paras.t: Sciebat enim ab initio æternitatis, et a principio incarnationis, Jesus, qui essent credentes futuri, et quis traditurus esset eum. Jesus, secundum quod Deus, novit ab æterno per scientiam increatam omnia occulta, contingentiaque futura; secundum naturam vero assumptam, scivit hujusmodi per scientiam infusam, ab exordio incarnationis. Ista sunt verba Joannis evangelistæ, qui consequenter recitat verba Christi.
paras.en: [[6:65|For Jesus knew from the beginning|Sciebat enim ab initio Jesus]], from the beginning of eternity and from the beginning of the incarnation, [[6:65|who they were that did not believe|qui essent credentes]] [Denis reads *qui essent credentes futuri*, “who they were that would believe”], [[6:65|and who he was that would betray him|et quis traditurus esset eum]]. Jesus, as God, knew from eternity by uncreated knowledge all hidden things and future contingents; but according to the nature assumed he knew such things by infused knowledge, from the beginning of the incarnation. These are the words of John the evangelist, who next relates the words of Christ.

paras.t: Et dicebat Jesus auditoribus suis: Propterea, id est, quia futura agnosco, et quosdam vestros non credere prævidebam, dixi vobis, quia nemo potest venire, id est per fidem converti ad me, nisi fuerit ei datum a Patre meo. Non enim omnium est fides, et novit Dominus qui sunt ejus. Atque ut Lucas profitetur in Actibus: Crediderunt quotquot præordinati erant ad vitam æternam. Hoc enim dixit Christus superius quantum ad sensum: Nemo, inquiens, potest venire ad me, nisi Pater qui misit me, traxerit eum. Omne enim datum optimum, et omne donum perfectum, est descendens a Patre luminum. — Sed dicet aliquis: Si nemo potest venire nisi Deus dederit, ergo qui non venit, per iimpotentiam exceusatur: Deus namque ultra vires nil exigit. Et respondendum, quod a nobis ipsis nil possumus, et tamen possumus quidquid Deus præcipit nobis: quia secundum Philosophum, id dicimur posse per nos, quod possumus per amicos. Quoniam ergo Deus, quantum in se est, paratus est opem impendere, imo et gratiam influit, dummodo fecerit homo quod in se est; ideo per impotentiam non exeusamur, sed possumus quod jubemur.
paras.en: [[6:66|And he said|Et dicebat]] Jesus to his hearers: [[6:66|Therefore did I say to you|Propterea dixi vobis]], that is, because I know the future and foresaw that some of you do not believe, [[6:66|that no man can come to me|quia nemo potest venire ad me]], that is, be converted by faith, [[6:66|unless it be given him by my Father|nisi fuerit ei datum a Patre meo]]. For [[2 Thess 3:2|for all men have not faith|Non enim omnium est fides]], and [[2 Tim 2:19|the Lord knoweth who are his|novit Dominus qui sunt ejus]]. And, as Luke professes in the Acts: [[Acts 13:48|as many as were ordained to life everlasting believed|crediderunt quotquot præordinati erant ad vitam æternam]] [Denis's order: “there believed as many as were ordained …”]. For Christ said this above as to the sense: [[6:44|No man can come to me, except the Father, who hath sent me, draw him|Nemo, inquiens, potest venire ad me, nisi Pater qui misit me, traxerit eum]]. For [[Jas 1:17|Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights|Omne … datum optimum, et omne donum perfectum … a Patre luminum]]. But someone will say: If no one can come unless God has given it, then he who does not come is excused by inability: for God demands nothing beyond our powers. The answer is that of ourselves we can do nothing, and yet we can do whatever God commands us: since, according to the Philosopher, we are said to be able by ourselves to do what we can do through our friends. Since, then, God, as far as lies in him, is ready to give his help, nay, pours in grace, provided that man does what is in him; therefore we are not excused by inability, but we can do what we are commanded.

paras.t: Ex hoc, id est istis auditis, præsertim ob id quod dixerat Christus, Nisi manducaveritis carnem Filii hominis, etc.; multi discipulorum ejus, non duodecim Apostoli, nee septuaginta duo discipuli, abierunt mente, per infidelitatem et apostasiam, et corpore, per localem recessum, retro post Satanam, non post Jesum, nolentes intellectum suum subjicere incomprehensibilibus testimoniis Christi ac fidei. Quocontra dicit Apostolus: In captivitatem redigentes omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi. Et jam non cum eo ambulabant. Dixit ergo Jesus ad duodecim Apostolos: Numquid et vos vultis abire? Non quasi ignorans sciscitatur; sed ut illorum fides manifestaretur, nobisque imitanda proponeretur, et ut ostendat quod coacta obsequia non acceptat.
paras.en: [[6:67|After this|Ex hoc]], that is, having heard these things, above all because Christ had said, [[6:54|except you eat the flesh of the Son of man|Nisi manducaveritis carnem Filii hominis]], etc., [[6:67|many of his disciples|multi discipulorum ejus]], not the twelve Apostles nor the seventy-two disciples, [[6:67|went back|abierunt retro]], in mind, by unbelief and apostasy, and in body, by going away from the place, back after Satan, not after Jesus, not willing to subject their understanding to the incomprehensible testimonies of Christ and to faith. Against which the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 10:5|bringing into captivity every understanding unto the obedience of Christ|In captivitatem redigentes omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi]]. [[6:67|and walked no more with him|Et jam non cum eo ambulabant]]. [[6:68|Then Jesus said to the twelve: Will you also go away|Dixit ergo Jesus ad duodecim Apostolos : Numquid et vos vultis abire?]]? He does not ask as one who does not know; but that their faith might be made manifest and set before us to imitate, and to show that he does not accept forced service.

paras.t: Respondit ergo ei Simon Petrus pro omnibus, quia ferventior ac principalior ceteris, unde et solito fervore nunc respondit pro sociis: Domine, ad quem ibimus? hoc est, si te relinquimus, alium tibi similem verumque Salvatorem invenire nequaquam valebimus; tu sufficis nobis, propter quem cuncta reliquimus. Verba vitæ æternæ habes: id est, doctrina tua cœlestis est, et obedientes tibi ad vitam æternam perducit: non enim temporalia bona, ut Moyses et Propheta, sed æterna promittis. In his verbis ostenditur vera et fervida caritas Petri ad Christum, a quo nullatenus voluit separari. Amor nempe nectit amantem amato tanto inseparabilius, validius atque intimius, quo fuerit major. Propter quod ait Paulus: Quis nos separabit a caritate Christi? Et nos credimus fide formata, quamvis nondum perfecta et stabilita, et cognovimus per donum intellectus, quod inest omnibus fidem formatam habentibus, et per illud perspicit anima quæ fidei sunt, videns per aliquam rationem qua fides ostenditur esse a Deo, quod vera sint quæ asserit fides. Et congrue ait, Credimus et cognovimus, quoniam credere præcedit intelligere. Quia tu es Christus, spirituali oleo, id est gratiarum plenitudine, unctus quantum ad naturam assumptam, in regem et sacerdotem altissimum, Filius Dei non adoptivus, sed naturalis. Hoc frequenter confessus est Petrus: et in verbis istis tangitur duplex natura unitasque personæ in Christo.
paras.en: [[6:69|And Simon Peter answered him|Respondit ergo ei Simon Petrus]] for all, since he was more fervent and more principal than the others, and so with his usual fervour he now answers for his companions: [[6:69|Lord, to whom shall we go|Domine, ad quem ibimus]]? that is, if we leave you, we shall never be able to find another like you and a true Saviour; you are enough for us, for whom we have left all things[[Matt 19:27||]]. [[6:69|Thou hast the words of eternal life|Verba vitæ æternæ habes]]: that is, your teaching is heavenly, and leads those who obey you to eternal life: for you promise not temporal goods, as Moses and the Prophets did, but eternal. In these words is shown the true and fervent love of Peter for Christ, from whom he would by no means be separated. For love binds the lover to the beloved the more inseparably, strongly and intimately, the greater it is. For this reason Paul says: [[Rom 8:35|Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ|Quis nos separabit a caritate Christi]]? [[6:70|And we have believed|Et nos credimus]] with formed faith [that is, faith given life by charity], though not yet perfect and established, [[6:70|and have known|et cognovimus]] by the gift of understanding, which is in all who have formed faith, and by which the soul sees into the things of faith, seeing by some reason by which faith is shown to be from God, that what faith asserts is true. And he fittingly says *we have believed and have known*, since believing goes before understanding. [[6:70|that thou art the Christ|Quia tu es Christus]], anointed with spiritual oil, that is, the fullness of graces, as to the nature assumed, as king and most high priest, [[6:70|the Son of God|Filius Dei]], not adoptive but natural. Peter often confessed this: and in these words the twofold nature and the unity of person in Christ are touched on.

paras.t: Verum, quia responsio Petri quantum ad Judam claudicavit, de quo tamen Petrus nil mali præsumpsit, ideo subditur: Respondit eis Jesus: Nonne ego vos duodecim elegi, id est, præ ceteris ad gratiam apostolatus vocavi, et unus ex vobis diabolus est? non per essentiam, sed mutationem, hoc est diabolicus propter malitiam, sicut Joannes Baptista dictus est angelus, et alio loco Salvator vocat diabolum hominem, dicens: Inimicus homo hoc fecit.
paras.en: But because Peter's answer limped as regards Judas, of whom Peter yet presumed nothing evil, there is added: [[6:71|Jesus answered them: Have not I chosen you twelve|Respondit eis Jesus: Nonne ego vos duodecim elegi]], that is, called you before the others to the grace of the apostolate, [[6:71|And one of you is a devil|et unus ex vobis diabolus est]]? not by essence, but by change, that is, devilish because of malice, as John the Baptist is called an angel[[Matt 11:10||]], and in another place the Saviour calls a man a devil [that is, an enemy], saying: [[Matt 13:28|An enemy hath done this|Inimicus homo hoc fecit]] [*inimicus homo*; Denis takes the enemy of the parable as the devil].

paras.t: Dicebat autem de Juda Simonis Iscariotæ. Fuit enim oriundus de vico nomine Carioth. Ista sunt verba Joannis Evangelistæ, non Christi. Christus enim non expressit Judam, quia occultus fuit, et ne diffamatus fierett pejor; vel potius, ut per ejus proditionem implerentur scriptura Prophetarum de traditione Christi a suo discipulo. Hic enim erat traditurus eum, quum esset unus ex duodecim. Implicite ergo Christus admonuit Judam, qui sibi de propria pravitate conscius fuit.
paras.en: [[6:72|Now he meant Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon|Dicebat autem de Juda Simonis Iscariote]]. For he was born in a village named Carioth. These are the words of John the Evangelist, not of Christ. For Christ did not name Judas, because he was hidden, and lest, being defamed, he should grow worse; or rather, so that by his betrayal the scriptures of the Prophets on the betraying of Christ by his disciple might be fulfilled. [[6:72|for this same was about to betray him, whereas he was one of the twelve|Hic enim erat traditurus eum, quum esset unus ex duodecim]]. Christ, then, implicitly warned Judas, who was conscious of his own wickedness.

paras.t: Circa hunc locum aliqua dieunt Augustinus et Beda, quæ sicut non audeo reprobare, ita nee approbare, quamvis aliqui reprobent ea. Dieunt ergo, quod Christus elegit Judam, ut per ejus proditionem compleret nostram salutem. Non tamen excusatur Judas a culpa, quia non ideo tradidit, quia electus, sed qui traditurus fuit, electus est. Quemadmodum enim iniqui male utuntur beneficiis Dei, sic Deus bene utitur maleficiis hominum, et sic Christus bene usus est malitia Judæ. Ego puto quod Christus elegit Judam ad apostolatum, ut videns tantam pietatem Christi, peeniteret, et apostolicum officium digne prosequeretur. Sed quoniam Christus novit aliter esse futurum, sustinuit Judam propter melius, scilicet, ut per eum impleretur prophetia de Christi proditione. Tanta quippe est bonitas Dei seu Christi, quod non sustineret neque permitteret malum, nisi posset et vellet inde elicere bonum.
paras.en: On this place Augustine and Bede say some things which, as I dare not reprove them, so I dare not approve them either, though some reprove them. They say, then, that Christ chose Judas so that by his betrayal he might accomplish our salvation. Yet Judas is not excused from guilt, since he did not betray because he was chosen, but he who was to betray was chosen. For as the wicked make ill use of God's benefits, so God makes good use of men's evil deeds: and so Christ made good use of the malice of Judas. I think that Christ chose Judas to the apostolate so that, seeing Christ's great kindness, he might repent and carry out the apostolic office worthily. But since Christ knew it would be otherwise, he bore with Judas for the better, namely that by him the prophecy of Christ's betrayal might be fulfilled. For so great is the goodness of God, or of Christ, that he would not bear with nor permit evil unless he could and would draw good from it.

paras.t: Prædicta autem assertio Augustini et Bedæ fundatur in hoc, quod dicunt Judam a principio suæ vocationis malum fuisse, et in malitia perstitisse. Cujus oppositum tenet et probat Lyra, quia distributio bonorum pertinet ad justitiam commutativam, secundum Philosophum, utpote ut melioribus major honor impendatur. Non ergo Judas vocatus fuisset ad apostolatum, nisi tune dignus fuisset, vel justificatus a Christo, sicut Matthæus, ut esset dignus tanto honore. Quidquid autem sit de veritate assertionis Augustini et Bedæ, tamen ratio ista nil obtinet. Primo, quoniam apostolatus, sicut et prophetia, pertinet ad gratias gratis datas, quæ seepe impiissimis dantur. Unde de facientibus miracula multa, et prophetantibus in nomine Christi, dicturus est Christus: Discedite a me, quoniam nunquam novi vos. Et Balaam perseveranti in malo datus est spiritus prophetiæ. Rursus, quoniam communicatio bonorum a Deo liberrima est, sine præviis meritis: ideireo non proprie pertinet ad justitiam commutativam, imo nec ad justitiam. Insuper quidam imponit Bedæ, quod dicat Judam non esse electum ad apostolatum, sed ad proditionem. Diligenter ergo inspiciens verba Bedæ super Joannem, inveni aliter. Dicit enim Beda, quod undecim erant electi ut in apostolica dignitate perseverarent, et per eos fides prædicaretur ubique. Per quod Beda dat intelligere, quod Judas non fuit electus ut in apostolica dignitate maneret; sed non negat eum ad apostolatum fuisse electum. Imo, si Beda hoc diceret, satis male sonaret: quia apud Matthæum Judas Iscariotes vocatur Apostolus; et in Marco legitur, quod Christus vocavit eum cum aliis undecim, fecitque eum Apostolum, committens ei sicut et aliis, prædicationis atque curationis officium. In Actibus quoque loquitur Petrus de Juda: Connumeratus est (inquit) in nobis, et sortitus est sortem ministerii hujus. Et post pauca leguntur Apostoli exorasse, ut Deus ostenderet quis inter Matthiam et Joseph acciperet sortem apostolatus, de quo prævaricatus est Judas. Vere igitur electus fuit in Apostolum. — Chrysostomus vero dicit, quod Judas tempore suæ vocationis fuit bonus.
paras.en: The assertion of Augustine and Bede just mentioned is founded on this, that they say Judas was evil from the beginning of his calling and persisted in malice. Lyra holds and proves the opposite, since the distribution of goods belongs to commutative justice, according to the Philosopher, namely that greater honour should be given to the better. Judas, then, would not have been called to the apostolate unless he had then been worthy, or justified by Christ, like Matthew, so as to be worthy of so great an honour. But whatever be the truth of the assertion of Augustine and Bede, this reason proves nothing. First, since the apostolate, like prophecy, belongs to the graces freely given [*gratiæ gratis datæ*, gifts for the good of others, which do not of themselves make their holder holy], which are often given to the most wicked. Hence of those who work many miracles and prophesy in the name of Christ, Christ will say: [[Matt 7:23|I never knew you: depart from me|Discedite a me, quoniam nunquam novi vos]] [Denis's order: “Depart from me, for I never knew you”]. And to Balaam, persevering in evil, the spirit of prophecy was given[[Num 22:1||]][[Num 24:2||]]. Again, since the sharing of goods by God is most free, without previous merits, it does not belong properly to commutative justice, nay, not to justice at all. Besides, someone charges Bede with saying that Judas was chosen not to the apostolate but to the betrayal. Looking carefully, then, at the words of Bede on John, I found otherwise. For Bede says that the eleven were chosen to persevere in the apostolic dignity, and that by them the faith might be preached everywhere. By which Bede gives us to understand that Judas was not chosen to remain in the apostolic dignity; but he does not deny that he was chosen to the apostolate. Nay, if Bede said that, it would sound ill enough: since in Matthew Judas Iscariot is called an Apostle[[Matt 10:4||]]; and in Mark we read that Christ called him with the other eleven and made him an Apostle, committing to him, as to the others, the office of preaching and healing[[Mark 3:14||]]. In the Acts also Peter speaks of Judas: [[Acts 1:17|Who was numbered with us, and had obtained part of this ministry|Connumeratus est (inquit) in nobis, et sortitus est sortem ministerii hujus]]. And a little after we read that the Apostles prayed that God would show which, between Matthias and Joseph, should take the lot of the apostleship from which Judas had fallen[[Acts 1:24||]][[Acts 1:25||]]. Truly, then, he was chosen as an Apostle. But Chrysostom says that Judas at the time of his calling was good.

paras.t: Quæritur, quum in Scripturis communiter electi accipiantur pro prædestinatis, juxta illud, Multi vocati, pauci vero electi, quomodo Christus dicit se elegisse duodecim, quorum unus fuit præscitus. Et respondendum, quod in Scripturis interdum electi dicuntur ad aliquam gratiam particularem gratis datam, vel etiam gratum facientem ad tempus durantem, promoti. Unde Saul vocatur electus. Et in Psalmo cantamus: Electos Israel impedivit. Et Salomon appellatus est, Amabilis Domino. In Isaia quoque Dominus ait de Cyro rege Persarum, viro gentili atque damnato: Elegi te, et non cognovisti me. Postremo omnino certum est, quod Judas fuit malus tune, quum Christus hæc verba de eo pronuntiavit. Et forte ex tunc permansit in malo, quousque prodito Christo, suspendit se ipsum.
paras.en: It is asked, since in the Scriptures the elect are commonly taken for the predestined, according to that, [[Matt 20:16|For many are called but few chosen|Multi vocati, pauci vero electi]][[Matt 22:14||]], how Christ says that he chose twelve, of whom one was foreknown [to damnation]. The answer is that in the Scriptures men are sometimes called elect who are advanced to some particular grace freely given, or even to sanctifying grace lasting for a time. Hence Saul is called chosen[[1 Kings 9:2||]]. And in the Psalm we sing: [[Ps 77:31|brought down the chosen men of Israel|electos Israel impedivit]]. And Solomon was called *Amiable to the Lord*[[2 Kings 12:25||]]. In Isaias also the Lord says of Cyrus king of the Persians, a Gentile and damned man: *I have chosen thee, and thou hast not known me*[[Is 45:4||]] [the margin gives Is. xlv, 3–5; the Vulgate has “I have made a likeness of thee, and thou hast not known me”]. Lastly, it is quite certain that Judas was evil at the time when Christ spoke these words of him. And perhaps from then on he remained in evil until, having betrayed Christ, he hanged himself[[Matt 27:5||]].

paras.t: Nos ergo cum beatissimo principe Apostolorum certissime credentes et cognoscentes quod Jesus est Christus Filius Dei, dicamus semper ad Jesum: Domine, verba vitæ æternæ habes, non me permittas abire a te. Integerrima itaque devotaque fide suscipiamus corpus et sanguinem Salvatoris, in quo est salus, vita et resurrectio nostra.
paras.en: Let us, then, with the most blessed prince of the Apostles, most surely believing and knowing that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, say always to Jesus: [[6:69|Lord|Domine]], [[6:69|Thou hast the words of eternal life|verba vitæ æternæ habes]]: do not let me go away from thee. With most entire and devout faith, then, let us receive the body and blood of the Saviour, in whom is our salvation, life and resurrection.

7.title: Declaratio capituli septimi: Post hæc autem ambulabat Jesus in Galilæam.
7.title_en: Explanation of the seventh chapter: “After these things, Jesus walked in Galilee.”

paras.t: Quid post mirabilem pastionem quinque millium virorum de quinque panibus duobusque piscibus, et cetera documenta Christi in præcedenti recitata capitulo, gestum sit, pandit Evangelista.
paras.en: What was done after the wonderful feeding of five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes, and the other teachings of Christ related in the preceding chapter, the Evangelist now sets out.

paras.t: Post hæc autem quæ in capitulo præcedenti descripta sunt, ambulabat Jesus in Galilæam, id est per diversa loca hujus provinciæ, prædicando in synagogis Galilæorum. Sermonem quippe immediate præhabitum, fecit in synagoga Capharnaum metropolis Galilææ; et inde egrediens, perambulabat urbes et villas Galilæ, faciendo diversa miracula, plurimaque docendo: quæ iste Evangelista omisit, quia ab aliis tribus Evangelistis novit esse sufficienter conscripta.
paras.en: [[7:1|After these things, Jesus walked in Galilee|Post hæc autem ambulabat Jesus in Galilæam]], which are described in the preceding chapter, that is, through the various places of this province, preaching in the synagogues of the Galileans. For the sermon given just before he gave in the synagogue of Capharnaum, the chief city of Galilee; and going out from there he went about the cities and villages of Galilee, working various miracles and teaching very many things: which this Evangelist left out, because he knew they had been written sufficiently by the other three Evangelists.

paras.t: Non enim volebat in Judæam, id est in terram duarum tribuum, scilicet Juda et Benjamin, ubi sacerdotes, Scribæ ac Pharisæi æmuli Christi communiter habitabant, ambulare passim ac publice, quia quærebant eum Judæi interficere. Idcirco declinavit ab eis: non quasi mortem vel eos qui corpus occidunt formidans, quum fuerit in omni virtute perfectus, et solo nutu omnes adversarios suos occidere potens; sed ut daret exemplum sepe pro causa, loco et tempore fugiendi persecutores, cedendo furori eorum, ne gravius peccent, vel bono communi inferant nocumentum. Noluit autem Christus in omnibus supernaturali modo procedere, ne putaretur incarnatio ejus phantastica, et ne viri religiosi sine magna causa quærant miraculosum effectum a Deo. Sed in aliquibus processit et habuit se modo humano, ut sciatur veraciter homo factus, et ut nos faciamus quod in nostra situm est potestate, non tentantes Deum.
paras.en: [[7:1|for he would not walk in Judea|non enim volebat in Judæam ambulare]], that is, in the land of the two tribes, namely Juda and Benjamin, where the priests, Scribes and Pharisees, Christ's rivals, commonly dwelt, here and there and publicly, [[7:1|because the Jews sought to kill him|quia quærebant eum Judæi interficere]]. Therefore he turned aside from them: not as fearing death or [[Matt 10:28|them that kill the body|eos qui corpus occidunt]], since he was perfect in every virtue and able with a nod to kill all his adversaries; but to give an example of fleeing from persecutors, often, according to cause, place and time, giving way to their fury lest they sin more grievously or do harm to the common good. And Christ did not will to proceed in a supernatural way in all things, lest his incarnation be thought a phantom, and lest religious men without great cause seek a miraculous effect from God. But in some things he proceeded and behaved in a human way, so that he might be known to have truly been made man, and that we may do what lies in our power, not tempting God[[Deut 6:16||]].

paras.t: Erat autem in proximo, id est, de propinquo imminebat, dies festus Judæorum, videlicet Scenopegia, id est festivitas Tabernaculorum, qua septem diebus duravit. Hanc celebraverunt Judæi in Jerusalem quintadecima die mensis septimi, in memoriam quod post egressum de Ægypto habitaverunt in deserto in umbraculis, tentoriis, tabernaculis seu papilionibus, per annos quadraginta. De hac festivitate præcepit Moyses in Deuteronomio.
paras.en: [[7:2|was at hand|Erat autem in proximo]], that is, it was close at hand, [[7:2|the Jews feast|dies festus Judæorum]], namely [[7:2|of tabernacles|Scenopegia]], that is, the feast of Tabernacles, which lasted seven days[[Lev 23:34||]]. The Jews kept it at Jerusalem on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, in memory of their having dwelt in the desert after the going out of Egypt in booths, tents, tabernacles or pavilions for forty years[[Lev 23:43||]]. Of this festival Moses gave commandment in Deuteronomy[[Deut 16:13||]].

paras.t: Dixerunt autem ad eum fratres ejus, id est consobrini sive affines. Non enim erant, secundum Bedam, filii Joseph ex alia conjuge: qui creditur virgo mansisse, ut purissimæ ac pudicissimæ Virginis esset custos atque minister condignus. Sed erant cognati Domini Jesu: non tamen de numero eorum quos Christus jam ad apostolatum vocavit, quia post pauca subjungitur, quod isti fratres ejus non credebant in eum; Apostoli autem credebant. Transi hinc, et vade in Judæam, præsertim in Jerusalem, Judææ regionis metropolim, ut et discipuli tui, quos habes in Judæa, vel nunc ascensuri sunt in Jerusalem, videant opera tua, id est miracula, quæ tu facis Habuit enim Christus in diversis locis quosdam discipulos qui eum corporaliter non sequebantur: et de illis jam agitur.
paras.en: [[7:3|And his brethren said to, him|Dixerunt autem ad eum fratres ejus]], that is, cousins or kinsmen. For, according to Bede, they were not sons of Joseph by another wife: he is believed to have remained a virgin, so as to be a worthy guardian and servant of the most pure and most chaste Virgin. But they were kinsmen of the Lord Jesus: yet not of the number of those whom Christ had already called to the apostolate, since a little after it is added that these his brethren did not believe in him, whereas the Apostles believed. [[7:3|Pass from hence and go into Judea|Transi hinc, et vade in Judæam]], above all to Jerusalem, the chief city of the region of Judea, [[7:3|that thy disciples also|ut et discipuli tui]], whom you have in Judea, or who are now about to go up to Jerusalem, [[7:3|may see thy works which thou dost|videant opera tua, quæ facis]], that is, miracles. For Christ had in various places some disciples who did not follow him in the body: and it is of these that there is now question.

paras.t: Nemo quippe in occulto quid, id est aliquid magnum, seu opus miraceulosum, facit, et quærit ipse in palam esse, id est, talia operando desiderat apparere, et in manifesto coram aliis operari. Miracula enim ordinantur ad declarationem divinæ potentiæ atque ad conversionem videntium: ideo in manifesto agenda sunt. Hæc sunt verba hominum adhuc carnalium, humanam laudem amantium, qui sic de omnibus judicant, quales ipsi intra se sunt. Vani enim et ambitiosi arbitrantur facile alios omnes eis esse conformes. Ceterum, verba istorum universaliter vera non sunt, quia non solum Christus suscitavit filiam archisynagogi occulte, multisque a se curatis præcepit ne publicarent ipsum; sed Elias quoque et Eliseus suscitaverunt pueros defunctos in cubiculo. Si hæc facis quæ tibi suggerimus, eundo Jerusalem versus, illicque signa agendo in festivitate jam imminente, coram omnibus qui ibi nunc confluent, manifestas te ipsum mundo, id est hominibus potentiam tuam ostendis, et quod sis Christus opere monstras.
paras.en: [[7:4|For there is no man that doth any thing in secret|Nemo quippe in occulto quid facit]], that is, anything great, or a miraculous work, [[7:4|and he himself seeketh to be known openly|et quærit ipse in palam esse]], that is, in working such things desires to appear, and to work openly before others. For miracles are ordered to the declaring of the divine power and to the conversion of those who see: so they are to be done openly. These are the words of men still carnal, loving human praise, who judge of all men as they themselves are within. For the vain and ambitious easily think all others like themselves. Besides, their words are not universally true, since not only did Christ raise the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue in secret[[Mark 5:40||]][[Luke 8:51||]], and command many whom he had cured not to make him known[[Matt 8:4||]][[Matt 9:30||]][[Mark 7:36||]] [the first of these margin notes prints Matth. vi, 4; Matt 8:4 is probably meant]; but Elias also and Eliseus raised dead boys in a chamber[[3 Kings 17:19||]][[4 Kings 4:32||]]. [[7:4|If thou do these things|Si hæc facis]] which we suggest to you, by going towards Jerusalem and doing signs there at the feast now at hand, before all who are now flocking there, [[7:4|manifest thyself to the world|manifesta te ipsum mundo]] [Denis reads *manifestas*, “thou showest thyself”], that is, you show men your power, and prove by deed that you are the Christ.

paras.t: Quod autem verba prædicta inordinata fuerunt innuit Evangelista, subdendo: Neque enim fratres ejus jam dicti credebant in eum: quia non est Propheta sine honore, nisi in domo sua et in cognatione sua. Unde et isti dubitabant an miracula Jesu essent vera miracula, facta virtute divina; vel si hæc crediderunt, non tamen tenuerunt eum pro Christo Unigenito Dei, veroque Deo, sed pro homine puro et Propheta.
paras.en: That the words just mentioned were disordered the Evangelist suggests by adding: [[7:5|For neither did his brethren believe in him|Neque enim fratres ejus jam dicti credebant in eum]], the brethren just spoken of: because [[Mark 6:4|A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and in his own house, and among his own kindred|non est Propheta sine honore, nisi in domo sua et in cognatione sua]] [Denis: “but in his own house and among his own kindred”]. Hence these too doubted whether Jesus' miracles were true miracles, done by divine power; or, if they believed this, yet they did not hold him to be the Christ, the Only-begotten of God and true God, but a mere man and a Prophet.

paras.t: Dixit ergo eis Jesus: Tempus meum, id est tempus manifestandi me ipsum eo modo quo vos desideratis, videlicet ad capiendum honorem ac gloriam ab hominibus, et ad dominandum in mundo, nondum advenit, quia non veni ministrari, sed ministrare. Primus enim Christi adventus usque ad passionem debuit esse occultus, et in abjectione ac humilitate, ut judicaretur; non in omnimoda manifestatione, ut quasi rex regum ab omnibus honoraretur: quoniam si sic, tunc utique nemo ausus fuisset judicare sive occidere eum. Sed post passionem fuit tempus glorificationis, manifestationis dominationisque suæ: quia ex tunc per prædicationem et signa Apostolorum aliorumque prædicatorum, cœpit Christus suam majestatem ostendere, et ubique regnare, ut omnes agnoscerent et adorarent sublimitatem ipsius. Ideo itaque dicit: Tempus meum nondum advenit. Novit enim Christus intentionem fratrum suorum, quod non invitarent eum ad ascendendum Jerusalem versus et ad signa illic agenda, ex devotione, sed vanitate, ut scilicet ipse Jesus eorum cognatus, et ipsi propter eum tanquam cognati ejus, humanam laudem, favorem et commodum, ex perpetratione miraculorum consequerentur. — Potest quoque ita exponi: Tempus meum, id est hora eundi ad Judæam, et prædicandi et faciendi illic miracula, nondum advenit, quoniam a Deo præordinatum non est ut in principio hujus festivitatis ibi sim, sed in medietate ipsius adveniam.
paras.en: [[7:6|Then Jesus said to them: My time|Dixit ergo eis Jesus: Tempus meum]], that is, the time of manifesting myself in the way you desire, namely to receive honour and glory from men and to rule in the world, [[7:6|is not yet come|nondum advenit]], because I came [[Matt 20:28|not come to be ministered unto, but to minister|non veni ministrari, sed ministrare]]. For Christ's first coming until the passion had to be hidden, and in lowliness and humility, so that he might be judged; not in full manifestation, so as to be honoured by all as King of kings: since if it had been so, no one would have dared to judge or kill him. But after the passion was the time of his glorification, manifestation and rule: since from then on, by the preaching and signs of the Apostles and other preachers, Christ began to show his majesty and to reign everywhere, so that all might acknowledge and adore his sublimity. So he says: *My time is not yet come*. For Christ knew the intention of his brethren, that they were not inviting him to go up towards Jerusalem and work signs there out of devotion, but out of vanity: namely that Jesus their kinsman, and they for his sake as his kinsmen, might gain human praise, favour and advantage from the working of miracles. It can also be explained thus: *My time*, that is, the hour of going into Judea and preaching and working miracles there, *is not yet come*, since it is not ordained by God that I be there at the beginning of this feast, but that I come in the middle of it.

paras.t: Tempus autem vestrum semper est paratum. Tempus dicitur bonum et malum, paratum et imparatum, propter ea quæ sunt vel fiunt in tempore. Unde ait Salvator: Sufficit diei malitia sua; et Apostolus, Redimentes tempus, quoniam dies mali sunt. Et tamen rursus dicit Apostolus: Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile, ecce nunc dies salutis. Et utique tempus acceptabile ac salutare non est malum nihilo minus unum et idem tempus dicitur malum, propter mala pœnæ et culpæ quæ sunt vel fiunt in eo, et acceptabile, propter misericordiam Dei, et cetera dona gratiæ operaque virtutum quæ fiunt in ipso. Simili modo dixit Salvator, tempus fratrum suorum esse semper paratum, quoniam quod quærebant, videlicet laus vana et favor humanus ac commodum temporale, quotidie inveniuntur, exhibentur et acquiruntur. Vel ideo dicit tempus suum nondum venisse, sed tempus illorum semper esse paratum, quoniam habuit multos insidiatores, illi vero sine periculo adversariorum ascendere poterant. Et huic consonant verba sequentia.
paras.en: [[7:6|but your time is always ready|Tempus autem vestrum semper est paratum]]. Time is called good and evil, ready and unready, because of what is or is done in time. Hence the Saviour says: [[Matt 6:34|Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof|Sufficit diei malitia sua]]; and the Apostle, [[Eph 5:16|redeeming the time, because the days are evil|Redimentes tempus, quoniam dies mali sunt]]. And yet again the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 6:2|Behold, now is the acceptable time: behold, now is the day of salvation|Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile, ecce nunc dies salutis]]. And of course the acceptable and saving time is not evil; nevertheless one and the same time is called evil because of the evils of punishment and of guilt that are or are done in it, and acceptable because of God's mercy and the other gifts of grace and works of virtue that are done in it. In like manner the Saviour said that his brethren's time was always ready, since what they sought, namely vain praise, human favour and temporal advantage, are daily found, offered and gained. Or he says that his own time had not yet come, but theirs was always ready, since he had many lying in wait for him, whereas they could go up without danger from adversaries. And the following words agree with this.

paras.t: Non potest mundus, id est homines mundani vobis similes in peccatis, odisse vos. Odium enim ex dissimilitudine oritur, et amor ex conformitate: ideo mali et sæculares se invicem amant carnali et cæco amore. Verumtamen similitudo est causa odii indirecte, sive per accidens, in quantum unus similium impedit alium a consecutione rei optatæ. Propter quod figuli invicem litigant, et homines ejusdem officii sibi invicem invident. Unus quoque multum eruditus, conatur deprimere alium sibi similem. Hinc inter superbos semper sunt jurgia, et inter iracundos discordiæ. Mundus ergo persequitur mundum, imo unus perversus odit atque interimit alium. Sed verum est quod Christus nunc loquitur, quoniam mundanus homo, secundum quod talis, non potest directe odio habere ac detestari similem sibi, quia affectu et opere sunt concordes; tamen indirecte et per accidens contingit oppositum, secundum quod unus sæcularis concipit alium quasi suo voto vel studio contrarium aut nocivum.
paras.en: [[7:7|The world cannot hate you|Non potest mundus odisse vos]], that is, worldly men like you in sins. For hatred arises from unlikeness, and love from likeness: so the wicked and worldly love one another with a carnal and blind love. Yet likeness is a cause of hatred indirectly, or by accident, in so far as one of those who are alike hinders the other from gaining a thing desired. This is why potters quarrel with one another, and men of the same calling envy one another. One very learned man, too, tries to put down another like himself. Hence [[Prov 13:10|Among the proud there are always contentions|inter superbos semper sunt jurgia]], and among the angry discords[[Prov 15:18||]][[Prov 29:22||]]. The world, then, persecutes the world; nay, one wicked man hates and kills another. But what Christ now says is true, since a worldly man, as such, cannot directly hate and detest one like himself, since they agree in affection and deed; yet indirectly and by accident the opposite happens, in so far as one worldly man conceives another as contrary or harmful to his wish or pursuit.

paras.t: Denique quum in divinis Scripturis dicitur, hominem malum non posse corrigi vel facere bonum, et hominem bonum non posse perverti vel facere malum, intelligendum est de hominibus bonis et malis formaliter, hoc est secundum quod tales sunt, non materialiter, quia personæ tales quum sint liberi arbitrii, possunt mutari, durante statu vitæ præsentis. In talibus quoque locutionibus frequenter accipitur impossibile pro difficili: quemadmodum peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum dicitur non posse remitti. Et Jeremias ait: Si mutare potest Æthiops pellem suam, et pardus varietates suas, et vos poteritis benefacere; et Christus in Evangelio: Non potest arbor bona fructus malos facere, neque arbor mala fructus bonos facere. Certumque est hoc de hominibus dici. Sic verissime dicimus: Impossibile est superbum Deo placere, homicidam salvari, iracundum a Spiritu Sancto inhabitari. Sed et pœnæ qua talibus determinantur, intelligenda sunt sub conditione, videlicet nisi pœniteant; vel per modum comminationis; vel quia frequenter sic accidit. Secundum hunc itaque sensum dicit nunc Christus fratribus istis mundanis: Non potest mundus odisse vos. Hine dicit Joannes in sua epistola: Nolite mirari si odit vos mundus. Hoc dicit de justis. De impiis vero adjecit: Ipsi de mundo sunt, et de mundo loquuntur, et mundus eos audit. Merito ergo amicitia hujus mundi inimica est Deo, in tantum quod Deus dissipavit ossa eorum qui hominibus placent.
paras.en: Further, when it is said in the divine Scriptures that a bad man cannot be corrected or do good, and that a good man cannot be perverted or do evil, it is to be understood of good and bad men formally, that is, in so far as they are such, not materially, since such persons, having free will, can be changed while the state of the present life lasts. In such expressions too *impossible* is often taken for *difficult*: as the sin against the Holy Ghost is said not to be able to be forgiven[[Matt 12:31||]]. And Jeremias says: [[Jer 13:23|If the Ethiopian can change his skin, or the leopard his spots: you also may do well|Si mutare potest Æthiops pellem suam, et pardus varietates suas, et vos poteritis benefacere]]; and Christ in the Gospel: [[Matt 7:18|A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can an evil tree bring forth good fruit|Non potest arbor bona fructus malos facere, neque arbor mala fructus bonos facere]]. And it is certain that this is said of men. So we say most truly: It is impossible for the proud to please God, for a murderer to be saved, for the angry to be indwelt by the Holy Ghost. And the punishments laid down for such are to be understood under a condition, namely unless they repent; or by way of threat; or because it often happens so. In this sense, then, Christ now says to these worldly brethren: [[7:7|The world cannot hate you|Non potest mundus odisse vos]]. Hence John says in his epistle: [[1 John 3:13|Wonder not, brethren, if the world hate you|Nolite mirari si odit vos mundus]]. This he says of the just. Of the wicked he added: [[1 John 4:5|They are of the world. Therefore of the world they speak: and the world heareth them|Ipsi de mundo sunt, et de mundo loquuntur, et mundus eos audit]]. Rightly, then, [[Jas 4:4|the friendship of this world is the enemy of God|amicitia hujus mundi inimica est Deo]], so much so that [[Ps 52:6|God hath scattered the bones of them that please men|Deus dissipavit ossa eorum qui hominibus placent]].

paras.t: Me autem odit mundus, id est homines vitiosi, præsertim principes sacerdotum cum suis fautoribus, quibus gravis fuit Christus ad videndum, quia ego testimonium perhibeo de illo, quia, id est quod, opera ejus mala sunt, id est, peccata eorum aperte redarguo. Veritas autem odium parit. Propter quod Salomon loquitur: Ambulans recto itinere et timens Deum, despicitur ab eo qui infami graditur via. Et denuo ait: Non amat pestilens eum qui se corripit. De talibus scribit Amos: Odio habuerunt corripientem, et loquentem perfecte abominati sunt. Hæc fuit prima atque præcipua causa odii et persecutionis Judæorum in Christum, quia increpavit pravitates eorum.
paras.en: [[7:7|but me it hateth|Me autem odit]] the world, that is, vicious men, above all the chief priests with their supporters, to whom Christ was grievous even to behold[[Wis 2:15||]], [[7:7|because I give testimony of it, that the works thereof are evil|quia ego testimonium perhibeo de illo, quia opera ejus mala sunt]] (*that*, that is), that is, I openly rebuke their sins. And truth breeds hatred. For this reason Solomon says: [[Prov 14:2|He that walketh in the right way, and feareth God, is despised by him that goeth by an infamous way|Ambulans recto itinere et timens Deum, despicitur ab eo qui infami graditur via]]. And again he says: [[Prov 15:12|A corrupt man loveth not one that reproveth him|Non amat pestilens eum qui se corripit]]. Of such Amos writes: [[Amos 5:10|They have hated him that rebuketh in the gate: and have abhorred him that speaketh perfectly|Odio habuerunt corripientem, et loquentem perfecte abominati sunt]]. This was the first and chief cause of the Jews' hatred and persecution of Christ, that he rebuked their wickedness.

paras.t: Vos ascendite ad diem festum hunc, hoc est ad principium solennitatis præfatæ secundum legem. Ego autem non ascendam ad diem festum istum, id est ad exordium festivitatis istius, sed postea veniam. Itaque, Non ascendam, eundo vobiscum et publice veniendo, quia tempus meum nondum impletum est (secundum sensum expositum).
paras.en: [[7:8|Go you up to this festival day|Vos ascendite ad diem festum hunc]], that is, to the beginning of the solemnity appointed by the law. [[7:8|but I go not up to this festival day|Ego autem non ascendam ad diem festum istum]], that is, to the beginning of this festivity, but I will come later. So: *I go not up*, going with you and coming publicly, [[7:8|because my time is not accomplished|quia tempus meum nondum impletum est]] (in the sense explained).

paras.t: Hoc quum dixisset, ipse mansit in Galilæa. Ut autem, id est postquam, ascenderunt fratres ejus ad Jerusalem, tunc et ipse ascendit, post paucos dies, quia ut cito patebit, ipse venit in templum quarto die festivitatis prædictæ. Fratres vero ipsius interfuerunt primo festivitatis hujus diei. Non manifeste, sed quasi in occulto, quia ut dictum est, ad hoc declinavit a suorum adversariorum adspectu, ut daret exemplum aliquando fugiendi persequentes, et ne daret illis incitamentum amplioris rancoris. Venit itaque non manifeste: vel quia sine magno comitatu processit, vel quia per rara itinera ivit, vel quia conspici noluit. Per quod dedit exemplum, ut interdum humiliter lateamus, atque occulte agamus bona qua agimus, ne alii contra nos provocentur.
paras.en: [[7:9|When he had said these things, he himself stayed in Galilee|Hoc quum dixisset, ipse mansit in Galilæa]]. [[7:10|But after his brethren were gone up|Ut autem ascenderunt fratres ejus]] (*after*, that is) to Jerusalem, [[7:10|then he also went up|tunc et ipse ascendit]], after a few days, since, as will soon appear, he came into the temple on the fourth day of the said feast[[7:14||]]. But his brethren were present at the first day of this feast. [[7:10|not openly, but, as it were, in secret|non manifeste, sed quasi in occulto]], since, as has been said, he turned aside from the sight of his adversaries in order to give an example of sometimes fleeing from persecutors, and not to give them an incitement to greater rancour. He came, then, not openly: either because he went without a large company, or because he went by little-used roads, or because he did not wish to be seen. By this he gave an example, that we should sometimes humbly hide ourselves, and do in secret the good we do, lest others be provoked against us.

paras.t: Juda ergo quærebant eum in die festo in Jerusalem, quoniam solitus fuit ibi adesse in præcipuis festis; et dicebant: Ubi est ille famosus, qui omnibus notus est, quia in omnibus singularis, in pulchritudine vultus, in habitudine corporis, in rectitudine æquitatis, in doctrina, in eloquentia, in miraculis? Hine ergo non exprimunt nomen ipsius: et forte quod quidam eorum ex contemptu, ut mali, quidam vero ex reverentia, ut credentes, hoc fecerunt. Et murmur multum, id est magna contentio et ingens confabulatio, erat de eo in turba, sicut de absentibus magna reputationis esse solet. Cujus ratio subditur. Quidam enim dicebant: Quia bonus est, id est, vera docens et juste vivens. Nullus tamen eorum æstimavit eum essentialiter bonum, tanquam verum Deum. Alii autem dicebant: Non est bonus, sed seducit turbas, per simulatam justitiam, falsa miracula pestiferamque doctrinam. Nemo tamen istorum palam loquebatur de illo, aliquid definiendo de bonitate vel pravitate ipsius in audientia publica, propter metum Judæorum. Istud dupliciter potest intelligi. Si enim quod ait, Propter metum Judæorum, intelligatur de Judæis qui quærebant Christum occidere, tunc id quod dictum est, Nemo palam loquebatur de eo, intelligendum erit dumtaxat de his qui dixerunt de Jesu, Quia bonus est. illi enim ne offenderent, tacuerunt. Si vero quod ait, Propter metum Judæorum, accipiatur simpliciter de Judæis, inter quos multi etiam magni atque potentes fuerunt qui bene senserunt de Jesu, tune quod dictum est, Nemo palam loquebatur de eo, intelligendum erit de omnibus qui murmuraverunt et loquebantur de Jesu, dicentes: Ubi est ille? Nam aliqui male sentientes de Jesu, non audebant coram omnibus Judæis detrahere ei.
paras.en: [[7:11|The Jews therefore sought him on the festival day|Judæi ergo quærebant eum in die festo]] at Jerusalem, since he was wont to be there at the chief feasts; [[7:11|and said: Where is he|et dicebant: Ubi est ille]], that famous man, known to all, since he is singular in all things, in beauty of face, in bearing of body, in uprightness of equity, in teaching, in eloquence, in miracles? So they do not express his name: and perhaps some of them did this out of contempt, as the wicked, but some out of reverence, as believers. [[7:12|And there was much murmuring among the multitude concerning him|Et murmur multum erat in turba de eo]], that is, great contention and much talk, as is wont to be about absent men of great repute. The reason of this is added. [[7:12|For some said: He is a good man|Quidam enim dicebant: Quia bonus est]], that is, teaching true things and living justly. Yet none of them thought him essentially good, as true God. [[7:12|And others said: No, but he seduceth the people|Alii autem dicebant : Non est bonus, sed seducit turbas]] [Denis reads *Non est bonus*, “He is not good”], by feigned justice, false miracles and pestilent doctrine. [[7:13|Yet no man spoke openly of him, for fear of the Jews|Nemo tamen palam loquebatur de illo propter metum Judæorum]], defining anything of his goodness or wickedness in public hearing. This can be understood in two ways. For if what he says, *for fear of the Jews*, is understood of the Jews who sought to kill Christ, then what was said, *no man spoke openly of him*, will have to be understood only of those who said of Jesus, *He is good*: for these kept silence so as not to give offence. But if *for fear of the Jews* is taken simply of the Jews, among whom there were many great and powerful men who thought well of Jesus, then *no man spoke openly of him* will be understood of all who murmured and spoke of Jesus, saying, *Where is he?* For some who thought ill of Jesus did not dare to disparage him before all the Jews.

paras.t: Jam autem de festo mediante, id est, prædicta festivitate Tabernaculorum septem diebus durante jam pro media parte elapsa, videlicet quarto die ejus. Sumitur ergo in isto capitulo dies festus, non pro uno die dumtaxat, sed totalitate dierum solennitatis istius. Ascendit Jesus in templum Jerosolymitanum, et docebat. Superius dixit Evangelista, quod noluit Jesus in Judæam transire, quia quærebant eum Judæi occidere: quomodo ergo nunc refert eum templum coram universis intrasse, manentibus Judæis in voluntate tam impia? Et respondendum, quod propter prædictam causam distulit Christus quandoque intrare Judæam, non ex timore, ut dictum est: non tamen semper, ut instruat prædicatores ne gregi sibi commisso subtrahant verbum salutis in necessitatis articulo; itemque, ut declaret Judæos nil posse contra ipsum, nisi quantum ipse permiserit. Docuit ergo Jesus in templo, introducendo documenta legis ac Prophetarum; et illa perfecit per propria documenta.
paras.en: [[7:14|Now, about the midst of the feast|Jam autem de festo mediante]], that is, when half of the said feast of Tabernacles, lasting seven days, had already gone by, namely on its fourth day. In this chapter, then, *the festival day* is taken not for one day only, but for the whole of the days of this solemnity. [[7:14|Jesus went up into the temple and taught|Ascendit Jesus in templum Jerosolymitanum, et docebat]], the temple of Jerusalem. Above, the Evangelist said that Jesus would not go into Judea, because the Jews sought to kill him: how then does he now relate that he entered the temple before all, while the Jews remained in so wicked a will? The answer is that for the reason given Christ put off going into Judea at times, not out of fear, as has been said: yet not always, in order to instruct preachers not to withdraw the word of salvation from the flock committed to them in a moment of need; and also to show that the Jews could do nothing against him except so far as he permitted. Jesus taught, then, in the temple, bringing in the teachings of the law and the Prophets; and he perfected them by his own teachings.

paras.t: Et mirabantur Judæi, dicentes: Quomodo hic litteras scit, id est scripturas legis ac Prophetarum, quum non didicerit eas ab homine? Audierunt namque excellentissima documenta Christi testimoniis Scripturarum firmata; et patuit eis quod Jesus non frequentavit [scholas], neque ab hominibus instructus fuit: ideo mirabantur. Admiratio quippe consurgit, quum aliquid novi apparet cujus causa nescitur. Istud vero novum atque insolitum fuit, et nescierunt quod Jesus esset ille de quo Isaias propheta prædixit: Requiescet super eum spiritus sapientiæ et intellectus, spiritus consilii et fortitudinis, etc. Latuit eos quod Jesus esset Deus et homo, in quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ et scientiæ absconditi, qui secundum naturam assumptam accepit a Deo Trinitate omnium præsentium, præteritorum ac futurorum plenam scientiam, ab incarnationis principio. Verumtamen admiratio horum partim rudis fuit et increpabilis. Quum enim vidissent plura signa per Jesum fieri, quam fecerunt Propheta, debebant attendere quod qui Prophetas docuit per inspirationem internam, docuisset et Jesum Christum similiter. Hinc est quod Matthæus et Marcus referunt dixisse Judæos: Unde huic sapientia hæc et virtutes? Nonne hic est filius fabri?
paras.en: [[7:15|And the Jews wondered, saying: How doth this man know letters, having never learned|Et mirabantur Judæi, dicentes: Quomodo hic litteras scit, cum non didicerit?]], that is, the scriptures of the law and the Prophets, having not learned them from man? For they heard the most excellent teachings of Christ confirmed by the testimonies of the Scriptures; and it was plain to them that Jesus had not frequented [schools], nor been instructed by men: so they wondered. For wonder arises when something new appears whose cause is not known. And this was new and unwonted, and they did not know that Jesus was he of whom Isaias the prophet foretold: [[Is 11:2|And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom, and of understanding, the spirit of counsel, and of fortitude|Requiescet super eum spiritus sapientiæ et intellectus, spiritus consilii et fortitudinis]], etc. It was hidden from them that Jesus was God and man, [[Col 2:3|In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge|in quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ et scientiæ absconditi]], who according to the nature assumed received from God the Trinity full knowledge of all things present, past and future, from the beginning of the incarnation. Yet their wonder was partly crude and blameworthy. For when they had seen more signs done by Jesus than the Prophets did, they ought to have reflected that he who taught the Prophets by inward inspiration had taught Jesus Christ likewise. Hence it is that Matthew and Mark relate that the Jews said: [[Matt 13:54|How came this man by this wisdom and miracles|Unde huic sapientia hæc et virtutes]]? [[Matt 13:55|Is not this the carpenter's son|Nonne hic est filius fabri?]]?[[Mark 6:2||]]

paras.t: Respondit eis Jesus, et dixit: Mea doctrina non est mea, sed ejus qui misit me. Juxta dialecticos, nulla propositio verior est quam in qua idem prædicatur de se ipso, et nulla falsior quam in qua idem de se ipso negatur. Quomodo ergo ait, Mea doctrina non est mea? Si enim sic est, ergo doctrina Christi non fuit Christi, et contraria simul stabunt. Dicendum, quod doctrina Christi fuit aliquo modo sua, et aliquo modo non fuit sua. Est igitur sensus: Mea doctrina, hoc est prædicatio evangelica qua est mea tanquam loquentis ac recipientis, non est mea tanquam a me ipso eam habentis. Christus enim non solum secundum naturam assumptam, )sed insuper secundum naturam divinam accepit a Patre quidquid habet et est, puta essentiam atque scientiam. Vel sic: Mea doctrina quæ est mea tanquam docentis, non est mea per studium instructionis humanæ, quia per infusionem eam accepi.
paras.en: [[7:16|Jesus answered them and said: My doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me|Respondit eis Jesus, et dixit: Mea doctrina non est mea, sed ejus qui misit me]]. According to the dialecticians, no proposition is truer than one in which the same thing is predicated of itself, and none falser than one in which the same thing is denied of itself. How then does he say, *My doctrine is not mine*? For if it is so, then the doctrine of Christ was not Christ's, and contraries will stand together. It must be said that Christ's doctrine was in some way his own, and in some way not his own. The sense therefore is: *My doctrine*, that is, the preaching of the Gospel, which is mine as the one speaking and receiving it, *is not mine* as having it from myself. For Christ, not only according to the nature assumed, but also according to the divine nature, received from the Father whatever he has and is, namely essence and knowledge. Or thus: My doctrine, which is mine as the one teaching, is not mine by study of human instruction, since I received it by infusion.

paras.t: Augustinus et Beda videntur subtiliorem tangere intellectum, tamen obscurum et pia interpretatione egentem. Pro quo sciendum, quod sieut Christus dicitur Verbum et sermo Patris quo omnia loquitur, sic dici potest doctrina Patris, quia per ipsum instruit omnes. Itaque ait: Mea doctrina, hoc est sapientia qua ego sum, non est mea, hoc est a me ipso, sed ejus qui misit me, scilicet Patris, tanquam primi æternique fontis atque datoris. Sic quilibet nostrum considerans se ex se nihil habere, sed totum quod habet vel est, divinitus recepisse, dicere potest ac debet: Mea anima, mea virtus, mea scientia, non est mea, sed Creatoris mei. Unde secundum Augustinum, doctrinam appellat hic Christus, non doctrinam volubilem et sonoram, sed essentialem seu increatam scientiam. Istam expositionem non arbitror litteralem, quia secundum eam Christus non directe solvisset quæstionem Judæorum dicentium, Quomodo hic litteras scit?
paras.en: Augustine and Bede seem to touch on a subtler meaning, yet an obscure one, needing a kindly interpretation. For which we must know that, as Christ is called the Word and the speech of the Father by which he speaks all things, so he can be called the doctrine of the Father, since by him he instructs all. So he says: *My doctrine*, that is, the wisdom which I am, *is not mine*, that is, from myself, *but his that sent me*, namely the Father's, as the first and eternal fountain and giver. So any of us, considering that he has nothing of himself, but has received from God all that he has or is, can and should say: My soul, my virtue, my knowledge, is not mine, but my Creator's. Hence, according to Augustine, Christ here calls his doctrine not a passing and sounding doctrine, but the essential or uncreated knowledge. I do not think this explanation literal, since by it Christ would not have directly answered the question of the Jews who said, *How doth this man know letters?*

paras.t: Si quis voluerit voluntate efficaci, procedente in opus quum potest, voluntatem ejus facere, hoc est Deo Patri obedire, ejus præcepta servando, atque in me unicum Filium ejus credendo, passionesque, propriam voluntatem, ac vitia rectum judicium impedientia, abjiciendo, cognoscet, per donum intellectus, per experientiam quamdam, et item per admirabilem certitudinem ex divina illustratione manantem, de doctrina, hoc est evangelica disciplina quam doceo, utrum ex Deo sit, id est, an vera et mihi a Patre collata consistat, an ego a me ipso loquar, hoc est, ex proprio corde eam confingam, et non missus a Deo, sed me ipsum ingerens, prædicem. Per fidem enim pervenitur ad intellectum, juxta illud Isaiæ: Nisi credideritis, non intelligetis. Et per obedientiam pervenitur ad gustum; per opera quoque, ad illuminationem. Qui ergo voluntatem Dei facit modo prætacto, meretur dono intellectus impleri ad cognoscendum ea qua fidei sunt; meretur quoque supernaturaliter consolari ineffabiliterque delectari in Domino, et certificari ab ipso: per qua fit in omni veritate fidei prorsus certissimus, ita ut nihil ei videatur rationabilius, certius, pulchrius, assertionibus fidei benedictæ.
paras.en: [[7:17|If any man will do the will of him|Si quis voluerit voluntatem ejus facere]], with an effective will, going on into deed when it can, that is, obey God the Father by keeping his precepts and believing in me his only Son, and casting away the passions, self-will and vices that hinder right judgment, [[7:17|he shall know of the doctrine|cognoscet de doctrina]], by the gift of understanding, by a certain experience, and also by a wonderful certainty flowing from divine enlightenment, the doctrine, that is, the Gospel teaching which I teach, [[7:17|whether it be of God|utrum ex Deo sit]], that is, whether it stands true and given me by the Father, [[7:17|or whether I speak of myself|an ego a me ipso loquar]], that is, make it up from my own heart, and preach not sent by God but thrusting myself forward. For by faith one comes to understanding, according to that of Isaias: *Unless you believe, you shall not understand*[[Is 7:9||]] [the margin gives Is. vii, 9, according to the Septuagint; the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have “If you will not believe, you shall not continue”]. And by obedience one comes to tasting; and by works also to enlightenment. He, then, who does God's will in the way just touched on deserves to be filled with the gift of understanding for knowing the things of faith; he deserves also to be consoled supernaturally, to delight ineffably in the Lord, and to be made certain by him: by which he becomes altogether most certain in every truth of the faith, so that nothing seems to him more reasonable, more certain, more beautiful than the assertions of the blessed faith.

paras.t: Talis quoque certissime scit, quod in christiana lege maxime condemnatur omne pactum eum dæmone, omnis operatio magicæ artis, omnis simulatio atque caliditas: sicque cognoscit miracula a Christianis uberrime facta, non esse facta ope diabolica arteque magica, aut circumventione et calliditate humana, sed potestate divina, qua falsam doctrinam miraculis non confirmat. Denique talis scit quam sancta, perfecta, simplex et pura sit christiana Religio, in qua omnia ad privati amoris plenam exstirpationem et ad divini amoris perfectionem, per ordinatissima media ordinantur. Scit etiam quam virtuosi fuerunt patres qui fecerunt miracula, quam patientes, casti et humiles, quam caritativi, contemplativi, veraces atque pacifici. Ex quibus cognoscunt quod divina sit Christi doctrina. Hine ergo viri interni, virtuosi et contemplativi, sunt in fide certissimi atque immobiles.
paras.en: Such a man also knows most certainly that in the Christian law every pact with the devil, every working of the magic art, every pretence and cunning is condemned in the highest degree: and so he knows that the miracles done most plentifully by Christians were not done by the devil's help and magic art, or by human trickery and cunning, but by divine power, which does not confirm false doctrine by miracles. Further, such a man knows how holy, perfect, simple and pure the Christian Religion is, in which all things are ordered, by most ordered means, to the full rooting out of private love and to the perfection of divine love. He knows also how virtuous were the fathers who worked miracles, how patient, chaste and humble, how charitable, contemplative, truthful and peaceable. From these things they know that the doctrine of Christ is divine. Hence inward, virtuous and contemplative men are most certain and immovable in the faith.

paras.t: Qui a semetipso loquitur, hoc est, proprias adinventiones, non veritates desuper revelatas, docet et predieat, gloriam propriam quærit. Operatur enim ex amore privato, non divino, et vanus est ac superbus. Tales fuerunt hæretici, et malarum legum doctores, ut Mahometus.
