paras.en: [[7:45|The ministers therefore came to the chief priests and the Pharisees|Venerunt ergo ministri ad pontifices et pharisæos]], who were sent to seize Jesus, by whom they had been sent, [[7:45|And they said to them|Et dixerunt eis illi]], that is, to the ministers: [[7:45|Why have you not brought him|Quare non adduxistis eum]], seized and bound? [[7:46|The ministers answered: Never did man speak like this man|Responderunt ministri: Nunquam sic locutus est homo, sicut hic loquitur]] [Denis: “as this man speaketh”]: that is, so great is the wisdom and eloquence of his mouth, he speaks so readily, in such order and so instructively, that no one was like him. Nor is it any wonder, since he is the only Word of God, who does not labour in speech. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 44:3|grace is poured abroad in thy lips|Diffusa est gratia in labiis tuis]]. And in Luke we read: [[Luke 4:22|And they wondered at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth|Omnes mirabantur in verbis gratiæ quæ procedebant de ore ejus]] [Denis: “All wondered …”].

paras.t: Responderunt ergo eis Pharisæi: Numquid et vos seducti estis, id est, decepti estis, putantes propter pulchritudinem verborum ejus, quod sit propheta aut Christus? Aliqui dicunt, quod isti ministri, quamvis mala intentione accesserunt ad Christum, tamen audiendo efficacissimam prædicationem ipsius, immutati fuerunt a malo proposito, incipientes aliqualiter bene sentire de eo. Unde Pharisæi hoc attendentes, voluerunt eos a fide Christi prorsus avertere, adjicientes: Numquid aliquis ex principibus, id est sacerdotibus et Scribis, per quos tunc regebantur Judæi, et doctores et ceteris doctiores fuerunt, credidit in eum, aut ex Pharisæis, qui ceteris religiosiores videbantur? Tanquam dicant: Nullus ex doctis et magnis atque devotis credit ei. Sed turba hæc currens post eum, quæ non novit legem, id est vulgus indoctum et ignobile, maledicti sunt, id est, miserabiliter fallitur, facile credens propter insipientiam suam et ruditatem.
paras.en: [[7:47|The Pharisees therefore answered them: Are you also seduced|Responderunt ergo eis Pharisæi: Numquid et vos seducti estis]], that is, deceived, thinking because of the beauty of his words that he is a prophet or the Christ? Some say that these ministers, though they came to Christ with an evil intention, yet, on hearing his most powerful preaching, were changed from their evil purpose, beginning to think somewhat well of him. Hence the Pharisees, noticing this, wished to turn them away altogether from faith in Christ, adding: [[7:48|Hath any one of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees|numquid ex principibus aliquis credidit in eum, aut ex pharisæis?]], of the rulers, that is, the priests and Scribes, by whom the Jews were then ruled, and who were teachers and more learned than the rest; of the Pharisees, who seemed more religious than the rest? As though they said: None of the learned, the great and the devout believes him. [[7:49|But this multitude, that knoweth not the law, are accursed|sed turba hæc, quæ non novit legem, maledicti sunt]], running after him, that is, the unlearned and base common people, that is, are wretchedly deceived, believing easily because of their foolishness and rudeness.

paras.t: Tota mentiuntur Pharisæi, quemadmodum moris est invidorum, quos in tantum excæcat invidia, ut sive per vera, sive per falsa, non cessent avertere alios ab eo quem odiunt. Nam et aliqui ex principibus crediderunt in Jesum, scilicet Nicodemus et Nathanael legis doctor. Infra quoque legitur, quod multi ex principibus crediderunt in Jesum. Sed et devotissimi Judæorum jam crediderunt in Jesum Pharisæi quoque pleni erant hypocrisi, avaritia, ambitione, invidia. Turba quoque non fuit maledicta, sed prælecta, quemadmodum fatur Apostolus: Quæ stulta sunt mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat sapientes; et infirma mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat fortia. Hoc ipse Salvator perpendens, exsultavit Spiritu Sancto, ut apud Lucam introducitur, et ait: Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine cœli et terræ, quia abscondisti hæc a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti ea parvulis. Et Psalmista: Testimonium (inquit) Domini fidele, sapientiam præstans parvulis. Quanto ergo quis minus de se ipso præsumit, quanto minus in propria subtilitate et scientia gloriatur, quanto minus alios vilipendit, tanto copiosius meretur illuminari a Christo. Hine quoque simplices et feminæ sunt devotiores quam multum litterati et viri, quia quo minus habent de excellentia in naturalibus, eo humiliores sunt, et per consequens pleniores sunt ex intima devotione, vera sapientia, illa videlicet qua est primum donum Spiritus Sancti. Unde Salomon ait: Cum simplicibus sermocinatio Dei.
paras.en: The Pharisees lie in everything, as is the way of the envious, whom envy blinds so much that, whether by true things or false, they do not cease to turn others away from the one they hate. For some of the rulers too believed in Jesus, namely Nicodemus[[John 3:1||]] and Nathanael, a doctor of the law[[John 1:49||]]. Below too it is read that many of the rulers believed in Jesus[[John 12:42||]]. And the most devout of the Jews had already believed in Jesus. The Pharisees too were full of hypocrisy, avarice, ambition and envy. Nor was the crowd accursed, but chosen, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 1:27|But the foolish things of the world hath God chosen, that he may confound the wise: and the weak things of the world hath God chosen, that he may confound the strong|Quæ stulta sunt mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat sapientes; et infirma mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat fortia]]. The Saviour himself, weighing this, rejoiced in the Holy Ghost, as is told in Luke, and said: [[Luke 10:21|I confess to thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent and hast revealed them to little ones|Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine cœli et terræ, quia abscondisti hæc a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti ea parvulis]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 18:8|the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to little ones|Testimonium (inquit) Domini fidele, sapientiam præstans parvulis]]. The less, then, a man presumes of himself, the less he glories in his own subtlety and knowledge, the less he despises others, the more abundantly he deserves to be enlightened by Christ. Hence too simple people and women are more devout than many learned men, since the less they have of excellence in natural things, the humbler they are, and in consequence the fuller of inward devotion and true wisdom, namely that which is the first gift of the Holy Ghost[[Is 11:2||]]. Hence Solomon says: [[Prov 3:32|and his communication is with the simple|Cum simplicibus sermocinatio Dei]] [Denis: “God's communication is with the simple”].

paras.t: Dicit Nicodemus ad eos, ille qui venit nocte ad eum, puta ad Jesum, ut dictum est, qui unus erat ex ipsis, id est de numero principum et Pharisæorum, ut patuit: Numquid lex nostra judicat, hoc est, judicandum per approbationem vel condemnationem docet, hominem, nisi audierit ab ipso prius, id est, verba de ore ejus audierit, et cognoverit per certitudinem quid faciat? Ubertim enim in lege præceptum fuit, ut causa judicandi investigaretur, audiretur, discuteretur, et ut ipse qui causam habuit, staret coram senioribus, sacerdotibus, vel judicibus, quorum fuit judicare, audireturque ab eis, sicque opera ejus vere cognoscerent. Hocque Nicodemus inseruit, ne incaute damnarent Jesum, vel aliquem ab ipso averterent, et ut induceret eos ad diligentem advertentiam atque præsentialem audientiam Christi, confidens eos, si hoc facerent, convertendos ad Christum, sicut ipse jam fuit conversus ad eum, cujus tantam expertus fuit virtutem, sapientiam eminentiamque in sermone.
paras.en: [[7:50|Nicodemus said to them|Dicit Nicodemus ad eos]], [[7:50|he that came to him by night|ille qui venit nocte ad eum]], namely to Jesus, as was said[[John 3:2||]], [[7:50|who was one of them|qui unus erat ex ipsis]], that is, of the number of the rulers and Pharisees, as was plain[[John 3:1||]]: [[7:51|Doth our law judge any man|Numquid lex nostra judicat hominem]], that is, teach that he is to be judged by approval or condemnation, [[7:51|unless it first hear him|nisi audierit ab ipso prius]], that is, hear words from his mouth, [[7:51|and know what he doth|et cognoverit per certitudinem quid faciat?]], with certainty? For in the law it was richly commanded that the cause to be judged be investigated, heard and discussed[[Lev 19:15||]][[Deut 1:16||]][[Deut 16:18||]][[Deut 19:16||]], and that he who had the cause should stand before the elders, priests or judges whose office it was to judge, and be heard by them, and so that they should truly know his works. And Nicodemus put this in lest they condemn Jesus rashly, or turn anyone away from him, and to lead them to attend carefully to Christ and hear him in person, trusting that if they did this they would be converted to Christ, as he himself had already been converted to him, whose great power, wisdom and pre-eminence in speech he had experienced.

paras.t: Responderunt Pharisæi, et dixerunt ei, utpote Nicodemo: Numquid et tu Galilæus es, id est a Jesu Galilæo deceptus, discipulusque illius effectus? Scrutare Scripturas, id est, tu qui legis doctor es, scripturas Moysis et Prophetarum diligenter inquire per actualem considerationem, quas nosti per habitualem notitiam, et vide, id est, si hoc feceris, ex Scripturis oculo interiori videbis, quia Propheta a Galilea, id est a tam vili terra et plebe, non surgit, id est, non nascitur, non procedit, non ascendit. Mirabilis cæcitas Pharisæorum, qui sic loquuntur ac si Deus eligeret gentem propter locum, et non potius locum propter gentem. Et quod asserunt a Galilea non surrexisse Prophetam, patet falsum de Eliseo propheta et Debora prophetissa. Tobias quoque, quem constat fuisse de Galilea, prophetico spiritu fulsit. Imo Deus frequenter in vilioribus locis efficit opera magis præclara. Unde et Nazareth civitatulam Galilææ elegit pro loco conceptionis et educationis; Bethlehem quoque civitatulam Judææ, pro loco nativitatis: non Romam caput mundi, neque Jerusalem Judææ metropolim, ne exaltatio Jesu ac divulgatio fidei christianæ adscriberetur potentiæ civium, vel eminentiæ loci, aut alicui causæ naturali, sed in omnibus agnosceretur operata Divinitas, cujus virtute et cooperatione scimus invaluisse fidem catholicam christianamque legem.
paras.en: [[7:52|They answered and said to him|Responderunt Pharisæi, et dixerunt ei]], the Pharisees, namely to Nicodemus: [[7:52|Art thou also a Galilean|Numquid et tu Galilæus es]], that is, deceived by Jesus the Galilean, and become his disciple? [[7:52|Search the scriptures|Scrutare Scripturas]], that is, you who are a doctor of the law, inquire diligently by actual consideration into the scriptures of Moses and the Prophets, which you know by habitual knowledge, [[7:52|and see|et vide]], that is, if you do this, you will see from the Scriptures with the inward eye, [[7:52|that out of Galilee a prophet riseth not|quia a Galilæa propheta non surgit]], that is, from so base a land and people, is not born, does not proceed, does not arise. Wonderful blindness of the Pharisees, who speak as if God chose a people for the sake of a place, and not rather the place for the sake of the people. And what they assert, that no Prophet has arisen from Galilee, is plainly false of Eliseus the prophet[[3 Kings 19:16||]] and Debbora the prophetess[[Judg 4:5||]]. Tobias too, who is known to have been from Galilee[[Tob 1:1||]], shone with the prophetic spirit. Nay, God often does his more splendid works in baser places. Hence he chose Nazareth too, a little city of Galilee, for the place of his conception and upbringing; and Bethlehem, a little city of Judea, for the place of his birth: not Rome, the head of the world, nor Jerusalem, the chief city of Judea, lest the exalting of Jesus and the spreading of the Christian faith be ascribed to the power of the citizens, or the eminence of the place, or any natural cause, but that in all things the Godhead might be acknowledged as having worked, by whose power and co-operation we know that the catholic faith and the Christian law have prevailed.

paras.t: Et reversi sunt unusquisque in domum suam. Nam propter prædictas dissensiones solutum est eorum consilium.
paras.en: [[7:53|And every man returned to his own house|Et reversi sunt unusquisque in domum suam]]. For because of the dissensions spoken of their council was broken up.

8.title: Elucidatio capituli octavi: Jesus autem perrexit in montem Oliveti.
8.title_en: Explanation of the eighth chapter: “And Jesus went unto mount Olivet.”

paras.t: […] post facta ac documenta in præcedenti capitulo recitata, egerit atque docuerit Christus, Evangelista explanat.
paras.en: The Evangelist sets out what Christ did and taught after the deeds and teachings related in the preceding chapter.

paras.t: Jesus autem perrexit in montem Oliveti, qui propter olivas illic nascentes et abundantes sic dictus est. Apud Lucam habetur, quod Jesus exiens noctibus, morabatur in monte qui dicitur Oliveti. Apud Matthæum vero et Marcum legitur, quod egressus a Jerusalem abiit in Bethaniam cum duodecim. Quod ergo nunc dicitur perrexisse in montem Oliveti, intelligendum est, vel quia intravit domum Marthæ in Bethania, quæ fuit juxta præfati montis radices, vel quia ad tempus morabatur in monte hoc, vacando orationi in loco quieto et separato: non quod indigeret hujusmodi adminiculo; sed ut cunctis fidelibus, et præsertim prædicatoribus, daret exemplum quærendi locum solitarium, orationi contemplationique aptum, post prædicationem, ut ibi recolligerent semetipsos, et quæ in strepitu populi minus recte egissent, discuterent atque corrigerent; idem quoque facerent ante prædicationem, quoniam ordinatus modus prædicandi consistit primo per orationem ad Deum recurrere pro illustratione sapientiæ suæ, et omnium vanitatum et imperfectionum evitatione, ut quod orando hauserunt, prædicando diffundant.
paras.en: [[8:1|And Jesus went unto mount Olivet|Jesus autem perrexit in montem Oliveti]], which is so called from the olives that grow there in abundance. In Luke we have that Jesus, [[Luke 21:37|at night going out, he abode in the mount that is called Olivet|exiens noctibus, morabatur in monte qui dicitur Oliveti]]. But in Matthew and Mark we read that, going out from Jerusalem[[Matt 21:17||]], [[Mark 11:11|he went out to Bethania with the twelve|abiit in Bethaniam cum duodecim]]. So when it is said here that He went to mount Olivet, it is to be understood either that He entered the house of Martha in Bethania, which lay near the foot of that mount[[Mark 11:1||]], or that for a time He stayed on this mount, giving Himself to prayer in a quiet and secluded place: not that He needed any such help, but to give all the faithful, and preachers above all, an example of seeking after preaching a solitary place, suited to prayer and contemplation, so that there they might gather themselves together again, and examine and correct whatever they had done less rightly amid the noise of the people; and that they should do the same before preaching too. For the ordered way of preaching consists first in turning to God in prayer, for the enlightening of His wisdom and the avoiding of all vanities and imperfections, so that what they have drawn in by praying they may pour out by preaching.

paras.t: Et diluculo iterum venit in templum: quia ut alibi ait, in his quæ Patris sui erant oportuit eum esse. In quo patet zelus suæ dilectionis quem habuit ad populum Judæorum, quemadmodum ait: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, quoties volui congregare filios tuos, quemadmodum gallina congregat pullos suos sub alas? Et omnis populus venit ad eum, maxime vulgus. Jam enim celeberrima fuit fama Jesu in doctrina et eloquentia, in sanctitate, in signis. Et sedens in templo, docebat eos.
paras.en: [[8:2|And early in the morning he came again into the temple|Et diluculo iterum venit in templum]], because, as He says elsewhere, [[Luke 2:49|I must be about my father's business|in his quæ Patris sui erant oportuit eum esse]]. In this the zeal of the love He had for the people of the Jews is plain, as He says: [[Matt 23:37|Jerusalem, Jerusalem|Jerusalem, Jerusalem]], [[Matt 23:37|how often would I have gathered together thy children, as the hen doth gather her chickens under her wings|quoties volui congregare filios tuos, quemadmodum gallina congregat pullos suos sub alas?]] [[8:2|and all the people came to him|Et omnis populus venit ad eum]], the common folk especially; for by now the fame of Jesus was very great, for His teaching and eloquence, for His holiness, and for His signs. [[8:2|And sitting down|Et sedens]] in the temple, [[8:2|he taught them|docebat eos]].

paras.t: Adducunt autem Scribæ, qui doctiores fuerunt, et Pharisæi, qui videbantur religiosiores. Unde et isti, quum fuerint vani, nomen scientiæ et sanctitatis affectantes, specialiter Christo inviderunt, eo quod in sapientia et sanctitate eos excederet, non solum secundum veritatem, sed et secundum populi reputationem. Amatores etenim excellentiæ ac laudis humanæ, invident jugiter his qui eis excellentiores vel pares videntur, timentes ne sibi præferantur.
paras.en: [[8:3|And the scribes|Adducunt autem Scribæ]], who were the more learned, [[8:3|and Pharisees|et Pharisæi]], who seemed the more religious, bring her. And these, being vain men who coveted a name for learning and holiness, envied Christ especially, because He surpassed them in wisdom and holiness, not only in truth but in the people's esteem as well. For those who love pre-eminence and human praise always envy those who seem to them their betters or their equals, fearing to be ranked below them.

paras.t: Adducunt itaque mulierem in adulterio deprehensam. Cur non adduxerunt adulterum, quum eamdem pœnam meruerit? Dicunt aliqui, ut facerent populo æstimationem quod fuit discipulus Jesu. Sed hoc est magis in contrarium. Quum enim studuerint Christum diffamare, si invenissent aliquem discipulorum ejus in tanto facinore, illum maxime publicassent ac produxissent in medium, quatenus crimen discipuli in magistrum redundaret. Quemadmodum enim filius sapiens est gloria patris, sic bonus discipulus est honor magistri. Forsitan ergo adulter evasit manus eorum, vel muneribus eos placavit. Sed potius reor quod ideo feminam adduxerunt, non virum, quia optabant ut Jesus parceret delinquenti, judicando ut dimitteretur adulterans, sicque accusarent eum de legis transgressione, quoniam lex jussit hujusmodi lapidare. Consuetudinarium est [enim] judicibus, feminis magis compati faciliusque indulgere quam viris, quia et ceteris paribus, minus peccant in eodem genere culpæ quam viri, quum sit in eis fragilitas major, carnalitas fortior, intellectus debilior. Propter quod mulier nomine carnis frequenter exprimitur in Scripturis.
paras.en: So they [[8:3|bring|Adducunt]] [[8:3|a woman taken in adultery|mulierem in adulterio deprehensam]]. Why did they not bring the adulterer, since he deserved the same punishment? Some say: to make the people think that he was a disciple of Jesus. But this tells rather the other way. For since they were bent on defaming Christ, had they found one of His disciples in so great a crime, they would above all have made him known and brought him out into the open, so that the disciple's crime might redound upon the master. For as a wise son is the glory of his father[[Prov 10:1||]][[Prov 15:20||]], so a good disciple is the honour of his master. Perhaps, then, the adulterer escaped their hands, or appeased them with gifts. But I rather think they brought the woman, not the man, because they hoped that Jesus would spare the offender, judging that the adulteress be let go, and so they might accuse Him of transgressing the law, since the law commanded such to be stoned[[Lev 20:10||]]. For it is customary with judges to feel more for women and to pardon them more readily than men, because, other things being equal, they sin less than men in the same kind of fault, since there is in them greater frailty, stronger carnality, and weaker understanding. For which reason woman is often expressed in the Scriptures by the name of flesh[[Gen 2:23||]][[Eph 5:29||]].

paras.t: Et statuerunt eam in medio templi vel populi, coram Christo, et dixerunt ei: Magister. Blande et reverenter, fraudulento corde loquuntur, ut Jesus minus caveat se ab eis; magistrumque nominant, cujus noluerunt esse discipuli. Tales sunt multi vulpini observatores Deo odibiles, a quibus tunc magis cavendum est, dum amplius se humiliant, arrident et applicant. Unde scriptum est: Ne credas inimico tuo in æternum, quoniam septem doli in corde ejus. Hæc mulier modo deprehensa est in adulterio, id est inventa in crimine, propter quod excusationi locus non patet.
paras.en: [[8:3|and they set her in the midst|Et statuerunt eam in medio]] of the temple, or of the people, before Christ, [[8:4|And said to him: Master|et dixerunt ei: Magister]]. They speak smoothly and respectfully, with a deceitful heart, so that Jesus may be less on His guard against them; and they call Him master whose disciples they would not be. Such are many foxlike watchers, hateful to God, of whom one must beware the more, the more they humble themselves, smile and draw close. Hence it is written: [[Ecclus 12:10|Never trust thy enemy|Ne credas inimico tuo in æternum]], [[Prov 26:25|because there are seven mischiefs in his heart|quoniam septem doli in corde ejus]] [Denis joins two verses here; where the Douay-Rheims has “mischiefs”, his Latin has *doli*, “deceits”]. [[8:4|this woman was even now taken in adultery|Hæc mulier modo deprehensa est in adulterio]], that is, found in the crime, so that there is no room for excuse.

paras.t: In lege autem Moyses mandavit nobis hujusmodi lapidare, id est jactibus saxorum occidere. Tu ergo, qui in aliquibus legem non servas, quasi vim dispensandi habens, et Dominus legis, quid dicis esse agendum cum ista nefaria?
paras.en: [[8:5|Now Moses in the law commanded us to stone such a one|In lege autem Moyses mandavit nobis hujusmodi lapidare]], that is, to kill by the throwing of stones. Thou therefore, who in some things keepest not the law, as one having power to dispense from it, and as Lord of the law, [[8:5|what sayest thou|quid dicis]] should be done with this wicked woman?

paras.t: Hæc autem dicebant tentantes eum, id est intentione fallendi, experiri volentes quid diceret, ut possent accusare eum. Proposuerunt enim sibi quæstionem, cujus responsio pro utraque parte increpabilis videbatur: quia si respondisset quod dimitteretur, accusarent eum de Mosaicæ legis destructione; si vero judicasset quod occideretur, objicerent ei quod contra propriam faceret prædicationem, qua in omnibus misericordiam docuit, non rigorem justitiæ. Magis tamen optabant quod judicaret eam dimitti, quia sic gravius videretur redarguendus.
paras.en: [[8:6|And this they said tempting him|Hæc autem dicebant tentantes eum]], that is, with the intention of deceiving, wishing to find out what He would say, [[8:6|that they might accuse him|ut possent accusare eum]]. For they put to Him a question whose answer seemed open to blame either way: for if He had answered that she be let go, they would accuse Him of destroying the law of Moses; but if He had judged that she be put to death, they would object to Him that He was acting against His own preaching, in which He had taught mercy in all things, not the rigour of justice. Yet they hoped rather that He would judge she be let go, since so He would seem more gravely to deserve reproof.

paras.t: Jesus autem inclinans se deorsum, digito scribebat in terra. Per hoc designavit quatuor: primo, quod ad mulierem peccatricem inclinavit suam clementiam; secundo, quod a malitiosis accusatoribus avertit suæ pietatis respectum, quasi detestans eorum calliditatem; tertio, quod sententia non sit subito et improvise promenda, sed cum deliberatione matura; quarto, quod judicium proferendum sit secundum scripta, vel primo scribendum, deinde publicandum: quod in pluribus locis ac populis observatur. Quid autem scripserit, non refert Evangelista. Sed aliqui dicunt, secundum quod tactum est, quod scripsit id quod postea protulit. Alii dicunt, quod scripsit eorum peccata, ut propria peccata videntes, erubescerent. Quidam affirmant, quod scripsit hæc verba: Terra judicat terram, id est peccator peccatorem.
paras.en: [[8:6|But Jesus bowing himself down, wrote with his finger on the ground|Jesus autem inclinans se deorsum, digito scribebat in terra]]. By this He signified four things: first, that He bowed down His clemency to the sinful woman; secondly, that He turned the regard of His kindness away from the malicious accusers, as though loathing their cunning; thirdly, that a sentence is not to be brought out suddenly and unadvisedly, but with ripe deliberation; fourthly, that judgment is to be given according to what is written, or is first to be written and then made public, which is observed in many places and among many peoples. What He wrote, however, the Evangelist does not relate. But some say, in keeping with what was just touched on, that He wrote what He afterwards spoke. Others say that He wrote their sins, so that seeing their own sins they might blush. Some affirm that He wrote these words: Earth judgeth earth, that is, a sinner judges a sinner.

paras.t: Quum autem perseverarent in studio decipiendi, interrogantes eum quid judicaret, erexit se, non corporaliter tantum, sed et spiritualiter, ab humili taciturnitate ad magnæ auctoritatis sublime ac judiciale eloquium. Porro, si Christus a Deo judex omnium constitutus, tam morosus fuit ad judicandum de alio, etiam in manifestis, cur nos tam proni sumus ad judicandum de aliis, etiam non commissis et subditis, et hoc in causis incertis parvisque rebus?
paras.en: [[8:7|When therefore they continued|Quum autem perseverarent]] in their effort to deceive, [[8:7|asking him|interrogantes eum]] what He judged, [[8:7|he lifted up himself|erexit se]], not in body only but also in spirit, from humble silence to the lofty, judicial speech of great authority. Moreover, if Christ, appointed by God the judge of all[[Acts 10:42||]], was so slow to judge another, even in plain matters, why are we so quick to judge others, even those not committed to us nor subject to us, and that in doubtful cases and small matters?

paras.t: Et dixit eis: Qui sine peccato mortali est vestrum. Sine venialibus enim nemo est, nisi forte ad horulam. Propter venialia quoque non fit homo ad judicandum seu puniendum magnos excessus indignus. Primus in illam lapidem mittat: id est, si imo vultis ut secundum legis rigorem puniatur, puniatur secundum congruum ordinem juris. Decet enim justitiam a justis exsecutioni mandari. Si igitur aliquis vestrum est qui legem transgressus non est, ab illo prævaricatrix legis debitam pœnam recipiat.
paras.en: [[8:7|and said to them|Et dixit eis]]: [[8:7|He that is without sin|Qui sine peccato]] (mortal sin) [[8:7|among you|est vestrum]]. For no one is without venial sins, except perhaps for a brief hour; and venial sins do not make a man unworthy to judge or punish great offences. [[8:7|let him first cast a stone at her|Primus in illam lapidem mittat]]: that is, if you will indeed have her punished according to the rigour of the law, let her be punished according to the fitting order of law; for it is fitting that justice be carried out by the just. If, then, there is any of you who has not transgressed the law, let the transgressor of the law receive her due punishment from him.

paras.t: O ineffabilis prudentiæ responsionem ex ore æternæ Sapientiæ profluentem! In qua utique responsione sic temperata est justitia per misericordiam, et econtra, quod nullatenus potuit judicans reprehendi. Quod enim dixit, Qui sine peccato est vestrum primus in illam lapidem mittat, ad justitiam pertinebat; quod vero per talem sententiam peccatricem de manu illorum eripuit, misericordiæ fuit. O quam facillime Sapientia Dei, Christus Dominus, laqueos sibi expansos dissolvit! Secundum quod Salomon ait: Non est sapientia, non est prudentia, non est consilium contra Dominum.
paras.en: O answer of unspeakable prudence, flowing from the mouth of the eternal Wisdom! In this answer justice is so tempered by mercy, and mercy by justice, that He who judged could in no way be blamed. For His saying, [[8:7|He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her|Qui sine peccato est vestrum primus in illam lapidem mittat]], belonged to justice; but His snatching the sinful woman out of their hands by such a sentence was of mercy. O how very easily the Wisdom of God, Christ the Lord, undid the snares spread for Him! As Solomon says: [[Prov 21:30|There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord|Non est sapientia, non est prudentia, non est consilium contra Dominum]].

paras.t: Et iterum se inclinans, scribebat in terra. Reiteratio facti, confirmationis exstat indicium seriositatisque signum. An vero secundo scripsit idem quod primo, non est penitus certum. Et aliqui dicunt quod primo scripsit sententiam, secundo Scribarum ac Pharisæorum peccata, ut considerantes propria crimina, desisterent a lapidatione adulteræ, atque se ipsos corrigerent. Dicitur quoque quod non scripsit omnia hæc quasi per singula verba, sed aliquem tractum seu figuram depinxit in terra, in qua illi viderunt sua peccata repræsentata quasi in signo. — Quæritur, quomodo Jesus scripsit in terra, quum fuerit in templo pavimentum habente. Et respondendum, quod terra frequenter accipitur pro quacumque re terrestri, in qua elementum terræ prædominatur: quemadmodum olim homini dictum est, Terra es. Si ergo super lapides scripsit, quomodo scripsit in tam dura materia? Dici potest, quod materia cessit ei, vel quod aliquid humoris ac pulveris superjacuit pavimento, in quibus scripsit.
paras.en: [[8:8|And again stooping down, he wrote on the ground|Et iterum se inclinans, scribebat in terra]]. The repeating of the act is a mark of confirmation and a sign of earnestness. Whether the second time He wrote the same as the first is not altogether certain. Some say that the first time He wrote the sentence, the second time the sins of the scribes and Pharisees, so that, considering their own crimes, they might leave off stoning the adulteress and correct themselves. It is also said that He did not write all this word by word, as it were, but drew some stroke or figure on the ground, in which they saw their sins represented as in a sign. — It is asked how Jesus wrote on the ground [*in terra*, literally “on the earth”], since He was in the temple, which had a pavement. And the answer is that *earth* is often taken for any earthly thing in which the element of earth predominates, as it was once said to man, Earth thou art[[Gen 3:19||]] [so Denis; the Vulgate has *pulvis es*, “dust thou art”]. If, then, He wrote upon stones, how did He write in so hard a material? It can be said that the material yielded to Him, or that some moisture and dust lay upon the pavement, in which He wrote.

paras.t: Secundum Bedam, ideo Christus se rursus inclinavit et scripsit, ut vultum ab illis sua responsione confusis divertendo, daret eis exeundi libertatem. Denique, juxta Bedam, per hoc quod Christus ante prolationem sententiæ, et statim post eam, scripsit in terra, docemur ut antequam fratrem vel proximum judicemus, et postquam eum corripuimus, ad nos ipsos mentis oculum convertamus, discutiendo conscientias proprias, ne forte in similibus vel gravioribus vitiis simus culpabiles.
paras.en: According to Bede, Christ stooped down again and wrote so that, by turning His face away from those confounded by His answer, He might leave them free to go out. Lastly, according to Bede, by Christ's writing on the ground before He uttered the sentence and straight after it, we are taught that before we judge a brother or neighbour, and after we have rebuked him, we should turn the eye of the mind upon ourselves, examining our own consciences, lest perhaps we be guilty of like or graver vices.

paras.t: Audientes autem Scribæ et Pharisæi sententiam Christi, unus post alium exibant de templo. Nam voce Salvatoris velut telo quodam percussa, confusa et victa erant corda eorum agnoscentium propria scelera: ideo verecundia quadam perfusi, quum se invicem adspexissent, dejecto capite egrediebantur. Et remansit solus Jesus, et mulier in medio stans. Quomodo solus remansit, quum nec discipuli ejus, nec populus videatur egressus, nisi cum eo vel post eum? Dicendum, quod mansit solus, id est sine prædictis insidiatoribus, et mulier in medio stans, quia incerta fuit adhuc quid Jesus judicaret de ea.
paras.en: [[8:9|But they hearing|Audientes autem]], the scribes and Pharisees, the sentence of Christ, [[8:9|went out one by one|unus post alium exibant]] [a note in the printed edition supplies here the words of the Gospel that Denis leaves out, *incipientes a senioribus*, “beginning at the eldest”] from the temple. For their hearts, struck by the Saviour's voice as by a dart, were confounded and overcome as they recognised their own crimes; and so, flushed with a kind of shame, when they had looked at one another, they went out with heads hung down. [[8:9|And Jesus alone remained, and the woman standing in the midst|Et remansit solus Jesus, et mulier in medio stans]]. How did He remain alone, since neither His disciples nor the people seem to have gone out, unless with Him or after Him? It must be said that He remained alone, that is, without the plotters just mentioned, [[8:9|and the woman standing in the midst|et mulier in medio stans]], because she was still unsure what Jesus would judge of her.

paras.t: Erigens autem se Jesus: per quam erectionem, suæ pietatis designatur respectus; dixit ei, interrogando non ex ignorantia, sed ut ad verba mulieris convenientius responderet: Mulier, ubi sunt qui te accusabant? Nemo te condemnavit, id est, lapidandam determinavit?
paras.en: [[8:10|Then Jesus lifting up himself|Erigens autem se Jesus]]: by this lifting up is signified the regard of His kindness; [[8:10|said to her|dixit ei]], asking not out of ignorance, but so as to answer the woman's words more fittingly: [[8:10|Woman, where are they that accused thee?|Mulier, ubi sunt qui te accusabant?]] [[8:10|Hath no man condemned thee|Nemo te condemnavit]], that is, decided that thou art to be stoned?

paras.t: Quæ dixit: Nemo, Domine: quia confusi abierunt qui eam accusaverunt. Dixit autem Jesus, cujus miserationes super omnia opera ejus, qui venit quærere et salvum facere quod perierat: Nec ego te condemnabo, id est, lapidandam dictabo, et si pœnitentiam egeris, non te condemnabo in hora mortis tuæ, nec in die judicii. Vade, non solum corporaliter recedendo, sed a pristinis malis te elongando, statum immutando, de virtute in virtutem eundo, et jam amplius noli peccare, id est, peccato non consentias, sed firmum propositum non peccandi habeto. Unde ait alibi Salvator: Non veni vocare justos, sed peccatores in pœnitentiam. Itaque, quod dixit, Nec ego te condemnabo, misericordia fuit; quod vero adjecit, Amplius noli peccare, fuit justitiæ.
paras.en: [[8:11|Who said: No man, Lord|Quæ dixit: Nemo, Domine]], because those who had accused her had gone away confounded. [[8:11|And Jesus said|Dixit autem Jesus]], He of whom it is written, [[Ps 144:9|his tender mercies are over all his works|cujus miserationes super omnia opera ejus]], He who [[Luke 19:10|is come to seek and to save that which was lost|venit quærere et salvum facere quod perierat]]: [[8:11|Neither will I condemn thee|Nec ego te condemnabo]], that is, I will not pronounce that thou be stoned; and if thou do penance, I will not condemn thee at the hour of thy death, nor on the day of judgment. [[8:11|Go|Vade]], not only going away in body, but removing thyself far from thy former evils, changing thy state, going [[Ps 83:8|from virtue to virtue|de virtute in virtutem]], [[8:11|and now sin no more|et jam amplius noli peccare]], that is, consent not to sin, but hold a firm purpose of not sinning. Hence the Saviour says elsewhere: [[Luke 5:32|I came not to call the just, but sinners to penance|Non veni vocare justos, sed peccatores in pœnitentiam]]. Thus His saying, [[8:11|Neither will I condemn thee|Nec ego te condemnabo]], was mercy; but His adding, [[8:11|sin no more|Amplius noli peccare]], was of justice.

paras.t: Dimisit ergo Salvator piissimus mulieri huic pœnam et culpam, sicut et latroni in cruce. Verumtamen ista forma absolvendi, non est ad imitationem trahenda, sed satisfactio imponenda est confitenti, secundum exigentiam culpæ. Christus autem habuit potestatem excellentiæ in sacramentis, potuitque sine exteriori satisfactione, tantæ contritionis gratiam peccatrici huic infundere, quod sufficiebat ad remissionem culpæ pœnæque. Et forte prævidit quod mulier tam efficaciter emendatura fuit vitam suam, quod non oportuit ei specialem satisfactionem imponere.
paras.en: So the most loving Saviour remitted to this woman both punishment and guilt, as He did also to the thief on the cross[[Luke 23:43||]]. Yet this manner of absolving is not to be drawn into imitation; rather, satisfaction is to be laid on one who confesses, according to what the fault requires. But Christ had the power of excellence in the sacraments [that is, the authority over the sacraments that belongs to Christ as their author, by which He can give their effect without their outward rite], and He could, without outward satisfaction, pour into this sinful woman the grace of so great a contrition as sufficed for the remission of guilt and punishment. And perhaps He foresaw that the woman would amend her life so effectually that there was no need to lay a special satisfaction on her.

paras.t: Iterum ergo locutus est eis, puta discipulis, populo, et cunctis qui aderant, Jesus, dicens: Ego sum lux mundi. Hoc Christus adjecit, ad ostendendum quod sua absolutio qua absolvit adulteram, fuit idonea, eo quod ipse sit lux mundi intus purgans, illuminans atque perficiens. Denique Christus secundum quod Deus, est lux increata, æterna, infinita, superessentialis, fontana, omnem mentem creatam intus illustrans lumine naturæ, gratiæ, vel gloriæ. Secundum naturam quoque assumptam, est lux mundi, id est hominum universorum: lux, inquam, participata, non substantialiter, sed propter plenitudinem gratiæ, sapientiæ et sanctitatis sibi infusæ: de cujus plenitudine accipiendo illuminamur ab eo. Illuminavit autem mundum docendo, conversando, miracula faciendo. Apostolis quoque ait Salvator: Vos estis lux mundi. Sed illi erant lumina particularia, et ministerialia seu instrumentalia, quoniam unusquisque eorum aliquam partem hominum illustravit, tanquam minister summæ lucis. Christus vero est lumen universale ac principale. Tamen ut homo, fuit lumen instrumentale, sed aliter quam ceteri Sancti: quia humanitas Christi est instrumentum Divinitatis proprium et conjunctum, quemadmodum caro est instrumentum animæ eam informantis; alii autem Sancti sunt instrumenta separata Divinitatis atque communia, sicut securis est instrumentum artificis.
paras.en: [[8:12|Again therefore, Jesus spoke to: them|Iterum ergo locutus est eis]], namely to the disciples, to the people, and to all who were present, [[8:12|saying: I am the light of the world|dicens: Ego sum lux mundi]]. Christ added this to show that the absolution by which He absolved the adulteress was valid, since He Himself is the light of the world, cleansing, enlightening and perfecting within. Moreover Christ, as God, is the uncreated light, eternal, infinite, superessential, the light that is the fountain of all light, enlightening every created mind inwardly with the light of nature, of grace, or of glory. According to the nature He assumed, too, He is the light of the world, that is, of all men[[John 1:9||]]: a light, I say, by participation, not by substance, but by reason of the fulness of grace, wisdom and holiness poured into Him[[John 1:14||]]; and receiving of His fulness, we are enlightened by Him[[John 1:16||]]. And He enlightened the world by teaching, by His life among men, and by working miracles. To the Apostles also the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:14|You are the light of the world|Vos estis lux mundi]]. But they were particular lights, ministerial or instrumental ones, since each of them enlightened some part of mankind, as a minister of the supreme light; whereas Christ is the universal and principal light. Yet as man He was an instrumental light, but otherwise than the other Saints: for the humanity of Christ is the proper and conjoined instrument of the Godhead [that is, an instrument united to the one who acts through it, as the hand is to a man, not a tool apart from him], as the flesh is the instrument of the soul that informs it; whereas the other Saints are separate and common instruments of the Godhead, as an axe is the instrument of the craftsman.

paras.t: Qui sequitur me per fidem, dilectionem et operum exhibitionem. Quod ad omnem pertinet Christianum, juxta illud: Qui se dicit in Christo manere, debet sicut ille ambulavit, et ipse ambulare. Et Paulus ad Ephesios: Imitatores Dei estote, et ambulate in dilectione, sicut et Christus dilexit nos. Non ambulat, id est, non conversatur, nec vivit, nec oblectatur, in tenebris ignorantiæ et peccati. De quibus tenebris habetur in Psalmo: Fiat via illorum tenebræ et lubricum. Hinc itaque via, id est conversatio impiorum, dicitur tenebrosa, via autem justorum, clara et luminosa, secundum quod Salomon asserit: Via impiorum tenebrosa, nesciunt ubi corruunt; justorum autem semita quasi lux splendens, procedit et crescit usque ad perfectum diem. Sed habebit pro præmio hujus imitationis, lumen vitæ, id est lumen gloriæ sempiternæ in patria: de quo canit Psalmista, In lumine tuo videbimus lumen. Habebit quoque in patria pro objecto et præmio objectali, lumen increatum, sanctam et superbenedictam Trinitatem, quæ est origo omnis vitæ naturalis, gratiosæ, et gloriosæ.
paras.en: [[8:12|He that followeth me|Qui sequitur me]] by faith, by love and by the showing forth of works. This belongs to every Christian, according to the text: [[1 John 2:6|He that saith he abideth in him ought himself also to walk even as he walked|Qui se dicit in Christo manere, debet sicut ille ambulavit, et ipse ambulare]] [the margin gives 1 John iii, 6; the words are 1 John 2:6]. And Paul to the Ephesians: [[Eph 5:1|Be ye therefore followers of God|Imitatores Dei estote]], [[Eph 5:2|And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us|et ambulate in dilectione, sicut et Christus dilexit nos]]. [[8:12|walketh not|Non ambulat]], that is, does not live his life, nor live, nor take his delight, [[8:12|in darkness|in tenebris]] of ignorance and sin; of which darkness we read in the Psalm: [[Ps 34:6|Let their way become dark and slippery|Fiat via illorum tenebræ et lubricum]]. Hence the way, that is, the life, of the wicked is called dark, but the way of the just clear and full of light, as Solomon declares: [[Prov 4:19|The way of the wicked is darksome: they know not where they fall|Via impiorum tenebrosa, nesciunt ubi corruunt]]; [[Prov 4:18|But the path of the just, as a shining light, goeth forwards, and increaseth even to perfect day|justorum autem semita quasi lux splendens, procedit et crescit usque ad perfectum diem]]. [[8:12|But shall have|Sed habebit]], as the reward of this imitation, [[8:12|the light of life|lumen vitæ]], that is, the light of everlasting glory in the fatherland, of which the Psalmist sings: [[Ps 35:10|in thy light we shall see light|In lumine tuo videbimus lumen]]. He shall have also in the fatherland, for his object and objective reward [that is, the reward which is the thing itself that the blessed see and enjoy, as distinct from the glory created in the soul], the uncreated light, the holy and superblessed Trinity, which is the origin of all life, of nature, of grace and of glory.

paras.t: Insuper, qui Christum sequitur, nunc habet vitæ lumen, videlicet Christum, per fidem, spem et dilectionem, quem in patria habiturus est per speciem, id est per claram visionem, tentionem et fruitionem, qui sunt tres dotes animæ correspondentes tribus virtutibus theologicis. His namque virtutibus et dotibus habemus, tenemus et possidemus Deum in præsenti et in futuro, quoniam Deus sublimis et benedictus, tam bonus, amorosus et liberalis consistit, quod præstando nobis dona sua, præstat se ipsum, ita ut fiducialiter veraciterque dicamus: Deus noster; et, Deus meus.
paras.en: Furthermore, he who follows Christ has the light of life even now, namely Christ, by faith, hope and charity; and he will have Him in the fatherland by sight, that is, by clear vision, possession and fruition, which are the three dowries of the soul answering to the three theological virtues [the *dotes* are the gifts of the glorified soul: vision answers to faith, *tentio* (holding fast, comprehension) to hope, and fruition to charity]. For by these virtues and dowries we have, hold and possess God, in the present and in the future; since God, sublime and blessed, is so good, so loving and so generous that in bestowing His gifts on us He bestows Himself, so that we may say with confidence and in truth: Our God; and: My God.

paras.t: Itaque, qui non sequitur Christum, currit et pertinget ad tenebras gehennæ; qui vero sequitur eum, currit atque perveniet ad lumen vitæ claritatemque patriæ, quemadmodum Isaias promisit: Non erit tibi sol amplius ad lucendum per diem, sed erit tibi Dominus in lucem sempiternam. — Quoniam Christus hoc loco asseruit, Ego sum lux mundi, Manichæi dixerunt quod Christus esset sol iste visibilis: quod quam stultum sit, non oportet probare.
paras.en: So then, he who does not follow Christ is running towards the darkness of hell and will reach it; but he who follows Him is running towards the light of life and the brightness of the fatherland, and will come to it, as Isaias promised: [[Is 60:19|Thou shalt no more have the sun for thy light by day|Non erit tibi sol amplius ad lucendum per diem]]; [[Is 60:19|but the Lord shall be unto thee for an everlasting light|sed erit tibi Dominus in lucem sempiternam]]. Because Christ asserted in this place, [[8:12|I am the light of the world|Ego sum lux mundi]], the Manichees said that Christ was this visible sun: how foolish that is there is no need to prove.

paras.t: Postremo sciendum, quod quum de ratione luminis sit manifestare seu clarificare, juxta illud Apostoli, Omnia quæ arguuntur, a lumine manifestantur; idcirco lumen seu lux proprie dicitur in spiritualibus ac divinis, quoniam manifestatio maxime spectat ad intellectum, in quo est veritatis inspectio. Hinc ergo Deus dicitur lux per essentiam, quia ab ipso omnis derivatur cognitio; et nulla creatura est lux secundum perfectam lucis proprietatem ac rationem, sed solus Deus. Omnis enim creatura habet aliquid tenebrositatis, defectibilitatis et imperfectionis admixtum, quum sit dependens, finita et indigens. Deus vero gloriosus et fortis sic lumen est, ut non sit in eo aliquid non luciditatis, seu imperfectionis vel ignobilitatis. Propter quod ait Joannes in prima sua Canonica: Deus lux est, et tenebræ non sunt in eo ullæ.
paras.en: Lastly, it is to be known that, since it belongs to the nature of light to make manifest or to make clear, according to the saying of the Apostle, [[Eph 5:13|all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light|Omnia quæ arguuntur, a lumine manifestantur]], light or brightness is therefore said properly of spiritual and divine things, since manifestation belongs above all to the intellect, in which is the beholding of truth. Hence God is called light by essence, because from Him all knowledge is derived; and no creature is light according to the perfect property and nature of light, but God alone. For every creature has something of darkness, of defectibility [that is, of the capacity to fail or fall short] and of imperfection mingled in it, since it is dependent, finite and needy; but God, glorious and mighty, is light in such a way that there is nothing in Him that is not brightness, nothing of imperfection or of baseness. That is why John says in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 1:5|God is light and in him there is no darkness|Deus lux est, et tenebræ non sunt in eo ullæ]].

paras.t: Dixerunt ergo ei Pharisæi. Jam dictum est quod Scribæ et Pharisæi qui adulteram adduxerunt, egressi sunt. Isti igitur Pharisæi de quibus nunc agitur, alii fuerunt ab illis. Tu de te ipso testimonium perhibes, laudando tuam personam sublimi præconio, quali nullus Propheta vel Patriarcha commendavit se ipsum; testimonium tuum non est verum, id est ratum et efficax, sed increpabile et suspectum, quum homo non sit bonus judex sui ipsius, nec morale est laudare se ipsum, quum Salomon protestetur: Laudet te alienus, et non os tuum; extraneus, et non labia tua. Unde Apostolus: Non qui se ipsum commendat, ille probatus est. Idcirco, quum Paulus commendasset quodammodo semetipsum, subjunxit: Factus sum insipiens, vos me coegistis; ego enim a vobis debui commendari.
paras.en: [[8:13|The Pharisees therefore said to him|Dixerunt ergo ei Pharisæi]]. It has already been said that the Scribes and Pharisees who brought the adulteress went out[[8:9||]]. These Pharisees of whom we now speak, then, were others than those. [[8:13|Thou givest testimony of thyself|Tu de te ipso testimonium perhibes]], praising Thy own person with a lofty commendation, such as no Prophet or Patriarch ever used in commending himself; [[8:13|Thy testimony is not true|testimonium tuum non est verum]], that is, not valid and effectual, but open to reproach and suspect; since a man is not a good judge of himself, nor is it seemly in conduct to praise oneself, as Solomon declares: [[Prov 27:2|Let another praise thee, and not thy own mouth: a stranger, and not thy own lips|Laudet te alienus, et non os tuum; extraneus, et non labia tua]]. Hence the Apostle: [[2 Cor 10:18|not he who commendeth himself is approved|Non qui se ipsum commendat, ille probatus est]]. Therefore, when Paul had in a manner commended himself, he added: [[2 Cor 12:11|I am become foolish. You have compelled me: for I ought to have been commended by you|Factus sum insipiens, vos me coegistis; ego enim a vobis debui commendari]].

paras.t: Sed quum hæc ita se habeant, quomodo salvatur quod Christus, cujus omnis actio nostra est instructio, recommendavit se ipsum? Et respondendum, quod non solum Christus, sed et multi Sanctorum Christi utriusque Testamenti, testimonium perhibuerunt de se, et laudaverunt se ipsos, non propter laudem humanam et gloriam vanam, sed ad Dei honorem et aliorum instructionem. Sic namque Prophetæ scribunt revelationes sibi divinitus factas, et quomodo Deus vel angeli eis locuti sunt. Et tale testimonium efficax fuit, quia ex multis aliis patuit verum esse quod asseruerunt, videlicet ex sanctitate conversationis et miraculis, ex effectu impletionis, aliisque diversis indiciis certis: et ita non ipsi dumtaxat, sed et Deus perhibuit testimonium eis. Simili modo testimonium Christi de se ipso efficacissimum fuit, quia ex eminentia suæ sapientiæ, ex magnis ac infinitis suis prodigiis, ex sanctimonia vitæ, multisque aliis, patuit eum esse virum sanctum et justum, omni fide dignissimum. Auctoritates vero præmemoratæ intelligendæ sunt secundum communem cursum, et de his quibus aliunde testimonium sive præconium non perhibetur; itemque, de laude ad se ipsum, non ad Dei honorem proximorumque utilitatem relata: talis etenim laus procedit ex vanitate, non ex caritate.
paras.en: But since these things are so, how is it to be defended that Christ, every action of whom is our instruction, commended Himself? The answer is that not only Christ, but many of Christ's Saints of both Testaments too, bore witness of themselves and praised themselves, not for the sake of human praise and vainglory, but for the honour of God and the instruction of others. For thus the Prophets write down the revelations made to them by God, and how God or the angels spoke to them. And such testimony was effectual, because what they asserted was shown to be true by many other things: by the holiness of their lives, by miracles, by the event of its fulfilment, and by various other sure signs; and so it was not they alone, but God also, who bore witness to them. In the same way Christ's testimony of Himself was most effectual, because from the eminence of His wisdom, from His great and countless wonders, from the holiness of His life, and from many other things, it was plain that He was a holy and just man, most worthy of all belief. The authorities cited above, then, are to be understood of the common course of things, and of those to whom testimony or commendation is not borne from elsewhere; and also of praise referred to oneself, not to the honour of God and the profit of one's neighbours: for such praise proceeds from vanity, not from charity.

paras.t: Præterea ratio cur testimonium et præconium a se ipso prolatum non est idoneum, hæc est, quoniam cognitio hominis de se ipso est sæpe incerta et fallax, propter inordinatum atque privatum affectum ad se. Propter quod homo in multis complacet sibi, in quibus displicet aliis. Et quamvis cognitio sui sit aliquando certa, tamen judicium ex affectu præfato frequenter pervertitur, juxta illud: Amor et odium pervertunt judicium. Illud ergo judicium firmum est, quod ex certitudine notitiæ et rectitudine affectionis emanat. Christus autem virtus et sapientia Patris, perfecte cognovit et juste amavit se ipsum in omnibus: ideo testimonium suum de se exstitit firmum. Propter quod subditur:
paras.en: Moreover, the reason why testimony and commendation given by oneself is not valid is this: that a man's knowledge of himself is often uncertain and deceptive, because of his disordered and private affection for himself. That is why a man is pleased with himself in many things in which he displeases others. And although his knowledge of himself is sometimes certain, yet his judgement is often perverted by that same affection, according to the saying: Love and hatred pervert judgement [a common saying, not a text of Scripture]. That judgement, then, is firm which springs from certainty of knowledge and rightness of affection. But Christ, the power and wisdom of the Father[[1 Cor 1:24||]], knew Himself perfectly and loved Himself justly in all things; therefore His testimony of Himself stood firm. That is why there follows:

paras.t: Respondit Jesus, et dicit eis: Etsi, id est quamvis, vel quia, ego testimonium perhibeo, id est do, de me ipso, verum est testimonium meum: quia scio, scientia increata comprehensive, atque creata apprehensive, unde, id est a quo, veni, utpote Deum Patrem, a quo natus sum ab æterno, et a quo sum missus in tempore; et quo vado, id est eumdem Patrem, ad quem cito revertar ascendendo ad cælum: et per consequens cognosco me ipsum, nec inordinate ad me ipsum afficior, quia cognitio ista non est informis, nuda et defectuosa. Dum enim principium rei et finis ejus cognoscitur, ipsa quoque cogno- […] dum utramque naturam exivit et venit a Patre, ita quod Pater, secundum utramque naturam est principium Christi, origo et fons; sed reverti ad Patrem tanquam ad finem, non competit Christo nisi se- […] est Patre, et distavit ab ipso quantum ad corporis passibilitatem, rediitque ad eum, a quo secundum divinitatem nusquam recessit. Nihilo minus unigenitus Filius, secundum divinitatem quoque ad Patrem convertitur per contemplationem ac dilectionem, sed non per dependentiam: sicque convertitur ad Patrem, tanquam ad objectum æquale, non tanquam ad finem superiorem; sed ipse et Pater ac Spiritus Sanctus sunt unus finis, in quem ordinanda sunt omnia, quoniam omnia propter se ipsum operatus est Dominus, ut Salomon ait.
paras.en: [[8:14|Jesus answered and said to them|Respondit Jesus, et dicit eis]]: [[8:14|Although|Etsi]], that is, though, or because, [[8:14|I give testimony|ego testimonium perhibeo]], that is, bear it, [[8:14|of myself, my testimony is true|de me ipso, verum est testimonium meum]]: [[8:14|for I know|quia scio]], by uncreated knowledge comprehensively, and by created knowledge apprehensively [that is, as God I know the Father fully, as man truly but not exhaustively], [[8:14|whence|unde]], that is, from whom, [[8:14|I came|veni]], namely God the Father, of whom I was born from eternity and by whom I was sent in time; [[8:14|and whither I go|et quo vado]], that is, the same Father, to whom I shall soon return by ascending into heaven; and consequently I know myself, and I am not disordered in my regard for myself, since this knowledge is not unformed, bare and defective. For when the beginning of a thing and its end are known, the thing itself also is kno- […] [a line is lost in the scan here] according to both natures he went forth and came from the Father, so that the Father is, according to both natures, the principle of Christ, his origin and fount; but to return to the Father as to an end does not befit Christ except ac- […] [another line is lost in the scan here] the Father, and was distant from him as regards the passibility of the body, and returned to him from whom, according to the divinity, he never withdrew. Nevertheless the only-begotten Son, according to the divinity also, turns towards the Father by contemplation and love, but not by dependence: and so he turns towards the Father as towards an equal object, not as towards a higher end; rather he and the Father and the Holy Ghost are one end, to which all things are to be ordered, since [[Prov 16:4|The Lord hath made all things for himself|omnia propter se ipsum operatus est Dominus]], as Solomon says.

paras.t: Vos autem nescitis unde venio, id est Patrem, a quo æternaliter gignor, et per incarnationem missus sum, imo continue mittor, quoniam quidquid ago, ex ejus inspiratione inclinationeque ago. Fuit quippe anima Christi donis Spiritus Sancti summe repleta, per quæ in omni actione movebatur a Deo. Aut quo vado, id est, terminum ad quem tendo nescitis, videlicet Patrem, seu corporis glorificationem, et sessionem ad dexteram Patris regnationemque in cælis. Idcirco non potestis bene judicare de me, quum non agnoscatis me, quem purum hominem æstimatis. Propterea sequitur:
paras.en: *But you know not whence I come* [these words, the end of v. 14 in the Vulgate, are wanting in the Douay-Rheims text used in this app], that is, the Father, of whom I am eternally begotten and by whom I was sent through the incarnation, nay, am continually sent, since whatever I do, I do by his inspiration and impulse. For the soul of Christ was filled in the highest degree with the gifts of the Holy Ghost, by which it was moved by God in every action. *Or whither I go*, that is, you know not the end towards which I tend, namely the Father, or the glorification of the body, and the sitting at the right hand of the Father, and reigning in heaven. Therefore you cannot judge rightly of me, since you do not know me, whom you reckon a mere man. Hence there follows:

paras.t: Vos secundum carnem judicatis, id est secundum ea quæ foris apparent, secundum sensum carnalem et vitiosum affectum, non secundum rectam rationem et Spiritus Sancti directionem. Unde superius dixit: Nolite secundum faciem judicare. Quoniam enim viderunt Jesum hominibus similem foris quantum ad corporis veritatem, passibilitatem, ceterosque indetrahibiles defectus, putabant quod esset homo purus, neque liceret sibi de se testimonium ferre.
paras.en: [[8:15|You judge according to the flesh|Vos secundum carnem judicatis]], that is, according to the things that appear outwardly, according to carnal sense and vicious affection, not according to right reason and the direction of the Holy Ghost. Whence he said above: [[John 7:24|Judge not according to the appearance|Nolite secundum faciem judicare]]. For since they saw Jesus outwardly like other men as regards the reality of his body, its passibility, and the other blameless defects [*indetrahibiles defectus*: the defects of our nature, such as hunger, weariness and death, which imply no sin or ignorance and so take nothing from Christ's dignity], they thought that he was a mere man, and that it was not lawful for him to bear witness of himself.

paras.t: Ego non judico quemquam. Quid est hoc? Nonne dicendo, Ego sum lux mundi, judicavit se ipsum judicio approbationis et discretionis? Itemque dicendo, Vos secundum carnem judicatis, judicavit Pharisæos judicio reprobationis seu redargutionis. Superius quoque dixit Salvator: Pater non judicat quemquam, sed omne judicium dedit Filio. Sed horum solutio aliqualiter patet ex his quæ dicta sunt super illud: Non enim misit Pater Filium suum in mundum ut judicet mundum, sed ut salvetur mundus per ipsum. In primo enim suo adventu non exercuit Christus judicium condemnationis et remunerationis, sed discretionis et increpationis ordinatæ ad emendationem, non ad pœnam. Itaque ait: Ego non judico quemquam in primo meo adventu, judicio finalis reprobationis ac remunerationis, quia hoc fiet in secundo adventu. Quidam exponunt sic: Ego non judico quemquam, eo modo quo vos, o Pharisæi, puta secundum carnem.
paras.en: [[8:15|I judge not any man|ego non judico quemquam]]. What does this mean? Did he not, by saying [[8:12|I am the light of the world|Ego sum lux mundi]], judge himself with a judgment of approval and discernment? And likewise, by saying [[8:15|You judge according to the flesh|Vos secundum carnem judicatis]], he judged the Pharisees with a judgment of reproof or rebuke. The Saviour also said above: [[John 5:22|neither does the Father judge any man: but hath given all judgment to the Son|Pater non judicat quemquam, sed omne judicium dedit Filio]]. But the solution of these is in some measure plain from what was said on the words: [[John 3:17|For God sent not his Son into the world, to judge the world: but that the world may be saved by him|Non enim misit Pater Filium suum in mundum ut judicet mundum, sed ut salvetur mundus per ipsum]] [Denis has *Pater*, “the Father”, for the Vulgate's *Deus*]. For in his first coming Christ did not exercise the judgment of condemnation and reward, but that of discernment, and of rebuke ordered to amendment, not to punishment. And so he says: [[8:15|I judge not any man|Ego non judico quemquam]] in my first coming, with the judgment of final reprobation and reward, since this will take place at the second coming. Some expound it thus: [[8:15|I judge not any man|Ego non judico quemquam]] in the way that you do, O Pharisees, that is, according to the flesh.

paras.t: Quod autem Christus aliquo modo judicaverit, constat ex eo quod subditur: Et si, id est quamvis et quia, judico ego, id est, sententiam definitivam profero de me ipso ac aliis, id est, quamvis judicium discretionis enuntio, inter bonos et malos discernendo, judicium meum tale verum est, id est rectum et efficax, quia non sum solus, id est sine teste et conjudicante, sed ego sum testans ac judicans, et qui me misit Pater, id est, Deus Pater mecum et in me est, mihi contestans atque conjudicans. In Trinitate enim non est solitudo, quoniam unaquæque Persona est in alia circumincessibiliter et inseparabiliter, et opera Trinitatis sunt indivisa. Omne quoque quod egit Christus secundum naturam assumptam, egit virtute Dei Patris, imo totius Trinitatis operantis per ipsum. Sic ergo Deus Pater approbavit et contestabatur verum esse quidquid Filius in humanitate judicavit. Propter quod Filius in judicando non fuit solus, nec sine teste et conjudicante.
paras.en: That Christ did judge in some way, however, is clear from what is added: [[8:16|And if|et si]], that is, although and because, [[8:16|I do judge|judico ego]], that is, pronounce a definitive sentence on myself and on others, that is, although I declare a judgment of discernment, discerning between the good and the wicked, [[8:16|my judgment is true|judicium meum tale verum est]], such a judgment, that is, right and effectual, [[8:16|because I am not alone|quia solus non sum]], that is, without a witness and fellow judge, [[8:16|but I|sed ego]] am witnessing and judging, [[8:16|and the Father that sent me|et qui misit me, Pater]], that is, God the Father is with me and in me, bearing witness with me and judging with me. For in the Trinity there is no solitude, since each Person is in the other by circumincession [that is, the mutual indwelling of the divine Persons] and inseparably, and the works of the Trinity are undivided. Also, all that Christ did according to the nature he had assumed he did by the power of God the Father, nay, of the whole Trinity working through him. Thus, then, God the Father approved, and bore witness that whatever the Son judged in his humanity was true. For this reason the Son was not alone in judging, nor without a witness and fellow judge.

paras.t: Ex his Christus ostendit auctoritate legis et per locum a majori, quod testimonium suum fuit idoneum. Et in lege vestra, id est vobis per Moysen data, scriptum est, quia duorum hominum testimonium verum est, id est, verum reputatur, et firmitatem sortitur. Hoc sumptum est ex eo quod Moyses ait: In ore duorum vel trium testium stabit omne verbum. In rebus enim requirenda est certitudo secundum qualitatem materiæ subjectæ, secundum Aristotelem et Boetium. Unde in actibus humanis, ubi non est certitudo demonstrativa, sufficit ut sint duo testes. Quamvis enim duo mentiri possint in testificando, hoc tamen non contingit de facili et frequenter. Propterea, quod ait, Duorum hominum testimonium verum est, non est sic intelligendum, quod sit semper verum, sed quia reputatur idoneum. Neque enim verum fuit testimonium duorum filiorum Belial, ad quorum testimonium lapidatus est Naboth; neque duorum senum contra Susannam; neque duorum qui in passione contra Christum testati sunt, dicentes: Nos audivimus eum dicentem: Possum destruere templum Dei.
paras.en: From these words Christ shows, by the authority of the law and by an argument from the greater [that is, if the witness of two men is accepted, much more that of the Father and the Son], that his testimony was sufficient. [[8:17|And in your law it is written|Et in lege vestra scriptum est]], that is, given to you through Moses, [[8:17|that the testimony of two men is true|quia duorum hominum testimonium verum est]], that is, is reckoned true and has force. This is taken from what Moses says: [[Deut 19:15|in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand|In ore duorum vel trium testium stabit omne verbum]]. For in things, certainty is to be required according to the nature of the subject matter, as Aristotle and Boethius teach. Hence in human acts, where there is no demonstrative certainty, it is enough that there be two witnesses. For although two may lie in bearing witness, yet this does not happen easily or often. Therefore when he says, [[8:17|the testimony of two men is true|duorum hominum testimonium verum est]], it is not to be understood that it is always true, but that it is reckoned sufficient. For neither was the testimony true of the two sons of Belial, on whose testimony Naboth was stoned[[3 Kings 21:13||]]; nor that of the two elders against Susanna[[Dan 13:36||]] [the verse number in the margin cannot be read in the scan; the elders' testimony is Dan 13:36–41]; nor that of the two who bore witness against Christ in the passion[[Matt 26:60||]], saying: We heard him say [Denis's wording here is that of Mark 14:58], [[Matt 26:61|I am able to destroy the temple of God|Possum destruere templum Dei]].

paras.t: Ego sum qui testimonium perhibeo de me ipso, Ego, inquiens, sum lux mundi; et testimonium perhibet de me qui misit me Pater: qui in baptismo et transfiguratione dixit de me, Hic est Filius meus dilectus: et per opera miraculosa in nomine ejus facta, testimonium perhibet mihi; itemque per Prophetarum scripturas, et aliis pluribus modis.
paras.en: [[8:18|I am one that give testimony of myself|Ego sum qui testimonium perhibeo de me ipso]], saying, [[8:12|I am the light of the world|Ego, inquiens, sum lux mundi]]; [[8:18|and the Father that sent me giveth testimony of me|et testimonium perhibet de me qui misit me Pater]]: who at the baptism and at the transfiguration[[Matt 17:5||]] said of me, [[Matt 3:17|This is my beloved Son|Hic est Filius meus dilectus]]; and through the miraculous works done in his name he gives testimony to me; and likewise through the writings of the Prophets, and in many other ways.

paras.t: Dicebant ergo ei: Ubi est Pater tuus? Putabant Jesum loqui de patre carnali, ideo ex contemptu cum irrisione interrogant ubinam sit. Quasi dicant: Tu scis quod Pater tuus sit tecum, et nos non videmus eum hoc loco: ne ergo videaris mentitus, dic ubi nunc sit. Sed quoniam malitiose et infideliter quæsierunt, ideo Dominus non respondit eis directe ad interrogatum, præsertim quoniam deteriores facti fuissent ex responsione aperta, sicut infra patebit.
paras.en: [[8:19|They said therefore to him: Where is thy Father?|Dicebant ergo ei: Ubi est Pater tuus?]] They thought Jesus was speaking of a father according to the flesh, and so in contempt and mockery they ask where he might be. As if to say: Thou sayest that thy Father is with thee, and we do not see him in this place; lest thou seem then to have lied, say where he is now. But since they asked maliciously and faithlessly, the Lord did not answer them directly to what was asked, especially since they would have been made worse by an open answer, as will be plain further on.

paras.t: Respondit Jesus: Neque me scitis, id est, non vere et intellectualiter me cognoscitis, præcipue secundum divinitatem, nec etiam secundum humanitatem ut a Verbo assumptam, quia putatis me purum hominem ex carnali commixtione progenitum, et vitiis subjacentem ad instar ceterorum. Noverunt tamen Christum quantum ad physionomiam, seu facialem notitiam, sicut superius dixit: Et me scitis, et unde sim scitis. Sed hæc erat omnino incompleta notitia. Neque Patrem meum. Quamvis enim Judæi noscerent Patrem per fidem, secundum rationem deitatis, vel quoad id quod est Deus, non tamen secundum proprietatem paternitatis, hoc est sub ratione relativa. Non enim habuerunt hi expressam fidem de Trinitate. Et quoniam Pater et Filius sunt correlativa, quorum unum per aliud definitur atque cognoscitur; idcirco qui nescit Filium, nescit et Patrem, et vice versa.
paras.en: [[8:19|Jesus answered: Neither me do you know|Respondit Jesus: Neque me scitis]], that is, you do not truly and with understanding know me, especially according to the divinity, nor even according to the humanity as assumed by the Word, since you think me a mere man begotten by carnal union, and subject to vices like the rest. Yet they knew Christ as to his features, that is, by knowledge of his face, as he said above: [[John 7:28|You both know me, and you know whence I am|Et me scitis, et unde sim scitis]]. But this was an altogether incomplete knowledge. [[8:19|nor my Father|Neque Patrem meum]]. For although the Jews knew the Father by faith, under the aspect of the Godhead, or as regards what God is, yet not according to the property of paternity, that is, under the aspect of relation; for these men had no explicit faith in the Trinity. And since Father and Son are correlatives, each of which is defined and known through the other, therefore he who knows not the Son knows not the Father either, and conversely.

paras.t: Si me sciretis fideli ac interiori notitia, sentiendo de me quia sim Filius Dei ac Virginis, forsitan et Patrem meum sciretis eodem modo quo me. Cognitio namque unius correlativi dependet ex cognitione alterius, quoniam per se invicem definiuntur, sicut dum dicimus: Pater est res habens filium, vel qui de sua substantia genuit filium; filius quoque est res habens patrem, vel ex substantia patris genitus. Quod ait, Forsitan, non dicitur dubitative, sed ad designandum arbitrii libertatem in credendo, et ut discamus sobrie, non pertinaciter, loqui. Imo hæc dictio, Forsitan, sæpe ponitur in Scripturis increpative, non dubitative: ut quum dicitur in Job, Tu forsitan cum Deo fabricatus es cælos. Hi ergo Judæi nullam divinam Personam noverunt secundum esse relativum, sed secundum esse absolutum, quoniam noverunt Deum per fidem, qui est substantialiter quælibet divina Persona, ac Trinitas tota. Propter quod fertur in Psalmo: Notus in Judæa Deus.
paras.en: [[8:19|If you did know me|si me sciretis]] with the knowledge of faith and from within, holding of me that I am the Son of God and of the Virgin, [[8:19|perhaps you would know my Father also|forsitan et Patrem meum sciretis]], in the same way as me. For the knowledge of one correlative depends on the knowledge of the other, since they are defined through each other, as when we say: A father is one who has a son, or who has begotten a son of his own substance; and a son is one who has a father, or who is begotten of the substance of a father. When he says *perhaps*, it is not said in doubt, but to signify the freedom of the will in believing, and that we may learn to speak soberly, not obstinately. Indeed this word *perhaps* is often used in the Scriptures by way of rebuke, not of doubt: as when it is said in Job, [[Job 37:18|Thou perhaps hast made the heavens|Tu forsitan cum Deo fabricatus es cælos]] [the margin reads Job xxxvi, 18; the words are at 37:18; Denis has *cum Deo* where the Vulgate has *cum eo*]. These Jews, then, knew none of the divine Persons according to their relative being [that is, as Father, Son or Holy Ghost], but according to their absolute being [that is, as the one God], since they knew by faith God, who is in substance each divine Person and the whole Trinity. For which reason it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 75:2|In Judea God is known|Notus in Judæa Deus]].

paras.t: Hæc verba locutus est Jesus in gazophylacio. Gazophylacium aliquando sumitur pro arca in qua oblationes pro ministrorum templi sustentatione ac templi reformatione ponebantur: aliquando vero, pro loco vel ædificio in quo fuit repositorium tale: sic modo accipitur. Docens in templo: quod est aptus locus pro cultu opereque divino. Et nemo adversariorum apprehendit eum, quamvis hoc sæpe proposuissent, quia necdum venerat hora ejus, id est tempus passioni dominicæ præordinatum, ante quod Jesus noluit comprehendi. Sicut enim oblatus est quia voluit, sic ante prædictum tempus captus non est, quoniam noluit.
paras.en: [[8:20|These words Jesus spoke in the treasury|Hæc verba locutus est Jesus in gazophylacio]]. *Gazophylacium* [treasury] is sometimes taken for the chest in which the offerings for the support of the ministers of the temple and for the repair of the temple were put; and sometimes for the place or building in which such a repository was: and so it is taken here. [[8:20|teaching in the temple|Docens in templo]], which is a fitting place for the worship and work of God. [[8:20|and no man laid hands on him|Et nemo adversariorum apprehendit eum]], none of his adversaries, although they had often purposed this, [[8:20|because his hour was not yet come|quia necdum venerat hora ejus]], that is, the time foreordained for the Lord's passion, before which Jesus would not be taken. For as [[Is 53:7|He was offered because it was his own will|oblatus est quia voluit]], so before the said time he was not taken, because he willed it not.

8.title: Expositio sequentis partis hujus capituli octavi, ab eo loco quo habetur: Ego vado, et quæretis me.
8.title_en: Exposition of the following part of this eighth chapter, from the place where it is had: “I go, and you shall seek me.”

paras.t: Dixit ergo iterum eis Jesus: Ego vado, id est, per passionem, resurrectionem et ascensionem revertor ad Patrem, secundum naturam assumptam, cui competit ire atque redire; et quæretis me, id est, sepe ante tempus passioni præfixum quæretis me capere et occidere. Vel, Quæretis me, id est, nomen meum et fidem christianam quæretis exstinguere, secundum quod dictum est a Jeremia in persona vestra: Eradamus eum de terra viventium, et nomen ejus non memoretur ultra. Vel, Quæretis me, id est, me in membris meis persecuturi estis post passionem, tribulando Apostolos ceterosque primitivæ Ecclesiæ filios. Unde et Paulo persequenti locutus est Jesus: Quid me persequeris? Et in peccato vestro moriemini formaliter, id est, peccatum vestrum contra me erit mors anima vestra, quia mortale fuit, et causa damnationis vestræ. Vel, In peccato vestro moriemini morte corporali, id est, usque in finem perseverabitis in peccatis tanquam indurati in malo. Vel, In peccato vestro moriemini, id est, propter peccata vestra perfidiæ et persecutionis in me, occidemini a Romanis: quemadmodum factum est tempore Titi et Vespasiani. Quo ego vado, puta ad patriam Patrisque dexteram, sessurus in throno gloriæ ejus, vos non potestis venire, quamdiu estis tales quales nunc estis. Peccata enim vestra separant inter Deum et vos, et ipsa prohibent bonum a vobis.
paras.en: [[8:21|Again therefore Jesus said to them: I go|Dixit ergo iterum eis Jesus: Ego vado]], that is, by the passion, resurrection and ascension I return to the Father, according to the nature assumed, to which it belongs to go and to return; [[8:21|and you shall seek me|et quæretis me]], that is, often before the time appointed for the passion you will seek to seize and kill me. Or, *you shall seek me*, that is, you will seek to blot out my name and the Christian faith, according to what was said by Jeremias in your person: [[Jer 11:19|Let us put wood on his bread, and cut him off from the land of the living, and let his name be remembered no more|Eradamus eum de terra viventium, et nomen ejus non memoretur ultra]]. Or, *you shall seek me*, that is, you will persecute me in my members after the passion, afflicting the Apostles and the other children of the early Church. Hence to Paul, persecuting him, Jesus said: [[Acts 9:4|why persecutest thou me|Quid me persequeris]]? [[8:21|And you shall die in your sin|Et in peccato vestro moriemini]], formally, that is, your sin against me will be the death of your soul, since it was mortal, and the cause of your damnation. Or, *you shall die in your sin* by bodily death, that is, you will persevere in your sins to the end, as hardened in evil. Or, *you shall die in your sin*, that is, for your sins of unbelief and persecution against me you will be slain by the Romans: as was done in the time of Titus and Vespasian. [[8:21|Whither I go|Quo ego vado]], namely to the fatherland and the Father's right hand, to sit on the throne of his glory, [[8:21|you cannot come|vos non potestis venire]], so long as you are such as you now are. For [[Is 59:2|your iniquities have divided between you and your God|Peccata enim vestra separant inter Deum et vos]] [Denis: “your sins divide between God and you”], and [[Jer 5:25|your sins have withholden good things from you|ipsa prohibent bonum a vobis]] [Denis: “they keep good from you”].

paras.t: Dicebant ergo Judæi: Numquid interficiet semetipsum, quia dicit, Quo ego vado, vos non potestis venire? id est, tam stulte loquitur, ut verisimile sit quod occidet se ipsum. Ecce quanta perversitas atque insania. Quid enim consequentiæ habet, Vadit quo nos non possumus eum sequi, ergo interficiet se? Imo interficientem se poterant sequi, inferendo sibi ipsis mortem nefariam. Passionati enim et invidi omnia interpretantur in pejus.
paras.en: [[8:22|The Jews therefore said: Will he kill himself, because he said: Whither I go, you cannot come|Dicebant ergo Judæi: Numquid interficiet semetipsum, quia dicit, Quo ego vado, vos non potestis venire]]? that is, he speaks so foolishly that it is likely he will kill himself.
