[[Ezech 28:17|And thy heart was lifted up with thy beauty|Elevatum est cor tuum in decore tuo]] … [[Ezech 28:16|and I cast thee out from the mountain of God, and destroyed thee, O covering cherub, out of the midst of the stones of fire|repleta sunt interiora tua iniquitate, et ejeci te de monte sancto Dei, et perdidi te, o Cherub, de medio lapidum ignitorum]] … [[Ezech 28:17|I have cast thee to the ground|in terram projeci te]]. Of the fall of the angels it is written also in the first chapter of Jude[[Jude 1:6||]], and in the second of Peter[[2 Pet 2:4||]].

paras.t: Quia veritas justitiæ, id est æquitas seu vera notitia per approbationem virtutis et veritatis ipsius amorem, non est in eo, id est diabolo et satellitibus ejus, a momento quo peccaverunt. veritate enim aversi sunt sponte, et falsitati iniquitatis inhæserunt. Fuit tamen et est in eis veritas naturæ, quoniam naturaliter mali non sunt. Et teste sancto atque divino Dionysio, naturalia in dæmonibus integra permanserunt: propter quod veram cognitionem, etiam vehementer profundam, habent de Deo et creaturis. Sed omnibus bonis abutuntur, et veritatem secundum se non amant: quin potius, convertunt eam ad hominum seductionem, quia et si bona veraque dicant, propterea dicunt, ut tandem mala et falsa ingerendo seducant. Transfigurant quippe se in angelos lucis: ideoque egemus gratia discretionis spirituum, ne ignoremus cogitationes et machinationes eorum.
paras.en: [[8:44|because truth is not in him|quia veritas non est in eo]], the truth of justice, that is, equity, or true knowledge with approval of virtue, and love of truth itself, is not in him, that is, in the devil and his followers, from the moment they sinned. For they turned away from the truth of their own will, and clung to the falsehood of iniquity. Yet there was and is in them the truth of nature, since they are not evil by nature. And by the testimony of the holy and divine Dionysius, the natural gifts remained whole in the demons: for which reason they have true knowledge, even exceedingly deep, of God and creatures. But they abuse all goods, and do not love truth for its own sake: rather, they turn it to the seducing of men, since even if they say good and true things, they say them in order at length to seduce by thrusting in evil and false things. For they [[2 Cor 11:14|transformeth himself into an angel of light|Transfigurant quippe se in angelos lucis]] [Denis: “transform themselves into angels of light”]: and so we need the grace of [the] discerning of spirits[[1 Cor 12:10||]], so as not to be ignorant of their thoughts and plots.

paras.t: Quum loquitur diabolus mendacium, ex propriis loquitur, id est ex malis habitibus atque nequitiis quibus in se plenus est, et quos primus invenit, concepit, et in alios genuit. Deo namque sortitus est esse et intelligere; sed peccatum propria voluntate incepit, non aliunde inductus ad malum, ut demones inferiores et primi parentes. Quia mendax est. Mentitus est enim dicendo: Similis ero Altissimo; itemque dicendo ad mulierem, Nequaquam moriemini, sed eritis sicut dii, scientes bonum et malum. Et pater ejus, id est primus inventor et actor mendacii. Mentita est autem iniquitas sibi, et ipse ad falsitatem angelos hominesque induxit. Quemadmodum vero triplex est veritas, utpote vitæ, justitiæ, et doctrinæ; sic est triplex mendacium triformi veritati oppositum, scilicet mendacium pravæ actionis, injustitia, et error, omniumque mendaciorum istorum pater exstat diabolus primus. Manichæi ponentes duo principia rerum, videlicet Deum lucis, et Deum tenebrarum, dixerunt quod diabolus esset mendax, et pater ejus, id est creator diaboli, etiam esset mendax. Sed ita intelligendum non est verbum Evangelistæ.
paras.en: [[8:44|When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own|Quum loquitur diabolus mendacium, ex propriis loquitur]], the devil, that is, out of the evil habits and wickednesses of which he is full in himself, and which he first invented, conceived, and begot in others. For from God he received being and understanding; but sin he began by his own will, not led to evil from elsewhere, like the lower demons and our first parents. [[8:44|for he is a liar|quia mendax est]]. For he lied in saying: [[Is 14:14|I will be like the most High|Similis ero Altissimo]]; and again in saying to the woman, [[Gen 3:4|No, you shall not die the death|Nequaquam moriemini]], [[Gen 3:5|and you shall be as Gods, knowing good and evil|sed eritis sicut dii, scientes bonum et malum]]. [[8:44|and the father thereof|Et pater ejus]], that is, the first inventor and doer of lying. For [[Ps 26:12|iniquity hath lied to itself|Mentita est autem iniquitas sibi]], and he led angels and men into falsehood. And as truth is threefold, namely of life, of justice and of doctrine, so lying is threefold, opposed to the threefold truth, namely the lie of wicked action, injustice, and error; and of all these lies the first devil is the father. The Manichees, positing two principles of things, namely the God of light and the God of darkness, said that the devil was a liar and his father, that is, the creator of the devil, was also a liar. But the Evangelist's word is not to be understood so.

paras.t: Ego autem quia veritatem dico, vera docendo, et vestra facinora veraciter arguendo, non creditis mihi: in quo patet quod sitis ex patre diabolo, qui in veritate non stetit, et mendacia ex propriis loquitur: cui et consentitis.
paras.en: [[8:45|But if I say the truth, you believe me not|Ego autem quia veritatem dico, non creditis mihi]] [Denis reads *quia*, “because”], teaching true things and truthfully rebuking your crimes: in which it is plain that you are of your father the devil, who stood not in the truth, and speaks lies of his own: and you consent to him.

8.title: Explanatio residuæ partis hujus capituli octavi: Quis ex vobis arguet me de peccato?
8.title_en: Explanation of the remaining part of this eighth chapter: Which of you shall convince me of sin?

paras.t: Superius redarguit Christus Judæorum incredulitatem et vitia, eo quod sibi non crediderint, neque obedire voluerint. Nunc ostendit se fide dignum, eo quod culpam non habeat. Quis ex vobis, o Scribæ, et Pharisæi, et sacerdotes, arguet me veraciter de peccato quocumque, magno vel parvo, mortali vel veniali, originali vel personali? Frequenter utique arguerunt Jesum de peccato, dicentes, quod sabbatum violaret, et de se ipso mendosum testimonium perhiberet; sed mendaciter id fecerunt. Innuit ergo Salvator vitam suam fuisse prorsus irreprehensibilem, seque omni peccato carere.
paras.en: Above, Christ rebuked the unbelief and the vices of the Jews, because they had not believed him and would not obey him. Now he shows himself worthy of belief, since he has no fault. [[8:46|Which of you|Quis ex vobis]], O Scribes and Pharisees and priests, [[8:46|shall convince me|arguet me]] truly [[8:46|of sin|de peccato]], of any sin whatever, great or small, mortal or venial, original or personal? They did indeed often accuse Jesus of sin, saying that he broke the sabbath[[John 5:18||]], and that he bore false witness of himself[[8:13||]]; but they did so falsely. The Saviour therefore intimates that his life was wholly irreprehensible, and that he was free of all sin.

paras.t: Christus enim secundum naturam divinam, essentialiter sanctus est, virtus virtutum et puritas infinita, tanquam candor lucis æternæ, et speculum sine macula majestatis paternæ. Porro secundum naturam assumptam, confirmatus fuit in bono ab incarnationis exordio, non solum propter beatificam animæ suæ fruitionem in Deo, sed multo amplius propter hypostaticam unionem cum Verbo, propter quam habuit omnium divinorum charismatum plenitudinem, gratiamque tam perfectam, quod major creaturæ communicari non potest. Unde secundum utramque naturam dici potest Sanctus Sanctorum, quia et sanctitas ejus creata omnium creaturarum sanctitatem simul sumptam excedit. Propter quod de ipso legitur apud Isaiam: Iniquitatem non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore ejus.
paras.en: For Christ according to his divine nature is essentially holy, the virtue of virtues and infinite purity, as [[Wis 7:26|the brightness of eternal light|candor lucis æternæ]], and [[Wis 7:26|the unspotted mirror|speculum sine macula]] of the Father's majesty. Further, according to the nature assumed, he was confirmed in good from the first moment of the incarnation, not only because of his soul's beatific enjoyment of God, but much more because of the hypostatic union with the Word, on account of which he had the fulness of all the divine charisms, and grace so perfect that no greater can be communicated to a creature. Hence according to both natures he can be called the Holy of Holies, since even his created holiness exceeds the holiness of all creatures taken together. For this reason we read of him in Isaias: [[Is 53:9|he hath done no iniquity, neither was there deceit in his mouth|Iniquitatem non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore ejus]] [the margin as read gives Is. vii, 9; the words are those of Is 53:9, in the form in which St Peter gives them, 1 Pet 2:22].

paras.t: Decuit autem Christum ut hominem esse sine omni peccato, non solum propter unionem cum Verbo, sed insuper quia salvator, mediator et advocatus totius generis humani. Si enim et ipse peccatum haberet, non esset idoneus omnes Deo reconciliare, et per se ipsum immediate ad Deum accedere, sed mediatore egeret. Idem quoque decuit propter privilegium sacerdotii ejus. Fuit enim primus et summus sacerdos, cujus hostia et obsequium non fuissent Deo perfecte accepta et ad satisfaciendum idonea, si et ipse subjacuisset peccato. Propter quod dicit Apostolus: Talis decebat ut esset nobis pontifex, sanctus, innocens, impollutus, segregatus a peccatoribus et excelsior cœlis factus.
paras.en: And it was fitting that Christ as man should be without any sin, not only because of the union with the Word, but also because he was the saviour, mediator and advocate of the whole human race[[Heb 9:15||]][[1 John 2:1||]] [the margin is partly unreadable here; Heb 9:15 (the mediator) and 1 John 2:1 (the advocate) fit]. For if he too had sin, he would not be fit to reconcile all men to God, and to approach God immediately by himself, but would himself need a mediator. The same was fitting also because of the privilege of his priesthood. For he was the first and supreme priest, whose victim and service would not have been perfectly acceptable to God and fit to make satisfaction, had he himself been subject to sin. Therefore the Apostle says: [[Heb 7:26|it was fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens|Talis decebat ut esset nobis pontifex, sanctus, innocens, impollutus, segregatus a peccatoribus et excelsior cœlis factus]].

paras.t: Si, pro Quia, veritatem dico, evangelicam legem prædicando, et vestra piacula increpando, futura atque secreta elucidando, quare vos non creditis mihi? quasi dicat: In hoc irrationabiliter facitis, quum scriptum sit: Quum videris sensatum, statim evigila ad illum. Sicut autem levitatis est statim credere indifferenter, sic duritiæ est non credere, dum sufficientia signa veritatis apparent. Quamvis vero doctrina Christi fuerit omnino insolita atque incomprehensibilis, propter quod nec faciliter recipienda fuit; tamen tanta tamque evidentissima argumenta patuerunt quod ipse esset verus Christus, verus magister et sanctus (puta testimonium Joannis Baptistæ, vaticinia Prophetarum, miracula Christi discipulorumque ejus, constantia ejus pro veritatis defensione, et zelus justitiæ), quod inexcusabiles erant Judæi de sua perfidia.
paras.en: [[8:46|If|Si]], that is, since, [[8:46|I say the truth|veritatem dico]], in preaching the law of the Gospel, in rebuking your crimes, in making plain things to come and things hidden, [[8:46|why do you not believe me|quare vos non creditis mihi?]]? As though he said: In this you act against reason, since it is written: [[Ecclus 6:36|if thou see a man of understanding, go to him early in the morning|Quum videris sensatum, statim evigila ad illum]]. Now as it is lightness to believe at once and without discernment[[Ecclus 19:4||]], so it is hardness not to believe when sufficient signs of the truth appear. And although the teaching of Christ was altogether unaccustomed and beyond comprehension, so that it could not easily be received, yet such and so very evident proofs appeared that he was the true Christ, the true master and the holy one (namely the testimony of John the Baptist[[John 1:19||]], the prophecies of the Prophets, the miracles of Christ and of his disciples, his constancy in defending the truth, and his zeal for justice), that the Jews were without excuse in their faithlessness.

paras.t: Qui est ex Deo per prædestinationem æternam, per gratiæ reformationem, per bonitatis divinæ imitationem, verba Dei audit, non solum auribus corporis, sed etiam mentis, id est, verba divina libenter audit, memoriter tenet, diligenter adimplet: quemadmodum ait Psalmista, In corde meo abscondi eloquia tua, ut non peccem tibi; et rursus, Bonum mihi lex oris tui super millia auri et argenti. Hinc scriptum est: Esto mansuetus ad audiendum verbum Dei; et iterum, Sit omnis homo velox ad audiendum. Propterea vos non auditis verba Dei auribus interioribus, id est, humiliter, reverenter et affectuose non recipitis verba divina quæ loquor, quia ex Deo non estis (modo prætacto). Omnes quidem, imo et omnia, sunt ex Deo tanquam ex causa efficienti, exemplari atque finali, dicente Apostolo: Ex ipso, per ipsum, et in ipso sunt omnia. Sed non omnes sunt ex Deo per spiritualem reformationem, per gratiæ conservationem, per divinam electionem. Qui enim sic est ex Deo, manet in eo, secundum quod ait Joannes in sua Canonica: Qui natus est ex Deo non peccat, quoniam semen Dei manet in eo. Denique unusquisque libenter audit loqui de re quam diligit. Qui ergo diligit Deum et vitam beatam, verba Dei libenter audit, et affectuose conservat. Et in hoc salus nostra consistit, secundum quod ait Salvator: Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei et custodiunt illud. Debemus ergo verba sacra cum magna attentione, intima affectione, humili reverentia legere, audire et proferre, tanquam epistolas nobis divinitus missas.
paras.en: [[8:47|He that is of God|Qui est ex Deo]], by eternal predestination, by the reforming of grace, by imitation of the divine goodness, [[8:47|heareth the words of God|verba Dei audit]], not only with the ears of the body but also with those of the mind; that is, he hears the divine words gladly, holds them in memory, and fulfils them diligently: as the Psalmist says, [[Ps 118:11|Thy words have I hidden in my heart, that I may not sin against thee|In corde meo abscondi eloquia tua, ut non peccem tibi]]; and again, [[Ps 118:72|The law of thy mouth is good to me, above thousands of gold and silver|Bonum mihi lex oris tui super millia auri et argenti]]. Hence it is written: [[Ecclus 5:13|Be meek to hear the word|Esto mansuetus ad audiendum verbum]] of God; and again, [[Jas 1:19|let every man be swift to hear|Sit omnis homo velox ad audiendum]]. [[8:47|Therefore you hear them not|Propterea vos non auditis]] with the inward ears, that is, you do not receive humbly, reverently and with love the divine words which I speak, [[8:47|because you are not of God|quia ex Deo non estis]] (in the way just touched on). All men indeed, nay all things, are of God as of their efficient, exemplary and final cause, as the Apostle says: [[Rom 11:36|of him, and by him, and in him, are all things|Ex ipso, per ipsum, et in ipso sunt omnia]]. But not all are of God by spiritual reforming, by the preserving of grace, by divine election. For he who is of God in this way abides in him, according to what John says in his Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 3:9|Whosoever is born of God committeth not sin: for his seed abideth in him|Qui natus est ex Deo non peccat, quoniam semen Dei manet in eo]]. Lastly, every man gladly hears talk of what he loves. He therefore who loves God and the blessed life gladly hears the words of God and keeps them with love. And in this our salvation consists, according to what the Saviour says: [[Luke 11:28|blessed are they who hear the word of God and keep it|Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei et custodiunt illud]]. We ought therefore to read, hear and speak the sacred words with great attention, inward affection and humble reverence, as letters sent to us from God.

paras.t: In his verbis dedit nobis Salvator saluberrimum documentum, maximam consolationem grandemque pœnitendi occasionem. Dicendo enim, Qui est ex Deo, etc., inter bonos et malos, inter electos reprobosque distinxit. Fidelibus quoque et timoratis, licet certitudinaliter nesciant an sint digni amore vel odio, contulit magnam spem confidendi quod sunt in statu salutis et filii Dei, quia experiuntur se verba Dei libenter audire, frequenter revolvere, et custodire. Propter quod probabiliter scire possunt quod sint in caritate et gratia, secundum quod ait Apostolus: Ipse Spiritus testimonium reddit spiritui nostro quod filii Dei sumus. Præterea, ex verbis his datur unicuique nostrum aperta et prompta occasio discutiendi se ipsum, an ad Deum pertineat. Dum enim audimus Christum dixisse, Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit, protinus admonemur nos ipsos investigare et sollicite indagare an verba Dei audimus amando et obediendo.
paras.en: In these words the Saviour has given us a most wholesome lesson, very great consolation, and a great occasion of repentance. For in saying, [[8:47|He that is of God|Qui est ex Deo]], etc., he distinguished between the good and the wicked, between the elect and the reprobate. To the faithful also and the God-fearing, although they do not know with certainty whether they are worthy of love or hatred[[Eccles 9:1||]], he gave great hope and confidence that they are in the state of salvation and are sons of God, since they find by experience that they hear the words of God gladly, turn them over often, and keep them. Hence they can know with probability that they are in charity and grace, according to what the Apostle says: [[Rom 8:16|the Spirit himself giveth testimony to our spirit that we are the sons of God|Ipse Spiritus testimonium reddit spiritui nostro quod filii Dei sumus]]. Moreover, these words give each of us a plain and ready occasion of examining himself, whether he belongs to God. For when we hear that Christ said, [[8:47|He that is of God heareth the words of God|Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit]], we are at once admonished to search ourselves and inquire carefully whether we hear the words of God by loving and obeying them.

paras.t: Postremo, quam diligenter et indesinenter conservanda sint verba Dei, patet ex eo quod Moyses scripsit: Erunt verba Domini in corde tuo, et narrabis ea filiis tuis, et meditaberis sedens in domo tua, et ambulans in itinere, et dormiens atque consurgens; et ligabis ea quasi signum in manu tua, eruntque et movebuntur inter oculos tuos, scribesque ea in limine et ostiis domus tuæ.
paras.en: Lastly, how diligently and unceasingly the words of God are to be kept is plain from what Moses wrote: The words of the Lord [[Deut 6:6|shall be in thy heart|Erunt verba Domini in corde tuo]], [[Deut 6:7|And thou shalt tell them to thy children, and thou shalt meditate upon them sitting in thy house, and walking on thy journey, sleeping and rising|et narrabis ea filiis tuis, et meditaberis sedens in domo tua, et ambulans in itinere, et dormiens atque consurgens]]; [[Deut 6:8|And thou shalt bind them as a sign on thy hand, and they shall be and shall move between thy eyes|et ligabis ea quasi signum in manu tua, eruntque et movebuntur inter oculos tuos]], [[Deut 6:9|thou shalt write them in the entry, and on the doors of thy house|scribesque ea in limine et ostiis domus tuæ]].

paras.t: Responderunt igitur Judæi, et dixerunt ei: Nonne bene dicimus nos quia Samaritanus es tu, id est hæreticus quidam, et dæmonium habes, cujus relatione et adjutorio dicis et facis alta ac mira, quæ alii te facere et dicere putant virtute divina! Samaritani erant natione gentiles, sed conversatione semijudæi, quoniam libros Moysis receperunt, et se circumciderunt. Noverant autem isti Judæi quod Jesus esset natione Judæus; sed ex contemptu appellabant eum Samaritanum, id est in parte legis observatorem, et in parte transgressorem. Sicque reputabant eum hæreticum: velut si nunc alicui diceremus: Hussita es tu.
paras.en: [[8:48|The Jews therefore answered and said to him|Responderunt igitur Judæi, et dixerunt ei]]: [[8:48|Do not we say well that thou art a Samaritan|Nonne bene dicimus nos quia Samaritanus es tu]], that is, a kind of heretic, [[8:48|and hast a devil|et dæmonium habes]], by whose information and help thou sayest and doest lofty and wonderful things, which others think thou doest and sayest by divine power? The Samaritans were Gentiles by nation, but half Jews in their way of life, since they received the books of Moses and were circumcised. Now these Jews knew that Jesus was a Jew by nation; but out of contempt they called him a Samaritan, that is, one who keeps the law in part and in part transgresses it. And so they reckoned him a heretic: as if we were now to say to someone, Thou art a Hussite [a follower of John Hus, condemned at the Council of Constance in 1415, in Denis's own lifetime].

paras.t: Secundum Gregorium, Christus non negavit se esse Samaritanum, sed hoc verum est quantum ad nominis interpretationem: non tamen admisit se esse Samaritanum eo modo quo Judæi sibi id imposuerunt. Samaritanus quippe interpretatur custos. Christus vero est custos electorum suorum: de quo Psalmista testatur, Custodiens parvulos Dominus; et Isaias, Custos, quid de nocte? Dixerunt quoque Christum habere dæmonium, non quod esset obsessus et amens, sed quod haberet occultum fœdus cum aliquo dæmone, imo cum summo diabolo, puta Beelzebub, secundum quod alibi dixisse leguntur: In Beelzebub principe dæmoniorum ejicit dæmonia. Hoc ergo perversi dixerunt, quoniam aliter salvare non poterant quomodo tot mirabilia facere, totque secreta et futura reserare, et tam subtilia ac profunda docere, non instructus ab homine, posset, nisi quod vel a Deo vel a diabolo hæc haberet. Noluerunt autem credere quod haberet ea a Deo, propter nimiam displicentiam atque invidiam quam conceperunt in eum: ideo omnia talia deputabant diabolo, quemadmodum magi et arreptitii atque pythones mira aliqua et occulta operantur ac pandunt. Sed in hoc elucescit Judæorum intoleranda perversitas. Nam multa miracula Christi omnem naturalem potestatem transcenderunt, et tota doctrina et conversatio ejus repugnabant diabolo. Propter quod subditur:
paras.en: According to Gregory, Christ did not deny that he was a Samaritan; and this is true as to the meaning of the name, though he did not admit that he was a Samaritan in the sense in which the Jews laid it on him. For Samaritan is interpreted keeper. And Christ is the keeper of his elect: of whom the Psalmist bears witness, [[Ps 114:6|The Lord is the keeper of little ones|Custodiens parvulos Dominus]]; and Isaias, [[Is 21:11|Watchman, what of the night|Custos, quid de nocte]]? [Latin *custos*, the same word as “keeper” in the Psalm.] They also said that Christ had a devil, not that he was possessed and out of his mind, but that he had a secret pact with some demon, nay with the chief devil, namely Beelzebub, according to what we read they said elsewhere: [[Luke 11:15|He casteth out devils by Beelzebub, the prince of devils|In Beelzebub principe dæmoniorum ejicit dæmonia]]. These perverse men said this because they could not otherwise account for how he could do so many wonders, disclose so many secret and future things, and teach things so subtle and deep, untaught by man, except that he had them either from God or from the devil. But they would not believe that he had them from God, because of the great displeasure and envy they had conceived against him: therefore they put all such things down to the devil, in the way that magicians, the possessed and pythons [that is, soothsayers possessed by a spirit of divination] work and disclose certain wonderful and hidden things. But herein shines out the intolerable perversity of the Jews. For many of Christ's miracles surpassed all natural power, and his whole teaching and way of life were opposed to the devil. Therefore it is added:

paras.t: Respondit Jesus: Ego dæmonium non habeo cooperatorem et familiarem: omnia tamen dæmonia mihi subjecta sunt. Sed honorifico Patrem meum, id est, verbo et opere, in omnibus exhibeo honorem, cultum et obedientiam Deo Patri, secundum quod homo sum: ex quo patet sanctitas vitæ meæ, et quod cum dæmonibus non concordo; sed eorum cultum destruo, idololatriam reprobo, vitia damno, hominesque ad Deum converto, ut eum in omnibus toto corde diligant ac honorent. Et vos inhonorastis me, id est, contempsistis, et falsa mihi imposuistis, opera Dei adscribentes diabolo. Et in hoc peccaverunt in Spiritum Sanctum.
paras.en: [[8:49|Jesus answered|Respondit Jesus]]: [[8:49|I have not a devil|Ego dæmonium non habeo]] as fellow worker and familiar; on the contrary, all the devils are subject to me. [[8:49|But I honour my Father|Sed honorifico Patrem meum]], that is, in word and deed, in all things I show honour, worship and obedience to God the Father, inasmuch as I am man: from which the holiness of my life is plain, and that I am not in league with the devils; rather I destroy their worship, condemn idolatry, condemn vices, and turn men to God, that they may love and honour him in all things with their whole heart. [[8:49|And you have dishonoured me|Et vos inhonorastis me]], that is, you have despised me, and laid false things upon me, ascribing the works of God to the devil. And in this they sinned against the Holy Ghost.

paras.t: Ecce quam patienter et mansuete Filius Dei, tanta accepta injuria, respondebat: quia ut Petrus testatur, Quum malediceretur, non maledicebat. Discamus et nos ejus exemplo, non reddere malum pro malo, non vinci a proprio animo, non passionari. Hoc facit facile qui non quærit propriam laudem gloriamque mundanam, qui privatum exstinxit amorem, et gaudet adversis. Nempe, ut ait S. Hieronymus, qui non quærit gloriam, non sentit contumeliam. Magnum est de nullo gaudere, nisi per quod promovemur apud Deum; de nullo quoque dolere, nisi per quod a Deo abducimur.
paras.en: See how patiently and meekly the Son of God answered, after so great an injury: for as Peter testifies, [[1 Pet 2:23|when he was reviled, did not revile|Quum malediceretur, non maledicebat]]. Let us too learn by his example not to [[1 Thess 5:15|render evil for evil|reddere malum pro malo]], not to be overcome by our own temper, not to be carried away by passion. He does this easily who does not seek his own praise and worldly glory, who has put out private love [that is, self-love], and rejoices in adversity. For, as St Jerome says, he who does not seek glory does not feel insult. It is a great thing to rejoice in nothing except what advances us with God, and to grieve at nothing except what draws us away from God.

paras.t: Et ne Judæi dicerent Christo, Inaniter te excusas, adjecit: Ego non quæro gloriam meam. Simile est quod supra ait: Claritatem ab hominibus non accipio. Quod quomodo verum sit, illic diligenter tractatum est. Certum est enim quod Christus jubet se adorari, honorari, suisque verbis in omnibus obediri: trium enim Personarum una est gloria. Verum Christus secundum quod homo, non quæsivit gloriam sæcularem, mundanum honorem, vel aliquam vanitatem, sicut opinabantur Judæi. Incomparabiliter igitur minus spectat ad nos vilissimos peccatores querere gloriam propriam, velle dominari, præesse, glorificari. Unde ex animo dicamus cum Apostolo: Soli Deo honor et gloria.
paras.en: And lest the Jews should say to Christ, Thou excusest thyself in vain, he added: [[8:50|But I seek not my own glory|Ego non quæro gloriam meam]]. Like this is what he said above: [[John 5:41|I receive not glory from men|Claritatem ab hominibus non accipio]]. How this is true was carefully treated there. For it is certain that Christ commands that he be adored and honoured, and obeyed in all his words: for of the three Persons the glory is one. But Christ as man did not seek worldly glory, earthly honour or any vanity, as the Jews supposed. Incomparably less, then, does it become us, most vile sinners, to seek our own glory, to wish to rule, to be set over others, to be glorified. Let us therefore say from the heart with the Apostle: [[1 Tim 1:17|the only God, be honour and glory|Soli Deo honor et gloria]].

paras.t: Est qui quærat et judicet, id est, Deus Pater vel Trinitas requiret a vobis quod non glorificastis me tanquam verum Filium Dei, et de hoc judicabit vos judicio condemnationis. Pater enim requirit et vult Filium .suum glorificari ab omnibus: idcirco qui non honorificat Filium, non honorificat Patrem. Unde in Daniele scriptum est quod Antiquus dierum, videlicet Pater æternus, dedit ei potestatem, honorem et regnum. Superius dixit Salvator: Pater non judicat quemquam. Quomodo ergo nunc ait de Patre, Est qui quærat et judicet? Respondendum, quod in judicio duo considerantur, videlicet ipsa discretio boni a malo, et prolatio sententiæ. Quantum ad primum, judicat Pater seu Trinitas tantum per auctoritatem; quantum ad secundum, judicat Christus secundum naturam assumptam, ut dictum est plenius supra.
paras.en: [[8:50|There is one that seeketh and judgeth|Est qui quærat et judicet]], that is, God the Father, or the Trinity, will require of you that you did not glorify me as the true Son of God, and for this will judge you with the judgment of condemnation. For the Father requires and wills that his Son be glorified by all: therefore [[John 5:23|He who honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father|qui non honorificat Filium, non honorificat Patrem]]. Hence it is written in Daniel that the Ancient of days[[Dan 7:13||]], that is, the eternal Father, [[Dan 7:14|gave him power, and glory, and a kingdom|dedit ei potestatem, honorem et regnum]]. Above, the Saviour said: [[John 5:22|neither does the Father judge any man|Pater non judicat quemquam]]. How then does he now say of the Father, There is one that seeketh and judgeth? The answer is that in judgment two things are considered, namely the discerning of good from evil, and the passing of sentence. As to the first, the Father, or the Trinity, judges by authority alone; as to the second, Christ judges according to the nature assumed, as was said more fully above.

paras.t: Amen, amen, id est vere, vere, dico vobis. Ingeminat, Amen, ad ampliorem certitudinem. Si quis sermonem meum servaverit, per fidem et caritatem, id est, verbis meis fideliter obedierit, mortem non videbit in æternum, id est, nunquam experietur seu sentiet mortem spiritualem: quia nec in presenti privabitur vita gratiæ, nec in futuro vita gloriæ, et nec pœnam sensus nec pœnam damni in inferno habebit. Justi enim in perpetuum vivent, ut Sapiens ait.
paras.en: [[8:51|Amen, amen|Amen, amen]], that is, truly, truly, [[8:51|I say to you|dico vobis]]. He doubles the Amen for greater certainty. [[8:51|If any man keep my word|Si quis sermonem meum servaverit]], by faith and charity, that is, if he faithfully obeys my words, [[8:51|he shall not see death for ever|mortem non videbit in æternum]], that is, he shall never experience or feel spiritual death: for neither in the present shall he be deprived of the life of grace, nor in the future of the life of glory, and he shall have neither the pain of sense nor the pain of loss in hell [the pain of sense: the torment of fire; the pain of loss: the loss of the sight of God]. For [[Wis 5:16|the just shall live for evermore|Justi enim in perpetuum vivent]], as the Wise Man says.

paras.t: Videre, in Scripturis ad omnes sensus refertur, et ad sensitivam atque intellectivam notitiam. Unde nunc sumitur pro gustare, vel experiri seu pati. Sic quoque accipitur in Psalmo, quo dicitur: Non dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem. Denique, ut habetur in Luca, Semen est verbum Dei. Quemadmodum ergo in corporalibus rebus qui semen custodit in terra, pertingit ad fructum; sic qui servat verbum Christi in corde, continuo tendit tandemque pertingit ad fructum seminis hujus, qui est vita eterna. Propter quod Salomon admonet: Serva mandata et legem quasi pupillam oculi tui; liga eam in digitis tuis, et in tabulis cordis tui scribe eam.
paras.en: To see, in the Scriptures, is said of all the senses, and of knowledge both of sense and of intellect. So here it is taken for to taste, or to experience or suffer. So too it is taken in the Psalm, where it is said: [[Ps 15:10|nor wilt thou give thy holy one to see corruption|Non dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem]]. Lastly, as we have it in Luke, [[Luke 8:11|The seed is the word of God|Semen est verbum Dei]]. As then in bodily things he who keeps the seed in the earth comes to the fruit, so he who keeps the word of Christ in his heart tends continually towards, and at last attains, the fruit of this seed, which is eternal life. Therefore Solomon admonishes: [[Prov 7:2|Keep my commandments|Serva mandata]], [[Prov 7:2|and my law as the apple of thy eye|et legem quasi pupillam oculi tui]]: [[Prov 7:3|Bind it upon thy fingers, write it upon the tables of thy heart.|liga eam in digitis tuis, et in tabulis cordis tui scribe eam]].

paras.t: Dixerunt ergo ei Judæi carnales, præinducta verba de morte naturali ac corporali intelligentes: Nunc cognovimus quia dæmonium habes, id est, tam insensate tamque manifeste mendaciter loqueris, quod qui paulo ante opinabamur te dæmonium habere, illoque instigante stultissime loqui, nunc certi sumus de hoc. Et hoc probant. Abraham mortuus est morte corporali, quum esset centum septuaginta quinque annorum; sepelieruntque eum Isaac et Ismael filii ejus, ut in Genesi dicitur; et Prophetæ mortui sunt. Quasi dicant: Tam sanctus patriarcha beatissimique Prophetæ, qui sermones Dei impleverunt, mortui sunt. Et tu filius fabri ac pauperis feminæ, dicis: Si quis sermonem meum servaverit, mortem non gustabit in æternum. Tanquam dicant: Intolerabilis est prassumptio tua, quia sic loqueris ac si verba tua essent amplioris efficaciæ quam verba Dei, et tibi obedientes beatiores essent Abraham ac Prophetis ceterisque Dei ministris, qui non obstante observatione divinorum verborum, defuncti noscuntur.
paras.en: [[8:52|The Jews therefore said|Dixerunt ergo ei Judæi]], the carnal Jews, understanding the words just spoken of natural and bodily death: [[8:52|Now we know that thou hast a devil|Nunc cognovimus quia dæmonium habes]], that is, thou speakest so senselessly and so plainly falsely that we, who a little before supposed that thou hadst a devil and spokest most foolishly at its prompting, are now certain of it. And they prove it: [[8:52|Abraham is dead|Abraham mortuus est]] by bodily death, when he was a hundred and seventy-five years old; and Isaac and Ismael his sons buried him, as is said in Genesis[[Gen 25:7||]][[Gen 25:9||]]; [[8:52|and the prophets|et Prophetæ]] are dead. As though they said: So holy a patriarch and the most blessed Prophets, who fulfilled the words of God, are dead. [[8:52|and thou|Et tu]], the son of a carpenter[[Matt 13:55||]] and of a poor woman, [[8:52|sayest: If any man keep my word, he shall not taste death for ever|dicis: Si quis sermonem meum servaverit, mortem non gustabit in æternum]]. As though they said: Thy presumption is intolerable, for thou speakest as though thy words were of greater efficacy than the words of God, and as though those who obey thee were more blessed than Abraham and the Prophets and the other ministers of God, who, for all their keeping of the divine words, are known to have died.

paras.t: Numquid tu major, id est sanctior, es patre nostro Abraham (qui amicus Dei vocatus est, sicut per Isaiam Dominus loquitur, Semen Abraham amici mei)? quasi dicant, Nequaquam. Loquuntur ergo de spirituali magnitudine, quæ præsertim in sapientia et virtute consistit. Unde in spiritualibus idem est esse majorem et meliorem. Ideo Deus, in quo nulla est quantitas, major est omnibus rebus in infinitum. Mira cæcitas Judæorum. Experimentaliter enim constabat, quod Jesus in gratia prophetiæ, in altitudine sapientiæ, in efficacia miraculorum, in conversatione spiritualium operum, excessit Abraham patriarcham. Sed omnia ista adscripserunt diabolo, quum tamen nec diabolo constent futura pure contingentia cordiumque secreta, sed soli Deo: quæ Christus ubertim prædixit ac reseravit. Unde per Isaiam Dominus ait: Quæ ventura sunt annuntiate, et sciemus quia dii estis vos. Et Prophetæ mortui sunt: id est, quomodo tu qui inferior es Abraham et Prophetis defunctis, citoque moriturus, aliis immortalitatem promittere audes? Quem te ipsum facis? id est, qualem vel quantum affirmas et reputas te, quem videmus esse hominem mortalem similem nobis? quasi dicant: Multum inaniter magnificas te ipsum.
paras.en: [[8:53|Art thou greater|Numquid tu major]], that is, holier, [[8:53|than our father Abraham|es patre nostro Abraham]] [the margin adds “who is dead”, which the verse has and Denis leaves out] (who was called the friend of God, as the Lord speaks by Isaias, [[Is 41:8|the seed of Abraham my friend|Semen Abraham amici mei]])? As though they said, By no means. They speak then of spiritual greatness, which consists chiefly in wisdom and virtue. Hence in spiritual things to be greater and to be better are the same. So God, in whom there is no quantity, is infinitely greater than all things. Wonderful is the blindness of the Jews! For it was known by experience that Jesus surpassed the patriarch Abraham in the grace of prophecy, in the height of wisdom, in the efficacy of miracles, in a life of spiritual works. But they put all these down to the devil, though neither purely contingent future things nor the secrets of hearts are known to the devil, but to God alone: and these Christ abundantly foretold and laid open. Hence the Lord says by Isaias: [[Is 41:23|Shew the things that are to come hereafter, and we shall know that ye are gods|Quæ ventura sunt annuntiate, et sciemus quia dii estis vos]]. [[8:53|And the prophets are dead|Et Prophetæ mortui sunt]]: that is, how darest thou, who art less than Abraham and the Prophets who are dead, and soon to die thyself, promise immortality to others? [[8:53|Whom dost thou make thyself|Quem te ipsum facis]]? that is, of what kind or how great dost thou declare and reckon thyself, whom we see to be a mortal man like ourselves? As though they said: Thou magnifiest thyself very vainly.

paras.t: Respondit Jesus, excusando se de tanto facinore: Si ego glorifico, id est, gloriosum seu magnum dico, me ipsum inordinate atque carnaliter, non sub ordine sapientiæ Dei, secundum quod mihi imponitis, gloria mea,id est dignitas quam mihi adseribo, nihil est, id est nullius reputationis, vana et falsa. Christus utique dicendo, Ego sum lux mundi, et multa similia, glorificavit se; sed non inordinate, prout Judæi ei imposuerunt. Idcirco respondet ad intentionem ipsorum.
paras.en: [[8:54|Jesus answered|Respondit Jesus]], clearing himself of so great a crime: [[8:54|If I glorify|Si ego glorifico]], that is, call glorious or great, [[8:54|myself|me ipsum]], inordinately and carnally, not under the order of God's wisdom, as you lay upon me, [[8:54|my glory|gloria mea]], that is, the dignity I ascribe to myself, [[8:54|is nothing|nihil est]], that is, of no account, vain and false. Christ, indeed, by saying [[8:12|I am the light of the world|Ego sum lux mundi]], and many like things, glorified himself; but not inordinately, as the Jews laid upon him. Therefore he answers to their meaning.

paras.t: Est Pater meus cœlestis qui glorificat, id est, gloriosum ostendit, me, dicendo, Hic est Filius meus dilectus, et per opera miraculosa, Prophetarum quoque eloquia. Denique Pater glorificavit, id est, beatum fecit Christum, secundum naturam assumptam, conferendo animæ ejus beatificam fruitionem. Nec mirum si Filius asserat se glorificari a Patre, quum infra Filius dicat ad Patrem: Ego te clarificavi super terram. Et in libris Regum Deus locutus est: Qui glorificaverit me, glorificabo eum. Quem, id est de quo Patre meo, vos dicitis quia Deus noster est per creationem et gubernationem, et per dilectionem et honorationem nostram ad eum. Quamvis enim Judæi Trinitatis mysterium ignorantes, non dixerint Deum Patrem esse Deum ipsorum, loquendo de Patre secundum quod Pater; tamen id quod est Pater, videlicet Deum absolute acceptum, dixerunt esse Deum suum.
paras.en: [[8:54|It is my Father|Est Pater meus]] in heaven [[8:54|that glorifieth|qui glorificat]], that is, shows to be glorious, me, by saying, [[Matt 3:17|This is my beloved Son|Hic est Filius meus dilectus]][[Matt 17:5||]], and by miraculous works, and by the sayings of the Prophets too. Again, the Father glorified, that is, made blessed, Christ according to the nature assumed, by conferring on his soul the beatific enjoyment. Nor is it any wonder if the Son declares that he is glorified by the Father, since further on the Son says to the Father: [[John 17:4|I have glorified thee on the earth|Ego te clarificavi super terram]]. And in the books of Kings God spoke: [[1 Kings 2:30|whosoever shall glorify me, him will I glorify|Qui glorificaverit me, glorificabo eum]]. [[8:54|of whom|Quem]], that is, of which Father of mine, [[8:54|you say that he is your God|vos dicitis quia Deus noster est]] [Denis: “our God”, as the Jews say it], by creation and governance, and by our love and honouring of him. For although the Jews, not knowing the mystery of the Trinity, did not say that God the Father was their God, speaking of the Father as Father, yet that which the Father is, namely God taken absolutely, they said was their God.

paras.t: Et non cognovistis eum: quoniam Patrem non cognoverunt secundum proprietatem relativam et propriam patris rationem, nec Deum cognoverunt cognitione formata, sed informi. Non enim obedierunt ejus præceptis. Ideo factis eum negabant, quemadmodum de impiis dicit Apostolus: Confitentur se nosse Deum, factis autem negant, quum sint abominati et reprobi. Unde Joannes ait in sua epistola: In hoc scimus quoniam cognovimus Deum, si mandata ejus observamus. De tali formata notitia dicit Apostolus: Si quis ignorat, ignorabitur. Porro de cognitione informi ait: Quum cognovissent Deum, non sicut Deum glorificaverunt, aut gratias egerunt, sed evanuerunt in cogitationibus suis.
paras.en: [[8:55|And you have not known him|Et non cognovistis eum]]: for they did not know the Father according to his relative property and the proper notion of father; nor did they know God with formed knowledge, but with unformed [formed knowledge: knowledge quickened by charity; unformed: without it]. For they did not obey his precepts. Therefore they denied him by their deeds, as the Apostle says of the wicked: [[Tit 1:16|They profess that they know God: but in their works they deny him: being abominable|Confitentur se nosse Deum, factis autem negant, quum sint abominati]] and reprobate. Hence John says in his Epistle: [[1 John 2:3|by this we know that we have known him, if we keep his commandments|In hoc scimus quoniam cognovimus Deum, si mandata ejus observamus]]. Of such formed knowledge the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 14:38|if any man know not, he shall not be known|Si quis ignorat, ignorabitur]]. But of unformed knowledge he says: [[Rom 1:21|when they knew God, they have not glorified him as God or given thanks: but became vain in their thoughts|Quum cognovissent Deum, non sicut Deum glorificaverunt, aut gratias egerunt, sed evanuerunt in cogitationibus suis]].

paras.t: Ego autem novi eum, secundum utramque meam naturam: quia ut Deus, cognosco eum per comprehensionem perfectam; et ut homo, cognosco eum notitia beatæ fruitionis per speciem. Tali nempe notitia novit anima Christi Deum Patrem seu Trinitatem indesinenter, in somno et vigilia: quia per somnum aliasque corporales occupationes, actiones et passiones, non impediebatur anima Christi ab interiori cognitione ac dilectione Dei, sed jugiter erat in actu. Et sermonem ejus servo memoriter et obedienter, secundum naturam humanam. Non enim negligentia vel oblivio locum habebat in Christo. Et si dixero quia non scio eum, id est, quod Patrem non cognosco: quod impossibile est me dicere, sicut impossibile est me mentiri; ero similis vobis, mendax, qui multa mendacia fingitis contra me; sed scio eum, et sermonem ejus servo (ut dictum est).
paras.en: [[8:55|but I know him|Ego autem novi eum]], according to both my natures: for as God I know him with perfect comprehension; and as man I know him with the knowledge of blessed enjoyment, by sight. With such knowledge the soul of Christ knew God the Father, or the Trinity, unceasingly, sleeping and waking: for through sleep and other bodily occupations, actions and passions, Christ's soul was not hindered from the inward knowledge and love of God, but was continually in act. [[8:55|and do keep his word|Et sermonem ejus servo]], in memory and in obedience, according to the human nature. For negligence or forgetfulness had no place in Christ. [[8:55|And if I shall say that I know him not|Et si dixero quia non scio eum]], that is, that I do not know the Father, which it is impossible for me to say, as it is impossible for me to lie, [[8:55|I shall be like to you, a liar|ero similis vobis, mendax]], who invent many lies against me; [[8:55|But I do know him and do keep his word|sed scio eum, et sermonem ejus servo]] (as has been said).

paras.t: Paulo ante dixerunt Judæi: Numquid tu major es patre nostro Abraham? Ad hoe Christus modo respondet: Abraham pater vester, secundum carnalem propaginem, non secundum fidei atque virtutum parilitatem, exsultavit, id est, spiritualiter letabatur, ut videret, id est de hoe quod visurus erat, diem meum, id est tempus adventus mei seu incarnationis. Facta enim sibi promissione quod Christum in spiritu cerneret, ejusque mysteria nosceret, cordialiter exsultavit. Vidit, id est, per spiritum prophetiae cognovit diem adventus mei, vel me tune venturum, et gavisus est. Cognovit enim Filium Dei in fine seculorum incarnandum, quum dictum est ei: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes. Nec dubium quin, ipse, aliique Prophetæ et Patriarchæ multa noverunt per revelationem divinam, de Christo ejusque adventu atque mysteriis, quæ non sunt descripta. An tamen Abraham novit determinate tempus adventus Christi, ut Daniel, qui determinavit hebdomades dominicæ passionis, certum non habeo.
paras.en: A little before, the Jews said: [[8:53|Art thou greater than our father Abraham|Numquid tu major es patre nostro Abraham]]? To this Christ now replies: [[8:56|Abraham your father|Abraham pater vester]], according to fleshly descent, not according to likeness in faith and virtues, [[8:56|rejoiced|exsultavit]], that is, was spiritually glad, [[8:56|that he might see|ut videret]], that is, at this, that he was to see, [[8:56|my day|diem meum]], that is, the time of my coming or incarnation. For when the promise was made to him that he should behold Christ in spirit and know his mysteries, he exulted in his heart. [[8:56|he saw it|Vidit]], that is, by the spirit of prophecy he knew the day of my coming, or me who was then to come, [[8:56|and was glad|et gavisus est]]. For he knew that the Son of God was to be incarnate at the end of the ages, when it was said to him: [[Gen 22:18|in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes]]. Nor is there any doubt that he, and many other Prophets and Patriarchs, knew by divine revelation many things about Christ and his coming and mysteries which are not written down. But whether Abraham knew determinately the time of Christ's coming, as Daniel did, who fixed the weeks to the Lord's passion[[Dan 9:24||]], I do not hold for certain.

paras.t: Potest quoque intelligi de die æternitatis Christi: qui dies aliud non est nisi ipsa eternitas, seu Deus æternus. Hujus diei beatificam visionem in claritate patriæ electorum, Deus promisit Abrahæ: Ego (inquiens) protector tuus et merces tua magna nimis. Hanc diem vidit Abraham in via per fidem, tendebat ad eam per spem, exsultavit in ejus prestolatione per caritatem. Hinc quoque dicit Apostolus: Exspectabat Abraham fundamenta habentem civitatem, cujus artifex et conditor Deus.
paras.en: It can also be understood of the day of Christ's eternity: which day is nothing other than eternity itself, or the eternal God. The beatific vision of this day, in the brightness of the fatherland of the elect, God promised to Abraham, saying: [[Gen 15:1|I am thy protector, and thy reward exceeding great|Ego (inquiens) protector tuus et merces tua magna nimis]]. This day Abraham saw on the way by faith, tended towards it by hope, and exulted in awaiting it by charity. Hence too the Apostle says: Abraham [[Heb 11:10|looked for a city that hath foundations: whose builder and maker is God|Exspectabat Abraham fundamenta habentem civitatem, cujus artifex et conditor Deus]].

paras.t: Sed his obviare videtur quod Christus alibi ait discipulis suis: Multi Prophetæ et justi cupierunt videre quæ vos videtis et non viderunt. Hoc enim apparet tam bene dictum de Abraham sicut de aliis Prophetis ac justis. Et respondendum, quod Christus loquitur ibi de visione intellectuali conjuncta visioni exteriori, quemadmodum plenius demonstravi super Matthæum. Sic autem Abraham non vidit diem et opera Christi, seu Christum in carne, nec alii Prophetæ ante Christi incarnationem defuncti.
paras.en: But against this seems to be what Christ says elsewhere to his disciples: [[Matt 13:17|many prophets and just men have desired to see the things that you see, and have not seen them|Multi Prophetæ et justi cupierunt videre quæ vos videtis et non viderunt]]. For this appears to be said as much of Abraham as of the other Prophets and just men. And the answer is that Christ speaks there of intellectual vision joined to outward vision, as I have shown more fully on Matthew. In this way Abraham did not see the day and works of Christ, or Christ in the flesh, nor did the other Prophets who died before Christ's incarnation.

paras.t: Dixerunt ergo Judæi ad eum: Quinquaginta annos nondum habes, et Abraham vidisti? Christus dixit quod Abraham vidit diem suum; et ipsi sic repetunt: Abraham vidisti? quia qua ratione verificaretur unum, verificaretur et reliquum. Quasi dicant: Si Abraham vidit diem tuum, ergo contemporanei exstitistis, et vos invicem conspexistis: quod patet falsum quum nondum sortitus sis annos quinquaginta. Potius autem dixerunt, Abraham vidisti? quam, Abraham vidit te? quasi magnum esset Jesu vidisse Abraham patriarcham, et non econtra, reputantes Abraham multo majorem Jesu.
paras.en: [[8:57|The Jews therefore said to him|Dixerunt ergo Judæi ad eum]]: [[8:57|Thou art not yet fifty years old. And hast thou seen Abraham|Quinquaginta annos nondum habes, et Abraham vidisti?]]? Christ said that Abraham saw his day; and they turn it about thus, Hast thou seen Abraham? because by the same reasoning by which the one would be true, the other would be true too. As though they said: If Abraham saw thy day, then you were contemporaries and saw one another: which is plainly false, since thou hast not yet reached fifty years. But they said, Hast thou seen Abraham? rather than, Did Abraham see thee? as though it were a great thing for Jesus to have seen the patriarch Abraham, and not the other way about, reckoning Abraham much greater than Jesus.

paras.t: Quæritur, cur nominaverunt annos quinquaginta, quum Jesus multo junior esset. Aliqui dicunt, quod a casu, quia sic occurrebat eis. Alii dicunt, quod propter reverentiam jubilæi, qui fuit quinquagesimus annus. Quasi dicant: Necdum attigisti unum jubilæum, et Abraham vidisti, qui pene per duo millia annorum dormivit cum patribus suis? Quidam dicunt, quod Christus, propter jejunia et labores et propter nimiam maturitatem, videbatur multo senior quam fuit. Unde ait in Psalmo: Genua mea infirmata sunt a jejunio, et caro mea immutata est propter oleum. Ego opinor quod ideo tantum excrementum annorum expresserunt, ut insinuarent quam plane ac facile possent falsificare verba Christi. Quasi dicant: Dato quod haberes multo plures annos quam habes, nihilo minus falsum esset quod dixisti Abraham te vidisse.
paras.en: It is asked why they named fifty years, when Jesus was much younger. Some say it was by chance, because it so came to them. Others say that it was out of reverence for the jubilee, which was the fiftieth year[[Lev 25:10||]]. As though they said: Thou hast not yet reached one jubilee, and hast thou seen Abraham, who has slept with his fathers for almost two thousand years? Some say that Christ, because of fasts and labours and his great gravity, looked much older than he was. Hence he says in the Psalm: [[Ps 108:24|My knees are weakened through fasting: and my flesh is changed for oil|Genua mea infirmata sunt a jejunio, et caro mea immutata est propter oleum]]. I think that they named so great a number of years to hint how plainly and easily they could prove Christ's words false. As though they said: Granted that thou hadst many more years than thou hast, it would none the less be false, what thou saidst, that Abraham saw thee.

paras.t: Erraverunt autem isti obtenebrati Judæi dupliciter: primo, quod verbum Christi de corporali visione intellexerunt; secundo, quod solum in Christo humanam nativitatem pensabant, putantes quod nequaquam fuisset prior sua matre. Hujus secundi falsitatem reprobat Christus. Dixit eis Jesus: Amen, amen dico vobis. Mitis humilisque magister semper patienter cum tranquillitate respondet, non commotus illorum injuriis. Hoc enim præcipue pertinet ad prædicatorem sive doctorem verbi Dei, quia ut Salomon loquitur: Doctrina viri per patientiam noscitur; et non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit. Propterea apud Gregorium: Tanto convincitur quisque minus doctus, quanto minus patiens.
paras.en: But these darkened Jews erred in two ways: first, in understanding Christ's word of bodily sight; second, in considering only the human birth in Christ, thinking that he was in no way prior to his mother. The falsity of this second error Christ refutes. [[8:58|Jesus said to them|Dixit eis Jesus]]: [[8:58|Amen, amen, I say to you|Amen, amen dico vobis]]. The meek and humble master always answers patiently and calmly, unmoved by their insults. For this belongs especially to the preacher or teacher of the word of God, since, as Solomon says: [[Prov 19:11|The learning of a man is known by patience|Doctrina viri per patientiam noscitur]]; and [[Prov 12:21|Whatsoever shall befall the just man, shall not make him sad|non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit]]. Hence in Gregory: The less patient a man is, the more he is shown to be the less learned.

paras.t: Antequam Abraham fieret, id est, crearetur quantum ad animam, vel generaretur quantum ad totum compositum, ego sum in natura divinitatis æternaliter, invariabiliterque subsisto. Porro dicendo, Ego sum, ostendit suam æternitatem, qua nec præteritum habet neque futurum, sed omne tempus ambit, includit, excedit. Ipse est qui olim locutus est Moysi: Ego sum qui sum. Unde ad Hebræos legitur: Jesus heri et hodie, ipse et in sæcula. Ipse namque est Sapientia quæ in Ecclesiastico protestatur: Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi, primogenita ante omnem creaturam.
paras.en: [[8:58|before Abraham was made|Antequam Abraham fieret]], that is, was created as to his soul, or begotten as to the whole composite, [[8:58|I AM|ego sum]] in the nature of the Godhead, that is, I subsist eternally and unchangeably. Further, by saying, I am, he shows his eternity, which has neither past nor future, but surrounds, includes and exceeds all time. He it is who once spoke to Moses: [[Ex 3:14|I AM WHO AM|Ego sum qui sum]]. Hence we read in Hebrews: [[Heb 13:8|Jesus Christ, yesterday, and today: and the same for ever.|Jesus heri et hodie, ipse et in sæcula]]. For he is the Wisdom who declares in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 24:5|I came out of the mouth of the most High, the firstborn before all creatures|Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi, primogenita ante omnem creaturam]].

paras.t: Tulerunt ergo lapides, ut jacerent in eum, obruendo eum lapidibus tanquam blasphemum. Lex quippe præcepit blasphemos lapidari. Jesus autem abscondit se, non retro maceriam seu columnam: sed, Abscondit se, id est, divina potestate præbuit se invisibilem Judæis, non discipulis suis, quia secuti sunt eum. Potest autem absconsio ista dupliciter intelligi: Primo, quod percussit eos cæcitate quæ dicitur aorasia, qua aliquid non videtur, quum tamen alia videantur, vel si videtur, non tamen cognoscitur: qua percussi fuerunt Sodomitæ, et Syri ad instantiam Elisei, ut legitur in Genesi et in libris Regum. Secundo, quod Jesus divina virtute fecit ne color corporis sui immutaret visum Judæorum. Imo hoc potuit virtute animæ suæ, quæ habuit perfectum dominium supra proprium corpus. Nam et animæ Beatorum corporibus glorificatis unitæ, facere possunt propria corpora visibilia uni, et invisibilia alteri. Corpora enim hujusmodi sunt in plenissima obedientia animarum Deo fruentium.
paras.en: [[8:59|They took up stones therefore to cast at him|Tulerunt ergo lapides, ut jacerent in eum]], to overwhelm him with stones as a blasphemer. For the Law commanded that blasphemers be stoned[[Lev 24:16||]]. [[8:59|But Jesus hid himself|Jesus autem abscondit se]], not behind a wall or a pillar; but, He hid himself, that is, by divine power he made himself invisible to the Jews, though not to his disciples, for they followed him. This hiding can be understood in two ways. First, that he struck them with the blindness called *aorasia* [Greek, “not seeing”: the eyes are sound but the thing is not perceived], by which something is not seen though other things are seen, or, if it is seen, is not recognised: with which the Sodomites were struck[[Gen 19:11||]], and the Syrians at the prayer of Eliseus[[4 Kings 6:18||]], as we read in Genesis and in the books of Kings. Second, that Jesus by divine power brought it about that the colour of his body did not act upon the sight of the Jews. Indeed he could do this by the power of his soul, which had perfect dominion over its own body. For the souls of the Blessed too, united to glorified bodies, can make their own bodies visible to one and invisible to another. For such bodies are in the fullest obedience to the souls that enjoy God.

paras.t: Et exivit de templo Jerusalem. Exivit autem pergendo per medium illorum, quemadmodum transiit per medium civium suorum eum præcipitare volentium, ut Lucas recitat. Noluit enim adhuc occidi, quoniam nondum venit hora quam propriæ passioni prævidit, præfixit, elegit. Per quod dedit exemplum fidelibus, quod sæpe possunt se persecutoribus suis occultare, quando videlicet fides aliorum non periclitatur, nec grande scandalum oritur pusillorum, nec justitia ipsa exstinguitur.
paras.en: [[8:59|and went out of the temple|et exivit de templo]] of Jerusalem. He went out by passing through the midst of them, as he passed through the midst of his fellow townsmen who wished to cast him down headlong, as Luke relates[[Luke 4:30||]] [the margin as read gives Luke 19:30; the passage is Luke 4:29–30]. For he did not yet will to be killed, since the hour had not yet come which he had foreseen, fixed and chosen for his own passion. By this he gave the faithful an example: that they may often hide themselves from their persecutors, namely when the faith of others is not endangered, nor great scandal arises among the little ones, nor justice itself is extinguished.

9.title: Expositio capituli noni: Et præteriens Jesus, vidit hominem cæcum a nativitate.
9.title_en: Exposition of the ninth chapter: “And Jesus passing by, saw a man who was blind from his birth.”

paras.t: Quia in superiori capitulo multa incomprehensibilia ac divina Christus de se ipso asseruit, quæ Judæi non intelligentes, voluerunt eum quasi blasphemum lapidare; idcirco nunc convenienter recitatur miraculum omnino divinum, quod naturali virtute effici nequit, quatenus per hoc confirmetur supernaturalis doctrina jam præinducta. Præmissæ enim correspondere et proportionari debent conclusioni. Propterea supernaturalis veritas fidei, per supernaturalia argumenta, hoc est per opera miraculosa, ostenditur.
paras.en: Since in the previous chapter Christ asserted many incomprehensible and divine things about Himself, which the Jews did not understand, and so wished to stone Him as a blasphemer, there is now fittingly related a miracle wholly divine, one that cannot be worked by natural power, so that the supernatural teaching already set out may be confirmed by it. For the premises must correspond and be proportioned to the conclusion. Therefore the supernatural truth of the faith is shown by supernatural arguments, that is, by miraculous works.

paras.t: Et præteriens Jesus, hoc est, locum circa templum pertransiens, vidit diligenti intuitu oculi corporalis, pio quoque respectu divinæ miserationis, hominem cæcum a nativitate, nomine Cedonium: qui postea cum Maria Magdalene, Martha, Maximino et Lazaro, a Judæa expulsus est, sicut habetur in legenda Mariæ Magdalenæ. Cæcus autem a nativitate non potest de coloribus judicare, quia orbatus a nativitate aliquo sensu, caret notitia sensibilium illius sensus. Ex quo concludit Aristoteles, quod nostra notitia intellectiva non est concreata, sed a sensu originata, atque ex prævia cognitione sensitiva causata.
paras.en: [[9:1|And Jesus passing by|Et præteriens Jesus]], that is, passing through the place near the temple, [[9:1|saw|vidit]] with the attentive gaze of His bodily eye, and also with the loving regard of divine compassion, [[9:1|a man who was blind from his birth|hominem cæcum a nativitate]], Cedonius by name, who afterwards was driven out of Judæa together with Mary Magdalene, Martha, Maximinus and Lazarus, as is found in the legend of Mary Magdalene. Now one blind from birth cannot judge of colours, since whoever is deprived of some sense from birth lacks all knowledge of the things perceived by that sense. From this Aristotle concludes that our intellectual knowledge is not concreated [that is, not created in the soul together with it, as inborn ideas], but has its origin in the senses and is caused by a prior knowledge through the senses.

paras.t: Mystice, quando Judæi increduli Christum repulerunt, ejus discipulos atque Apostolos a suis finibus expellendo, conversus est Jesus, et oculo pietatis adspexit populum gentilem penitus cæcum et in tenebris natum ac enutritum, eumque per Apostolorum prædicationem et gratiæ infusionem edocuit. Propter quod Paulus et Barnabas dicunt Judæis: Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei; sed quoniam repulistis illud, ecce convertimur ad gentes: sic enim præcepit nobis Dominus. In Isaia quoque Dominus ad Christum ait: Dedi te in lucem gentium, ut aperires oculos cæcorum.
paras.en: Mystically: when the unbelieving Jews rejected Christ, driving His disciples and Apostles out of their borders, Jesus turned and with the eye of mercy looked upon the gentile people, wholly blind, born and brought up in darkness, and taught them through the preaching of the Apostles and the infusion of grace. Hence Paul and Barnabas say to the Jews: [[Acts 13:46|To you it behoved us first to speak the word of God|Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei]]: but since you have rejected it, [[Acts 13:46|behold we turn to the Gentiles|ecce convertimur ad gentes]]. [[Acts 13:47|For so the Lord hath commanded us|sic enim præcepit nobis Dominus]]. In Isaias too the Lord says to Christ: [[Is 42:6|I have given thee|Dedi te]] [[Is 42:6|for a light of the Gentiles|in lucem gentium]], [[Is 42:7|That thou mightest open the eyes of the blind|ut aperires oculos cæcorum]].

paras.t: Et interrogaverunt eum discipuli ejus. Ex quo viderunt Jesum diligenter intueri hunc cæcum, quasi aliquid circa eum acturus, sciscitati sunt magistrum discipuli. Rabbi, quis peccavit, hic cæcus, aut parentes ejus, ut, hoc est propter quod peccatum, cæcus nasceretur? Discipuli isti præsupponebant quod pœna non infligitur rationali creaturæ, nisi propter culpam, quum pœna sit præmium culpæ. Et hoc aliquo modo verum est, quia nisi originale peccatum præcessisset, sequentes pœnæ hominibus inflictæ non essent. Non tamen omnis pœna propter originale peccatum inducitur, quasi in vindictam illius, nec propter actuale peccatum patientis, sed et propter alias causas, ut jam dicetur.
paras.en: [[9:2|And his disciples asked him|Et interrogaverunt eum discipuli ejus]]. When they saw Jesus looking attentively at this blind man, as though about to do something for him, the disciples questioned their Master: [[9:2|Rabbi, who hath sinned, this man|Rabbi, quis peccavit, hic]], the blind man, [[9:2|or his parents|aut parentes ejus]], [[9:2|that|ut]], that is, for what sin, [[9:2|he should be born blind|cæcus nasceretur]]? These disciples took it for granted that punishment is not inflicted on a rational creature except for guilt, since punishment is the wages of guilt. And this is true in a certain way, for had original sin not gone before, the punishments that followed would not have been inflicted on men. Yet not every punishment is brought on because of original sin, as if in vengeance for it, nor because of an actual sin of the one who suffers it, but also for other causes, as will now be said.

paras.t: Videntur autem discipuli interrogasse, ac si putassent hominem antequam nasceretur peccasse, quemadmodum Platonici et Origenes dixerunt animas hominum simul creatas a principio mundi in cœlo, illicque peccasse, et ob id corporibus quasi carceribus alligatas in ultionem peccatorum vitæ alterius sæculi. Sed hoc discipuli non putabant, neque a Christo hoc didicerunt; sed quum essent rudes et simplices, simpliciter quæsierunt. Potest tamen eorum inquisitio colorari dupliciter: primo, ut intelligantur quæsisse de peccato originali ipsius cæci; secundo ut intelligantur interrogasse de peccato ejus futuro, videlicet an Deus universa prænoscens, fecerit eum cæcum propter iniquitates ejus futuras. Est namque quorumdam opinio, quod Deus interdum dat præmium ante meritum, scilicet propter meritum futurum.
paras.en: The disciples seem to have asked as if they thought the man had sinned before he was born, just as the Platonists and Origen said that the souls of men were created all together at the beginning of the world in heaven, and sinned there, and for that reason were bound to bodies as to prisons, in punishment for the sins of a life in another age. But the disciples did not think this, nor had they learned it from Christ; being unlettered and simple men, they simply asked. Their question can, however, be given a sound sense [literally "coloured", that is, given a fair construction] in two ways: first, so that they are understood to have asked about the original sin of the blind man himself; second, so that they are understood to have asked about his future sin, namely whether God, foreknowing all things, had made him blind on account of his future iniquities. For it is the opinion of some that God sometimes gives the requital before the desert, that is, on account of a desert still to come.

paras.t: Considerandum vero, quod punitio consistit in subtractione alicujus boni et inflictione mali. Bonum autem est duplex, et malum similiter. Est enim bonum spirituale ad animam pertinens, scilicet gratia, virtus, et dona Spiritus Sancti. Aliud est bonum corporale, ut sanitas, divitiæ. Unus ergo non punitur propter peccatum alterius, in privatione spiritualium bonorum et inflictione oppositorum malorum, sed in privatione corporalium bonorum. Cujus ratio est, quoniam unus punitur propter peccatum alterius, in quantum est aliquid ejus, ita quod pœna ejus redundat in illum propter quem punitur: sicut punitur populus propter regem, et filius propter parentes, quemadmodum in libris Regum et Paralipomenon legitur populus Judæorum percussus propter numerationem factam seu fieri jussam a David. Unus autem non est aliquid alterius quantum ad animam, quoniam anima simplex est, et immediate a Deo creatur atque infunditur. Unde per Ezechielem Dominus loquitur: Omnes animæ meæ sunt; sicut anima filii, sic anima patris. Sed quantum ad corpus, filius est aliquid parentum, tanquam de eorum semine natus, et populus est aliquid principis. Ideo propter peccatum unius, alter quandoque punitur, vel in corpore per infirmitatem, vel in membris per monstruositatem. Quandoque enim nascuntur filii monstruosi propter peccata parentum, qui in filiis talibus affliguntur ac puniuntur, vel in exterioribus bonis, vel in subditis.
paras.en: It must be considered, however, that punishment consists in the taking away of some good and the infliction of evil. Now good is twofold, and so is evil. For there is spiritual good, belonging to the soul, namely grace, virtue and the gifts of the Holy Spirit; and there is bodily good, such as health and riches. One man, then, is not punished for another's sin by being deprived of spiritual goods and having the opposite evils inflicted on him, but by being deprived of bodily goods. The reason is this: one man is punished for another's sin in so far as he is something of his, so that the punishment of the one overflows onto him for whose sake he is punished; as a people is punished for its king, and a son for his parents, just as we read in the books of Kings[[2 Kings 24:1||]] and Paralipomenon[[1 Par 21:1||]] that the people of the Jews was struck because of the numbering made, or ordered to be made, by David. But one man is not something of another as regards the soul, since the soul is simple, and is created and infused immediately by God. Hence the Lord speaks through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 18:4|all souls are mine|Omnes animæ meæ sunt]]; as the soul of the son, so the soul of the father. But as regards the body, a son is something of his parents, being born of their seed, and a people is something of its prince. Therefore for the sin of one, another is sometimes punished, either in the body by sickness, or in the limbs by deformity. For sometimes children are born deformed because of the sins of their parents, who are afflicted and punished in such children; or in outward goods, or in their subjects.

paras.t: Per hanc distinctionem concordantur Scripturæ quæ prima facie videntur contrariæ. Illæ enim quæ asserunt filios puniri propter parentes, intelligendæ sunt de punitione in corporalibus bonis quæ subtrahuntur, et corporalibus malis quæ infliguntur: ut quum Moyses ait in Exodo, Dominator Domine, qui reddis iniquitatem patrum filiis ac nepotibus, in tertiam et quartam generationem. Et apud Jeremiam: Domine Deus, qui facis misericordiam in millibus, et reddis iniquitatem patrum in sinum filiorum post eos. Porro auctoritates quæ dicunt oppositum, intelliguntur de punitione in spiritualibus bonis (talis enim punitio non ordinaretur ad bonum puniti) ut per Ezechielem inducitur: Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris, et pater non portabit iniquitatem filii. Hinc apud eumdem Dominus increpat filios Israel dicentes: Patres comederunt uvam acerbam, et dentes filiorum obstupuerunt.
paras.en: By this distinction the Scriptures that at first sight seem contrary are brought into agreement. Those which assert that children are punished for their parents are to be understood of punishment in bodily goods that are taken away and in bodily evils that are inflicted; as when Moses says in Exodus: [[Ex 34:6|O the Lord|Dominator Domine]], [[Ex 34:7|Who renderest the iniquity of the fathers to the children, and to the grandchildren unto the third and fourth generation|qui reddis iniquitatem patrum filiis ac nepotibus, in tertiam et quartam generationem]]. And in Jeremias: [[Jer 32:17|O Lord God|Domine Deus]], [[Jer 32:18|Thou shewest mercy unto thousands, and returnest the iniquity of the fathers into the bosom of their children after them|qui facis misericordiam in millibus, et reddis iniquitatem patrum in sinum filiorum post eos]]. But the authorities that say the opposite are understood of punishment in spiritual goods (for such punishment would not be ordered to the good of the one punished), as is brought forward through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 18:20|the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son|Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris, et pater non portabit iniquitatem filii]]. Hence in the same prophet the Lord rebukes the children of Israel who say: [[Ezech 18:2|The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge|Patres comederunt uvam acerbam, et dentes filiorum obstupuerunt]].

paras.t: Respondit Jesus: Neque hic peccavit neque parentes ejus, peccato de quo vos inquiritis, id est, tale crimen non commiserunt, propter quod iste natus est cæcus. Non ergo vult Christus dicere, quod nullatenus peccaverunt: quoniam Salomone testante, Non est homo super terram qui faciat bonum et non peccet; et Jacobus, In multis (inquit) offendimus omnes. Sed intentioni discipulorum respondit, qui de certo peccato interrogaverunt. Sed ut manifestentur opera Dei in illo, id est, ideo natus est cæcus, ut miraculosa opera a me in eo fiant, ad manifestationem divinæ potentiæ atque ad gloriam Creatoris. Ponit autem Salvator plurale pro singulari, quia per opera Dei designat supernaturalem illuminationem cæci istius. Vel potest pluraliter accipi, intelligendo per opera Dei, omnia quæ ad illuminationem hujus cæci concurrebant, videlicet linitionem oculorum ejus ex sputo, etc.
paras.en: [[9:3|Jesus answered: Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents|Respondit Jesus: Neque hic peccavit neque parentes ejus]], with the sin you are asking about; that is, they did not commit such a crime that on account of it this man was born blind. So Christ does not mean to say that they had not sinned at all, since, as Solomon testifies, [[Eccles 7:21|there is no just man upon earth, that doth good, and sinneth not|Non est homo super terram qui faciat bonum et non peccet]]; and James: [[Jas 3:2|In many things|In multis]] (he says) [[Jas 3:2|we all offend|offendimus omnes]]. But He answered the disciples' intention, for they asked about a particular sin. [[9:3|but that the works of God should be made manifest in him|Sed ut manifestentur opera Dei in illo]]: that is, he was born blind for this, that miraculous works might be done in him by Me, for the manifestation of the divine power and for the glory of the Creator. The Saviour puts the plural for the singular, since by "the works of God" He means the supernatural giving of sight to this blind man. Or it can be taken as a true plural, understanding by "the works of God" all that went together to give this blind man sight, namely the anointing of his eyes with spittle, etc.

paras.t: Denique, secundum doctores sex modis flagellat Dominus hominem: Primo, propter meritorum augmentum, et ad virtutis probationem seu manifestationem, quemadmodum Job et Tobiam: secundum quod Job ait, Probavit me Dominus quasi aurum quod per ignem transit; et Tobiæ dicitur, Quia acceptus eras Deo, necesse fuit ut tentatio probaret te. Secundo, propter virtutum spiritualiumque bonorum custodiam, ne propter superbiam amittantur: ut Paulum, qui profitetur, Ne magnitudo revelationum extollat me, datus est mihi angelus Satanæ. Tertio, ut virtus divina manifestetur ad gloriam Creatoris: ut hunc cæcum, et Lazarum, qui ideo obiit, ut a Christo ad gloriam Dei suscitaretur, sicut infra Salvator testatur: Infirmitas hæc non est ad mortem, sed pro gloria Dei, ut clarificetur Filius hominis per eam. Quarto, propter peccata, ut per pœnam inflictam purgentur, expientur, seu dimittantur: ut paralyticum, de quo dictum est quinto capitulo, et Mariam sororem Moysis, filios quoque Israel in deserto, ut aliqui dicunt. Quinto, propter nimia scelera, ut futura atque æterna pœna in præsenti quodammodo inchoetur: ut Antiochum, et Herodem, Sodomitas, Dathan et Abiron et Core. Sexto, propter divini consilii dispensationem, ad satisfaciendum pro aliis: sicut Christum, juxta illud Isaiæ, Propter scelus populi mei percussi eum.
paras.en: Lastly, according to the doctors, the Lord scourges a man in six ways. First, for the increase of merit, and for the proving or showing forth of virtue, as He did Job and Tobias[[Tob 2:12||]]; according to which Job says, The Lord [[Job 23:10|has tried me as gold that passeth through the fire|Probavit me Dominus quasi aurum quod per ignem transit]]; and to Tobias it is said, [[Tob 12:13|because thou wast acceptable to God, it was necessary that temptation should prove thee|Quia acceptus eras Deo, necesse fuit ut tentatio probaret te]]. Second, for the safekeeping of the virtues and spiritual goods, lest they be lost through pride, as He did Paul, who declares: [[2 Cor 12:7|lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me|Ne magnitudo revelationum extollat me]], [[2 Cor 12:7|there was given me|datus est mihi]] [[2 Cor 12:7|an angel of Satan|angelus Satanæ]]. Third, that the divine power may be shown forth to the glory of the Creator, as He did this blind man, and Lazarus, who died for this, that he might be raised by Christ to the glory of God, as the Saviour testifies below: [[John 11:4|This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God|Infirmitas hæc non est ad mortem, sed pro gloria Dei]], that the Son of man may be glorified by it [so Denis; the Vulgate has "the Son of God"]. Fourth, for sins, that through the punishment inflicted they may be purged, expiated or forgiven, as He did the paralytic spoken of in the fifth chapter[[John 5:5||]], and Mary the sister of Moses[[Num 12:1||]], and also the children of Israel in the desert, as some say. Fifth, for exceeding great crimes, that the future and eternal punishment may in some way begin in the present, as He did Antiochus[[2 Mach 9:5||]], and Herod[[Acts 12:23||]], the Sodomites[[Gen 19:13||]], Dathan and Abiron and Core[[Num 16:1||]]. Sixth, by the dispensation of the divine counsel, to make satisfaction for others, as He did Christ, according to that of Isaias: [[Is 53:8|for the wickedness of my people have I struck him|Propter scelus populi mei percussi eum]].

paras.t: Me oportet, non aliqua coactione, sed magna utilitate atque immobili complacentia, et propter invariabilem dispositionem ordinationis divinæ, a qua deviare non possum, operari opera ejus qui me misit, hoc est opera Dei Patris quæ per me fieri decrevit, quæ ordinantur vel pertinent ad humani generis liberationem, videlicet signa per quæ homines sciunt me esse Filium Dei et convertuntur ad me, cetera quoque opera sancta et virtuosa quæ pro nostra salute Christus fecit, docendo, orando, discurrendo. Opera autem miraculosa, sunt opera Patris vel Trinitatis, tanquam principalis actoris: de quo cantatur, Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, qui facit mirabilia solus. Et sunt opera Christi hominis, tanquam instrumentaliter exsequentis. Unde infra ait: Pater in me manens, ipse facit opera. Donec dies est, hoc est, quamdiu in mundo visibiliter maneo, cum hominibus conversando. Quemadmodum enim sol materialis sua præsentia causat diem, et sua absentia noctem, sic Christus præsentialiter exsistendo in mundo in humanitate assumpta, tanquam sol intelligentiæ solque justitiæ, fecit diem specialis gratiæ spiritualem. De qua die loquitur Isaias: In die illa erit germen Domini in gloria et magnificentia; et Zacharias, In die illa applicabuntur gentes multæ ad Dominum. Dies ista præsertim consistit in cordibus divino lumine illustratis, duravitque a Christi nativitate usque ad ejus ascensionem.
