paras.en: [[9:4|I must|Me oportet]], not by any constraint, but by reason of the great good it brings and of My unchanging good pleasure, and on account of the unalterable disposition of the divine ordinance, from which I cannot depart, [[9:4|work the works of him that sent me|operari opera ejus qui me misit]], that is, the works of God the Father which He has decreed shall be done through Me, which are ordered to, or belong to, the deliverance of mankind: namely the signs by which men know that I am the Son of God and are converted to Me, and also the other holy and virtuous works which Christ did for our salvation, by teaching, praying and going about. Now the miraculous works are the works of the Father, or of the Trinity, as their principal agent, of whom it is sung: [[Ps 71:18|Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone doth wonderful things|Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, qui facit mirabilia solus]]. And they are the works of Christ as man, as carrying them out instrumentally. Hence He says below: [[John 14:10|the Father who abideth in me, he doth the works|Pater in me manens, ipse facit opera]]. [[9:4|whilst it is day|Donec dies est]], that is, as long as I remain visibly in the world, living among men. For as the material sun by its presence causes day, and by its absence night, so Christ, being present in the world in the humanity He had taken, as the sun of understanding and the sun of justice, made a spiritual day of special grace. Of this day Isaias speaks: [[Is 4:2|In that day the bud of the Lord|In die illa erit germen Domini]] in glory and magnificence; and Zacharias: In that day [[Zach 2:11|many nations shall be joined to the Lord|applicabuntur gentes multæ ad Dominum]]. This day consists above all in hearts enlightened by the divine light, and it lasted from the birth of Christ until His ascension.

paras.t: Verum, quoniam Christus etiam post ascensionem operabatur opus nostræ salutis, mittendo Paracletum, et per Apostolos faciendo miracula, imo per eos ceterosque discipulos atque vicarios suos multos illuminando et convertendo, quod et nunc agit, et usque sæculi finem facturus est; ideo potest hoc modo exponi: Me oportet operari opera ejus qui me misit, hoc est miseris subvenire, peccatores convertere, infirma sanare, debilia confortare, electos custodire, donec dies est, hoc est durante tempore gratiæ seu vitæ præsentis sub evangelica lege. De quo tempore per Isaiam Dominus asserit: Tempore accepto exaudivi te, et in die salutis adjuvi te; et Apostolus, Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile, ecce nunc dies salutis.
paras.en: But since Christ, even after his Ascension, was working the work of our salvation, by sending the Paraclete and working miracles through the Apostles, nay, by enlightening and converting many through them and through his other disciples and vicars (as he does now too, and will do until the end of the world), the verse can also be expounded in this way: [[9:4|I must work the works of him that sent me|Me oportet operari opera ejus qui me misit]], that is, to succour the wretched, convert sinners, heal the sick, strengthen the weak, and guard the elect, [[9:4|whilst it is day|donec dies est]], that is, while the time of grace lasts, or of the present life under the law of the Gospel. Of this time the Lord declares through Isaias: [[Is 49:8|In an acceptable time I have heard thee, and in the day of salvation I have helped thee|Tempore accepto exaudivi te, et in die salutis adjuvi te]]; and the Apostle: [[2 Cor 6:2|Behold, now is the acceptable time: behold, now is the day of salvation|Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile, ecce nunc dies salutis]].

paras.t: Venit, id est, incessabiliter appropinquat, nox, id est finis vitæ præsentis, vel hora judicii, quando nemo potest operari, id est meritorie agere, quoniam via finita est status. Quum ergo hæc vita sit via et cursus ad aliam vitam, nemo potest post hanc vitam mereri vel pœnitere. In hora quoque judicii erit tempus præmiorum, non meritorum. Non ergo indulta pœnitentiæ tempora negligamus, non diem aliquem infructuose perdamus; sed juxta Salomonis doctrinam, quodcumque potest manus nostra instanter operemur, quoniam cito erit terminus vitæ istius.
paras.en: [[9:4|cometh|Venit]], that is, draws ever nearer without ceasing, [[9:4|the night|nox]], that is, the end of the present life, or the hour of judgement, [[9:4|when no man can work|quando nemo potest operari]], that is, act meritoriously, since the way is then finished, and the state of the wayfarer with it [the state of the viator, the soul still on the road to its goal, in which alone merit and repentance are possible]. Since, then, this life is the way and the course to another life, no one can merit or repent after this life. And the hour of judgement will be the time of rewards, not of merits. Let us not, therefore, neglect the times granted for penance, nor lose any day fruitlessly; but, according to the teaching of Solomon, whatever our hand is able to do, let us do earnestly,[[Eccles 9:10||]] for the end of this life will soon come.

paras.t: Quamdiu in mundo sum, id est, inter homines corporaliter vivo et ambulo, lux sum mundi, id est, hominum corda illustro verbo prædicationis, exemplo conversationis, signis divinæ virtutis.
paras.en: [[9:5|As long as I am in the world|Quamdiu in mundo sum]], that is, as long as I live and walk bodily among men, [[9:5|I am the light of the world|lux sum mundi]], that is, I enlighten the hearts of men by the word of my preaching, the example of my life, and the signs of divine power.

paras.t: Sed nonne Salvator semper in mundo est? vel post ascensionem desiit esse lux hominum? Non utique, quoniam ipse ait apud Matthæum: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem sæculi. Est autem Christus in hoc mundo inferiori et cum fidelibus, per majestatem deitatis, per Sacramentum proprii corporis et sanguinis, atque per spiritualem inhabitationem qua mentes devotas per caritatem et cetera gratiæ dona inhabitat. Denique, post ascensionem magis illuminavit mundum quam ante, tam Apostolos quam alios per Apostolos. Dixit enim Apostolis ante passionem: Expedit vobis ut ego vadam. Si enim non abiero, Paracletus non veniet ad vos; si autem abiero, mittam eum ad vos. Ante ascensionem quoque non illuminavit nisi Judæos et aliquas gentes illis vicinas; post ascensionem vero, universum mundum. Nihilominus quamdiu fuit in mundo modo prætacto, fuit lux mundi specialiter, utpote per se ipsum immediate homines illustrando.
paras.en: But is not the Saviour always in the world? Or did he cease to be the light of men after his Ascension? Certainly not, for he himself says in Matthew: [[Matt 28:20|behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world|Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem sæculi]]. Christ is in this lower world, and with the faithful, by the majesty of his Godhead, by the Sacrament of his own Body and Blood, and by the spiritual indwelling by which he dwells in devout minds through charity and the other gifts of grace. Indeed, after his Ascension he enlightened the world more than before, both the Apostles and others through the Apostles. For he said to the Apostles before his Passion: [[John 16:7|it is expedient to you that I go. For if I go not, the Paraclete will not come to you: but if I go, I will send him to you|Expedit vobis ut ego vadam. Si enim non abiero, Paracletus non veniet ad vos; si autem abiero, mittam eum ad vos]]. Before his Ascension, too, he enlightened only the Jews and some nations bordering on them, but after his Ascension the whole world. Nevertheless, as long as he was in the world in the manner just mentioned, he was the light of the world in a special way, since he enlightened men by himself, immediately.

paras.t: Hoc quum dixisset Jesus, exspuit in terram, et fecit lutum ex sputo et terra seu pulvere, et linivit lutum super oculos ejus, id est super organum clausum hujus cæci, et dixit ei: Vade, lava oculos in natatoria, id est piscina vel aqua, Siloe (quod nomen Hebraicum interpretatur Missus). Siloe fons fuit oriens in pede montis Sion, descendensque in vallem Josaphat: cujus aqua in quodam stagno recepta atque collecta non longe a monte Sion, vocata est natatoria Siloe, id est piscina ex fonte illo collecta.
paras.en: [[9:6|When he had said these things|Hoc quum dixisset]], Jesus [[9:6|spat on the ground|exspuit in terram]], [[9:6|and made clay of the spittle|et fecit lutum ex sputo]] and earth or dust, [[9:6|and spread the clay upon his eyes|et linivit lutum super oculos ejus]], that is, upon the closed organ of sight of this blind man, [[9:7|And said to him|et dixit ei]]: [[9:7|Go, wash|Vade, lava]] your eyes [[9:7|in the pool|in natatoria]], that is, in the basin or water, [[9:7|of Siloe|Siloe]] (which Hebrew name [[9:7|is interpreted, Sent|interpretatur Missus]]). Siloe was a spring rising at the foot of Mount Sion and running down into the valley of Josaphat; its water was received and collected in a certain pool not far from Mount Sion, and this was called the pool of Siloe, that is, the basin collected from that spring.

paras.t: Quærendum est diligenter, cur Christus sapientia Patris, nihil sine legitima causa efficiens, qui potuit solo nutu, solo verbo, solo imperio, cæco huic visum præstare, ita non fecit, sed juxta ordinem explicatum, exspuendo fecit lutum, quo unxit oculos cæci, quem misit ad aquas Siloe ad lavandum. Et respondendum, quod non sine grandi mysterio, non sine mystica ratione id contigit. Nempe, per exteriora ista quæ fecit, insinuavit quo modo et ordine interior oculus illustretur. Exspuitio ergo in terram, figuravit effusionem divinæ sapientiæ super corda humana: quoniam per salivam, qua gustus cibos dijudicat et lingua verba pronuntiat, sapientia designatur, quæ præstat in rebus divinis saporem, et linguam erudit ad loquendum quæ Dei sunt cum discretione rectissima, prout docet Apostolus: Sermo vester semper in gratia sale sit conditus. Lutum vero est cor humanum, quoniam sensus et cogitatio hominis proni sunt in malum, et ad terrena jugiter inclinantur, nisi cor ipsum divina gratia perfundatur ac elevetur. Propter quod mentes peccatorum dicuntur carnales, non per essentiam, sed inclinationem et inhæsionem.
paras.en: We must ask carefully why Christ, the Wisdom of the Father, who does nothing without a just cause, and who could have given this blind man his sight by a nod alone, a word alone, a command alone, did not do so, but in the order set out, made clay by spitting, anointed the blind man's eyes with it, and sent him to the waters of Siloe to wash. And the answer is that this did not happen without a great mystery, without a mystical reason. For by these outward things that he did he showed in what way and order the inward eye is enlightened. The spitting on the ground, then, figured the outpouring of divine wisdom upon human hearts: for by the saliva, by which the taste judges food and the tongue utters words, is signified wisdom [sapientia, from sapere, "to taste"], which gives a relish for divine things and teaches the tongue to speak the things of God with the most upright discretion, as the Apostle teaches: [[Col 4:6|Let your speech be always in grace seasoned with salt|Sermo vester semper in gratia sale sit conditus]]. The clay is the human heart, since [[Gen 8:21|the imagination and thought of man's heart are prone to evil|sensus et cogitatio hominis proni sunt in malum]] and are continually bent towards earthly things, unless the heart itself is steeped and raised up by divine grace. That is why the minds of sinners are called carnal, not in their essence, but by their inclination and clinging.

paras.t: Præterea, per linitionem luti istius super oculos cæci, designatur unctio spiritualis qua Verbum incarnatum, vel homo quicumque divina sapientia illustratus, docet intellectum fratris seu proximi sui, applicando radium sapientiæ Dei ad certam personam. Quo facto jubetur homo ire, id est a vitiis ad virtutes migrare, atque de virtute in virtutem procedere, ne infusam sapientiam perdat; et lavare oculos suos in natatoria Siloe, id est cor suum ab omni vitiorum caligine atque ignorantiæ cæcitate in fonte sapientiæ, scilicet Christo, purgare, quatenus sciat se sine virtute et gratia Christi et sine dominicæ passionis merito, nil posse, secundum quod infra testatur: Sine me nihil potestis facere. Christus enim quum sit Sapientia incarnata missa in mundum, recte per natatoriam Siloe, quæ interpretatur missus, exprimitur. Potest quoque per natatoriam hanc, fons lacrimarum ex vera compunctione vel patriæ desiderio emanantium designari, in quibus anima ab omni macula purificatur; vel certe Baptismus, quantum ad catechumenos bene instructos atque contritos. Ad insinuandum ergo quod ista ad interioris oculi perfectam illustrationem requiruntur, fecit Christus quæ dicta sunt.
paras.en: Further, the spreading of this clay upon the blind man's eyes signifies the spiritual anointing by which the incarnate Word, or any man enlightened by divine wisdom, teaches the understanding of his brother or neighbour, applying the ray of God's wisdom to a particular person. When this is done, the man is bidden to go, that is, to pass from vices to virtues, and to go on [[Ps 83:8|from virtue to virtue|de virtute in virtutem]], lest he lose the wisdom poured into him; and to wash his eyes in the pool of Siloe, that is, to cleanse his heart from all the darkness of vice and the blindness of ignorance in the fountain of wisdom, that is, in Christ, so that he may know that without the power and grace of Christ and without the merit of the Lord's Passion he can do nothing, according to what Christ testifies below: [[John 15:5|without me you can do nothing|Sine me nihil potestis facere]]. For since Christ is Wisdom incarnate, sent into the world, he is rightly expressed by the pool of Siloe, which is interpreted "Sent". This pool can also signify the fountain of tears flowing from true compunction or from longing for our heavenly country, in which the soul is cleansed from every stain; or else Baptism, as regards catechumens who are well instructed and contrite. To show, then, that these things are required for the perfect enlightenment of the inward eye, Christ did what has been described.

paras.t: Alii dicunt, ut Chrysostomus, quod fecit lutum, ad ostendendum quod ipse sit qui in exordio mundi operatus est hominem de limo terræ. Salivam quoque emisit, ad declarandum quod virtus curativa esset a Divinitate, quæ est caput Christi hominis, tanquam a principali principio, et ab ejus humanitate, quasi ab instrumento. Saliva quippe fluit a capite, et caput Christi Deus, secundum Apostolum; Christus quoque, secundum naturam assumptam, caput est omnium electorum. Sicque per exspuitionem salivæ descendentis a capite, signatur quod potestas sanativa esset a Divinitate et Christi humanitate, sicut ostensum est. Oculos quoque cæci linivit, ostendens se humanorum corporum formatorem et reformatorem, qui reformabit corpus humilitatis nostræ configuratum corpori claritatis suæ. Jussit autem cæcum sic luto linitum ire ad natatoriam Siloe, ut obediendo aliquid mereretur, ejusque fides et obedientia notificaretur, et ipsum miraculum amplius divulgaretur.
paras.en: Others, such as Chrysostom, say that he made clay to show that it was he who in the beginning of the world made man [[Gen 2:7|of the slime of the earth|de limo terræ]]. He also put forth saliva to declare that the healing power came from the Godhead, which is the head of Christ the man, as from its principal source, and from his humanity as from an instrument. For saliva flows from the head, and, according to the Apostle, [[1 Cor 11:3|the head of Christ is God|caput Christi Deus]]; Christ too, in the nature he assumed, is the head of all the elect.[[Eph 1:22||]][[Col 1:18||]] And so by the spitting forth of saliva coming down from the head it is signified that the power of healing came from the Godhead and from the humanity of Christ, as has been shown. He also anointed the blind man's eyes, showing himself to be the maker and remaker of human bodies, [[Phil 3:21|Who will reform the body of our lowness, made like to the body of his glory|qui reformabit corpus humilitatis nostræ configuratum corpori claritatis suæ]]. And he ordered the blind man, his eyes thus spread with clay, to go to the pool of Siloe, so that by obeying he might gain some merit, that his faith and obedience might be made known, and that the miracle itself might be spread abroad the more.

paras.t: Abiit ergo cæcus natus, et lavit oculos suos in natatoria Siloe, lutum abstergendo ab oculis: in quo commendatur fides ac obedientia ejus. Et venit videns. Nam obediendo Christo, in ipsa piscina visum recepit: quo significatur, quod qui Deo obedit, copiosius illustrari meretur.
paras.en: [[9:7|He went therefore|Abiit ergo]], the man born blind, [[9:7|and washed|et lavit]] his eyes in the pool of Siloe, wiping the clay from his eyes; and in this his faith and obedience are commended. [[9:7|and he came seeing|Et venit videns]]. For by obeying Christ he received his sight in the pool itself; by which it is signified that he who obeys God deserves to be enlightened more abundantly.

paras.t: Itaque vicini cæci istius, et qui viderant eum prius, antequam visum recepit, quia mendicus erat, id est, ideo eum frequenter inspexerant, quoniam more debilium sedit in publico, eleemosynam a prætergredientibus postulando, dicebant: Nonne hic est qui sedebat in loco pauperum, et mendicabat? quasi dicant, Utique. Ex longa enim experimentalique notitia, certi erant de hoc. Alii dicebant: Quia hic est. Isti consenserunt judicio vicinorum.
paras.en: [[9:8|The neighbours, therefore|Itaque vicini]] of this blind man, [[9:8|and they who had seen him before|et qui viderant eum prius]], before he received his sight, [[9:8|that he was a beggar|quia mendicus erat]] [Denis takes quia, "that", as "because": they had seen him because he was a beggar], that is, they had often looked at him for this reason, that he sat in a public place, as the infirm do, begging alms of the passers-by, said: [[9:8|Is not this he that sat|Nonne hic est qui sedebat]] in the place of the poor, [[9:8|and begged|et mendicabat]]? As if to say: Yes, surely. For they were certain of this from long acquaintance and experience. [[9:8|Some said: This is he|Alii dicebant: Quia hic est]]. These agreed with the judgement of the neighbours.

paras.t: Alii autem dicebant: Nequaquam, id est, non est sic, sed similis est ejus. Hoc dixerunt duplici ratione: primo, quoniam possibilius reputabant duos esse in omni dispositione corporali simillimos, ita ut discerni non possent, quam cæcum a nativitate visum recepisse; secundo, quia et cæcus iste in vultu aliqualiter fuit mutatus, propter oculorum apertionem, partiumque oculis vicinarum alterationem et relaxationem. Ille vero, quia se ipsum optime novit quantum ad identitatem personæ, dicebat: Quia ego sum. Voluit enim suum curatorem magnificare atque honorare.
paras.en: [[9:9|But others said: No|Alii autem dicebant: Nequaquam]], that is, it is not so, [[9:9|but he is like him|sed similis est ejus]]. They said this for two reasons: first, because they thought it more possible that two men should be so alike in their whole bodily make that they could not be told apart, than that one blind from birth should have received his sight; second, because this blind man was also somewhat changed in his face, through the opening of his eyes and the altering and loosening of the parts around the eyes. He, however, because he knew himself perfectly as to the identity of his person, [[9:9|said: I am he|dicebat: Quia ego sum]]. For he wished to magnify and honour the one who had healed him.

paras.t: Dicebant ergo ei: Quomodo aperti sunt tibi oculi? Respondit: Ille homo qui dicitur Jesus. Nondum agnovit hic cæcus Christi divinitatem; sed humanitatem ejusque nomen ex aliorum relatu didicerat. Lutum fecit. Non dicit quomodo, utpote ex sputo et terra, quia forte non scivit hoc, quia nec vidit illud. Et unxit oculos meos, videlicet pellem extrinsecus, et dixit mihi: Vade ad natatoriam Siloe, et lava oculos. Et abii, et lavi, et vidi, postquam illi obediendo, oculos aquis rigavi. Et dixerunt ei: Ubi est ille? Hoc forte quærebant, ut traderent Jesum Pharisæis et Scribis, eo quod sabbato hæc egisset. Ait, Nescio. Jesus namque recessit a loco illo antequam cæcus jam illustratus reversus fuit; nec audivit quo abisset, nec scivit quod Jesus per divinitatis immensitatem esset ubique.
paras.en: [[9:10|They said therefore to him: How were thy eyes opened?|Dicebant ergo ei: Quomodo aperti sunt tibi oculi?]] [[9:11|He answered: That man that is called Jesus|Respondit: Ille homo qui dicitur Jesus]]. This blind man did not yet acknowledge Christ's divinity; but he had learned of His humanity and His name from what others told him. [[9:11|made clay|Lutum fecit]]. He does not say how, namely of spittle and earth, because perhaps he did not know this, since he had not seen it either. [[9:11|and anointed my eyes|Et unxit oculos meos]], that is, the skin on the outside, [[9:11|and said to me: Go to the pool of Siloe and wash|et dixit mihi: Vade ad natatoriam Siloe, et lava]] my eyes. [[9:11|And I went: I washed: and I see|Et abii, et lavi, et vidi]], after I had bathed my eyes in the water in obedience to Him. [[9:12|And they said to him: Where is he?|Et dixerunt ei: Ubi est ille?]] Perhaps they asked this in order to hand Jesus over to the Pharisees and Scribes, because He had done these things on the sabbath. [[9:12|He saith: I know not|Ait, Nescio]]. For Jesus had withdrawn from that place before the blind man, now given light, came back; and he had not heard where He had gone, nor did he know that Jesus, by the immensity of His divinity, is everywhere.

paras.t: Adducunt eum ad Pharisæos qui cæcus fuerat, ut ipsi tanquam majores ac religiosiores judicarent de opere isto, remque diligentius examinarent; vel ut Jesum de violatione sabbati coram Pharisæis accusarent; vel ut placerent Pharisæis, a quibus noverant Jesum odiri. Erat autem sabbatum, videlicet septima dies festiva, quando lutum fecit Jesus, et aperuit oculos ejus. Hoc inserit Evangelista, ut pandat causam adductionis cæci ad Pharisæos, et dissensionis Pharisæorum ad invicem. Iterum ergo interrogabant eum Pharisæi quomodo vidisset, ut possent aliquam calumniandi occasionem ex verbis cæci illuminati elicere. Ille autem dixit eis: Lutum posuit mihi super oculos, et lavi oculos in præfata piscina, et video.
paras.en: [[9:13|They bring him that had been blind to the Pharisees|Adducunt eum ad Pharisæos qui cæcus fuerat]], so that they, as men of greater standing and more religious, might judge of this work and examine the matter more carefully; or in order to accuse Jesus before the Pharisees of breaking the sabbath; or to please the Pharisees, by whom they knew Jesus was hated. [[9:14|Now it was the sabbath|Erat autem sabbatum]], that is, the seventh day, a feast day, [[9:14|when Jesus made the clay and opened his eyes|quando lutum fecit Jesus, et aperuit oculos ejus]]. The Evangelist puts this in to show the reason why the blind man was brought to the Pharisees, and why the Pharisees disagreed among themselves. [[9:15|Again therefore the Pharisees asked him how he had received his sight|Iterum ergo interrogabant eum Pharisæi quomodo vidisset]], so that they might draw out of the words of the enlightened blind man some occasion for slander. [[9:15|But he said to them: He put clay upon my eyes: and I washed|Ille autem dixit eis: Lutum posuit mihi super oculos, et lavi]] my eyes in the pool already mentioned, [[9:15|and I see|et video]].

paras.t: Dicebant ergo ex Pharisæis quidam indurati et excæcati, festucam in aliis, non trabem in se ipsis pensantes, atque ex beneficiis Dei pejores effecti: Non est hic homo a Deo per vitæ bonitatem, hoc est, secundum Dei beneplacitum non operatur, neque a Deo missus est, nec ejus adjutorio, sed dæmonis agit subsidio, qui sabbatum non custodit. Mentiti sunt dicendo quod Christus sabbatum violavit faciendo quæ dicta sunt: quoniam opera exteriora ad divinæ majestatis honorem et declarationem directe pertinentia, licita erant in sabbato, utpote occidere et excoriare pecora immolanda, templum ornare, atque similia. Factura autem luti et unctio oculorum prædicta, ordinabantur directe ad gloriam Dei ejusque omnipotentiæ sublimitatem declarandam, itemque ad glorificationem Filii sui, ut Christus esse sciretur. Præterea, Christus quum esset Dominus sabbati, et legislator, non tenebatur ad litteralem sabbati observationem. De hoc dicta sunt plura quinto capitulo. Alii autem, qui magis veritati propinquabant, minusque Christo invidebant, dicebant: Quomodo potest homo peccator, legis transgressor, et sabbati violator, hæc signa facere quæ facit iste, sanando paralyticum natumque cæcum? Isti videntur melius intellexisse præceptum de sabbati custoditione quam illi, quia non reputabant Jesum peccatorem. Et schisma erat inter eos, videlicet inter Pharisæos, hoc est, divisi atque discordes erant, diversa loquendo ac sentiendo de Jesu.
paras.en: [[9:16|Some therefore of the Pharisees said|Dicebant ergo ex Pharisæis quidam]], hardened and blinded, weighing the mote in others and not the beam in themselves[[Matt 7:3||]], and made worse by the benefits of God: [[9:16|This man is not of God|Non est hic homo a Deo]] by goodness of life, that is, he does not work according to God's good pleasure, nor is he sent by God, nor does he act with His help, but by the aid of the devil, [[9:16|who keepeth not the sabbath|qui sabbatum non custodit]]. They lied in saying that Christ broke the sabbath by doing what has been described: for outward works that belong directly to the honour and showing forth of the divine majesty were lawful on the sabbath[[Num 28:9||]], such as killing and flaying the beasts to be sacrificed, adorning the temple, and the like. Now the making of the clay and the anointing of the eyes just mentioned were directly ordered to the glory of God and to showing forth the sublimity of His omnipotence, and likewise to the glorification of His Son, that He might be known to be the Christ. Moreover, since Christ was Lord of the sabbath[[Matt 12:8||]] and the lawgiver, He was not bound to the literal observance of the sabbath. Much was said of this in the fifth chapter[[John 5:10||]]. [[9:16|But others|Alii autem]], who came nearer to the truth and envied Christ less, said: [[9:16|How can a man that is a sinner|Quomodo potest homo peccator]], a transgressor of the law and a breaker of the sabbath, [[9:16|do such miracles|hæc signa facere]] as this man does, healing a paralytic[[John 5:8||]] and one born blind? These seem to have understood the precept of keeping the sabbath better than the others, since they did not consider Jesus a sinner. [[9:16|And there was a division among them|Et schisma erat inter eos]], that is, among the Pharisees; in other words, they were divided and at odds, saying and thinking different things about Jesus.

paras.t: Huic quod dictum est, Quomodo potest homo peccator hæc signa facere? consonat quod Christo locutus est Nicodemus: Scimus quia a Deo venisti magister; nemo enim potest hæc signa facere quæ tu facis, nisi fuerit Deus cum illo. Quæritur ergo, an vera sint hæc. Et apparet quod non, quoniam operatio miraculorum pertinet ad gratias gratis datas, quæ bonis malisque communes sunt. Christus quoque affirmat apud Matthæum septimo capitulo: Multi (inquiens) dicent mihi in illa die: Domine, Domine, nonne in nomine tuo prophetavimus, et in nomine tuo signa multa fecimus? Et tunc (inquit) confitebor illis: Quia non novi vos; discedite a me, operarii iniquitatis. Oppositum vero arguitur, quia si miracula fieri possunt a malis, perit firmitas fidei christianæ, quæ miraculis præsertim innititur: quod enim a malo homine fieri valet, non videtur sufficiens fidei argumentum. Rursus, miracula fiunt divina virtute. Deus autem preces malorum non audit, faciendo prodigia ad eorum instantiam. Respondendum, quod miracula proprie dicta, sunt effectus totam virtutem creatam excedentes: unde a solo Deo fiunt. Idcirco id ad cujus confirmationem fit tale miraculum, semper est verum, quum Deus non sit confirmator erroris, nec testis falsitatis. Miracula vero divinitus facta, quandoque fiunt ad testificandum de veritate doctrinæ: et tunc illa doctrina immobiliter vera est, a quocumque doceatur, vel quantumcumque perversus sit doctor; non tamen consequens est, quod docens sit justus, vel Deo placens. Sicque per malos prædicatores frequenter sunt facta quædam miracula, ad fidei confirmationem: exaudivitque Deus precem illorum, non propter illorum merita, sed propter Ecclesiæ utilitatem, et ad insinuandum efficaciam fidei christianæ, cujus tanta est virtus, ut per eam fiant miracula etiam a malis. Interdum vero miracula fiunt ad testificandum de bonitate docentis: et tunc doctor hujusmodi veraciter bonus et justus est. Miracula autem Christi facta sunt a Deo propter utrumque, videlicet ad ostendendum quod vera sit ejus doctrina, et quod ipse sit verus Christus, Sanctus Sanctorum et justus in omnibus. Imo, si quis dixerit quod miracula Christi facta sint ad suæ doctrinæ confirmationem, sequitur quod etiam facta sint ad suæ sanctitatis testimonium. Docuit enim se esse Christum, sanctum et justum, omni peccato carentem: quam doctrinam Deus nequaquam miraculis confirmasset, nisi ita fuisset. Sed hoc in aliis non sequitur, qui non propriam, sed Christi legem prædicant et doctrinam. Sive ergo a bonis sive a malis fiant proprie sumpta miracula, demonstratur fidei veritas, tanquam a Deo data atque firmata. Verum, quoniam ad credendum multum confert justitia asserentis, idcirco decentius est miracula fieri a justis quam impiis: quod et ita fit.
paras.en: With what was said, [[9:16|How can a man that is a sinner do such miracles?|Quomodo potest homo peccator hæc signa facere?]] agrees what Nicodemus said to Christ: [[John 3:2|we know that thou art come a teacher from God; for no man can do these signs which thou dost, unless God be with him|Scimus quia a Deo venisti magister; nemo enim potest hæc signa facere quæ tu facis, nisi fuerit Deus cum illo]]. The question therefore is whether these things are true. And it seems that they are not, since the working of miracles belongs to the graces freely given [gratiæ gratis datæ: gifts such as prophecy and miracles, given for the good of others rather than for the holiness of the one who receives them], which are common to the good and the wicked. Christ too affirms in the seventh chapter of Matthew, saying: [[Matt 7:22|Many will say to me in that day: Lord, Lord, have not we prophesied in thy name|Multi (inquiens) dicent mihi in illa die: Domine, Domine, nonne in nomine tuo prophetavimus]], [[Matt 7:22|and done many miracles in thy name|et in nomine tuo signa multa fecimus]]? And He goes on: [[Matt 7:23|And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you|Et tunc (inquit) confitebor illis: Quia non novi vos]]; [[Luke 13:27|Depart from me|discedite a me]], [[Luke 13:27|workers of iniquity|operarii iniquitatis]]. On the other side it is argued that, if miracles can be done by the wicked, the firmness of the Christian faith perishes, since it rests chiefly on miracles: for what can be done by a wicked man does not seem a sufficient argument for the faith. Again, miracles are done by divine power; but God does not hear the prayers of the wicked by working wonders at their request. The answer is that miracles properly so called are effects that exceed all created power, and so they are done by God alone. Therefore that for whose confirmation such a miracle is done is always true, since God does not confirm error, nor bear witness to falsehood. Now miracles done by God are sometimes done to bear witness to the truth of a doctrine: and then that doctrine is unshakeably true, whoever teaches it, however perverse the teacher may be; yet it does not follow that the one who teaches it is just, or pleasing to God. And so certain miracles have often been done through wicked preachers for the confirmation of the faith: and God heard their prayer, not for their merits, but for the good of the Church, and to make known the efficacy of the Christian faith, whose power is so great that through it miracles are done even by the wicked. At other times, however, miracles are done to bear witness to the goodness of the one who teaches: and then such a teacher is truly good and just. Now the miracles of Christ were done by God for both reasons, namely to show that His doctrine is true, and that He Himself is the true Christ, the Holy of Holies, and just in all things[[Ps 144:13||]]. Indeed, if anyone says that Christ's miracles were done to confirm His doctrine, it follows that they were also done as a testimony to His holiness. For He taught that He was the Christ, holy and just, free of all sin: a doctrine God would never have confirmed with miracles had it not been so. But this does not follow in the case of others, who preach not their own law and doctrine but Christ's. Whether, then, miracles properly so called are done by the good or by the wicked, the truth of the faith is shown, as given and confirmed by God. Yet since the justice of the one who asserts a thing does much to make it believed, it is more fitting that miracles be done by the just than by the wicked: and so in fact it happens.

paras.t: Dicunt ergo cæco, sed nunc videnti, iterum Pharisæi: Tu quid dicis de eo qui aperuit oculos tuos? id est, quale testimonium perhibes illuminatori tuo? Aliqui dicunt hanc quæstionem factam ab illis qui dixerunt, Non est hic homo a Deo, qui sabbatum non custodit: ad hoc, ut vel terrendo vel circumveniendo, inducerent cæcum ad proferendum aliquid mali de Jesu; vel ut cæcum ex sua responsione arguerent, atque de synagoga ejicerent. Hoc asserit Augustinus et Beda. Theophilus autem et alii dicunt, quod facta sit a fautoribus Christi dicentibus, Quomodo potest peccator hæc signa facere? quoniam verisimile erat quod cæcus bona de suo curatore contestaretur. Potius tamen videtur facta ab ambabus inter se discordantibus partibus, qui quum inter se discordarent, recurrebant ad testimonium ejus qui expertus fuit Christi potentiam, si forte ex ejus responsione possent aliquam invenire concordiam.
paras.en: [[9:17|They say therefore to the blind man|Dicunt ergo cæco]] (but one who now saw) [[9:17|again|iterum]], the Pharisees: [[9:17|What sayest thou of him that hath opened thy eyes?|Tu quid dicis de eo qui aperuit oculos tuos?]] that is, what testimony do you give to the one who gave you light? Some say that this question was put by those who said, [[9:16|This man is not of God, who keepeth not the sabbath|Non est hic homo a Deo, qui sabbatum non custodit]]: so that, either by frightening him or by getting round him, they might bring the blind man to say something bad about Jesus; or that they might convict the blind man by his own answer and cast him out of the synagogue. So Augustine and Bede assert. But Theophilus [probably Theophylact, the Greek commentator] and others say that it was put by those who favoured Christ, who said, [[9:16|How can a man that is a sinner do such miracles?|Quomodo potest peccator hæc signa facere?]] since it was likely that the blind man would testify to good things of the one who had cured him. Yet it seems rather to have been put by both parties, who were at odds with each other: since they disagreed among themselves, they turned to the testimony of the man who had experienced Christ's power, in case from his answer they might find some agreement.

paras.t: Ille autem dixit: Quia propheta est. Putavit enim quod Jesus fuisset solum propheta, non finis et Dominus Prophetarum. Implicite tamen credidit eum esse Christum, quoniam firmiter tenuit quod esset homo justus et verax, et per consequens talis, qualem ipse se esse perhibuit.
paras.en: [[9:17|And he said: He is a prophet|Ille autem dixit: Quia propheta est]]. For he thought that Jesus was only a prophet, not the end and Lord of the Prophets. Yet he implicitly believed Him to be the Christ, since he firmly held that He was a just and truthful man, and consequently such as He declared Himself to be.

paras.t: Sed contra hoc videtur, quia quos Christus sanavit in corpore, curavit in anima. Ergo et cæcum istum a tali errore curavit. Dicendum, quod cæcus pro tunc non tenebatur ad explicitam fidem de hoc, quod Jesus esset Christus. Unde prædictus error excusabatur a culpa, maxime quia non fuit per absolutam affirmationem. Quidam dicit, quod cæcus iste, dicendo de Jesu, Propheta est, nomine propheta intellexit Christum, ita quod cæcus asseruit Jesum esse Christum. Sed huic obviat, quod post pauca cæcus hic ait de Jesu: Si peccator est, nescio. Si autem tenuisset eum pro Christo, scivisset quod non esset peccator. Istud tamen satis faciliter solvi potest. Non tamen dicendum est quod nomine propheta intellexerit Christum, quia non fuit consuetudo Judæis, in communi modo loquendi, per prophetam intelligere Christum.
paras.en: But against this it seems that those whom Christ healed in body, he cured in soul; therefore he cured this blind man too of such an error. It must be said that the blind man was not at that time bound to explicit faith in this, that Jesus was the Christ. Hence the error just mentioned was excused from fault, above all because it was not made by an absolute affirmation. A certain writer says that this blind man, in saying of Jesus, [[9:17|He is a prophet|Propheta est]], understood Christ by the name of prophet, so that the blind man asserted that Jesus was the Christ. But against this stands the fact that a little later this blind man says of Jesus: [[9:25|If he be a sinner, I know not|Si peccator est, nescio]]. Yet if he had held him for the Christ, he would have known that he was not a sinner. This, however, can be answered easily enough. Still, it must not be said that by the name of prophet he understood Christ, because it was not the custom of the Jews, in the common way of speaking, to understand Christ by a prophet.

paras.t: Non crediderunt ergo Judæi quidam, de quibus dictum est quod dixerunt istum similem esse cæco nato, vel Pharisæi opera Christi calumniantes; quia cæcus fuisset a nativitate, et vidisset, beneficio Christi, donec vocaverunt parentes ejus qui viderat; et interrogaverunt eos, dicentes: Hic est filius vester, quem vos dicitis, id est, de quo affirmatis, quia cæcus natus est? Quomodo ergo nunc videt? Tria inquirunt: primo, an iste sit filius eorum; secundo, an cæcus a nativitate; tertio, qualiter visum recepit, si natus est cæcus. Et quia ad duo prima poterant parentes sine periculo respondere, non autem ad tertium, idcirco respondent ad duo hæc, quemadmodum subditur.
paras.en: [[9:18|The Jews then did not believe|Non crediderunt ergo Judæi]]: certain Jews, of whom it was said that they said this man was like the man born blind, or the Pharisees who slandered the works of Christ; [[9:18|that he had been blind|quia cæcus fuisset]] from his birth, [[9:18|and had received his sight|et vidisset]] by the kindness of Christ, [[9:18|until they called the parents of him that had received his sight|donec vocaverunt parentes ejus qui viderat]]; [[9:19|And asked them, saying: Is this your son, who you say|et interrogaverunt eos, dicentes: Hic est filius vester, quem vos dicitis]], that is, of whom you affirm, [[9:19|was born blind? How then doth he now see?|quia cæcus natus est? Quomodo ergo nunc videt?]] They ask three things: first, whether this is their son; second, whether he was blind from birth; third, how he received his sight, if he was born blind. And because the parents could answer the first two without danger, but not the third, they therefore answer these two, as follows.

paras.t: Responderunt eis parentes ejus, et dixerunt: Scimus quia hic est filius noster (de prole cujus sit, certior est mater quam pater), et quia cæcus natus est. Quomodo autem nunc videat, nescimus, id est, modum et ordinem facti ignoramus; aut quis ejus aperuit oculos, hoc est auctorem tanti prodigii, nos nescimus. Ipsum interrogate; ætatem habet, id est annos discretionis, ipse de se loquatur, quoniam nemo certior eo.
paras.en: [[9:20|His parents answered them and said: We know that this is our son|Responderunt eis parentes ejus, et dixerunt: Scimus quia hic est filius noster]] (whose a child is, the mother is surer than the father), [[9:20|and that he was born blind|et quia cæcus natus est]]. [[9:21|But how he now seeth, we know not|Quomodo autem nunc videat, nescimus]], that is, we do not know the manner and order of the deed; or [[9:21|who hath opened his eyes|quis ejus aperuit oculos]], that is, the author of so great a wonder, [[9:21|we know not. Ask himself|nos nescimus. Ipsum interrogate]]: [[9:21|he is of age|ætatem habet]], that is, he has the years of discretion: [[9:21|Let him speak for himself|ipse de se loquatur]], since no one is surer of it than he.

paras.t: Hæc dixerunt parentes ejus, quoniam timebant Judæos, hoc est principales Judæos, videlicet Pharisæos, Scribas et sacerdotes, inordinato et carnali timore: ex quo et mentiti sunt, et opera Christi pia atque præclara maluerunt tacere, quam a Judæis persecutionem sufferre. Unde non excusantur a culpa. Causa timoris subjungitur. Jam enim conspiraverant Judæi principales, de quibus jam dixi, ut si quis eum confiteretur Christum, extra synagogam fieret, id est, quicumque diceret Jesum esse Christum, excluderetur a populo Judæorum tanquam excommunicatus et perfidus: quod erat tunc grande opprobrium. Propterea, scilicet, ne de synagoga expellerentur, parentes ejus dixerunt: Quia ætatem habet, ipsum interrogate. Et in hoc multum errabant, magisque dilexerunt gloriam hominum quam divinam. Nonne salubrius eis fuisset a Christo recipi, qui propter se expulsos clementer recepit, quam in synagoga manere, in qua erant inimici Filii Dei?
paras.en: [[9:22|These things his parents said, because they feared the Jews|Hæc dixerunt parentes ejus, quoniam timebant Judæos]], that is, the chief Jews, namely the Pharisees, Scribes and priests, with an inordinate and carnal fear: out of which they both lied and preferred to keep silent about the holy and glorious works of Christ rather than suffer persecution from the Jews. Hence they are not excused from fault. The cause of their fear is added: [[9:22|for the Jews had already agreed among themselves|Jam enim conspiraverant Judæi]], the chief ones, of whom I have just spoken, [[9:22|that if any man should confess him to be Christ|ut si quis eum confiteretur Christum]], [[9:22|he should be put out of the synagogue|extra synagogam fieret]], that is, whoever said that Jesus was the Christ would be shut out from the people of the Jews as one excommunicated and faithless: which was then a great disgrace. [[9:23|Therefore did his parents say: He is of age. Ask himself|Propterea parentes ejus dixerunt: Quia ætatem habet, ipsum interrogate]]: that is, so as not to be driven out of the synagogue. And in this they erred greatly, and loved the glory of men more than the glory of God. Would it not have been more wholesome for them to be received by Christ, who mercifully received those driven out for his sake, than to remain in the synagogue, in which were the enemies of the Son of God?

paras.t: Vocaverunt ergo Pharisæi rursus hominem qui fuerat cæcus. Invidia enim non quiescit, sed indefesso animo molitur malum ei quem odit; et qui veritatem nituntur obruere, variis, exquisitis falsissimisque cautelis utuntur. Et dixerunt ei: Da gloriam Deo, hoc est, Deum honora, nobis religiosis consentiendo, et tuam curationem non huic Jesu, quasi divina potestate agenti, adscribendo, sed quod aliquo alio modo visum recepisti. Nos scimus quia hic homo peccator est, id est assiduus in peccato, seductor plebis et simulator, magicis artibus utens, nec divina virtute te illuminavit. Ecce quomodo malitia excæcavit eos, et quam studiose satagebant decipere cæcum istum. Quasi dicant: Ex quo nos docti et religiosi hoc scimus, tu simplex et idiota non debes contradicere nobis.
paras.en: [[9:24|They therefore called the man again that had been blind|Vocaverunt ergo Pharisæi rursus hominem qui fuerat cæcus]]: the Pharisees. For envy does not rest, but with untiring mind contrives evil against the one it hates; and those who strive to bury the truth use various, far-fetched and utterly false stratagems. And they said to him: [[9:24|Give glory to God|Da gloriam Deo]], that is, honour God, by agreeing with us, who are religious men, and by ascribing your cure not to this Jesus, as though he acted by divine power, but saying that you received your sight in some other way. [[9:24|We know that this man is a sinner|Nos scimus quia hic homo peccator est]], that is, constant in sin, a seducer of the people and a deceiver, using magic arts, and he did not give you light by divine power. See how malice blinded them, and how busily they laboured to deceive this blind man. As if they said: Since we, learned and religious men, know this, you, a simple and unlettered man, ought not to contradict us.

paras.t: Dixit ergo ille cæcus nondum in anima perfecte de Christo illustratus: Si peccator est, nescio, id est, dubius sum vel incertus an aliquo fuerit interdum peccato saltem veniali obstrictus, quemadmodum ceteri Prophetarum. Nemo enim mundus a sorde, et justus septies cadit in die. Alii exponunt sic: Si peccator est, nescio, id est, ego non scio verum esse quod vos dicitis vobis esse notorium, utpote quod sit peccator: quin potius, oppositum sentio. Cæcus iste non dubitavit de sanctitate Jesu, quem dixit esse prophetam; sed an fuit prorsus ab omni culpa immunis, non scivit, quoniam nondum scivit eum esse Christum Filium Dei. Unum scio, quia cæcus quum essem paulo ante, nunc video. Securus et imperterritus fuit hic cæcus.
paras.en: [[9:25|He said therefore|Dixit ergo]] that blind man, not yet perfectly enlightened in soul about Christ: [[9:25|If he be a sinner, I know not|Si peccator est, nescio]], that is, I am in doubt or uncertain whether he has at times been bound by some sin, at least a venial one [that is, a lesser sin that does not destroy charity], as the rest of the Prophets were. For no one is clean from stain[[Job 14:4||]] [so Job 14:4 in the Septuagint, as the margin notes; the Vulgate reads “Who can make him clean that is conceived of unclean seed?”], and [[Prov 24:16|a just man shall fall seven times|justus septies cadit]] a day. Others explain it thus: [[9:25|If he be a sinner, I know not|Si peccator est, nescio]], that is, I do not know it to be true, what you say is well known to you, namely that he is a sinner; rather, I think the opposite. This blind man did not doubt the holiness of Jesus, whom he called a prophet; but whether he was wholly free from all fault he did not know, since he did not yet know him to be the Christ, the Son of God. [[9:25|One thing I know, that whereas I was blind|Unum scio, quia cæcus quum essem]] a little while ago, [[9:25|now I see|nunc video]]. This blind man was secure and undaunted.

paras.t: Dixerunt ergo illi: Quid fecit tibi? quomodo aperuit tibi oculos? Hoc rursus quærebant insidiose, ut possent aliquid reprehensionis elicere, tantumque miraculum obfuscare. Timebant enim, si miraculum istud divulgaretur, quod propter novitatem et magnitudinem ejus, multi acciperent Jesum pro Christo. Respondit eis: Dixi vobis jam, et audistis, quid fecerit mihi, et quomodo dederit mihi visum. Quid iterum vultis audire? quasi dicat: Non bono animo quæritis, quatenus cognita veritate credatis in illum, sed ut aliquam objectionem fingatis. Ideo subditur: Numquid et vos vultis discipuli ejus fieri, cujus ego jam discipulus fieri cupio? tanquam dicat: Scio quod non. Magna fuit constantia hujus cæci, qui tam pertinenter atque audacter respondit pro suo benefactore. Nec dubium quin Christus hanc ei concessit constantiam.
paras.en: [[9:26|They said then to him: What did he to thee? How did he open thy eyes?|Dixerunt ergo illi: Quid fecit tibi? quomodo aperuit tibi oculos?]] This they asked again insidiously, so that they might draw out something to find fault with, and obscure so great a miracle. For they feared that if this miracle were spread abroad, many, because of its newness and greatness, would take Jesus for the Christ. [[9:27|He answered them: I have told you already, and you have heard|Respondit eis: Dixi vobis jam, et audistis]] what he did to me, and how he gave me sight. [[9:27|Why would you hear it again?|Quid iterum vultis audire]] As if he said: You do not ask in a good spirit, so that, knowing the truth, you may believe in him, but in order to invent some objection. Therefore he adds: [[9:27|Will you also become his disciples?|Numquid et vos vultis discipuli ejus fieri]], whose disciple I already desire to become? As if he said: I know you will not. Great was the constancy of this blind man, who answered so steadfastly and boldly on behalf of his benefactor. Nor is there any doubt that Christ granted him this constancy.

paras.t: Maledixerunt, id est, malum imprecati sunt, ei, videlicet cæco huic, Pharisæi, et dixerunt: Tu discipulus illius sis. Hoc narrat Evangelista secundum intentionem illorum, qui reputabant discipulatum sub magisterio Jesu esse miseriam, seductionem et perditionem, quum secundum veritatem fuerit benedictio, salus et gratia magna. Nos autem Moysis discipuli sumus. Nec hoc vere locuti sunt, quoniam mandatum Dei de honoratione parentum per Moysen datum, per suam traditionem irritum fecerunt, ut probat Christus apud Matthæum. Scripturam quoque Moysis non vere exposuerunt. Propter quod supra dixit eis Salvator: Si crederetis Moysi, crederetis et mihi; de me enim ille scripsit.
paras.en: [[9:28|They reviled him|Maledixerunt]], that is, they called down evil upon him, namely upon this blind man, the Pharisees, [[9:28|and said: Be thou his disciple|et dixerunt: Tu discipulus illius sis]]. The Evangelist relates this according to the intention of those who reckoned discipleship under the teaching of Jesus to be misery, seduction and perdition, whereas in truth it was a blessing, salvation and a great grace. [[9:28|but we are the disciples of Moses|Nos autem Moysis discipuli sumus]]. Nor did they say this truly, since the commandment of God about honouring parents, given through Moses, they made void by their tradition[[Matt 15:6||]], as Christ proves in Matthew [the margin gives Matt 15:3–6]. Nor did they expound the Scripture of Moses truly either. For this reason the Saviour said to them above: [[John 5:46|if you did believe Moses, you would perhaps believe me also: for he wrote of me|Si crederetis Moysi, crederetis et mihi; de me enim ille scripsit]].

paras.t: Nos scimus auctoritate Scripturæ, quia Moysi locutus est Deus per angelum in persona Dei loquentem. Unde in Exodo scriptum est: Loquebatur Dominus cum Moyse facie ad faciem, sicut loqui solet homo ad amicum suum. Hunc autem Jesum nescimus unde sit. Paulo ante locuti sunt Pharisæi isti increduli: Non est hic homo a Deo; et, Nos scimus quia hic homo peccator est. Opinabantur ergo se scire quod non esset a Deo. Patriam quoque ejus et genus noverunt. Unde superius locuti sunt Nicodemo: Scrutare Scripturas, et vide quia a Galilæa Propheta non surgit. Quomodo ergo nunc dicunt, Hunc nescimus unde sit? præsertim quum putarent eum a diabolo esse et magicis artibus inhærere. Dicendum, quod ex magno contemptu sic loquebantur, ad insinuandum vilitatem Jesu.
paras.en: [[9:29|We know|Nos scimus]] by the authority of Scripture [[9:29|that God spoke to Moses|quia Moysi locutus est Deus]], through an angel speaking in the person of God. Hence it is written in Exodus: [[Ex 33:11|the Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is wont to speak to his friend|Loquebatur Dominus cum Moyse facie ad faciem, sicut loqui solet homo ad amicum suum]]. [[9:29|but as to this man, we know not from whence he is|Hunc autem Jesum nescimus unde sit]]. A little before, these unbelieving Pharisees had said: [[9:16|This man is not of God|Non est hic homo a Deo]]; and, [[9:24|We know that this man is a sinner|Nos scimus quia hic homo peccator est]]. So they supposed they knew that he was not of God. They also knew his country and his family. Hence they had said above to Nicodemus: [[John 7:52|Search the scriptures, and see that out of Galilee a prophet riseth not|Scrutare Scripturas, et vide quia a Galilæa Propheta non surgit]]. How then do they now say, [[9:29|we know not from whence he is|Hunc nescimus unde sit]]? Especially since they thought that he was from the devil and given to magic arts. It must be said that they spoke thus out of great contempt, to suggest the worthlessness of Jesus.

paras.t: Tanquam dicerent: Velut inventicium hunc reputamus, quum ignoremus eum a Deo missum. Vel dicendum, quod loquebantur sicut homines passionati, et ideo mirum non est si verba eorum sint falsa atque ad invicem repugnantia.
paras.en: As though they said: We reckon him as one found by chance [that is, as a foundling, of unknown origin], since we do not know that he was sent by God. Or it must be said that they spoke as men swayed by passion, and so it is no wonder if their words are false and contradict one another.

paras.t: Respondit ille homo mente et corpore illustratus, et dixit eis, increpando eorum duritiam perfidiamque reprobando: In hoc enim mirabile est, id est, in eo quod dicam patet mirabile esse, quia, id est quod, vos nescitis unde sit, id est, quod Jesus iste a Deo sit. Deinceps ponit in quo patet quod miranda sit ignorantia Pharisæorum: et aperuit oculos meos: id est, per hoc quod aperuit oculos meos a nativitate clausos et cæcos, merito agnosceretis eum esse a Deo, quum hoc sit supernaturalis effectus, soli Deo possibilis, qui et fecit istum effectum in testimonium veritatis sanctitatisque Jesu: et mirum quod non attenditis hoc, quum consuetum semper fuerit populo Judæorum signa quærere illisque credere. Propter quod dicit Apostolus: Judæi signa quærunt.
paras.en: [[9:30|The man answered|Respondit ille homo]], enlightened in mind and in body, [[9:30|and said to them|et dixit eis]], rebuking their hardness and reproving their faithlessness: [[9:30|why, herein is a wonderful thing|In hoc enim mirabile est]], that is, in what I shall say it is plain that there is a wonderful thing, [[9:30|that you know not from whence he is|vos nescitis unde sit]] [Denis glosses *quia* as *quod*: "that", not "because"], that is, that this Jesus is from God. Next he sets down that by which it is plain that the ignorance of the Pharisees is to be wondered at: [[9:30|and he hath opened my eyes|et aperuit oculos meos]]: that is, by this, that he opened my eyes, shut and blind from birth, you would rightly acknowledge that he is from God, since this is a supernatural effect, possible to God alone, who also wrought this effect in witness to the truth and holiness of Jesus; and it is a wonder that you do not heed this, since it was ever the custom of the Jewish people to seek signs and to believe them. Wherefore the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 1:22|the Jews require signs|Judæi signa quærunt]].

paras.t: Scimus autem quia peccatores Deus non audit. Omnia verba cæci hic introducta, uno modo exponuntur determinate, ad probandum suum propositum: et sic vera sunt. Alio modo exponuntur communiter: sicque, secundum Augustinum, sunt verba cæci nondum perfecte interius illustrati, unde nec vera sunt absolute. — Primo sic: Scimus autem ex Scripturis, quia peccatores in vitiis permanentes Deus non audit, propter præces eorum faciendo miracula ad testimonium bonitatis ipsorum. Tamen, ut dictum est, interdum per malos fiunt vera miracula. Nam et ad instantiam Alexandri Magni legitur Deus maxima fecisse miracula. Denique, licet quis sit in statu salutis, raro tamen vel nunquam facit miracula modo prædicto, nisi sit vir heroicus et perfectus. Unde per peccatores intelligi possunt insipientes, animales et imperfecti, quamvis sint pœnitentes. Propterea subditur: Sed si quis Dei cultor est, id est Deo devotus per interiores latriæ actus, et voluntatem ejus facit, divinis præceptis et admonitionibus obediendo in omnibus, hunc exaudit, faciendo ad præcem ejus miracula pro testimonio virtutis talis cultoris. Sic autem maxime exaudivit Deus Jesum, sicut cæcus subjungit.
paras.en: [[9:31|Now we know that God doth not hear sinners|Scimus autem quia peccatores Deus non audit]]. All the words of the blind man brought in here are expounded in one way in a determinate sense, to prove his point: and so they are true. In another way they are expounded in a general sense; and so, according to Augustine, they are the words of a blind man not yet perfectly enlightened within, and hence they are not true absolutely. — First, then, thus: Now we know from the Scriptures that God does not hear sinners who remain in their vices, by working miracles at their prayers in witness to their goodness. Yet, as has been said, true miracles are sometimes done through the wicked. For we read that God worked very great miracles even at the instance of Alexander the Great. Moreover, though a man be in the state of salvation, yet he rarely or never works miracles in the way just said, unless he be a heroic and perfect man. Hence by *sinners* may be understood the unwise, the carnal [*animales*, that is, those living by the senses rather than the spirit] and the imperfect, even though they be penitent. Therefore it is added: [[9:31|but if a man be a server of God|Sed si quis Dei cultor est]], that is, devoted to God by inward acts of latria [that is, the worship due to God alone], [[9:31|and doth his, will|et voluntatem ejus facit]], obeying the divine precepts and counsels in all things, [[9:31|him he heareth|hunc exaudit]], by working miracles at his prayer in witness to the virtue of such a worshipper. And in this way God heard Jesus above all, as the blind man goes on to say.

paras.t: A sæculo non est auditum, id est, nunquam contigit vel perceptum est, quia aperuit quis oculos cæci nati. In nulla enim scriptura hoc legitur factum, nisi hoc loco. Ex his infert cæcus suum intentum. Nisi esset hic a Deo, quasi missus ab illo, ejusque gratia juvaretur, non poterat facere quidquam, id est aliquid tale quale fecit in me.
paras.en: [[9:32|From the beginning of the world it hath not been heard|A sæculo non est auditum]], that is, it never happened nor was it known, [[9:32|that any man hath opened the eyes of one born blind|quia aperuit quis oculos cæci nati]]. For in no writing do we read that this was done, save in this place. From these things the blind man draws his conclusion: [[9:33|Unless this man were of God|Nisi esset hic a Deo]], as sent by him, and helped by his grace, [[9:33|he could not do anything|non poterat facere quidquam]], that is, anything such as he did in me.

paras.t: Pro secunda explanatione hujus scripturæ, sciendum quod aliquis dicitur peccator multipliciter: Primo, quia aliquando magna peccata commisit, quamvis postea perfectus et virtuosus sit factus. Sic Paulus vocat se peccatorem, dicendo: Venit Jesus peccatores salvos facere, quorum ego primus sum. Nihilo minus de se ipso fatetur: Nihil mihi conscius sum. Secundo, quia de peccatis suis non satisfecit, quamvis pœniteat. Sic publicanus peccator fuit, quum dixit: Deus, propitius esto mihi peccatori. Tunc enim dimissa erant ei peccata, quantum ad culpam. Tertio, quoniam in peccatis mortalibus est, habet tamen propositum se emendandi, habetque sæpe motum attritionis, quamvis non habeat veram contritionem. Quarto, quia in vitiis jacet, nec pœnitet, sed in pravo manet proposito et affectu.
paras.en: For the second explanation of this text, it is to be known that a man is called a sinner in several ways. First, because at some time he committed great sins, though afterwards he became perfect and virtuous. So Paul calls himself a sinner, saying: [[1 Tim 1:15|Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the chief|Venit Jesus peccatores salvos facere, quorum ego primus sum]]. And yet he confesses of himself: [[1 Cor 4:4|I am not conscious to myself of anything|Nihil mihi conscius sum]]. Secondly, because he has not made satisfaction for his sins, though he repents. So the publican was a sinner when he said: [[Luke 18:13|O God, be merciful to me a sinner|Deus, propitius esto mihi peccatori]]. For then his sins had already been forgiven him, as to the guilt[[Luke 18:14||]] [that is, the guilt was remitted, though the debt of satisfaction remained]. Thirdly, because he is in mortal sins, yet has the purpose of amending himself, and often has a movement of attrition [that is, sorrow for sin from a lower motive, such as fear of punishment, which falls short of contrition], though he has not true contrition. Fourthly, because he lies in his vices and does not repent, but abides in a wicked purpose and affection.

paras.t: Itaque, quod ait, Scimus quia peccatores Deus non audit, verum est de peccatoribus quarto modo, utpote quod non exaudiuntur ad utilitatem, quamdiu sunt tales. Ideo enim Sapiens dicit: Qui declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis. Et apud Isaiam Dominus loquitur: Quum multiplicaveritis præces, non exaudiam; manus enim vestræ sanguine plenæ sunt. Et pene innumerabilia sunt loca Scripturæ hoc idem testantia: ut quum in libro Proverbiorum Dominus asserit: Tunc invocabunt me, et non exaudiam; mane consurgent ad me, et non invenient me. Nihilo minus verum est quod Dominus ait per Ezechielem: In quacumque hora peccator ingemuerit, omnium iniquitatum ejus non recordabor. Elucescit ergo quod peccatorem secundo modo dictum, videlicet pœnitentem, exaudiat Dominus, dummodo salubriter et instanter pro se ipso oraverit. Sed de peccatore tertio modo major est difficultas, an exaudiatur in spiritualibus bonis. Et dicendum, quod non exauditur de condigno, sed de congruo, maxime si faciat quod in se est. Certum est autem quod qui in peccato mortali est, non potest aliquid promereri, seu de condigno exaudiri, nisi misericorditer præveniatur a Deo gratiam gratum facientem infundente: qua adepta, habet homo motum contritionis, meritoriæ actionis et dignæ atque idoneæ orationis.
paras.en: So then, what he says, [[9:31|we know that God doth not hear sinners|Scimus quia peccatores Deus non audit]], is true of sinners in the fourth way, in that they are not heard to their profit so long as they are such. For this is why the Wise Man says: [[Prov 28:9|He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination|Qui declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis]]. And in Isaias the Lord says: [[Is 1:15|when you multiply prayer, I will not hear: for your hands are full of blood|Quum multiplicaveritis præces, non exaudiam; manus enim vestræ sanguine plenæ sunt]]. And the places of Scripture that bear witness to this same thing are almost without number: as when in the book of Proverbs the Lord declares: [[Prov 1:28|Then shall they call upon me, and I will not hear: they shall rise in the morning, and shall not find me|Tunc invocabunt me, et non exaudiam; mane consurgent ad me, et non invenient me]]. Nevertheless, what the Lord says through Ezechiel is true: In what hour soever the sinner shall groan[[Ezech 18:21||]], [[Ezech 18:22|I will not remember all his iniquities|omnium iniquitatum ejus non recordabor]] [the first words are the familiar form of the saying, not the Vulgate's; the sense is that of Ezech 18:21, which the margin cites with 18:22]. It is clear, then, that the Lord hears the sinner called so in the second way, namely the penitent, provided that he has prayed for himself to his salvation and with perseverance. But concerning the sinner in the third way there is greater difficulty, whether he is heard in spiritual goods. And it must be said that he is not heard *de condigno*, but *de congruo* [that is, not as of strict merit, but as is fitting to God's liberality], especially if he does what lies in him. But it is certain that one who is in mortal sin cannot merit anything, or be heard *de condigno*, unless he be mercifully prevented by God, who pours in sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes a man pleasing to God]: and once a man has obtained this, he has the movement of contrition, of meritorious action, and of worthy and fitting prayer.

paras.t: Sed si quis Dei cultor est, et voluntatem ejus facit, id est, signa divinæ voluntatis implet, videlicet præcepta et hortamenta, hunc exaudit ad utilitatem, quamvis non semper ad libitum: imo, quandoque negando quod postulatur, dat meliora ac viciniora saluti. Hinc scriptum est: Si diluculo consurrexeris ad Deum, et Omnipotentem fueris deprecatus, si mundus et rectus incesseris, statim evigilabit ad te; itemque: Deus non projiciet simplicem, nec porriget manum malignis. Si ergo a Deo exaudiri optamus, si aliquam specialem gratiam adipisci appetimus, non contradicat operatio orationi, nec ostendamus per opera iniqua, nos amare id quod per orationem dicimus nos odire; sed faciamus quod in nobis est, laborem debitum continuamque diligentiam apponendo, et effectum affectui conformando. Tunc Deus protinus aderit, nostrumque imperfectum supplebit, optatam perfectionem virtutum præstando. Hæc quippe in Job legitur: Si iniquitatem quæ est in manu tua abstuleris, tunc levare poteris faciem tuam; et in Psalmo: Voluntatem timentium se faciet, et deprecationem eorum exaudiet, et salvos faciet eos.
paras.en: [[9:31|but if a man be a server of God|Sed si quis Dei cultor est]], [[9:31|and doth his, will|et voluntatem ejus facit]], that is, fulfils the signs of the divine will [that is, the outward tokens by which God's will is made known to us], namely his precepts and exhortations, [[9:31|him he heareth|hunc exaudit]] to his profit, though not always as he pleases: nay, sometimes, by denying what is asked, he gives things better and nearer to salvation[[Heb 6:9||]]. Hence it is written: [[Job 8:5|if thou wilt arise early to God, and wilt beseech the Almighty|Si diluculo consurrexeris ad Deum, et Omnipotentem fueris deprecatus]], [[Job 8:6|If thou wilt walk clean and upright, he will presently awake unto thee|si mundus et rectus incesseris, statim evigilabit ad te]]; and again: [[Job 8:20|God will not cast away the simple, nor reach out his hand to the evil doer|Deus non projiciet simplicem, nec porriget manum malignis]]. If then we desire to be heard by God, if we long to obtain some special grace, let not our working contradict our praying, nor let us show by wicked works that we love what by our prayer we say we hate; but let us do what lies in us, putting in due labour and constant diligence, and making the deed conform to the desire. Then God will at once be at hand, and will make up what is lacking in us, granting the perfection of the virtues we long for. For this is what we read in Job: [[Job 11:14|If thou wilt put away from thee the iniquity that is in thy hand|Si iniquitatem quæ est in manu tua abstuleris]], [[Job 11:15|Then mayst thou lift up thy face|tunc levare poteris faciem tuam]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 144:19|He will do the will of them that fear him: and he will hear their prayer, and save them|Voluntatem timentium se faciet, et deprecationem eorum exaudiet, et salvos faciet eos]].

paras.t: Responderunt Pharisæi, et dixerunt ei: In peccatis natus es totus, id est, in originali peccato quantum ad animam, et in speciali pœna peccati quantum ad corpus, videlicet in cæcitate tibi congenita. Sicque innuebant eum cæcum natum propter peccatum parentum vel proprium: cujus contrarium dixit Salvator. Monstruositas autem prolis, quamvis interdum sit propter culpam parentum, vel unius eorum, communiter tamen procedit ex causa naturali, puta ex disproportione materiæ, superfluitate vel parvitate, aut ex debilitate virtutis formativæ in semine. Sicque monstruositas est a casu, quoad naturam creatam; sed quoad divinam providentiam, est ordinata. Quandoque enim, ut dictum est, ordinatur ad manifestationem divinæ potentiæ in opere miraculoso. Semper quoque valet ad ampliorem declarationem naturalis perfectionis in rebus ejusdem speciei non monstruosis: in qua perfectione repræsentatur divina sapientia atque potentia, quoniam opposita juxta se posita clarius elucescunt.
paras.en: The Pharisees [[9:34|answered and said to him|Responderunt Pharisæi, et dixerunt ei]]: [[9:34|Thou wast wholly born in sins|In peccatis natus es totus]], that is, in original sin as to the soul, and in a special penalty of sin as to the body, namely in the blindness you were born with. And so they hinted that he had been born blind because of the sin of his parents or his own: the contrary of which the Saviour had said. Now deformity in offspring, though it is sometimes on account of the fault of the parents, or of one of them, commonly proceeds from a natural cause, for instance from a disproportion of the matter, through excess or deficiency, or from a weakness of the formative power in the seed. And so deformity is by chance as regards created nature; but as regards divine providence it is ordained. For sometimes, as has been said, it is ordained to the showing forth of the divine power in a miraculous work. And it always serves to set forth more fully the natural perfection in things of the same species that are not deformed: in which perfection the divine wisdom and power are represented, since opposites set side by side shine out more clearly.

paras.t: Sed quum originale peccatum sit unum, quomodo pluraliter dicunt: In peccatis natus es totus? Et respondendum, quod originale peccatum formaliter seu essentialiter unum est, scilicet carentia originalis justitiæ debitæ inesse, secundum Anselmum. Materialiter autem est multa, quoniam multas animæ vires inficit, et alia peccata virtualiter continet: præcipue vero propter quatuor vulnera animæ, ex originali peccato inflicta, secundum Bedam, quæ sunt: ignorantia, exsistens in ratione; malitia, exsistens in voluntate; concupiscentia, quæ est in appetitu concupiscibili, sumendo concupiscentiam pro pronitate ad concupiscendum inordinate; et infirmitas, quæ est in irascibili. Hæ enim quatuor vires animæ sunt subjecta virtutum.
paras.en: But since original sin is one, how is it that they say in the plural: [[9:34|Thou wast wholly born in sins|In peccatis natus es totus]]? The answer is that original sin is formally or essentially one, namely the lack of the original justice that ought to be present, according to Anselm. But materially it is many, since it infects many powers of the soul and contains other sins virtually [that is, in its power, as a cause contains its effects]: and above all because of the four wounds of the soul inflicted by original sin, according to Bede, which are: ignorance, which is in the reason; malice, which is in the will; concupiscence, which is in the concupiscible appetite, taking concupiscence for a proneness to desire inordinately; and infirmity, which is in the irascible [the concupiscible and irascible appetites are the soul's powers of desire and of resistance to what is hard]. For these four powers of the soul are the subjects of the virtues.

paras.t: Et tu doces nos? hoc est, quum sis tam vilis, præsumptuosum est nimis quod per modum docentis et redarguentis alloqueris nos, qui seniores et majores sumus in populo. Solent enim superiores ac doctiores inferiorum informationem despicere. Verumtamen veraciter sapientes et docti, diligenter atque humiliter pensant quæ eis dicuntur, informarique appetunt, nec propter dicentis parvitatem contemnunt quod prædicatur: quoniam veritas propter se ipsam digna est acceptione. Ideo Salomon ait: Argue sapientem, et diliget te; doce justum, et festinabit accipere.
paras.en: [[9:34|and dost thou teach us|Et tu doces nos]]? That is: since you are so base, it is too presumptuous that you address us by way of one teaching and reproving, us who are the elders and the greater ones among the people. For superiors and the more learned are wont to despise instruction from their inferiors. Yet those who are truly wise and learned weigh carefully and humbly what is said to them, and are eager to be instructed, and do not despise what is preached because of the lowliness of the speaker: since truth is worthy of acceptance for its own sake. Therefore Solomon says: [[Prov 9:8|Rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee|Argue sapientem, et diliget te]]; [[Prov 9:9|Teach a just man, and he shall make haste to receive it|doce justum, et festinabit accipere]].

paras.t: Et ejecerunt eum foras, id est, ex templo et synagoga seu populo expulerunt, et tanquam excommunicatum habuerunt. Et sicut paulo ante nescientes benedixerunt eum verbis, dicendo, Tu discipulus illius sis; sic modo ignorantes benedicunt eum factis, expellendo eum a synagoga Satanæ. Quos enim ipsi expellebant crudeliter, Christus recepit clementer.
paras.en: [[9:34|And they cast him out|Et ejecerunt eum foras]], that is, they drove him out of the temple and the synagogue or the people, and held him as excommunicated. And as a little before they had unknowingly blessed him in words, saying, [[9:28|Be thou his disciple|Tu discipulus illius sis]], so now, not knowing it, they bless him in deeds, driving him out of the synagogue of Satan. For those whom they cruelly drove out, Christ mercifully received.

paras.t: Audivit Jesus a narrantibus: quod tamen antequam fieret novit futurum, et dum fiebat inspexit, et antequam sibi recitaretur, scivit jam accidisse; quia ejecerunt eum foras, id est, quod Pharisæi cæcum a synagoga sequestraverunt. Et quum invenisset eum. Secundum Bedam, Jesus quæsivit eum. Dixit ei jam invento: Tu credis in Filium Dei? Non quasi ignorans id quærit, sed ut cæcum ad perfectiorem sui agnitionem promoveat. Quanto enim quis magis opprimitur propter veritatem, tanto apud Deum meretur ampliorem exaltationem et gratiam. Cæcus iste nondum determinate credebat in Filium Dei; sed paratus fuit ad hoc. Ideo interrogatur a Christo, quia qui boni propositi sunt, merentur gratiam Dei auxiliatricem per quam deducantur in exsecutionem salubrem.
paras.en: [[9:35|Jesus heard|Audivit Jesus]] from those who told Him: though He knew before it happened that it would be, and saw it while it was happening, and knew it had already happened before it was recounted to Him; [[9:35|that they had cast him out|quia ejecerunt eum foras]], that is, that the Pharisees had cut the blind man off from the synagogue. [[9:35|And when he had found him|Et quum invenisset eum]]. According to Bede, Jesus sought him out. [[9:35|He said to him|Dixit ei]], now that He had found him: [[9:35|Dost thou believe in the Son of God|Tu credis in Filium Dei]]? He does not ask this as if not knowing, but to bring the blind man on to a more perfect knowledge of Himself. For the more one is oppressed for the sake of the truth, the more ample the exaltation and grace he merits with God. This blind man did not yet believe distinctly in the Son of God, but he was ready for it. Therefore he is questioned by Christ, because those who are of good purpose merit the helping grace of God, by which they are led on to carry it out to their salvation.

paras.t: Respondit ille cæcus: Quis est, o Domine, Filius Dei? quod quæro ut credam in eum. Nondum enim cognovit Jesum secundum faciem, quoniam cæcus ab eo recessit, et nondum ad eum reversus fuit: et si cognovisset eum secundum faciem, non tamen scivisset quod esset Filius Dei, quia ut dictum est, tenuit eum pro Propheta. Et dixit ei Jesus: Et vidisti eum nunc, ad me accedendo, et qui loquitur tecum, ipse est, id est, ego ipse quem nunc inspexisti oculo corporali, qui præsentialiter tecum loquor, sum Filius Dei.
paras.en: [[9:36|He answered|Respondit ille]], the blind man: [[9:36|Who is he, Lord|Quis est, o Domine]], the Son of God? This I ask [[9:36|that I may believe in him|ut credam in eum]]. For he did not yet know Jesus by His face, since he had gone away from Him blind and had not yet come back to Him: and even if he had known Him by His face, he would still not have known that He was the Son of God, because, as has been said, he held Him for a Prophet. [[9:37|And Jesus said to him: Thou hast both seen him|Et dixit ei Jesus: Et vidisti eum]] now, by coming to me, [[9:37|and it is he that talketh with thee|et qui loquitur tecum, ipse est]], that is: I myself, whom you have now looked upon with the eye of the body, who am speaking with you here present, am the Son of God.

paras.t: At ille ait: Credo, Domine, in Filium Dei. His nempe verbis auditis, cognovit quod is qui eum alloquebatur, fuit Jesus, oculorum suorum apertor; et quia tenuit eum pro vero Propheta justoque viro, credidit omnia verba ejus esse vera. Idcirco quum audisset ab ore ejus quod esset Filius Dei, mox credidit, sciens Deum esse cum illo cui credebat. Et procidens adoravit eum. Si credidit explicite quod esset Filius Dei naturalis, adoravit eum adoratione latriæ. Si vero credidit quod esset Filius Dei per gratiam singularem, adoravit eum adoratione duliæ. Paucissimi autem discipulorum habebant explicitam fixamque fidem de hoc quod Christus esset Dei Unigenitus verusque Deus: sic tamen dispositi erant quod mox fidem talem reciperent.
paras.en: [[9:38|And he said: I believe, Lord|At ille ait: Credo, Domine]], in the Son of God. For when he heard these words he knew that the one speaking to him was Jesus, the opener of his eyes; and because he held Him for a true Prophet and a just man, he believed all His words to be true. Therefore, when he heard from His mouth that He was the Son of God, he believed at once, knowing that God was with Him whom he believed. [[9:38|And falling down, he adored him|Et procidens adoravit eum]]. If he believed explicitly that He was the natural Son of God, he adored Him with the adoration of latria [the worship due to God alone]. But if he believed that He was the Son of God by a singular grace, he adored Him with the adoration of dulia [the honour given to a creature for its excellence, as to the saints]. Very few of the disciples had an explicit and firm faith that Christ was the Only-begotten of God and true God: yet they were so disposed that they would soon receive such faith.

paras.t: Dixit ei Jesus: In judicium ego in hunc mundum veni, id est, ad faciendum judicium discretionis, hoc est, discretionem judicialem, inter electos ac reprobos. De quo judicio infra habetur: Nunc judicium est mundi. In primo ergo suo adventu venit Christus discernere inter electos ac præscitos, illos gratiose et pie convertendo, hos juste deserendo. In secundo autem adventu veniet facere judicium retributionis, de quo dixit: Non misit Deus Filium suum ut judicet mundum; et, Ego non judico quemquam. Ut qui non vident, id est, simplices et indocti, quales fuerunt discipuli Christi et cæcus iste, videant, id est, spiritualiter illuminentur a me, meque lucem mundi fidei oculis contemplentur: et qui vident, id est, Scribæ et Pharisæi ceterique in propriis oculis sapientes, litterati ac providi, cæci fiant, id est, lumine fidei ceterisque donis gratiæ Spiritus Sancti priventur, et gravius quam ante obtenebrentur, propter eorum superbiam atque demerita. Huic verbo Christi consonat quod Simeon justus prædixisse legitur: Ecce positus est hic in ruinam et resurrectionem multorum in Israel. Christus quoque alio loco ait concorditer istis: Confiteor tibi, Pater, quoniam abscondisti hæc a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti ea parvulis.
paras.en: Jesus said to him: [[9:39|For judgment I am come into this world|In judicium ego in hunc mundum veni]], that is, to make a judgment of discernment, that is, a judicial separation, between the elect and the reprobate.
